subject: english
note: Descriptor text: Australian Curriculum v9 (ACARA, CC BY 4.0). Waypoints and prior knowledge: Learning Waypoints. Made by tools/import-curriculum.mjs; do not edit by hand.

descriptors.title: Language use at home and school
descriptors.description: explore how language is used differently at home and school depending on the relationships between people
descriptors.knowledge: Students bring informal oral language from home, family and community contexts. They have not yet been asked to consciously observe and reflect on how language changes across different relationship contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can explain that language choices (words, tone, phrasing) change depending on the relationship between speakers, giving examples from both home and school contexts.

nodes.label: Language varies by context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that different situations call for different language — that how you speak changes depending on where you are.
criteria: Student can name at least one situation where they would speak differently (e.g. talking to a teacher vs talking to a friend).
Student can say why the language is different in those two situations.

width.minimum: Identify one example of language that is used at school but not at home, or vice versa.
width.typical: Identify and discuss examples of language used differently at school versus home, noting that the setting affects how we speak.
wider: Compare language used in multiple school settings — in the classroom, at lunch, on the playground — and discuss how it shifts across each
Compare language used in multiple home settings — with parents, siblings, grandparents — and identify what changes

modes.reason: Students at Foundation may initially treat 'school language' as a fixed thing — the misconception is that language is constant rather than contextually variable. More settings help break the exemplar convergence on a single school/home contrast.

nodes.label: Relationships shape language choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that the relationship between people — not just the setting — is what shapes language choices.
criteria: Student can name at least two different relationships and explain how language would be different in each.
Student can give a specific example of a word or phrase that would or wouldn't be used in a particular relationship context.

width.minimum: Give one example of how language changes depending on whether you are talking to a teacher or a friend.
width.typical: Identify how language changes across relationship types: teacher/student, parent/child, sibling/friend, shopkeeper/customer; recognise that formal vs informal language choices relate to relationship roles.
wider: Examine characters in picture books and identify language that shows the relationship between them
Explore how language in texts by First Nations Australian authors reflects relationship protocols and community roles
Investigate how language might differ when interacting with a known versus unknown adult

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of relationship types and associated language patterns — parent/child, teacher/student, peers, community members — before the generalisation becomes robust. A single contrast pair is insufficient.

nodes.label: Asking, expressing and requesting appropriately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use context-appropriate language when asking for things, expressing opinions or making requests, and can explain why they chose those words.
criteria: Student can make an appropriate request or express an opinion in a school context using suitable words and tone.
Student can explain why they chose the language they used for that context.
Student can identify at least one adjustment they would make to the same request in a different relationship context.

width.minimum: Use appropriate language to make one request or express one opinion in a school context.
width.typical: Ask relevant questions, express requests and share opinions in ways that suit the context; reflect on why the language chosen was appropriate for that context.
wider: Role-play the same request (e.g. asking for help) in three different contexts — with a teacher, a classmate, and a family member — and compare the language used
Explore how characters in stories ask for things and evaluate whether their language was appropriate for the relationship
Investigate how language used in requests differs across culturally diverse contexts represented in classroom texts

modes.reason: Students must bring together: knowing the relationship context, choosing appropriate register, and producing the language — three elements that now need to work together in performance. This is where the concept and the capability unite.

descriptors.title: Language to express preferences
descriptors.description: explore different ways of using language to express preferences, likes and dislikes
descriptors.knowledge: Students bring natural oral language for expressing feelings. They have not yet been asked to consciously identify or compare the specific language choices used to express preferences, or to recognise how these are conveyed in visual and media texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify and use a range of language choices for expressing preferences, likes and dislikes — in speech, gesture and visual forms — and can compare how different choices work.

nodes.label: Preferences can be put into words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express a like, dislike or preference using words, and recognise that language is one way to communicate feelings.
criteria: Student uses at least one specific word or phrase to express a preference beyond 'like' or 'don't like'.
Student can identify that language was used to express a feeling or preference.

width.minimum: Express one like or dislike using a word or phrase (e.g. 'I love...', 'I don't like...').
width.typical: Express preferences, likes and dislikes in words; explore different word choices for the same feeling (e.g. 'like', 'love', 'enjoy', 'prefer').
wider: Collect and compare words for positive and negative preferences from classroom picture books
Explore vocabulary for feelings and preferences in languages other than English known to students in the class

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of preference language beyond the immediate 'like/don't like' binary. A vocabulary repertoire is what this node is building.

nodes.label: Gesture and speech work together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that feelings and preferences are communicated through both language and body — speech and gesture work together.
criteria: Student can describe how both words and gesture are used to show how a character or person feels.
Student can demonstrate expressing a preference using both spoken language and an appropriate gesture.

width.minimum: Demonstrate one gesture (e.g. thumbs up, facial expression) that communicates a preference, and pair it with a spoken word.
width.typical: Recognise how feelings and preferences are communicated in speech and gesture; practise combining gesture and language to express preferences more fully.
wider: Compare how preferences are expressed through gesture in different cultural contexts — noticing that gestures are not universal
Explore how animated characters (in animations or picture books) use body language and speech together to communicate feelings

modes.reason: Students may initially treat gesture as decoration — the misconception is that words alone carry meaning. Multiple contexts showing gesture as a meaning-making system help resolve this.

nodes.label: Preferences in visual and media texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how emotions and preferences are conveyed in visual and media texts — not just through words but through images, colour, and sound.
criteria: Student can identify at least one visual or sound feature in a media text that communicates a feeling or preference.
Student can explain how that feature communicates the feeling — not just say that it does.

width.minimum: Identify how one visual text (e.g. an advertisement or animation) shows a character or person feeling a preference.
width.typical: Recognise how emotions and feelings are conveyed in visual and media texts such as advertising and animations; identify specific visual and multimodal choices that communicate preference.
wider: Compare how two different advertisements or animations convey emotions and preferences — what visual choices do they make?
Explore how texts by First Nations Australian creators use visual language to convey feelings and preferences
Investigate how colour and facial expression in picture book illustrations signal character preferences without words

modes.reason: The concept (preferences communicated through multiple modes) requires multiple text types before it generalises — advertising and animation are explicitly named in elaborations, and each medium uses different conventions.
Here students bring together language, gesture and visual knowledge — connecting all three as modes for expressing preferences. The coordination across modes is the learning.

descriptors.title: Texts take many forms
descriptors.description: understand that texts can take many forms such as signs, books and digital texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have interacted with texts in home and community settings. They have not yet been asked to consciously categorise and compare text forms, or to understand that form and purpose are connected.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify a range of text forms, explain what each is for, and recognise that the purpose of a text shapes its form — including that First Nations Australians' stories may be oral or image-based rather than print.

nodes.label: Texts are all around us
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that texts are present in many places and take different physical forms.
criteria: Student can name at least two different text forms encountered in everyday settings.
Student can distinguish a text from a non-text (e.g. a picture vs a labelled diagram).
nodes.hinge_reason: Without recognising that texts exist in multiple forms in the world, students cannot reason in Node 2 about why different forms serve different purposes — form-purpose reasoning requires having a repertoire of text forms to reason about.

width.minimum: Name at least two different types of text seen in the world (e.g. a book and a sign).
width.typical: Identify texts in school, home and community settings across multiple forms: signs, books, digital texts, labels, instructions; recognise these as different types of text.
wider: Create a class collection or photo record of texts found in the school and local community, sorting them by form
Investigate texts in culturally diverse contexts — including community languages and First Nations Australian contexts — identifying forms that may not appear in school settings

modes.reason: Text form recognition must be reliable and broad before form-purpose reasoning can be applied. Practice identifying texts across multiple settings builds the necessary repertoire.

nodes.label: Form follows purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that different text forms exist because they serve different purposes — form and purpose are connected.
criteria: Student can explain why a particular text takes the form it does — connecting form to purpose.
Student can give an example of a text form that would not suit a particular purpose and explain why.

width.minimum: Match at least one text form to its purpose (e.g. a crossing sign tells you when it is safe to cross).
width.typical: Identify texts and explain what each is for; compare different ways information might be presented (e.g. on a sign vs in a set of instructions); identify similarities and differences in text forms.
wider: Compare how the same information (e.g. 'wash your hands') is presented in different forms — a sign, a set of written instructions, a picture — and discuss what each form is best for
Investigate how digital texts serve different purposes from print texts — exploring apps, websites and e-books alongside paper forms

modes.reason: Students may initially think that purpose and form are arbitrary — the misconception is that a text could be in any form. Multiple specific examples where form matches purpose (a crossing sign cannot be a novel) help consolidate the connection.

nodes.label: First Nations texts — oral and image-based forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that texts can be oral and image-based — not only written — and that First Nations Australians' stories are examples of this.
criteria: Student can name at least one type of text that is not written and explain that it is still a text.
Student can identify a First Nations Australian text form and describe what form it takes.
Student can explain why not all texts are books or written texts.

width.minimum: Recognise that a story can be told through speech or images, not only through writing.
width.typical: Understand that many First Nations Australians' stories are oral narrations and cultural accounts that may be represented as or with images; identify examples of oral and image-based texts and discuss what form they take.
wider: Engage with First Nations Australian stories from multiple forms — oral, visual, digital and multimodal sources — and compare how each form presents the story
Discuss how oral and image-based texts have been transmitted across generations and why this matters for the communities that created them
Compare images in First Nations Australian texts with images in non-Indigenous picture books — exploring how images carry cultural meaning

modes.reason: The risk is that students form a 'texts are written' misconception — this node explicitly widens that schema. Multiple First Nations examples from different sources are needed to ensure the understanding generalises beyond a single example.

descriptors.title: Conventions of print and screen
descriptors.description: understand conventions of print and screen, including how books and simple digital texts are usually organised
descriptors.knowledge: Students have been handled books and interacted with digital devices at home and in early childhood settings. They have not yet been explicitly taught or asked to name the conventions that organise print and screen texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can demonstrate and explain the key conventions of print and screen texts — directionality, title identification, image/word placement, and basic digital navigation — and understand that these are conventions rather than arbitrary arrangements.

nodes.label: Print is directional
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate that written English is read left to right and top to bottom, and can apply this when approaching a new text.
criteria: Student tracks print from left to right without prompting.
Student correctly returns to the start of the next line when text wraps.
nodes.hinge_reason: Print directionality is a prerequisite for both Node 2 (identifying title and starting point requires knowing where reading begins) and LY04 (reading connected text requires correct directional tracking) — without it, all print-based literacy tasks collapse.

width.minimum: Demonstrate left-to-right, top-to-bottom reading direction when approaching a familiar book or text.
width.typical: Understand and apply print conventions for directionality; indicate where to start reading on a page; return correctly to the next line when reading.
wider: Compare English print direction with texts written in other directions — right-to-left or vertical scripts — and discuss why conventions differ
Explore how directionality affects the layout of a page — where images appear, how text is positioned

modes.reason: Directionality is a mechanical habit — it must become automatic. Students need to practise the correct left-to-right, return sweep movement until it is habituated. Width is thin here; accuracy and fluency are what matter.

nodes.label: Books have structure — title and starting point
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the title of a book and show where to start reading.
criteria: Student can point to the title of a book when asked.
Student can indicate the correct starting point for reading.

width.minimum: Indicate the title of a book and point to where reading begins.
width.typical: Identify the title and starting point of a book; discuss the placement of images and words on the page; begin to understand that these placements are intentional choices.
wider: Compare title placement and starting points across different book formats — picture books, simple chapter books, big books
Explore how image and word placement varies across a range of text types and discuss why designers make those choices

nodes.label: Digital texts have their own conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that digital texts are organised differently from print texts and can use at least one navigation feature (e.g. a tab or scroll).
criteria: Student can identify at least one feature of a digital text that is not found in print books.
Student can use a basic digital navigation feature independently.
Student can explain that print and digital texts have different but consistent conventions.

width.minimum: Identify one digital navigation feature (e.g. a tab, a button) and explain what it is for.
width.typical: Identify tabs and other navigation features in simple digital texts; recognise that screen texts are organised using different conventions from print books; discuss image and word placement in digital contexts.
wider: Compare navigation across multiple digital text forms — a website, an e-book, a simple app — identifying similarities and differences
Explore how touch-based navigation (swiping, tapping) differs from button-based navigation and what this means for how a reader moves through a text
Compare a print book and its digital equivalent — what conventions stay the same and what changes?

modes.reason: Students may over-generalise from print conventions — assuming digital texts work the same way. Multiple digital contexts (app, website, e-book) help build a distinct digital text schema.

descriptors.title: Sentences express ideas
descriptors.description: recognise that sentences are key units for expressing ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students use spoken sentences naturally but have not yet reflected on what makes a sentence. They have not yet been asked to distinguish a sentence from a fragment or to identify word order as meaningful.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify a sentence as a complete unit that expresses a single idea, distinguish it from a fragment, and recognise that word order affects meaning.

nodes.label: A sentence is complete
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that a sentence expresses a complete idea — it makes sense on its own.
criteria: Student can identify a sentence as expressing a complete idea.
Student can say why a fragment does not make sense on its own.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that a sentence is a complete unit is a prerequisite for Node 2 — students cannot reason about word order affecting sentence meaning if they do not yet have a concept of what a sentence is as a unit.

width.minimum: Identify whether a group of words is a complete sentence or a fragment in one example.
width.typical: Recognise the difference between a sentence fragment and a complete sentence; identify sentences in familiar texts; understand that a sentence expresses a single complete idea.
wider: Sort a range of written phrases and sentences into 'complete' and 'not complete' groups and explain the sorting
Identify sentences and fragments across different text types — labels, books, signs — comparing how completeness shows up in different contexts

modes.reason: The sentence/fragment distinction can feel arbitrary when only one or two examples are used. Multiple contrasting pairs help build the concept of 'completeness' as a stable criterion.

nodes.label: Word order carries meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate that changing word order in a sentence changes — or destroys — its meaning.
criteria: Student can explain that moving words around in a sentence changes what it means.
Student can produce or identify at least one example of the same words in different order making different sense.

width.minimum: Identify that two sentences with the same words in different order mean different things (e.g. 'The boy sat on the dog' vs 'The dog sat on the boy').
width.typical: Understand that word order in sentences is important for meaning; experiment with reordering words in simple sentences and observe what happens to meaning.
wider: Create multiple sentences from a small set of words in different orders — exploring which orders make sense and which don't
Compare word order in English sentences with word order in other languages familiar to students in the class

modes.reason: Students may think order is arbitrary or that meaning comes only from individual words. Multiple examples — including deliberately nonsensical reorderings — are needed to consolidate that word order is systematically meaningful in English.

descriptors.title: Words work together in sentences
descriptors.description: recognise that sentences are made up of groups of words that work together in particular ways to make meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise that sentences express ideas (AC9EFLA05). They have not yet examined how words within a sentence work as a system — how nouns connect to verbs, or adjectives to nouns.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify that words in a sentence have particular roles and work together — nouns, verbs and adjectives connect to make meaning — and can demonstrate this across multiple simple examples.

nodes.label: Words have jobs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that words in a sentence do different things — some name things, some describe actions, some describe qualities.
criteria: Student can point to a noun and a verb in a simple sentence.
Student can say what job each word is doing — naming, doing or describing.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without distinguishing word roles (naming, doing, describing), students cannot identify how those words connect and relate to each other in Node 2 — word connection reasoning presupposes that the roles are already distinguished.

width.minimum: Identify one noun (a naming word) and one verb (a doing word) in a simple sentence.
width.typical: Recognise that words play different roles in sentences: nouns name things, verbs describe actions or states, adjectives describe qualities; identify examples in simple sentences.
wider: Sort word cards from familiar sentences into 'naming words', 'doing words' and 'describing words' categories
Identify the same word playing different roles in different sentences — for example, 'run' as a noun vs a verb

modes.reason: Students need to encounter many examples of each word class before the categories become robust — a single example of a noun or verb is insufficient. Accumulating examples is the learning work.

nodes.label: Words connect to each other
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how specific words in a sentence relate to each other — how a noun connects to a verb, or an adjective to a noun.
criteria: Student can identify the noun-verb relationship in a simple sentence.
Student can identify what an adjective is describing in a simple sentence.
Student can explain how removing one word affects the meaning of the sentence as a whole.

width.minimum: Show how a noun and verb connect in one simple sentence (e.g. 'the cat ate').
width.typical: Identify how words in a sentence relate to one another: how a noun connects to a verb (the subject doing the action), and how an adjective connects to a noun (describing it); apply this to multiple simple sentences.
wider: Use physical sentence-building activities — word cards, sentence strips — to construct and break sentences, discussing which words connect
Explore how changing the connecting word (adjective or verb) changes the meaning of the whole sentence
Identify word connections across a range of text types — picture books, labels, captions — noting how the same patterns appear in different contexts

modes.reason: The relationship between words in a sentence is not immediately obvious — students need a visible reasoning scaffold (which word connects to which, and how) before they can apply the pattern independently. Worked examples that make the connection explicit are important here.

descriptors.title: Images and words make meaning
descriptors.description: explore the contribution of images and words to meaning in stories and informative texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have been read picture books and interacted with illustrated texts. They have not yet been explicitly asked to separate and compare what words contribute versus what images contribute to meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can describe what images add to a text beyond the words, and what words add beyond the images — recognising that words and images work together in different ways across different texts.

nodes.label: Images carry meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that images in a text communicate meaning — that looking at images alone tells us something.
criteria: Student can name something an image communicates that is not stated in the written text.
Student can explain that images are a source of meaning, not just decoration.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students treat images as decoration rather than meaning-carriers, they cannot compare what images and words contribute differently in Node 2 — the comparative analysis depends on images already being understood as independent sources of meaning.

width.minimum: Identify at least one thing a picture tells us in a familiar text that is not said in words.
width.typical: Explore what images communicate in stories and informative texts; identify information that comes from images alone; recognise that images extend meaning beyond the words.
wider: Cover the words in a picture book and try to tell the story from images only — then uncover words and compare
Compare illustrations in a picture book by a First Nations Australian illustrator with illustrations in another picture book — what different types of meaning do images carry?

modes.reason: The understanding that images carry meaning independently of words needs to be established reliably before students can compare the distinctive contributions of each mode. Practice across multiple texts — including with words covered — builds this understanding.

nodes.label: Words and images work differently
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that words and images each contribute different things to a text's meaning — what each mode does distinctively.
criteria: Student can describe what the images contribute to a text beyond what the words say.
Student can describe what the words contribute beyond what the images show.
Student can explain why both modes are needed to understand the text fully.

width.minimum: Identify one thing the words tell us and one thing the images tell us in the same text.
width.typical: Identify where written text is reflected in images and where it is not; recognise that texts can be understood differently when only words or only images are attended to; explore this across stories and informative texts.
wider: Compare two texts on the same topic — one image-heavy, one mostly words — and discuss how the balance of modes affects meaning
Create a brief multimodal text (drawing + labels) where each mode contributes something different, then explain what each contributes
Explore texts by First Nations Australian authors/illustrators where visual elements carry cultural meaning — identifying what images communicate that words alone would not

modes.reason: The risk is that students see words and images as simply 'the same information twice'. Multiple text types — where images sometimes extend, contradict or add cultural meaning not in words — are needed to break this exemplar.

descriptors.title: Vocabulary in familiar contexts
descriptors.description: recognise and develop awareness of vocabulary used in familiar contexts related to everyday experiences, personal interests and topics taught at school
descriptors.knowledge: Students bring oral vocabulary from home and community contexts. They have not yet been asked to consciously attend to vocabulary — to notice, collect and develop awareness of words in relation to specific topics and contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise and use vocabulary relevant to everyday experiences, personal interests and school topics — drawing on multiple sources to expand their word knowledge and applying vocabulary in both imaginative and informative contexts.

nodes.label: Topics have words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that topics and contexts have specific vocabulary — particular words that go with particular subjects or activities.
criteria: Student can name at least three words associated with a familiar topic.
Student can identify a word as a 'topic word' when it is introduced in a new context.

width.minimum: Name at least three words that belong to one familiar topic (e.g. words related to families, or words used in a current class topic).
width.typical: Identify and collect vocabulary associated with school topics; recognise learning area–specific words across multiple topics; notice when new words are introduced.
wider: Build a word wall for a current topic and continue adding to it as new vocabulary is encountered across the unit
Compare the vocabulary of two different topics — what words appear in both? What words are unique to each?

modes.reason: Vocabulary acquisition at Foundation is fundamentally about accumulation — students need to encounter and retain many words across many contexts before vocabulary awareness becomes a generative habit.

nodes.label: Vocabulary grows through experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify multiple ways of encountering and learning new vocabulary — through interactions, texts, images, objects and play.
criteria: Student can identify at least two different ways they have encountered new vocabulary.
Student can use a recently acquired vocabulary word appropriately in speech or in a text they are creating.

width.minimum: Identify one new word encountered in class and explain where or how they came across it.
width.typical: Recognise that vocabulary can be expanded through informal interactions, planned experiences, texts, images, artefacts and objects; draw on vocabulary encountered in multiple ways — including imaginative play — to use words in context.
wider: Investigate how role-play activities generate new vocabulary — comparing words used in different dramatic contexts (shopkeeper, scientist, storyteller)
Explore vocabulary from different cultural contexts in the class — including words from First Nations Australian languages or other community languages
Compare vocabulary encountered through visual texts (picture books, films) with vocabulary encountered through oral interaction and real objects

modes.reason: Students may think vocabulary grows only through 'word learning lessons'. Multiple sources — play, objects, images, community language — help build the broader understanding that vocabulary is encountered everywhere.

descriptors.title: Punctuation and capital letters
descriptors.description: identify punctuation as a feature of written text different from letters; recognise that capital letters are used for names, and that capital letters also signal the beginning of sentences while punctuation marks signal the end
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise some letters and have encountered written text. They have not yet been asked to distinguish punctuation marks from letters or to understand the systematic roles of capital letters and end-of-sentence punctuation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify punctuation marks as distinct from letters, recognise capital letters in names and at sentence beginnings, and identify end-of-sentence punctuation marks — understanding that these are consistent, rule-based conventions in written English.

nodes.label: Punctuation is not letters
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify punctuation marks in a text and distinguish them from letters.
criteria: Student can reliably point to punctuation marks and identify them as distinct from letters.
Student can name at least one punctuation mark by name (e.g. full stop, question mark).
nodes.hinge_reason: Without reliably distinguishing punctuation from letters, students cannot identify what capital letters or end punctuation marks are — both Nodes 2 and 3 depend on punctuation marks being already separated from the letter system.

width.minimum: Point to at least one punctuation mark in a written text and say it is not a letter.
width.typical: Identify punctuation marks as distinct features of written text; sort punctuation marks from letters across several familiar examples; begin to name common punctuation marks.
wider: Collect and classify all punctuation marks encountered in a class text — grouping them and counting how many of each type appear
Explore punctuation marks in digital texts — including emoji — and discuss which ones follow the same rules as print punctuation

modes.reason: Students need reliable letter–punctuation discrimination as a prerequisite for all subsequent print literacy. This is a precision skill: errors (treating punctuation as letters) cascade into reading and writing. Practice with a range of texts is the remedy.

nodes.label: Capital letters signal names and sentence starts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify capital letters used for names and at the beginning of sentences, and explain the rule behind each use.
criteria: Student can identify a capital letter used for a name and say why it is capitalised.
Student can identify a capital letter at the start of a sentence and say why it is capitalised.
Student can explain that capital letters follow rules — they are not placed randomly.

width.minimum: Identify a capital letter in a familiar word and say why it is capitalised (name, or start of sentence).
width.typical: Recognise that capital letters are used for proper names (people, places, school names); recognise that capital letters signal the beginning of sentences; identify these in everyday and classroom texts.
wider: Investigate capital letters across a wide range of text types — books, signs, labels, digital texts — and confirm consistency of the rules
Compare own name, classmates' names, the school name and the class name — noting that the capital letter rule applies consistently
Explore how capital letters appear in other alphabetic writing systems and compare with English conventions

modes.reason: The two uses of capitals (names and sentence starts) can be confused — students may think only one rule exists. Multiple contexts showing both uses, alongside consistent exceptions (mid-sentence common nouns), help build a complete schema.

nodes.label: Punctuation signals sentence endings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify end-of-sentence punctuation marks (full stop, question mark, exclamation mark) and understand that they signal the end of a sentence.
criteria: Student can identify a full stop, question mark and exclamation mark in a text.
Student can explain that each of these signals the end of a sentence.
Student can use a full stop in their own writing at the end of a sentence.

width.minimum: Identify a full stop in a text and say that it means the sentence has ended.
width.typical: Identify full stops, question marks and exclamation marks as sentence-end signals; recognise the rule that punctuation marks — not new lines — signal sentence endings; apply this in reading and beginning writing.
wider: Compare sentences ending with different punctuation marks and discuss how each affects how the sentence is read or spoken
Investigate how punctuation functions differently in digital informal writing (texts, posts) vs formal written texts
Sort sentences by end punctuation type and read each aloud — exploring how punctuation signals prosody

modes.reason: Students may know full stops but not question marks or exclamation marks as sentence-enders — each requires its own contextual exposure before the general 'punctuation ends sentences' concept is robust.

descriptors.title: Share ideas about literature
descriptors.description: share ideas about stories, poems and images in literature, reflecting on experiences that are similar or different to their own by engaging with texts by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators
descriptors.knowledge: Students have heard and interacted with stories at home and in early childhood settings. They have not yet been explicitly asked to reflect on how literary experiences connect to or differ from their own lives, or to engage with literature from a culturally diverse range of authors.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can share ideas about stories, poems and images from a diverse range of authors — connecting literary experiences to their own lives and identifying cultural features that reveal characters' worlds.

nodes.label: Literature reflects experiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect events or characters in a story to their own experiences, identifying at least one similarity or difference.
criteria: Student can identify at least one similarity or difference between their own experience and a character or event in a text.
Student can share this observation verbally or through drawing.

width.minimum: Share one connection between a story event or character and their own life.
width.typical: Engage with stories and identify experiences that are similar or different to their own; reflect on how characters' lives might feel familiar or unfamiliar; share ideas with the class.
wider: Compare personal responses to two different stories — one with familiar experiences and one with unfamiliar experiences — discussing what each evokes
Engage with stories that portray Australian family life in different settings (suburban, remote, regional) and connect each to own experiences

nodes.label: Cultural details reveal characters' worlds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify cultural features in stories — dress, food, daily routines — and explain what these reveal about characters' lives.
criteria: Student can name a cultural detail from a story and explain what it shows about the character's life.
Student can identify at least one way a character's life in a story is different from their own, with reference to a specific cultural detail.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students interpret unfamiliar cultural details as errors or oddities rather than as culturally meaningful, they cannot engage substantively with the diversity of authoring voices in Node 3 — the understanding that cultural difference is meaningful is a prerequisite for appreciating diverse author perspectives.

width.minimum: Identify one cultural detail (e.g. what a character eats, wears or does daily) and say something about what it shows.
width.typical: Identify features of culture revealed by characters and events in stories — dress, food, daily routines; discuss how these differ from or connect to students' own cultural contexts.
wider: Compare cultural details across stories from two different cultural contexts — identifying specific similarities and differences
Explore stories that portray First Nations Australian cultural life — identifying cultural features and discussing their significance with reference to the text
Discuss how cultural features in stories from other countries or time periods reveal differences in daily life

modes.reason: Students may interpret unfamiliar cultural details as errors or oddities rather than as culturally meaningful. Multiple cultural contexts — particularly First Nations Australian texts — help build the understanding that cultural difference is meaningful, not random.

nodes.label: Literature from diverse authors and illustrators
nodes.checkpoint: Students can engage with texts from First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors and illustrators — sharing ideas that reflect awareness of diverse authoring voices.
criteria: Student can share an idea about a text by a First Nations Australian author or illustrator.
Student can identify that different authors bring different experiences and cultural knowledge to their stories.
Student can give an example of how a story from another country or culture reflects a different world.

width.minimum: Engage with at least one text by a First Nations Australian author or illustrator and share one idea about it.
width.typical: Engage with stories, poems and images from First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors; share ideas that reflect on how different authors and illustrators bring different cultural perspectives; compare texts from diverse sources.
wider: Engage with First Nations Australian storytelling from multiple forms — print, visual, digital, multimodal — and compare how the story is presented across forms
Compare perspectives: read two versions of a similar story from different cultural contexts and discuss how the authoring context shapes what the story values
Investigate how the cultural background of an illustrator is visible in their artistic choices

modes.reason: Engagement with diverse authoring voices requires accumulating exposure — a single First Nations text or a single world literature text is insufficient to build genuine awareness of diverse authoring. Range is what matters here.

descriptors.title: Respond to stories and characters
descriptors.description: respond to stories and share feelings and thoughts about their events and characters
descriptors.knowledge: Students have listened to and engaged with stories. They have not yet been explicitly asked to formulate and share a personal response — to reflect on their feelings about events and characters and communicate this response in a deliberate way.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can share personal feelings and thoughts about story events and characters through multiple modes — oral, drawing or beginning writing — connecting events and characters to their own experiences.

nodes.label: Stories prompt feelings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a feeling evoked by a story or character and name it.
criteria: Student can name at least one feeling evoked by a story event or character.
Student can connect the feeling to a specific event or character in the text.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify and name a feeling evoked by a story, they have no content for the sharing and mode-selection task in Node 2 — the deliberate response that Node 2 requires is built on the raw material of named feelings from this node.

width.minimum: Name one feeling a story evoked (e.g. 'I felt happy/sad/scared') when discussing a text.
width.typical: Identify and name feelings evoked by story events and characters; discuss what caused the feeling — connecting events to emotional responses.
wider: Compare feelings evoked by different types of stories — funny stories, sad stories, scary stories — and discuss what makes each evoke different responses
Explore how characters' feelings in a story differ from student responses to those same events

modes.reason: Students need to encounter multiple stories and name feelings across them — a single story is insufficient to build the habit of noticing and naming emotional responses. Accumulating examples is what makes the naming automatic.

nodes.label: Responses can be shared in multiple ways
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share a personal response to a story through drawing, beginning writing or oral sharing — choosing a mode appropriate to the response.
criteria: Student can share a feeling or thought about a story event or character through drawing, speech or beginning writing.
Student can connect their response to a specific event or character.
Student can explain their response when asked — articulating why they felt or thought that.

width.minimum: Share a response to one story through drawing or oral expression.
width.typical: Respond to stories using drawing and beginning forms of writing to express personal responses; discuss events and characters, connecting them to personal experiences; share responses orally with peers.
wider: Respond to the same story through multiple modes — oral, drawing, movement or drama — and compare what each allows
Create a shared class response text (collaborative drawing or dictated writing) about a favourite story
Respond to First Nations Australian stories and discuss responses with attention to cultural context

modes.reason: Students bring together: having a personal response, reflecting on it, and translating it into a shareable form (drawing, writing, speech). The coordination of these acts is the learning.

descriptors.title: Recognise literary text types
descriptors.description: recognise different types of literary texts and identify features including events, characters, and beginnings and endings
descriptors.knowledge: Students have encountered stories and poems. They have not yet been asked to distinguish literary text types from each other, or to identify the structural features (beginnings, endings, characters, events) that define and differentiate them.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise and name different types of literary texts; identify features including events, characters, and beginnings and endings; and recognise that different literary forms (fairytales, realistic stories, poetry) have characteristic patterns.

nodes.label: Literary texts have features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least one key feature (character, event, beginning, or ending) in a familiar literary text.
criteria: Student can identify a character in a literary text.
Student can identify a key event from the story.
Student can identify the beginning and ending of a story.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without being able to identify characters, events, beginnings and endings, students cannot recognise the patterns that distinguish literary text types in Node 2 — type-level pattern recognition depends on feature-level identification being secure.

width.minimum: Name a character and an event in one story.
width.typical: Identify characters, events, beginnings and endings across multiple literary texts; recognise that these are features that literary texts share.
wider: Compare how different texts begin — story openings across picture books and fairytales — noting patterns and conventions
Map the events in a familiar story in order — from beginning to ending — using drawings or a simple timeline

modes.reason: Feature identification must become reliable across multiple texts before students can abstract text-type patterns from those features. Practice across a range of stories builds the consistent recognition habit.

nodes.label: Literary text types have patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different types of literary texts and describe at least one pattern or feature that is typical of each type.
criteria: Student can name at least two different types of literary texts.
Student can identify at least one feature typical of each type named.
Student can say something about how First Nations Australian storytelling patterns differ from or are similar to fairytales.

width.minimum: Name one literary text type (e.g. fairytale, poem) and identify one feature typical of it.
width.typical: Recognise different types of literary texts — fairytales, realistic stories, poetry; identify typical features (e.g. fairytale openings, story structure, poetic features); recognise First Nations Australian cultural storytelling patterns.
wider: Compare fairytales from different cultural traditions — European, Asian, First Nations Australian — and identify shared and distinctive patterns
Explore how stories are told in poetry and compare this to prose narrative — examining what each form can and cannot do
Investigate how First Nations Australian authors use cultural storytelling patterns distinctively, compared with fairytales or European story conventions

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate examples of each literary text type before the category becomes robust — a single fairytale is not enough to understand 'fairytale' as a type — the pattern emerges from the repertoire.

descriptors.title: Explore rhythms and sound patterns
descriptors.description: explore and replicate the rhythms and sound patterns of literary texts such as poems, rhymes and songs
descriptors.knowledge: Students have heard and participated in rhymes, songs and chants in home and early childhood settings. They have not yet been asked to consciously attend to, describe or replicate the rhythmic and sound patterns that structure these texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify and replicate rhythmic and sound patterns in poems, rhymes and songs — including exploring rhythms from First Nations Australian poetry — demonstrating attention to the patterns through performance and participation.

nodes.label: Poems and songs have rhythm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that a poem, rhyme or song has a rhythmic beat — a repeating pattern of strong and weak sounds.
criteria: Student can clap or tap the beat of a familiar rhyme without losing the pattern.
Student can identify that a poem or song has a rhythm.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without recognising that rhythmic beat is a pattern, students cannot identify rhyming and sound patterns in Node 2, nor replicate them in Node 3 — replication requires holding the pattern in mind, which is impossible if the pattern has not yet been consciously perceived.

width.minimum: Clap or tap the beat of one familiar rhyme or song.
width.typical: Recognise that poems, rhymes and songs have rhythm; clap, tap or move to the beat of multiple rhymes and songs; identify rhythm as a pattern that repeats.
wider: Compare the rhythms of different poem types — a nursery rhyme, a marching chant, a lullaby — and discuss how the rhythm feels different
Explore rhythms from First Nations Australian songs or chants and compare the rhythmic patterns with familiar English nursery rhymes

modes.reason: Rhythmic beat recognition must become automatic through repeated clapping and moving to diverse rhymes — students need to internalise the pattern before they can transfer it to identifying and replicating sound patterns in subsequent nodes.

nodes.label: Rhyme and sound patterns repeat
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify rhyming patterns and other sound patterns (e.g. alliteration) in poems and songs.
criteria: Student can identify rhyming words in a poem or song.
Student can describe the sound pattern they hear — where it repeats or changes.

width.minimum: Identify the rhyming words at the end of two lines in a familiar poem or song.
width.typical: Identify rhyme patterns in poems and songs; recognise that sound patterns (rhyme, repetition of sounds) contribute to the text's effect; explore poems with both rhyme and alliteration.
wider: Compare how rhyme patterns differ across several poems — some rhyme every line, some alternate, some don't rhyme — and discuss the effect
Create a short class rhyme or chant using a familiar sound pattern as a model
Explore sound patterns in First Nations Australian poetry and songs — attending to patterns that may be different from typical English rhyme schemes

modes.reason: Students may conflate 'poem' with 'rhyme' — the misconception that poems must rhyme. Multiple examples including non-rhyming poems and First Nations patterns that differ from English rhyme schemes are needed.

nodes.label: Replicating rhythms and patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can replicate the rhythm and sound pattern of a familiar poem, rhyme or song — performing it with attention to the pattern.
criteria: Student can recite or perform a poem, rhyme or song with the rhythm intact.
Student can identify the pattern they are replicating.
Student can clap or move to the beat of a poem they have not practised before.

width.minimum: Recite or perform one rhyme with actions, maintaining the rhythm throughout.
width.typical: Replicate rhythms and sound patterns through recitation with actions, clapping, or movement; use music to enhance appreciation; perform familiar poems and songs with rhythmic accuracy.
wider: Perform the same poem in multiple ways — with actions, with instruments, with movement — and compare how each performance changes the experience
Explore and replicate rhythms from First Nations Australian poetry, using accompaniment where culturally appropriate
Compose a simple original chant using a pattern learned from a familiar poem

modes.reason: Replication brings together: recognising the pattern, holding it in memory, and producing it in performance. These must be coordinated — and performance is how the learning becomes visible.

descriptors.title: Retell and adapt familiar texts
descriptors.description: retell and adapt familiar literary texts through play, performance, images or writing
descriptors.knowledge: Students have encountered and enjoyed literary texts. They have not yet been explicitly asked to retell a story in sequence or to adapt one — changing elements while maintaining its recognisable structure.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can retell a familiar literary text in sequence through play, performance, images or beginning writing, and can adapt elements of it — changing characters, settings or events — while maintaining story structure.

nodes.label: Retelling maintains sequence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can retell key events from a familiar story in the correct sequence.
criteria: Student can retell at least three events from a familiar story in the correct order.
Student's retelling includes the beginning and ending of the story.
nodes.hinge_reason: Sequential retelling establishes the structural knowledge of the story that adaptation in Node 3 depends on — students cannot adapt a story while maintaining its recognisable structure if they have not yet internalised that structure through accurate retelling.

width.minimum: Retell at least three events from a familiar story in order — orally, through drawing, or through sequenced pictures.
width.typical: Retell familiar literary texts in sequence using oral retelling, drawings or sequenced pictures; include key characters and events; maintain the story's beginning, middle and end.
wider: Retell the same story through two different modes — oral and sequenced pictures — and compare what each mode captures
Use digital tools to sequence images for a retelling and share with the class
Retell a First Nations Australian story with attention to its cultural sequence of events

modes.reason: Sequencing events correctly is a foundational narrative literacy skill — precision matters, and errors (missing events, wrong sequence) propagate into later story writing. Practice across multiple stories builds the habit.

nodes.label: Role-play brings characters to life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can take on a character role from a familiar text through play or performance, enacting key events.
criteria: Student can enact at least one scene from a story in role.
Student maintains the character's identity and the event's logic during play or performance.

width.minimum: Role-play or act out at least one scene from a familiar story, taking on a character role.
width.typical: Retell familiar literary texts through play and performance; draw and role-play characters or events; maintain character identity and event logic during dramatic play.
wider: Perform a familiar story as a class drama, allocating roles and rehearsing key events
Role-play the same story with different students in each role across multiple performances — discussing how different portrayals affect the story
Dramatise scenes from First Nations Australian literary texts, attending to cultural context and meaning

nodes.label: Adaptation changes elements while keeping structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adapt a familiar story — changing a character, setting or event — while maintaining its recognisable structure.
criteria: Student can retell an adapted version of a familiar story where at least one element has been changed.
Student's adaptation maintains a recognisable story structure — beginning, key events, ending.
Student can explain what they changed and why.

width.minimum: Change one element of a familiar story (e.g. 'What if the bear was a dog instead?') and explain what would be different.
width.typical: Adapt familiar literary texts by changing characters, settings or events; use play, performance, drawing or digital tools to represent the adaptation; maintain story structure during adaptation.
wider: Adapt the same story into a different setting or cultural context — discussing what changes and what must stay the same for the story to still work
Retell a story from a different character's perspective, adapting events as needed
Adapt a familiar text into a different mode — for example, turning a poem into a picture story or a story into a chant

modes.reason: Adaptation requires students to hold the original structure in mind while simultaneously generating changes — coordinating prior knowledge of the text with creative generation. This integration of memory and creativity is the endpoint of this descriptor.

descriptors.title: Identify familiar texts and purpose
descriptors.description: identify familiar texts and some features that indicate their purposes
descriptors.knowledge: Students encounter texts in home and community settings daily. They have not yet been explicitly asked to identify text features that signal purpose, or to connect specific features (ingredients list, numbered steps, images) to the purpose of the text.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify a range of familiar texts and name features that indicate their purposes — connecting observable features (lists, headings, images, numbered steps) to the texts' communicative functions.

nodes.label: Texts have features we can see
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify observable features of a familiar text — noting what is on the page or screen beyond just the words.
criteria: Student can point to at least two distinct features in a familiar text.
Student can name what each feature is (e.g. 'That's a list', 'That's a heading').
nodes.hinge_reason: Without being able to observe and name specific text features, students cannot connect those features to purpose in Node 2 — feature identification is the perceptual prerequisite for the feature-purpose reasoning that follows.

width.minimum: Name at least one visible feature of a familiar text beyond words alone (e.g. pictures, a list, numbers).
width.typical: Identify multiple visual and structural features of familiar texts — headings, images, lists, numbered steps, labels; discuss what these features look like across different text types.
wider: Compare the features of two different text types side by side — noting what is the same and what is different
Collect and sort examples of text features (lists, headings, pictures, numbered steps) from a range of classroom and everyday texts

modes.reason: Feature recognition must become reliable across multiple text types before students can reason about what those features signal. Practice across diverse texts builds the naming habit.

nodes.label: Features signal purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect specific text features to the text's purpose — explaining why a recipe has a list or why instructions are numbered.
criteria: Student can identify a text feature and explain what purpose it serves.
Student can use a text feature to select an appropriate text for a given purpose.

width.minimum: Match one text feature to the purpose it serves (e.g. 'The picture shows what the food looks like so you know what to make').
width.typical: Identify features that indicate text purposes — a recipe with an ingredients list and numbered steps is for cooking; a label is for identifying; a set of instructions is for doing something; discuss why each feature serves the purpose it does.
wider: Select a text for a specific purpose from a collection (e.g. 'Find a text that would help you learn how to do something') and explain the feature that told you it would help
Explore how the same feature (e.g. numbered steps) is used across multiple text types — and whether it always signals the same purpose
Investigate how First Nations Australian texts may serve community purposes through features different from standard school texts

modes.reason: The feature-purpose connection can over-generalise from one example — e.g. students may think 'pictures mean it's for children'. Multiple text types with different feature-purpose pairings are needed to build a flexible rather than rigid schema.

descriptors.title: Listen and use voice features
descriptors.description: interact in informal and structured situations by listening while others speak and using features of voice including volume levels
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed oral interaction skills through home and play contexts. They have not yet been explicitly required to practise structured listening behaviours or to consciously vary and control voice features such as volume across different interaction contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can interact in both informal and structured situations — listening appropriately while others speak and controlling voice features including volume — across a range of classroom and social contexts.

nodes.label: Listening is active
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate active listening behaviours when others are speaking — attending without interrupting and showing they understand.
criteria: Student listens without interrupting while another student or the teacher speaks.
Student can retell or respond to what was said, showing they were listening.
nodes.hinge_reason: Active listening is a prerequisite for the structured interaction in Node 3 — students who have not established listening behaviours cannot meaningfully participate in exchanges where they must listen, contribute and respond, since the listening component collapses.

width.minimum: Demonstrate listening without interrupting in one structured interaction (e.g. group discussion).
width.typical: Use active listening behaviours — listening without interrupting, looking at the speaker (where culturally appropriate), showing understanding; apply in pairs, small groups and whole-class contexts.
wider: Practise listening for a specific purpose — to answer a question, to find a detail — and report back what was heard
Explore how listening conventions differ across cultural contexts — including First Nations Australian conversational protocols where relevant to the class community
Apply active listening skills in play-based interaction and compare to structured discussion — noting similarities and differences

modes.reason: Active listening is a behavioural habit requiring practice to become reliable. Students need repeated structured opportunities rather than broader contexts. Precision and consistency are what matter here.

nodes.label: Volume varies by context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adjust their speaking volume appropriately for different contexts — indoor/outdoor, one-to-one, speaking to an audience.
criteria: Student uses an appropriate volume level for the context without prompting.
Student can identify when their volume is too loud or too quiet and adjust.

width.minimum: Use an appropriate volume level in one specified context (e.g. group discussion volume vs playground volume).
width.typical: Alter volume for different contexts — inside vs outside, informal interaction vs speaking to an audience; recognise that different contexts require different volume levels.
wider: Practise the same message at different volume levels across different contexts — comparing what feels appropriate in each
Explore other voice features — pacing, tone — and how they work alongside volume in different interaction contexts
Investigate how volume and voice norms differ across community and cultural contexts

modes.reason: Volume adjustment requires context-reading — students need exposure to multiple situations (inside, outside, audience) to generalise the principle rather than memorising a rule for one specific situation.

nodes.label: Interact in structured and informal situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in both informal and structured interaction situations — contributing ideas, exchanging with peers and following instructions — using appropriate listening and voice behaviours.
criteria: Student can contribute an idea in a structured interaction without prompting.
Student demonstrates active listening while others speak.
Student uses an appropriate voice volume for the interaction context.

width.minimum: Contribute at least one idea in a structured group discussion and listen to at least one other contribution.
width.typical: Participate in informal and structured situations — pair work, small groups, class discussions, play-based experiences; contribute ideas and questions; listen to others and respond; follow spoken instructions.
wider: Participate in a range of structured interaction formats — paired discussion, small group, whole class, and performance audience — applying appropriate behaviours in each
Engage in play-based interaction requiring imaginative use of spoken language across different roles
Lead a short interaction (e.g. ask a question to the group) and manage the response

modes.reason: Structured interaction requires simultaneously managing listening behaviours, voice features, and contribution — these previously practised skills must now work together in real interaction contexts.

descriptors.title: Differences between text types
descriptors.description: identify some differences between imaginative and informative texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have been read imaginative and informative texts. They have not yet been explicitly asked to name and compare the differences between these two broad text types as categories.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify and describe differences between imaginative and informative texts — including purpose, content and image use — and can select texts for information purposes.

nodes.label: Some texts are stories, some give information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a text is imaginative (a story) or informative (giving facts) and say how they know.
criteria: Student can identify an imaginative text and an informative text from a selection.
Student can say at least one reason for the classification.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without the imaginative/informative distinction, students cannot compare how images function differently across text types in Node 2 — the image comparison depends on the category distinction being secure.

width.minimum: Identify one imaginative and one informative text and say one way they are different.
width.typical: Distinguish between imaginative and informative texts; discuss what is 'real' and what is imagined; identify informative texts for information purposes.
wider: Sort a collection of texts into imaginative and informative categories and explain the reasoning for each sort
Find examples where the boundary between imaginative and informative is blurred — for example, narrative non-fiction — and discuss

modes.reason: Students may use a surface feature (pictures = stories) to classify — the misconception is that visual richness signals imaginative purpose. Multiple examples, including illustrated informative texts and wordless stories, help build a more robust criterion.

nodes.label: Images differ between text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how images are used differently in imaginative and informative texts.
criteria: Student can describe how images are used differently in an imaginative and an informative text.
Student can give a reason why images in informative texts look different from illustrations in stories.

width.minimum: Identify one difference in how images are used in an imaginative text and an informative text.
width.typical: Compare images in imaginative and informative texts — noting that imaginative texts often use illustrations to evoke emotion or narrative while informative texts use images to show, label or explain real content.
wider: Compare the same topic presented in an imaginative and an informative text — examining how images serve different purposes in each
Investigate First Nations Australian texts that serve both imaginative and informative purposes and discuss how images function in them
Discuss how digital informative texts (websites, simple apps) use images differently from print informative texts

descriptors.title: Read using phonic knowledge
descriptors.description: read decodable and authentic texts using developing phonic knowledge, and monitor meaning using context and emerging grammatical knowledge
descriptors.knowledge: Students are developing letter-sound knowledge (AC9EFLY11, AC9EFLY12). They have not yet been asked to apply phonic decoding strategies within connected text, or to monitor for meaning breakdown and self-correct using context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can read decodable and authentic texts using developing phonic knowledge — navigating correctly, attempting unknown words using phonics, and monitoring for meaning using context and grammatical knowledge.

nodes.label: Navigate a text correctly
nodes.checkpoint: Students can navigate a text from left to right, top to bottom, matching one spoken word to one written word.
criteria: Student tracks from left to right consistently across a full page of text.
Student correctly matches each spoken word to one written word.
Student returns correctly to the start of the next line.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without accurate directional tracking and one-to-one word matching, phonic decoding in Node 2 cannot function — students cannot attempt to decode a word they have not correctly isolated on the page.

width.minimum: Read a short familiar text pointing to each word, maintaining left-to-right directionality and one-to-one word matching.
width.typical: Navigate a text correctly — starting at the right place, reading left to right and top to bottom, returning to the next line correctly, matching one spoken word to one written word.
wider: Apply navigation skills across a range of text formats — big books, small books, and simple digital texts
Read familiar texts at varying speeds while maintaining accurate tracking and word matching

modes.reason: Accurate tracking and one-to-one word matching must become automatic — they are the foundation of all reading. Practice across multiple texts builds the habit. Errors (losing track, skipping lines) cascade into comprehension breakdown.

nodes.label: Use phonic knowledge to decode
nodes.checkpoint: Students can attempt to decode unknown words using their developing letter-sound knowledge and high-frequency word knowledge.
criteria: Student attempts an unknown word using phonics rather than guessing randomly.
Student can blend sounds to produce a recognisable word in at least one attempt.
nodes.hinge_reason: Decoding is the prerequisite for meaning monitoring in Node 3 — students cannot notice that their reading does not make sense if they are not producing an approximation of the word through phonic attempt. Without decoding, self-correction has no raw material to work with.

width.minimum: Attempt at least one unknown word in a familiar text using letter-sound decoding.
width.typical: Attempt to work out unknown words using phonic decoding and knowledge of high-frequency words; blend sounds to decode CVC and simple words encountered in text.
wider: Apply decoding strategies to an increasing range of text types — decodable readers, picture books, simple information texts
Apply phonic decoding to names and topic words from culturally diverse contexts in classroom texts
Use multiple decoding strategies (phonics, word recognition, context) and explain which strategy was used

modes.reason: Students may apply phonics only in isolated word tasks and not carry the strategy into connected text. Multiple connected text contexts — including authentic texts not just decodables — help generalise the strategy.

nodes.label: Monitor meaning and self-correct
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise when their reading does not make sense and pause or seek support — using context and emerging grammatical knowledge as a check.
criteria: Student notices when their reading does not make sense.
Student pauses or attempts to self-correct without needing a prompt.
Student can say what they tried when meaning broke down.

width.minimum: Pause when reading breaks down and attempt to self-correct or seek support.
width.typical: Monitor meaning while reading — pause or ask for support when something does not make sense; use context (what would make sense here?) and emerging grammatical knowledge (does that sound right?) alongside phonics to monitor and repair.
wider: Apply monitoring strategies across texts of increasing length and complexity
Explicitly articulate what strategy was used when meaning broke down — identifying the source of difficulty
Apply monitoring strategies to texts with culturally unfamiliar content, using context more heavily when phonics alone is insufficient

modes.reason: Monitoring meaning requires integrating multiple cueing systems simultaneously — phonics, context and grammar — rather than relying on one. Coordinating these is the endpoint of Foundation-level reading.

descriptors.title: Use comprehension strategies
descriptors.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising and questioning to understand and discuss texts listened to, viewed or read independently
descriptors.knowledge: Students listen to and view texts in classroom read-alouds. They have not yet been explicitly taught comprehension strategies as named, deliberate moves that can be applied intentionally to construct meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can use a range of comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, questioning — when listening, viewing and reading, and can discuss texts using what they have understood.

nodes.label: Predicting uses what we know
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make a prediction about what a text will be about using available information (title, cover, images).
criteria: Student makes a prediction with reasoning — using a visible text feature (title, image) to justify the prediction.
Student can revisit and evaluate their prediction after reading.

width.minimum: Make one prediction about a text before reading, using the title or cover image.
width.typical: Predict what might happen in a text based on title and cover; connect predictions to prior knowledge; revisit predictions after reading.
wider: Make predictions at multiple points in a text — before, during, and after — comparing how predictions change
Make predictions about texts from unfamiliar cultural contexts and discuss what prior knowledge was and wasn't useful

nodes.label: Connecting links text to experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make a connection between a text and their own experiences or prior knowledge.
criteria: Student makes a connection between a text event and their own experience.
Student can explain how the connection helped them understand the text.

width.minimum: Make one connection between a text and their own life or prior knowledge.
width.typical: Connect texts to personal experiences; identify similarities and differences between text events and own life; use connections to deepen understanding.
wider: Make text-to-text connections — identifying how two texts are similar or different
Connect texts to knowledge from other learning areas — identifying when prior curriculum knowledge helps understand a text
Make connections to First Nations Australian stories and cultural accounts when engaging with relevant texts

nodes.label: Retelling and summarising shows understanding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can retell or summarise key content from a text they have listened to, viewed or read — selecting what was most important.
criteria: Student retells at least two key events or facts from a text in the correct sequence.
Student's retelling captures the main content, not just an interesting detail.

width.minimum: Retell at least two key events or facts from a text in sequence.
width.typical: Retell stories using picture cues or prompts; relate one or two key facts from informative texts; sequence events in retelling; retell events from First Nations Australians' stories in sequence.
wider: Retell the same text in two different modes (oral and drawing) and compare what each captures
Summarise an informative text by identifying and reporting the most important facts — distinguishing from interesting details
Retell events from First Nations Australian cultural accounts attending to cultural sequence and significance

modes.reason: Retelling accurately and sequentially is a fundamental comprehension output skill — precision matters and sequence errors signal comprehension gaps. Practice across multiple text types builds accuracy.

nodes.label: Questioning deepens understanding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can ask a genuine question about a text — identifying something they want to understand or find out more about.
criteria: Student asks at least one genuine question about a text — not just a yes/no question.
Student can identify whether their question was answered by the text or requires another source.
Student can listen to a text with a specific question in mind and report the answer.

width.minimum: Ask one question about a text listened to or read (e.g. 'Why did the character do that?').
width.typical: Ask questions about texts before, during and after reading; listen for specific purposes — to answer a given question or find a specific detail; generate and pursue genuine questions.
wider: Generate questions about a text and discuss which questions the text answers and which it doesn't — exploring how texts have limits
Listen to a text for a specific purpose set by the teacher and then for a purpose generated by the student — comparing the experience
Ask questions about texts from culturally unfamiliar contexts — identifying what additional knowledge is needed to fully understand them

modes.reason: Questioning as a comprehension strategy risks becoming rote ('ask a question') rather than genuinely purposeful. Multiple text types — including informative and First Nations Australian texts — help students develop questioning as a real meaning-making move.

descriptors.title: Create short written texts
descriptors.description: create and participate in shared editing of short written texts to record and report ideas and events using some learnt vocabulary, basic sentence boundary punctuation and spelling some consonant–vowel–consonant words correctly
descriptors.knowledge: Students have beginning letter-sound and word knowledge (AC9EFLY09–15). They have not yet been asked to compose and edit connected written text — integrating spelling, vocabulary, punctuation and ideas into a coherent short text.
