descriptors.endpoint: Students can create short written texts to record or report ideas and events — using learnt vocabulary, CVC spelling and basic sentence punctuation — and can participate in shared editing to improve a text.

nodes.label: Writing communicates an idea
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce a short text (drawing and/or beginning writing) that communicates one idea or event.
criteria: Student produces a text that communicates a recognisable idea or event.
Student's text includes at least one written word alongside or within a drawing.

width.minimum: Produce a text with at least one written word or sentence (and/or drawing) that communicates an idea.
width.typical: Create short written texts using beginning writing knowledge, sound-letter relationships and known words; combine writing and drawing to communicate personal responses to ideas and events.
wider: Create texts for different purposes — recording an event, responding to a story, reporting an observation — and compare how purpose affects what is written
Create multimodal texts using digital tools that combine writing and images

nodes.label: CVC spelling, vocabulary and punctuation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply CVC spelling, use some learnt vocabulary, and include a capital letter at the sentence start and a full stop at the end.
criteria: Student uses a capital letter at the start of a sentence and a full stop at the end.
Student spells at least one CVC word correctly without prompting.
Student uses at least one learnt vocabulary word accurately in context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without these conventions being at least partially established, students cannot productively participate in shared editing in Node 3 — they need something to read back and review, and the editing process presupposes that conventions have been attempted.

width.minimum: Write at least one sentence with a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end, spelling at least one CVC word correctly.
width.typical: Use learnt vocabulary in writing; spell some CVC words correctly; apply basic sentence boundary punctuation (capital letter and full stop); demonstrate growing control of these conventions in short texts.
wider: Write short texts across different topics, applying vocabulary and spelling knowledge to new content
Experiment with question marks and exclamation marks in appropriate writing contexts
Use topic-specific vocabulary from cross-curricular learning in written texts

modes.reason: CVC spelling accuracy and sentence punctuation conventions are precision skills — errors cascade into illegible or misleading texts. Practice across multiple writing tasks consolidates these as reliable conventions rather than occasional correct applications.

nodes.label: Reading back and shared editing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can 'read' their own text back and participate in shared editing — identifying at least one thing to change or correct.
criteria: Student can read their own text back and identify what it says.
Student can participate in shared editing and identify at least one feature to change.
Student makes at least one improvement following feedback.

width.minimum: Read their own text back to an experienced writer and identify at least one capital letter at a sentence start.
width.typical: Read own texts back; participate in shared editing by identifying capital letters at sentence beginnings; respond to feedback from an experienced writer and make at least one improvement.
wider: Participate in shared editing with a focus on a chosen feature — punctuation, vocabulary, spelling — applying what is learned to future writing
Read back texts from multiple writing events and identify growth over time
Contribute to editing of a class-shared text, justifying each editing decision

modes.reason: Reading back and editing requires coordinating all previously learned conventions — punctuation, spelling, vocabulary — as a self-monitoring and improvement process. The act of authoring and reviewing one's own text integrates the learning.

descriptors.title: Deliver short spoken texts
descriptors.description: create and deliver short spoken texts to report ideas and events to peers, using features of voice such as appropriate volume
descriptors.knowledge: Students interact orally in informal settings. They have not yet been asked to prepare and deliver a deliberately constructed spoken text to an audience of peers — with conscious attention to voice features such as volume.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can create and deliver a short spoken text to peers — reporting an idea or event — using appropriate volume and staying on topic.

nodes.label: A spoken text has a topic
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the topic they want to talk about and share at least one idea or event related to it.
criteria: Student's spoken text is identifiably about a topic.
Student shares at least one idea or event related to the topic.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without identifying a topic and having content to share, the audience-directed delivery in Node 2 has nothing to work with — volume adjustment and visual prompt use are tools for delivering content, not a substitute for it.

width.minimum: Name what their spoken text will be about and share one idea or fact.
width.typical: Share a personal experience, interest or discovery with peers; stay on the topic selected; sequence ideas or events with support from visual prompts.
wider: Share spoken texts on topics from different areas — personal experience, a book shared in class, something learned in another subject
Compare what is easy to share orally versus in writing — identifying what each mode does well

modes.reason: Topic focus and content generation must be reliable before students can attend to delivery features. Practice at identifying a topic and sharing ideas builds the foundation for Node 2 delivery.

nodes.label: Volume and focus for an audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adjust their volume for an audience of peers and use visual prompts to stay on topic.
criteria: Student can be heard clearly by peers without shouting.
Student stays on topic with or without visual prompts.
Student delivers a text of at least two to three connected ideas or events.

width.minimum: Deliver a short spoken text at an audible volume to peers using at least one visual prompt.
width.typical: Use appropriate volume for a semi-formal peer audience; use visual prompts (objects, drawings, digital images) to stay on topic and sequence ideas.
wider: Deliver the same spoken text in different contexts — to one partner, to a small group, to the whole class — adapting volume accordingly
Create and use visual prompts for a spoken text — selecting images or drawings that sequence ideas effectively
Deliver a short response to a First Nations Australian story or cultural account with attention to appropriate ways of sharing

modes.reason: Audience-directed delivery requires integrating topic focus, volume control, and use of visual supports simultaneously. These skills were practised separately; here they must work together in performance.

descriptors.title: Letter formation
descriptors.description: form most lower-case and upper-case letters using learnt letter formations
descriptors.knowledge: Students may have pre-writing experience (drawing, mark-making) but have not yet been explicitly taught and practised standardised letter formations for most of the alphabet.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can form most lower-case and upper-case letters using learnt formations — with a functional pencil grip and consistent starting points, direction and size.

nodes.label: Functional grip and starting point
nodes.checkpoint: Students use a functional pencil grip and can demonstrate the correct starting point for a modelled letter.
criteria: Student uses a recognisably functional pencil grip.
Student starts letters at the correct point without prompting for practised letters.
nodes.hinge_reason: Incorrect pencil grip and starting-point habits established here directly impair the accuracy and legibility of letter formation in Nodes 2 and 3 — motor habits are increasingly difficult to correct once established.

width.minimum: Demonstrate a functional pencil grip and correctly start at least one letter from the top.
width.typical: Develop and use a functional pencil grip; follow demonstrations of where to start and in which direction to write letters; apply consistently across practised letters.
wider: Practise grip and formation with different writing tools — pencil, marker, chalk — noting how grip adapts
Use letter formation across different media — sand tray, whiteboard, digital stylus — attending to starting point consistency

modes.reason: Pencil grip and starting-point habits must be established early and consistently — errors in these mechanics become increasingly hard to correct. Repetition across tools and contexts is the remedy, not breadth.

nodes.label: Form lower-case letters accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can form most lower-case letters using learnt formations — with correct direction and legible shape.
criteria: Student produces most lower-case letters in a recognisable, legible form.
Student's letter formation is consistent across a short piece of writing.
nodes.hinge_reason: Lower-case letter formation must be sufficiently established before upper-case letters in Node 3, since upper-case letters are used in conjunction with lower-case in all real writing tasks — inconsistent lower-case production undermines legibility in any written work from this point forward.

width.minimum: Form at least fifteen lower-case letters using learnt formations legibly.
width.typical: Form most lower-case letters using learnt letter formations; demonstrate correct directionality and size; produce legible letterforms in writing tasks.
wider: Apply lower-case letter formations in the context of real writing tasks — labelling drawings, writing names, copying short sentences
Compare letter formation consistency across different surfaces and tools
Explore how printed lower-case letters vary in font and compare with handwritten forms — understanding that the letterform has a consistent structure

modes.reason: Letter formation is a motor skill — accuracy and consistency require practice. The width axis is thin here; the issue is reliable production, not contextual breadth.

nodes.label: Form upper-case letters accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can form most upper-case letters using learnt formations.
criteria: Student produces most upper-case letters in a recognisable, legible form.
Student uses upper-case letters correctly in their own name.

width.minimum: Form at least ten upper-case letters using learnt formations legibly.
width.typical: Form most upper-case letters using learnt letter formations; apply in contexts where capitals are required (names, sentence starts).
wider: Use upper-case letters in authentic writing contexts — own name, classmates' names, titles — attending to when capitalisation is required
Compare upper-case and lower-case letter pairs and discuss how formation relates to the letter's identity

modes.reason: As with lower-case, upper-case formation is a motor skill requiring practice. Application in authentic contexts (names, titles) reinforces both formation and the rule for when to use capitals.

descriptors.title: Recognise rhyme, alliteration and phonemes
descriptors.description: recognise and generate rhyming words, alliteration patterns, syllables and sounds (phonemes) in spoken words (phonological awareness)
descriptors.knowledge: Students may have heard rhymes and songs. They have not yet been asked to consciously attend to, name and generate the phonological patterns in spoken words — rhyme, alliteration, syllables and phonemes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise and generate rhyming words, identify alliteration patterns, identify syllables in spoken words, and isolate phonemes — demonstrating phonological awareness across multiple word types.

nodes.label: Rhyming words share endings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a rhyming pair and produce a rhyming word when given a target.
criteria: Student can identify whether two words rhyme when heard.
Student can generate at least one rhyming word when given a target word.
nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable rhyme recognition signals that phoneme-level auditory discrimination is developing — without this, phoneme isolation in Node 4 and the blending and segmenting tasks in LY10 will be unreliable, as they all depend on the ability to hear and attend to sounds within words.

width.minimum: Identify whether two words rhyme; generate one word that rhymes with a given word.
width.typical: Recognise and produce rhyming words; identify rhyming patterns in familiar stories and rhymes; generate rhyming strings.
wider: Generate rhyming strings across multiple word families — exploring how many words share the same rime
Compare rhyming conventions in English with other languages or First Nations Australian language patterns known to students
Create simple rhyming couplets orally — applying rhyme generation to creative language play

modes.reason: Reliable rhyme recognition and production is foundational to phonological awareness — errors here indicate the phoneme-level awareness needed for decoding is not yet secure. Practice across many word pairs is the remedy.

nodes.label: Alliteration is repeated initial sounds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify alliteration patterns in spoken words — recognising that initial sounds repeat.
criteria: Student can identify two words that start with the same sound.
Student can produce at least one alliterative phrase orally.

width.minimum: Identify an alliteration pattern in two words (e.g. 'helpful Henry').
width.typical: Identify alliteration patterns in spoken words and familiar texts; produce simple alliterative phrases; understand that alliteration is about the initial sound, not the initial letter.
wider: Create alliterative name phrases for each class member — exploring alliteration productively
Identify alliteration in poems, picture book titles and tongue twisters across a range of texts
Compare alliteration in English with sound-play patterns in other languages

nodes.label: Words have syllables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the number of syllables in spoken words by clapping, tapping or counting.
criteria: Student can clap the correct number of syllables in a spoken word.
Student correctly distinguishes one-syllable and two-syllable words.

width.minimum: Correctly identify the number of syllables in at least five words of varying length (one to three syllables).
width.typical: Identify syllables in spoken words by clapping or tapping; segment multi-syllable words; understand that every syllable contains a vowel sound.
wider: Clap syllables across names of class members, local area names and topic words — exploring syllable patterns in real vocabulary
Compare syllable counts in familiar words across different languages — noting that syllable structure differs across languages
Sort word cards by syllable count — building a syllable-based word awareness

nodes.label: Words are made of phonemes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can isolate individual phonemes in spoken words — hearing the discrete sounds that make up a word.
criteria: Student can isolate the first phoneme in a spoken word.
Student can isolate the final phoneme in a spoken CVC word.
Student understands that words are made of more than one sound.
nodes.hinge_reason: Phoneme isolation is a prerequisite for blending and segmenting in LY10 — students cannot blend phonemes they cannot yet isolate, and cannot segment words into phonemes they cannot hear as discrete units.

width.minimum: Identify the first phoneme in at least three spoken words.
width.typical: Recognise individual phonemes in spoken words; isolate initial, medial and final phonemes; understand that words are made of discrete sounds.
wider: Practise phoneme isolation across a range of word types — varying initial, medial and final positions
Compare phonemes in English words with sounds in other languages or names familiar to students — noticing sounds that English does and doesn't have
Use phoneme awareness as a bridge to letter-sound knowledge — connecting isolated phonemes to their grapheme representations

modes.reason: Phoneme isolation is a prerequisite for blending and segmenting (AC9EFLY10) — without reliable phoneme isolation, decoding will be unreliable. Practice to accuracy is required before width is productive.

descriptors.title: Segment and blend phonemes
descriptors.description: segment sentences into individual words; orally blend and segment single-syllable spoken words; isolate, blend and manipulate phonemes in single-syllable words (phonological awareness)
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise phonemes (AC9EFLY09). They have not yet been explicitly taught to blend phonemes into words, segment words into phonemes, or manipulate individual phonemes by substitution, addition or deletion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can blend phonemes into words, segment single-syllable words into phonemes, and manipulate phonemes by addition, deletion and substitution — demonstrating secure phoneme-level awareness across a range of single-syllable word types.

nodes.label: Sentences are strings of words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can segment a spoken sentence into its individual words — identifying where word boundaries fall.
criteria: Student correctly segments a spoken sentence into its individual words.
Student can count the number of words in a spoken sentence.

width.minimum: Segment a spoken sentence of three to four words into individual words by clapping or tapping.
width.typical: Segment sentences into individual words; understand that words are the units within sentences; count words in short spoken sentences.
wider: Apply word segmentation to sentences of varying length — including sentences with contractions and function words
Connect spoken word segmentation to written word spaces — matching oral and print word boundaries

nodes.label: Blending: sounds into words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can blend a sequence of separately spoken phonemes into a recognisable word.
criteria: Student blends three separately spoken phonemes into a recognisable word.
Student can blend words of varying CVC, CVCC and CCVC patterns.
nodes.hinge_reason: Blending fluency is the core decoding mechanism in LY04 and LY12 — students who cannot reliably blend phonemes into words cannot read connected text using phonics, and their decoding will remain halting and inaccurate.

width.minimum: Blend three phonemes into a CVC word when given the sounds separately (e.g. /l/-/i/-/p/ → 'lip').
width.typical: Blend phonemes of single-syllable spoken words — including CVC, CVCC and CCVC patterns; produce the target word correctly from the phoneme sequence.
wider: Blend phoneme sequences across a wide range of single-syllable word types — varying vowels, clusters and codas
Apply blending to words containing digraphs once grapheme knowledge is established
Practise blending through word games, oral riddles and chants — building fluent blending as a reading tool

modes.reason: Blending fluency is the core decoding mechanism — it must become fast and accurate. Slow or inaccurate blending limits reading. Practice to fluency across word types is required before width adds value.

nodes.label: Segmenting: words into sounds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can segment a single-syllable spoken word into its constituent phonemes — saying each sound separately.
criteria: Student segments a CVC word into three separate phonemes.
Student can segment both onset and rime of a word.
nodes.hinge_reason: Segmenting is the prerequisite for spelling — students who cannot segment a spoken word into phonemes cannot apply letter-sound knowledge to encode it in writing (LY12, LY13). Segmenting errors propagate directly into misspelling.

width.minimum: Segment a CVC word into three phonemes (e.g. 'can' → /c/-/a/-/n/).
width.typical: Segment single-syllable spoken words into phonemes — including CVC, CVCC and CCVC patterns; say each phoneme distinctly; understand this as the inverse of blending.
wider: Segment words across a wide range of single-syllable types — varying onset, vowel and coda
Apply segmenting to words with digraphs (once grapheme knowledge supports this) — recognising that 'sh' is one phoneme
Connect segmenting to spelling — use segmentation to support encoding in writing tasks

modes.reason: Segmenting is the inverse of blending and equally foundational for spelling. Consistent accuracy across word types is required — errors propagate directly into misspelling.

nodes.label: Phoneme manipulation: add, delete, substitute
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate phonemes in single-syllable words by addition, deletion and substitution — generating new words.
criteria: Student can substitute the initial phoneme to make a new word.
Student can delete the initial phoneme and say what remains.
Student can add a phoneme to generate a new word.

width.minimum: Substitute the initial phoneme in a given word to make a new word (e.g. 'run' → 'fun').
width.typical: Manipulate phonemes by addition, deletion and substitution at initial, medial and final positions; generate new words through each manipulation type; understand that changing one phoneme changes the word.
wider: Practise phoneme manipulation across all positions — initial, medial, final — systematically exploring minimal pairs
Apply phoneme manipulation to generate a range of words for a rime family — building awareness of word families as phonemic units
Explore phoneme manipulation through word games, chants and minimal pair comparisons

modes.reason: Phoneme substitution and deletion can feel arbitrary without multiple examples — students need to work across initial, medial and final positions, and across addition/deletion/substitution, before the principle that phonemes are independently manipulable is secure.

descriptors.title: Name letters and common sounds
descriptors.description: recognise and name all upper- and lower-case letters (graphemes) and know the most common sound that each letter represents
descriptors.knowledge: Students may recognise letters in their own name and in familiar texts. They have not yet been explicitly taught all upper- and lower-case letter names and their most common associated sounds.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise and name all upper- and lower-case letters and identify the most common sound each letter represents — demonstrating complete alphabet knowledge across both cases.

nodes.label: Letters have names
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and name most upper- and lower-case letters when shown them.
criteria: Student can name all twenty-six upper-case letters.
Student can name all twenty-six lower-case letters.
Student can match upper- and lower-case letter pairs.
nodes.hinge_reason: Letter name knowledge is a prerequisite for letter-sound learning in Node 2 — without reliable letter identification, students cannot associate sounds with specific letters, and phonics instruction cannot proceed effectively.

width.minimum: Recognise and name at least fifteen lower-case letters.
width.typical: Recognise and name all upper- and lower-case letters; match upper- and lower-case pairs; apply letter naming in the context of familiar words and texts.
wider: Recognise letters across a range of fonts and handwriting styles — understanding that the same letter takes different visual forms
Identify letters in environmental print, books, signs and digital texts — building multi-context letter recognition
Compare the English alphabet with other alphabetic writing systems — noting similarities and differences

modes.reason: Complete and automatic letter name knowledge is a prerequisite for phonics instruction — uncertain letter names slow decoding and letter-sound learning. Practice to automaticity is required.

nodes.label: Letters represent sounds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the most common sound represented by each letter.
criteria: Student can produce the most common sound for each letter of the alphabet.
Student can connect a letter to its sound when prompted by either the letter name or the letter form.
nodes.hinge_reason: Letter-sound associations are the prerequisite for all phonic decoding in LY04, LY12 and LY13 — without automatic letter-to-sound retrieval, students cannot blend or segment, and reading and spelling both fail at the letter level.

width.minimum: Produce the most common sound for at least fifteen letters.
width.typical: Know the most common sound each letter represents; connect letter names to letter sounds; apply letter-sound knowledge in the context of simple reading and spelling.
wider: Identify the most common sound for all twenty-six letters, then explore that some letters have more than one common sound (e.g. 'c' in 'cat' vs 'city')
Connect letter-sound knowledge to words encountered in reading — applying the knowledge in context rather than isolation
Explore sounds in other languages — noting that the same letter may represent different sounds in different languages

modes.reason: Letter-sound associations require practice to automaticity — slow retrieval directly limits decoding speed. The 'most common sound' must be the automatic first response before alternative sounds are introduced.

descriptors.title: Write and read CVC words
descriptors.description: write consonant–vowel–consonant (CVC) words by representing sounds with the appropriate letters, and blend sounds associated with letters when reading CVC words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can name letters, produce letter sounds (AC9EFLY11), and segment and blend phonemes (AC9EFLY10). They have not yet been asked to connect phoneme-grapheme knowledge in both directions: encoding (writing) and decoding (reading) CVC words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can write CVC words by encoding phonemes as letters, and read CVC words by blending the letter sounds — demonstrating bidirectional phoneme-grapheme correspondence at the CVC level.

nodes.label: Sounds can be written as letters
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent each phoneme in a CVC word with the correct letter when writing.
criteria: Student correctly writes at least five CVC words, including words with different vowels.
Student represents each phoneme with the correct letter — not just onset and final consonant.
nodes.hinge_reason: CVC encoding is the prerequisite for the spelling strategy in LY13 — students who cannot reliably encode CVC words cannot extend phoneme-grapheme correspondence to unknown words. Encoding errors also propagate directly into the writing tasks in LY06.

width.minimum: Write at least five CVC words correctly from dictation, representing each phoneme with the appropriate letter.
width.typical: Write CVC words across all short vowel sounds by representing each phoneme with the appropriate letter; spell common CVC patterns reliably.
wider: Write CVC words across all five short vowel sounds — ensuring the vowel discrimination is secure
Write CVC words in the context of real writing tasks — labelling drawings, completing simple sentences
Sort CVC words by vowel sound — building awareness of short vowel patterns

modes.reason: CVC encoding must become reliable and accurate — encoding errors cascade directly into unintelligible writing. Practice across all short vowels is required before accuracy is secure.

nodes.label: Letters can be blended into words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read CVC words by blending the sounds associated with the letters left to right.
criteria: Student reads at least five CVC words by blending, including unfamiliar words.
Student reads CVC words within a short decodable text rather than only in isolation.
nodes.hinge_reason: CVC decoding is the prerequisite for reading connected text in LY04 — students who cannot blend CVC words cannot apply phonic decoding to unknown words in authentic texts, and their reading remains dependent on memorisation.

width.minimum: Read at least five CVC words by blending letter sounds.
width.typical: Blend the sounds of CVC words when reading; apply blending to new CVC words not previously seen; read CVC words in the context of simple texts.
wider: Read CVC words in connected text — applying blending in the context of meaning-making
Read CVC words across a range of vowel patterns — not limited to familiar words
Identify CVC words in a familiar text and read them aloud — connecting letter-sound knowledge to reading fluency

modes.reason: Blending at the word level must become fluent — slow, halting blending interferes with comprehension. Accuracy first, then fluency across multiple CVC words.

descriptors.title: Use letters and sounds to spell
descriptors.description: use knowledge of letters and sounds to spell words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can write CVC words (AC9EFLY12) and have letter-sound knowledge. They have not yet been explicitly asked to apply letter-sound knowledge independently as a self-directed spelling strategy across unknown words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can use letter-sound knowledge as a spelling strategy — making plausible attempts at unknown words by representing phonemes with appropriate graphemes.

nodes.label: Spelling is a strategy, not just memory
nodes.checkpoint: Students can attempt to spell an unknown word by applying letter-sound knowledge — producing a plausible spelling attempt rather than random letters.
criteria: Student makes a plausible spelling attempt — each phoneme in the word is represented by a letter.
Student uses the spelling strategy without needing to be told 'try to spell it'.
Student's spelling attempt reflects the sounds in the word, even if not conventionally correct.

width.minimum: Produce a plausible letter-sound attempt for at least one unknown word encountered in writing.
width.typical: Use knowledge of letters and sounds to make plausible spelling attempts; understand that spelling unknown words involves applying phoneme-grapheme knowledge; produce attempts where each phoneme is represented.
wider: Apply the spelling strategy to unknown topic words in different learning areas — practising transfer of the skill
Compare a plausible phonemic spelling attempt with the conventional spelling — identifying where letter-sound rules were applied correctly and where other knowledge is needed
Use the spelling strategy in independent writing tasks across different text purposes

modes.reason: Students may apply the spelling strategy only in explicit phonics tasks and not in independent writing. Multiple writing contexts — across different purposes and topics — help generalise the strategy so it is used independently.

descriptors.title: Read and write high-frequency words
descriptors.description: read and write some high-frequency words and other familiar words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can decode CVC words phonically (AC9EFLY12). They have not yet been asked to build a set of words that are recognised and written automatically — including high-frequency words that cannot always be decoded phonically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can read and write an increasing number of high-frequency words and other familiar words — including words that cannot be fully decoded phonically — with sufficient automaticity to support fluent reading and independent writing.

nodes.label: Some words are recognised at sight
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise at least ten high-frequency words automatically — without needing to decode them phoneme by phoneme.
criteria: Student reads at least ten high-frequency words automatically without sounding out.
Student recognises their own name and at least five other familiar words on sight.
nodes.hinge_reason: Sight recognition of high-frequency words is a prerequisite for fluent written production in Node 2 — students who cannot recognise these words automatically in reading also cannot write them automatically, and their writing composition is impeded by the need to decode or invent every common word.

width.minimum: Read at least ten high-frequency words on sight without decoding.
width.typical: Read an increasing number of high-frequency words recognised in shared and independent texts; recognise some familiar words (own name, character names, school name).
wider: Read high-frequency words in connected text — applying recognition in the context of reading rather than word list drills only
Compare which words appear most often across multiple familiar texts — building a text-grounded high-frequency word list
Investigate high-frequency words in digital texts — noting which appear on screens, websites, apps and digital books

modes.reason: High-frequency word recognition must become automatic — slow recognition of common words significantly limits reading fluency. Repeated exposure across many encounters is the mechanism. Width is thin here: the issue is automaticity, not contextual breadth.

nodes.label: High-frequency words can be written
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write at least some high-frequency words correctly from memory.
criteria: Student can write at least five high-frequency words correctly from memory.
Student uses high-frequency words in independent writing without needing to copy them.

width.minimum: Write at least five high-frequency words correctly without copying.
width.typical: Read and write an increasing number of high-frequency words; write familiar words from memory in the context of independent writing tasks.
wider: Use high-frequency words in independent writing and self-check for correct spelling
Build a personal word card collection — connecting reading recognition with written production
Apply known high-frequency words as anchors in independent writing — using them alongside phonemic spelling strategies for unknown words

modes.reason: Written production of high-frequency words must be automatic — looking up or sounding out every common word in writing impedes composition. Practice to accuracy across multiple words is required.

descriptors.title: Words as units of meaning
descriptors.description: understand that words are units of meaning and can be made of more than one meaningful part
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that words exist as units within sentences. They have not yet been introduced to the idea that words themselves can be decomposed into meaningful parts — morphemes — that each carry meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can explain that words are units of meaning and that some words contain more than one meaningful part — demonstrating beginning morphemic awareness.

nodes.label: Words carry meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that each word in a sentence carries meaning — removing a word changes what the sentence communicates.
criteria: Student can explain that a word contributes meaning to a sentence.
Student can identify that removing a word changes what a sentence says.
nodes.hinge_reason: Unless students understand that words are independently meaningful units, the concept of a word having multiple meaningful parts in Node 2 has no foundation — morphemic awareness builds on the prior understanding that words carry separable meaning.

width.minimum: Identify that removing one word from a familiar sentence changes its meaning.
width.typical: Understand that words are units of meaning; identify what specific words contribute to a sentence's meaning; recognise that different words carry different types of meaning.
wider: Explore how swapping one word in a sentence for another word changes meaning — including substituting synonyms and antonyms
Investigate words from different topic areas and discuss what meaning each contributes to understanding the topic

modes.reason: Students need a visible reasoning scaffold — removing a word, then observing what changes — to grasp that individual words carry independent meaning. Worked examples make the word-meaning relationship explicit before students can apply it.

nodes.label: Some words have more than one meaningful part
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that some words are made of more than one meaningful part (e.g. 'dogs' = 'dog' + 's' meaning more than one).
criteria: Student can identify a word that has more than one meaningful part.
Student can explain what each part of the word means.
Student can give at least one more example of a word with multiple meaningful parts.

width.minimum: Identify one word made of two meaningful parts and explain what each part means (e.g. 'dogs' — the dog part means the animal, the 's' means more than one).
width.typical: Understand that words can be made of more than one meaningful part; identify simple examples of plurals ('s'), past tense markers and familiar compounds; explain what each part contributes.
wider: Sort words into 'one meaning part' and 'more than one meaning part' categories across a range of familiar words
Explore compound words (e.g. 'sunflower', 'raincoat') as another form of words with multiple meaningful parts
Investigate words with meaningful parts from other languages familiar to students — discussing how different languages build meaning through word parts

modes.reason: The morpheme concept requires a visible reasoning scaffold — students need to be shown the analysis (here is the word, here is where it breaks, here is what each part means) before they can apply it independently. This is the first introduction to morphemic thinking.

descriptors.title: Language, expressions and gestures
descriptors.description: understand how language, facial expressions and gestures are used to interact with others when asking for and providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore how language is used differently at home and school depending on relationships and contexts (AC9EFLA01). They have not yet understood the specific functions of language, facial expressions and gestures across distinct interaction types such as requesting, exclaiming, and commanding.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how language, facial expressions and gestures work together across different types of interaction — providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands.

nodes.label: Communication is multimodal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that communication involves more than words — gestures, facial expressions and body language all carry meaning.
criteria: Student names at least two non-verbal communication modes and gives an example of each
Student explains that gestures or facial expressions can change how a message is received
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who equate communication with speech only cannot engage with N4's analysis of how language, expression and gesture combine — the multimodal frame is definitionally required before the combination can be examined.

width.minimum: Identify at least two non-verbal communication modes (e.g. gesture, facial expression) and explain that they contribute meaning alongside words.
width.typical: Recognise and discuss how words, facial expressions, gestures and body language each contribute to meaning in everyday interactions, including in short film or picture book examples.
wider: Explore how symbols and body language function as primary communication modes in First Nations Australian communities, comparing with verbal-dominant communication
Investigate how meaning changes when body language and words send conflicting signals (e.g. saying 'fine' while frowning)

modes.reason: Students often conflate communication with speech only. Encountering diverse multimodal examples — film, picture books, First Nations contexts — helps build the understanding that non-verbal modes carry independent meaning, not just accompaniment.

nodes.label: Interaction types have distinct features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different types of interaction — providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting, giving commands — and recognise that each uses different language.
criteria: Student correctly names and gives an example of at least three different interaction types
Student identifies how the language used differs between at least two interaction types

width.minimum: Name and give an example of at least three interaction types (e.g. asking a question, giving a command, making an offer).
width.typical: Identify and discuss the full range of interaction types from the descriptor, recognising differences in language and tone across providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands.
wider: Compare how the same interaction type (e.g. requesting) sounds different in formal versus informal contexts
Identify interaction types in short film clips and discuss how character relationships affect language choices

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a working set of interaction type examples — the learning is in recognising the range, not in any single instance. More examples across varied contexts build the category.

nodes.label: Open and closed questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between open and closed questions and understand that question type shapes the kind of response expected.
criteria: Student correctly classifies a given question as open or closed
Student explains what kind of response an open question invites versus a closed question

width.minimum: Identify whether a given question is open or closed and explain what kind of answer each invites.
width.typical: Distinguish open questions (inviting extended response) from closed questions (yes/no or single answer), give examples of each, and discuss how question choice affects conversation.
wider: Explore how open questions are used in discussions to invite opinion versus closed questions used to check facts
Investigate how question type shifts in different interaction contexts — classroom discussion, playground, storytelling

modes.reason: Students frequently confuse open/closed question distinction in practice. Repeated sorting and labelling of examples builds the precision needed to reliably apply the distinction.

nodes.label: Language, expression and gesture work together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how language choices, facial expressions and gestures combine to shape how an interaction is received by others.
criteria: Student gives an example showing how body language and words together affect how a message is received
Student explains, for at least one interaction type, how changing the gesture or expression would change the meaning

width.minimum: Describe how a speaker's words and body language together affect how their message is received in at least one interaction type.
width.typical: Explain how the combination of language, facial expression and gesture shapes meaning across multiple interaction types, using examples from texts or familiar situations.
wider: Discuss how the same verbal request can be received differently depending on facial expression and tone — e.g. a polite request vs an impatient demand
Explore representations of interaction in literature by First Nations Australian authors, discussing how visual and verbal elements together create meaning

modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate their understanding of verbal and non-verbal modes together — it's not adding new content but assembling the components from nodes 1–3 into a unified explanation of how communication works.

descriptors.title: Language to justify preferences
descriptors.description: explore language to provide reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore different ways of using language to express preferences, likes and dislikes (AC9EFLA02). They have not yet used connective language such as 'because' to provide reasons, or comparative adjectives to express degrees of preference.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore language that provides reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences, including connective and comparative language.

nodes.label: Stating a preference
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express a like, dislike or preference using appropriate language (e.g. 'I like...', 'I prefer...', 'My favourite is...').
criteria: Student uses at least two different language forms to express a preference
Student applies preference language in a new context when prompted

width.minimum: Use at least two different language forms to express a preference or dislike.
width.typical: Express likes, dislikes and preferences using a range of language forms across different topic contexts — books, activities, foods, stories.
wider: Explore how preference language differs between informal speech and written opinion texts
Compare how characters in picture books or stories express preferences, identifying the language used

nodes.label: Giving reasons with 'because'
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use 'because' and similar connectives to link a preference to a reason.
criteria: Student produces a sentence using 'because' where the reason is specific to the stated preference
Student can identify the reason part of a given 'because' sentence
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who append comments rather than genuinely linking a reason with 'because' cannot produce the reasoned opinion required for AC9E1LY06 opinion writing — the connective structure is a prerequisite for coherent opinion text production.

width.minimum: Construct at least one sentence using 'because' to give a reason for a preference or dislike.
width.typical: Use 'because' and similar connectives to provide reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences across a range of topics, with reasons that are specific to the preference stated.
wider: Explore other reason-giving connectives (e.g. 'since', 'as') and compare how they feel in spoken versus written contexts
Examine how reasons in opinion texts are structured, linking to AC9E1LA03 text organisation

modes.reason: Using 'because' to genuinely link a reason (not just append a comment) requires repeated practice. Students frequently produce 'I like dogs because dogs are nice' — consolidation builds the habit of a substantive, specific reason.

nodes.label: Comparative language for degree
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use comparative adjectives to express the degree of a preference (e.g. 'better', 'faster', 'more exciting').
criteria: Student uses a comparative adjective correctly in a sentence expressing preference
Student identifies what two things are being compared in a given comparative sentence

width.minimum: Use at least one comparative adjective to express a preference and explain what it is comparing.
width.typical: Use comparative adjectives (including irregular forms like 'better') to express degrees of preference, naming what is being compared.
wider: Explore superlatives ('best', 'fastest') as an extension of comparative degree language
Investigate how comparative adjectives are used in advertising and persuasive texts to express preference or recommendation

modes.reason: Students often use comparatives without a clear referent ('it's better' — better than what?). Encountering comparatives across varied contexts — speech, picture books, advertising — helps establish that comparison requires two things to compare.

descriptors.title: Texts organised by purpose
descriptors.description: explore how texts are organised according to their purpose, such as to recount, narrate, express opinion, inform, report and explain
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand that texts can take many forms and be used for different purposes (AC9EFLA03). They have not yet explored how organisation (stages and structure) differs systematically across text types such as recount, narrative, and information text.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how texts are organised differently according to purpose, identifying the typical stages of familiar text types including recount, narrative, opinion, information, report and explanation.

nodes.label: Texts have a purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a familiar text (e.g. to tell a story, to give information, to give instructions).
criteria: Student correctly identifies the purpose of a given text
Student gives a reason for their identification (e.g. 'it tells me how to do something, so it's a procedure')

width.minimum: Identify the purpose of at least two different texts from familiar text types.
width.typical: Identify and discuss the purpose of a range of familiar text types — story, information text, recount, procedure — and explain how they know.
wider: Compare digital and print versions of texts with the same purpose and discuss whether the purpose is served differently
Explore how some texts serve more than one purpose (e.g. a picture book can entertain and inform)

nodes.label: Text stages differ by type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the typical stages of at least two text types and explain how those stages serve the text's purpose.
criteria: Student identifies the stages of a given text and names at least the opening and purpose-serving stages
Student explains what a specific stage does for the reader (e.g. 'the orientation tells you who and when')
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who apply the beginning-middle-end narrative schema to all texts cannot distinguish the stages of recounts, procedures or informative texts — this misconception, if uncorrected, flows into N3's multimodal organisation work and into AC9E1LY06 writing-for-purpose.

width.minimum: Identify the opening, middle and end of two different text types and describe what each stage does.
width.typical: Describe the typical stages of familiar text types — recount (orientation, events, reorientation), narrative (orientation, complication, resolution), procedure (goal, steps) — and explain how stages serve the purpose.
wider: Compare the stages of a recount and a narrative to identify where they overlap and where they differ
Examine informative texts to identify stages (introduction, information sections, conclusion/summary)

modes.reason: Students readily grasp that stories have a beginning, middle and end but often apply this schema to all texts. Encountering multiple distinct text types with different stage names helps resolve the misconception that all text structure is narrative structure.

nodes.label: Words and images both organise texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that text organisation includes both words and visual/graphical elements, and that these work together to serve the text's purpose.
criteria: Student identifies a visual element in an informative text and describes what information it provides
Student explains how the image and the words work together in that text

width.minimum: Identify at least one visual or graphical element in an informative text and explain what it contributes to the text's organisation.
width.typical: Recognise that informative and other texts use images, diagrams, headings and captions alongside words to organise information, and discuss how these visual elements serve the text's purpose.
wider: Compare how a purely verbal text and a multimodal text with diagrams serve the same informative purpose differently
Explore how picture books use image sequences as a structural element — images tell part of the story that words don't

modes.reason: Students frequently focus on verbal structure only. Examining informative texts where diagrams carry organisational load — where understanding depends on reading image and text together — resolves the misconception that structure is only verbal.

descriptors.title: Repetition, rhyme and rhythm
descriptors.description: explore how repetition, rhyme and rhythm create cohesion in simple poems, chants and songs
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand conventions of print and screen including how books and simple digital texts are organised (AC9EFLA04) and have explored rhythms and sound patterns in literary texts at Foundation level (AC9EFLE04). They have not yet explored how repetition, rhyme and rhythm function specifically as cohesion-creating devices within the text as a whole.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how repetition, rhyme and rhythm create cohesion in simple poems, chants and songs.

nodes.label: Recognising rhyme and repetition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify rhyming words and repeated patterns in poems, chants and songs.
criteria: Student identifies at least one rhyming pair in a given text
Student identifies a repeated phrase or sentence pattern in a poem or chant

width.minimum: Identify rhyming word pairs and a repeated sentence pattern in a given poem or chant.
width.typical: Identify rhyming words (including end-of-line rhyme), alliterative patterns, and repeated sentence or phrase structures across a range of simple poems, chants and songs.
wider: Identify different types of rhyme (end rhyme, internal rhyme) across a variety of poems
Collect and compare examples of repetition patterns across poems from different cultures or traditions

nodes.label: Repetition and rhyme hold the text together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how repetition and rhyme create a sense of pattern and predictability that holds a poem, chant or song together.
criteria: Student explains, with reference to a specific example, how a repeated pattern helps the text feel connected
Student identifies at least one way repetition or rhyme signals to the reader or listener what comes next

width.minimum: Explain how a repeated pattern in a given poem or chant helps the reader or listener know what comes next.
width.typical: Discuss how repetition and rhyme create cohesion — a sense of wholeness and connection — in poems, chants and songs, using specific examples from familiar texts.
wider: Compare two versions of a poem — one with repetition removed — and discuss how cohesion changes
Explore how chants and songs use repetition functionally to aid memory and communal participation

modes.reason: The concept of cohesion is abstract for Year 1 students. Multiple text examples — poems, chants, songs — where students can feel the 'pull' of repetition and rhyme help make the abstract idea concrete and transferable.

nodes.label: Rhythm creates pattern in sound
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify rhythm in a poem or chant and describe how it contributes to the text's pattern and flow.
criteria: Student can mark or demonstrate the beat pattern of a given poem or chant
Student describes how rhythm combines with rhyme or repetition to give the text its pattern

width.minimum: Clap or mark the beat of a familiar poem or chant and describe the rhythmic pattern.
width.typical: Identify rhythm in poems, chants and songs by marking beats, describe the rhythmic pattern, and discuss how rhythm contributes to the text's flow and cohesion alongside rhyme and repetition.
wider: Compare fast and slow rhythms across poems and discuss how rhythm affects mood
Explore rhythm in First Nations Australian songs or chants and discuss how rhythm serves cultural and communal purposes

modes.reason: Rhythm, rhyme and repetition are three distinct devices that work together — this node requires students to see how rhythm joins the other devices to create overall cohesion, not just identify another isolated feature.

descriptors.title: Print and screen text features
descriptors.description: understand how print and screen texts are organised using features such as page numbers, tables of content, headings and titles, navigation buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands, links and images
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand conventions of print and screen including how books and simple digital texts are organised at Foundation level. They have not yet systematically compared the full range of navigational and organisational features specific to print versus screen texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how print and screen texts are organised using navigational and structural features including page numbers, tables of contents, headings, titles, navigation buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands, links and images.

nodes.label: Print texts use structural features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify structural features of print texts — page numbers, headings, titles, table of contents — and explain what each one does.
criteria: Student identifies at least two print structural features by name
Student explains what purpose each identified feature serves for the reader

width.minimum: Identify at least two structural features in a print information text and explain the purpose of each.
width.typical: Identify and explain the purpose of page numbers, headings, titles and tables of contents in print information texts, and use these features to locate information.
wider: Compare structural features across different print text types — information book, magazine, dictionary — and discuss how features vary by purpose
Use a table of contents to locate specific information and evaluate its usefulness

nodes.label: Screen texts use navigation features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify navigation features of screen texts — navigation buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands, links — and explain how they are used to move through the text.
criteria: Student identifies at least two screen navigation features and names them correctly
Student explains how to use a specific navigation feature to move through a screen text

width.minimum: Identify at least two navigation features of a screen text and explain how each is used.
width.typical: Identify and explain navigation buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands and links in screen texts, discussing how each allows the reader to move through or interact with the text.
wider: Explore how navigation features differ across different screen text types — informative website, e-book, educational app
Discuss how verbal commands and gesture-based navigation (swiping) represent different modes of interaction with a text

modes.reason: Students encounter many different screen interfaces but may not have a conceptual vocabulary for navigation features. Multiple screen text examples build the generalisation that navigation features serve the same orientation purpose across different interfaces.

nodes.label: Print and screen texts compared
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how print and screen texts use different features to serve the same organisational purposes, and identify features unique to each.
criteria: Student identifies one feature that print texts have but screen texts do not (or vice versa)
Student explains how a print feature and a screen feature serve the same purpose in different ways

width.minimum: Compare at least one print feature and its screen equivalent, explaining how they serve the same purpose differently.
width.typical: Compare the layout and features of a print information text with a screen text on the same or similar topic, identifying shared purposes (navigation, heading, image) served by different features.
wider: Discuss which features a reader might find easier to use in print versus screen for locating specific information
Explore how images serve structural roles differently in print (fixed position) versus screen texts (interactive, linked)

modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of print and screen features — students coordinate their knowledge of both to make a comparison, which is the descriptor's core demand ('comparing the layout of print and digital texts').

descriptors.title: Simple sentences
descriptors.description: understand that a simple sentence consists of a single independent clause representing a single event or idea
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise that sentences are key units for expressing ideas (AC9EFLA05). They have not yet understood the internal structure of a simple sentence — that it consists of a single independent clause with a process (verb), participants (noun groups) and optional circumstances (adverbs).
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that a simple sentence is a single independent clause representing one event or idea, containing a process, participants and optional circumstances.

nodes.label: A sentence expresses one event or idea
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that a sentence expresses one complete event or idea and recognise when a sentence is complete.
criteria: Student correctly identifies at least three complete sentences in a mixed set
Student explains why a given fragment is not a complete sentence
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably identify a complete sentence cannot identify the participant and process structure in N2 — the completeness concept is definitionally prior to analysis of what a complete sentence contains.

width.minimum: Identify whether a given group of words is a complete sentence (expresses a complete event or idea) or is incomplete.
width.typical: Identify complete sentences and explain what makes them complete — they express a whole event or idea. Distinguish complete sentences from fragments and from sequences of multiple events.
wider: Sort a set of word groups into complete sentences and fragments, explaining the decision for each
Find examples of single-event sentences in a familiar picture book and discuss what each one expresses

modes.reason: Recognising a complete sentence requires repeated exposure to both examples and non-examples. Students need practice judging completeness across varied sentence types before moving to internal structure.

nodes.label: Sentences have participants and processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the participant (who or what) and the process (what is happening) in a simple sentence.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the participant and process in at least three simple sentences
Student explains what the participant and process each contribute to the meaning

width.minimum: In a given simple sentence, identify who or what is involved and what is happening.
width.typical: Identify the participant (noun group) and process (verb) in simple sentences, and explain what each contributes to the sentence's meaning — who/what is doing or being something, and what that doing or being is.
wider: Explore sentences with more than one participant (e.g. 'The cat chased the mouse') and identify both participants and the process
Investigate how changing the participant or process changes the meaning of a sentence

modes.reason: Students often focus on identifying the 'doing word' without grasping that participant and process work together as a minimum sentence unit. Varied sentence examples — different participant types, different verb types — help establish the interdependence of these elements.

nodes.label: Circumstances add detail
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify circumstantial detail (when, where, how) in simple sentences and explain that these details are optional additions to the core event.
criteria: Student identifies a circumstantial detail in a sentence and names what it answers (when/where/how)
Student confirms the sentence's core event is still expressed without the circumstance

width.minimum: In a given sentence, identify one circumstantial detail (where, when or how) and confirm the sentence would still make sense without it.
width.typical: Identify circumstantial details (adverb groups/phrases answering when, where, how) in simple sentences, and understand that these extend the sentence without creating a new independent clause.
wider: Construct simple sentences that express the same core event with and without circumstances, discussing how meaning changes
Sort circumstantial details by type (when/where/how) across a range of simple sentences

nodes.label: The clause as a unit
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that a simple sentence is a single independent clause — one complete event or idea expressed with a participant, process and optional circumstances.
criteria: Student explains, in their own words, what makes a sentence a 'simple sentence'
Student correctly identifies participant, process and any circumstances in a new example sentence

width.minimum: Explain that a simple sentence contains one clause representing one event, with a who/what, a doing/being, and optional details.
width.typical: Explain the structure of a simple sentence as a single independent clause, identifying its key elements (participant, process, optional circumstances) and understanding that adding circumstances does not create a new clause.
wider: Identify simple sentences and multi-clause sentences in a short text and discuss the difference
Examine how authors use simple sentences for effect — pace, clarity, emphasis — in narrative and informative texts

modes.reason: This final node integrates participant, process and circumstance into the unified concept of the independent clause — the core schema students need before Year 2 work on compound sentences.

descriptors.title: Word classes
descriptors.description: understand that words can represent people, places and things (nouns, including pronouns), happenings and states (verbs), qualities (adjectives) and details such as when, where and how (adverbs)
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise that sentences are made up of groups of words that work together in particular ways (AC9EFLA06). They have not yet understood the distinct semantic roles that different word classes play — nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs as categories with specific functions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand the major word classes — nouns (including pronouns), verbs, adjectives and adverbs — and the semantic roles each plays in a sentence.

nodes.label: Nouns name people, places and things
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify nouns in sentences and explain that they name people, places or things.
criteria: Student identifies at least three nouns in a sentence and gives the category each belongs to (person/place/thing)
Student recognises a pronoun as a noun substitute

width.minimum: Identify at least three nouns in a given sentence or short text and confirm each names a person, place or thing.
width.typical: Identify nouns across a range of sentence contexts, including common nouns, proper nouns and pronouns, and explain the semantic role of nouns as participants in a sentence.
wider: Explore abstract nouns (e.g. happiness, time) and discuss how they extend the category beyond concrete people, places and things
Investigate how pronouns replace nouns and discuss why this matters for cohesion in a text

nodes.label: Verbs represent happenings and states
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify verbs in sentences and explain that they represent what is happening or a state of being.
criteria: Student identifies the verb in sentences containing both action and state verbs
Student distinguishes between a happening verb and a state verb in given examples
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only recognise action verbs will miss state verbs in sentences, producing systematic misidentification of the process element — this error propagates into N5's integration work and into the participant/process identification required for AC9E1LA06.

width.minimum: Identify the verb in at least three given sentences and explain whether it represents a happening (doing) or a state (being).
width.typical: Identify verbs across a range of sentence contexts — action verbs (doing, saying) and state verbs (being, thinking, feeling) — and explain their role as the process element of the sentence.
wider: Sort a set of verbs into action/doing verbs and state/being verbs, and discuss whether the boundary is always clear
Investigate how changing the verb changes what a sentence expresses, even when participants stay the same

modes.reason: Students readily identify 'doing words' (action verbs) but often miss state verbs like 'is', 'feels', 'knows'. Encountering sentences where the verb is a state rather than an action — and where the 'doing word' frame fails — is the key to broadening the category.

nodes.label: Adjectives describe qualities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify adjectives and explain that they describe the qualities of nouns.
criteria: Student identifies at least two adjectives and links each to the noun it modifies
Student explains what quality the adjective adds to the noun

width.minimum: Identify at least two adjectives in a given sentence and explain what quality each adds to the noun it describes.
width.typical: Identify adjectives in sentences, explain how they add quality information to nouns, and use adjectives to make sentences more specific.
wider: Compare sentences with and without adjectives and discuss how precision and vividness change
Explore how adjectives are used differently in informative texts (precise, factual) versus narrative texts (evocative, sensory)

nodes.label: Adverbs add circumstantial detail
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify adverbs and explain that they add circumstantial detail answering when, where or how.
criteria: Student identifies an adverb in a sentence and states what question it answers
Student correctly distinguishes an adverb from an adjective in a given example
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who confuse adverbs with adjectives cannot reliably identify the circumstantial elements in N5's integration task — the adverb/adjective distinction is prerequisite for the full word-class analysis that N5 requires.

width.minimum: Identify an adverb in a given sentence and state whether it answers when, where or how.
width.typical: Identify adverbs across a range of sentence contexts, distinguish the circumstantial question each answers (when/where/how), and understand adverbs as optional details that extend but do not change the core clause.
wider: Explore adverb placement (beginning, middle, end of sentence) and discuss how position affects emphasis
Distinguish adverbs modifying verbs from adjectives modifying nouns in context

modes.reason: Adverbs are the most easily confused word class at Year 1 — students frequently label any descriptive word as an adjective. Sorting practice (does this describe the noun or the action?) builds the discrimination needed.

nodes.label: Word classes work together in sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify all four word classes in a sentence and explain the role each plays in building meaning.
criteria: Student correctly identifies noun, verb and at least one of adjective/adverb in a sentence
Student explains the role each identified word plays in the sentence's meaning

width.minimum: In a given sentence, identify at least one noun, one verb and one adjective or adverb, and explain the role of each.
width.typical: Identify nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs in sentences and explain how each word class contributes to the meaning — who/what, process, quality, and circumstance.
wider: Analyse how an author's word class choices shape the meaning and effect of a sentence in a literary text
Construct sentences that include all four word classes and discuss how each element contributes

modes.reason: This node requires coordinating all four word classes as a functional system — not just labelling each in isolation but understanding how they fit together in a sentence to build complete meaning.

descriptors.title: Images contribute to meaning
descriptors.description: compare how images in different types of texts contribute to meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore the contribution of images and words to meaning in stories and informative texts (AC9EFLA07). They have not yet compared how images function differently across different text types, or how image sequences build meaning, or how images can carry meaning not present in the verbal text.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare how images in different types of texts contribute to meaning, including how image sequences build meaning, how images carry meaning independent of words, and how First Nations Australian authors use images.

nodes.label: Images carry meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe what meaning an image contributes to a text, independent of the words.
criteria: Student describes at least one piece of meaning that an image carries independently of the words
Student identifies whether the image repeats, extends or contrasts the meaning of the accompanying words
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat images as mere word-repetition cannot engage with N2's analysis of image sequences or N3's comparison of image types — both depend on students already accepting that images carry independent meaning.

width.minimum: Cover the words in a given illustrated text and describe what the image alone communicates.
width.typical: Identify and describe the meaning carried by images in texts — what information, emotion or story detail the image communicates — and discuss how this meaning relates to the accompanying words.
wider: Examine texts where the image and words tell different things — discuss what each contributes and why the author might have made that choice
Compare a cartoon image, a photograph and a diagram of the same subject and discuss how each conveys meaning differently

modes.reason: Students often treat images as illustrations that simply repeat what words say. Encountering examples where images carry distinct or additional meaning — diagrams that explain what words only describe, images that show emotion not stated — resolves this misconception.

nodes.label: Image sequences build meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a sequence of images builds meaning across a text, not just within a single image.
criteria: Student explains how two consecutive images connect to show change or progression
Student identifies what a reader learns from an image sequence that a single image could not convey

width.minimum: Describe how two consecutive images in a picture book connect to build a sense of progression or change.
width.typical: Explain how authors and illustrators build meaning across a sequence of images — how each image relates to what came before and sets up what comes next, contributing to narrative progression or informational structure.
wider: Investigate wordless picture books where the entire narrative is carried by image sequences
Compare how image sequences function in narrative texts versus informative texts

nodes.label: Images differ by text type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how images function differently in different text types — narrative, informative, advertising — and explain how each type of image serves the text's purpose.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the text type of two different texts and describes how the image in each serves that text's purpose
Student gives at least one way that images in an informative text and a narrative text function differently

width.minimum: Compare images from two different text types (e.g. a story illustration and a diagram) and explain how each serves its text's purpose differently.
width.typical: Compare images across narrative texts (illustrations, character images), informative texts (diagrams, photographs, captions) and other text types (advertisements), explaining how each type of image serves the text's purpose.
wider: Explore how digital images (animations, interactive images) in screen texts function differently from static print images
Examine images in stories and cultural accounts by First Nations Australian authors, discussing how visual choices reflect cultural perspectives and meaning-making

modes.reason: Comparing across text types is the core demand of the descriptor. Students who have only examined narrative illustration will transfer a narrow schema. Informative diagrams and advertisement images are qualitatively different and require distinct encounters.

descriptors.title: Learning area vocabulary
descriptors.description: recognise the vocabulary of learning area topics
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and develop awareness of vocabulary used in familiar contexts related to personal experiences (AC9EFLA08). They have not yet systematically recognised topic-specific vocabulary tied to learning area disciplines, or understood the cultural and contextual dimension of vocabulary such as Acknowledgement of Country.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise vocabulary associated with learning area topics, including topic-specific terms used in classroom discussions and protocols such as Acknowledgement of Country.

nodes.label: Topics have their own words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that different learning areas use their own topic-specific vocabulary and can name examples from a familiar topic.
criteria: Student names at least three topic-specific words from a current learning area topic
Student explains that these words are associated with that particular topic or subject

width.minimum: Name at least three topic-specific words from a learning area topic currently studied and explain that these words belong to that topic.
width.typical: Identify topic-specific vocabulary from at least two different learning area topics, explain that each discipline has words that belong to it, and use those words when discussing the topic.
wider: Compare vocabulary from two different learning area topics and discuss what makes words 'belong' to a particular field
Investigate how some words are used in everyday language and in a technical sense in a learning area (e.g. 'force' in science versus everyday use)

nodes.label: Using topic vocabulary in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use appropriate topic-specific vocabulary when discussing a learning area topic.
criteria: Student uses at least two topic-specific words correctly in discussion or writing about a learning area topic
Student demonstrates understanding of a term by using it in a meaningful sentence

width.minimum: Use at least two topic-specific words correctly in a discussion or explanation of a learning area topic.
width.typical: Use appropriate topic-specific vocabulary when discussing or writing about learning area topics, selecting words that accurately name the concepts or phenomena being described.
wider: Compare how the same topic is discussed using everyday words versus topic-specific vocabulary, and discuss why precision matters
Explore topic vocabulary across multiple learning areas studied this year and build a personal vocabulary collection

modes.reason: Recognising topic vocabulary and reliably using it in the right context are distinct competencies. Students need repeated practice using terms in discussion before they become reliably part of active vocabulary.

nodes.label: Cultural and community vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use appropriate vocabulary in cultural and community protocols, including Acknowledgement of Country, and understand these as a specific vocabulary context.
criteria: Student uses appropriate vocabulary for an Acknowledgement of Country in a school context
Student explains, in their own words, what 'Traditional Owners' means in this context

width.minimum: Use appropriate vocabulary for an Acknowledgement of Country in a relevant school context and explain the purpose of this protocol.
width.typical: Use appropriate vocabulary for an Acknowledgement of Country and other school community protocols, understanding these as a culturally significant vocabulary context where word choice reflects respect and recognition of Traditional Owners.
