wider: Explore the meaning of key terms used in Acknowledgement of Country (e.g. Traditional Owners, Country, Place) and why precise language matters in this context
Investigate how Acknowledgement of Country varies in different school and community settings and discuss why

modes.reason: Acknowledgement of Country vocabulary is culturally situated and carries specific meaning that differs from general topic vocabulary. Students need to understand this as a distinct vocabulary register, not just a list of words to memorise.

descriptors.title: Sentence boundary punctuation
descriptors.description: understand that written language uses punctuation such as full stops, question marks and exclamation marks, and uses capital letters for familiar proper nouns
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify punctuation as a feature of written text different from letters, and recognise capital letters at sentence beginnings (AC9EFLA09). They have not yet understood the specific signalling functions of sentence-ending punctuation marks or the use of capital letters for proper nouns.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand sentence boundary punctuation — full stops, question marks, exclamation marks — and use capital letters for familiar proper nouns.

nodes.label: Punctuation marks signal sentence endings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify full stops, question marks and exclamation marks as sentence-ending punctuation and explain that each signals a different type of sentence.
criteria: Student identifies and names all three sentence-ending punctuation marks correctly
Student matches each punctuation mark to its sentence type

width.minimum: Identify all three sentence-ending punctuation marks by name and match each to its sentence type (statement, question, exclamation).
width.typical: Identify full stops, question marks and exclamation marks in written texts, name each correctly, explain which sentence type each signals, and respond to them when reading aloud (pausing, intonation change).
wider: Explore how the same words with different end punctuation create different sentences — e.g. 'You did it.' vs 'You did it?' vs 'You did it!'
Examine how writers use exclamation marks for effect and discuss whether overuse reduces their impact

nodes.label: Punctuation guides reading aloud
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use intonation and pauses in response to sentence-ending punctuation when reading.
criteria: Student pauses at full stops and end-of-sentence marks when reading aloud
Student adjusts intonation at question marks (rising) and exclamation marks (emphasis)

width.minimum: Read a short passage aloud, pausing at full stops and adjusting intonation at question marks and exclamation marks.
width.typical: Consistently use appropriate intonation and pausing in response to sentence boundary punctuation when reading aloud — full stops signal pause and drop, question marks signal rising intonation, exclamation marks signal emphasis.
wider: Listen to recordings of the same text read with and without attention to punctuation, and discuss the difference in meaning and expression
Practise reading dialogue that includes multiple punctuation types, attending to how each mark shapes the character's voice

modes.reason: Translating punctuation knowledge into consistent oral reading requires repeated rehearsal. Students may know the rule but not yet apply it automatically — oral reading practice across varied texts builds the habit.

nodes.label: Capital letters for proper nouns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify familiar proper nouns and explain that they require capital letters.
criteria: Student correctly identifies at least two proper nouns in a text and explains why each is capitalised
Student writes familiar proper nouns with correct capitalisation in their own writing
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who limit capitalisation to personal names will systematically miscapitalise place names, days and months in writing — this pattern, once established, persists into N4's application task and beyond into independent writing.

width.minimum: Identify at least two familiar proper nouns in a text and explain why they use capital letters.
width.typical: Identify proper nouns — names of people, places, days, months, holidays — in texts and writing, apply capital letters to familiar proper nouns, and explain that proper nouns are specific names that always take capitals.
wider: Distinguish between common nouns and proper nouns in context (e.g. 'city' vs 'Sydney'), and write sentences using both
Explore why days and months are capitalised — link to the concept of proper names

modes.reason: Students typically know names of people take capitals but often miss place names, days of the week, months and holidays. Encountering a range of proper noun categories resolves the misconception that only personal names require capitalisation.

nodes.label: Writing with sentence punctuation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply sentence boundary punctuation and proper noun capitalisation in their own writing.
criteria: Student correctly punctuates at least two different sentence types in their own writing
Student capitalises proper nouns correctly in at least two examples in their writing

width.minimum: Write at least two different sentence types (statement and question) using correct end punctuation, and capitalise at least one proper noun.
width.typical: Write statements, questions and exclamations using correct end punctuation, capitalise proper nouns and sentence-opening capitals, and identify and correct punctuation errors in given sentences.
wider: Write a short dialogue using multiple sentence types with correct punctuation throughout
Edit a deliberately un-punctuated passage, adding sentence boundary punctuation and proper noun capitalisation

modes.reason: Applying punctuation consistently in writing requires sustained practice beyond recognition tasks. Writing and editing tasks build the automatic application that transfers into independent writing.

descriptors.title: Language and images create meaning in literature
descriptors.description: discuss how language and images are used to create characters, settings and events in literature by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share ideas about stories, poems and images in literature, reflecting on experiences (AC9EFLE01). They have not yet discussed specifically how language choices and image choices work to construct characters, settings and events, or engaged with the diversity of literature from First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss how language and images are used to create characters, settings and events in literature from First Nations Australian, wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators.

nodes.label: Characters are constructed through language and image
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how an author or illustrator uses specific words or images to create a character — what they look like, how they feel, what kind of person or creature they are.
criteria: Student identifies at least two specific language or image choices and links each to what it tells the reader about the character
Student uses the language of author/illustrator craft (e.g. 'the author chose... to show that...')

width.minimum: Identify at least two language or image choices in a text and explain what each tells the reader about a character.
width.typical: Discuss how authors use word choices (describing words, dialogue, actions) and illustrators use image choices (appearance, expression, colour) to create characters, using specific examples from familiar texts.
wider: Compare how the same type of character (e.g. an animal with human qualities) is created differently across two texts from different authors or cultures
Discuss how characters in literature by First Nations Australian authors and illustrators are depicted, exploring what the choices tell us about the character and their world

modes.reason: Students need to encounter diverse author and illustrator choices — not just one familiar style — to understand that character construction is a crafted decision, not a natural consequence. Texts from different cultural contexts make this especially visible.

nodes.label: Settings are created through detail
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how authors and illustrators use language and images to create settings — where and when stories take place.
criteria: Student describes the setting of a text and identifies at least one language or image choice that creates it
Student states whether the setting seems realistic or imagined and gives a reason

width.minimum: Identify at least one language or image choice that creates a sense of place or time in a text, and describe the setting it creates.
width.typical: Discuss how authors use descriptive language and illustrators use visual details (colour, scale, perspective) to create settings, including whether settings feel real or imagined.
wider: Compare settings in texts from Australian and world authors — discuss how setting reflects the author's cultural context
Discuss whether a setting feels realistic or imagined and what specific choices create that effect

nodes.label: Events unfold through language and image choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how authors and illustrators use language and images to depict events — what happens, how it happens, and why it matters.
criteria: Student describes an event and explains how both words and images contribute to the reader's understanding of it
Student identifies at least one specific choice (language or image) that shapes how the event feels to the reader

width.minimum: Identify how at least one event in a text is conveyed through both words and images, and describe what each contributes.
width.typical: Discuss how events are depicted through language (action verbs, dialogue, description) and images (sequence, expression, movement), including how the two modes work together to create the full event.
wider: Explore how events in texts by First Nations Australian authors may be depicted in ways that differ from familiar narrative conventions
Examine how the same event depicted with different language or image choices would create a different reader experience

modes.reason: Events require students to coordinate understanding of character and setting — events happen to characters in settings. This node integrates the prior two nodes into a full discussion of how literature uses all its resources together.

descriptors.title: Connect literature to personal experience
descriptors.description: discuss literary texts and share responses by making connections with students' own experiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can respond to stories and share feelings and thoughts about events and characters (AC9EFLE02). They have not yet systematically connected literary texts to their own experiences as an interpretive strategy, or asked questions about texts to deepen response.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss literary texts and share responses by making connections with their own experiences, using drawing, role-play and discussion.

nodes.label: Responding to characters and events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share a personal response to a character or event in a literary text — expressing what they think, feel or wonder.
criteria: Student shares a response that goes beyond plot retelling to express a personal reaction
Student uses language that signals thinking or feeling ('I think', 'I felt', 'I wonder')

width.minimum: Share at least one response to a character or event in a text, using language that expresses thinking or feeling (e.g. 'I think...', 'I wonder...', 'I felt...').
width.typical: Share responses to characters, events and situations in texts using language of thinking and feeling, across multiple texts and in varied modes (discussion, drawing, role-play).
wider: Explore how different readers can have different responses to the same character or event — discuss why this might be
Examine responses to characters that are morally complex or whose actions are hard to understand

nodes.label: Connecting text to personal experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make an explicit connection between something in a literary text and their own experience, and explain how the connection helps them understand the text.
criteria: Student states an explicit connection between something in the text and their own experience
Student explains how the connection helps them understand the character, event or feeling

width.minimum: Identify at least one connection between a text and personal experience and explain what it helps them understand.
width.typical: Make text-to-self connections across a range of literary texts, explaining how personal experience helps them understand characters, events or feelings depicted in the text.
wider: Discuss what happens when a text depicts an experience the reader has not had — how do they make sense of it?
Compare personal connections made by different readers in a class discussion — explore why different things connect for different people

modes.reason: Making text-to-self connections is a transferable strategy that students build through repeated practice across varied texts. The more varied the texts and experiences engaged with, the more robust the strategy becomes.

nodes.label: Questioning and narrating story
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate questions about characters, settings and events, and identify who is telling the story in a text.
criteria: Student generates at least one question about the text that is not answered directly on the page
Student identifies who is telling the story and gives a reason for their identification
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify who is telling the story cannot engage with perspective, point of view or narrator reliability in Year 2 and beyond — the concept of narrator is a definitional prerequisite for downstream literary response work.

width.minimum: Ask at least one question about a character, setting or event in a text; identify who is telling the story.
width.typical: Generate questions about characters, settings and events that probe beyond the literal; identify who tells the story (first person narrator, third person narrator) and discuss how this shapes the reader's experience.
wider: Compare a story told from a character's own perspective with one told by an outside narrator — discuss how the storyteller's identity shapes what we know
Explore how identifying the narrator changes the questions a reader might ask

modes.reason: Identifying the narrator requires a deliberate reasoning move — 'who is speaking?' is not always obvious to Year 1 students. A simple scaffold (Is the narrator in the story or outside it? How do we know?) helps students make this judgment reliably.

descriptors.title: Plot, character and setting
descriptors.description: discuss plot, character and setting, which are features of stories
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise different types of literary texts and identify features including events and characters (AC9EFLE03). They have not yet discussed plot, character and setting as the three core structural features of stories, or explored how these features operate across different story types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss plot, character and setting as features of stories, recognising these across different story types including traditional tales and narratives.

nodes.label: Stories have characters
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify characters in stories and describe what kind of character they are — their qualities, roles and relationships.
criteria: Student identifies the main character and describes at least two of their qualities
Student uses evidence from the text to support their description

width.minimum: Identify the main character(s) in a story and describe at least two qualities or characteristics of one.
width.typical: Identify and describe characters across a range of story types, discussing character qualities, roles (protagonist, antagonist, helper), and how characters are similar or different across texts.
wider: Compare how the same character type (e.g. a trickster, a helper) appears in stories from different traditions
Discuss how animal characters in fables reflect human characteristics — what human qualities the author has given the animal and why

nodes.label: Stories have a setting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the setting of a story — where and when it takes place — and discuss whether it is realistic or imagined.
criteria: Student describes the setting with reference to both place and time
Student states whether the setting is realistic or imagined and gives a reason

width.minimum: Describe the setting of a given story (where and when) and state whether it seems realistic or imagined.
width.typical: Identify and describe settings across a range of texts, discussing time and place, whether settings are realistic or imagined, and how setting shapes the story's feel or events.
wider: Compare settings from stories set in the past, present and imagined worlds — discuss how setting shapes what is possible in the story
Explore how settings in Australian stories reflect Australian landscape and culture

nodes.label: Stories have a plot
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the plot of a story — the sequence of events including a problem and how it is resolved.
criteria: Student retells main plot events in order
Student identifies the problem and resolution in the story
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify the problem and resolution in a plot cannot engage with N4's analysis of how plot, character and setting interact — that integration depends on students having a functional concept of plot as a problem-resolution sequence.

width.minimum: Retell the main events of a story in order, identifying the problem and how it is resolved.
width.typical: Describe the plot of a story including the key events, the problem or challenge faced by characters, and the resolution, across a range of story types.
wider: Compare plots across two texts of the same story type (e.g. two traditional tales) and identify similarities in plot structure
Discuss what would happen to the plot if the setting or character were changed

modes.reason: Identifying 'the problem' in a story requires a reasoning move beyond sequencing — students need to judge which events constitute the complication versus background events. A scaffold ('What did the character want? What stopped them? How did it get fixed?') supports this.

nodes.label: Plot, character and setting work together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how plot, character and setting work together as features of a story — how each influences the others.
criteria: Student explains how at least one of plot, character or setting influences another element in a story
Student discusses all three features in relation to a given text

width.minimum: Explain how the setting or a character quality influences an event in the plot of a given story.
width.typical: Discuss how plot, character and setting interact in a story — how the setting shapes what events are possible, how character qualities drive plot events, and how these three elements together create the story.
wider: Identify similar characters and settings in different story types (traditional tales, narrative poems, fables) and discuss how the three features function across these forms
Explore how changing one element — e.g. moving a traditional tale to a different setting — would affect the other elements

modes.reason: Understanding plot, character and setting as a system — not three separate checklists — is the endpoint of this descriptor. Students need to see how these features depend on each other to form a coherent story.

descriptors.title: Sound patterns in poetry
descriptors.description: listen to and discuss poems, chants, rhymes and songs, and imitate and invent sound patterns including alliteration and rhyme
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore and replicate the rhythms and sound patterns of literary texts such as poems and chants at Foundation level (AC9EFLE04). They have not yet specifically identified and invented alliteration, or systematically imitated and created their own sound patterns.
descriptors.endpoint: Students listen to and discuss poems, chants, rhymes and songs, and imitate and invent sound patterns including alliteration and rhyme.

nodes.label: Recognising sound patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify alliteration and rhyme in poems, chants and songs and describe the sound pattern they create.
criteria: Student correctly identifies alliteration in a given example and describes the repeated sound
Student identifies a rhyming pair and explains why they rhyme (same ending sound)

width.minimum: Identify alliteration and at least one rhyme pattern in given examples and describe what they sound like.
width.typical: Identify alliteration (repeated initial sounds) and rhyme (matching end sounds) across a range of poems, chants and songs, and describe the sound patterns they create.
wider: Identify other sound devices such as assonance (repeated vowel sounds) in poems read aloud
Compare how alliteration and rhyme create different sound effects — one at the start of words, one at the end

nodes.label: Discussing the effect of sound patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how sound patterns such as alliteration and rhyme create effects in poems, chants and songs — how they sound and feel.
criteria: Student describes the sound effect created by a specific sound pattern in a poem
Student uses language that describes the aesthetic quality of the pattern (not just labels it)

width.minimum: Describe how alliteration or rhyme makes a poem or chant sound and explain the effect it creates for the listener.
width.typical: Discuss how alliteration and rhyme shape the sound, rhythm and feel of poems, chants and songs, using language that describes aesthetic response (e.g. 'it sounds bouncy', 'it feels soft and slow').
wider: Compare poems with heavy alliteration versus heavy rhyme and discuss the different sound effects each creates
Discuss how sound patterns in poems serve purposes beyond aesthetics — memory, participation, cultural transmission

modes.reason: Students need to hear sound patterns across varied tonal contexts — playful, serious, ceremonial — to understand that alliteration and rhyme create different effects depending on how and where they are used. Multiple text encounters build this differentiated understanding.

nodes.label: Imitating sound patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can imitate a sound pattern from a poem or chant by creating their own example using the same pattern.
criteria: Student produces an imitation that correctly follows the alliterative or rhyme pattern of the model
Student's substituted words make sense in context

width.minimum: Imitate either an alliterative phrase or a rhyming couplet from a model poem, substituting new words that follow the same pattern.
width.typical: Imitate alliteration and rhyme patterns from model texts, creating new examples that follow the pattern in new contexts or with new content.
wider: Imitate more complex patterns — e.g. a poem with a repeating structure where alliteration occurs at the start of each line
Experiment with combining alliteration and rhyme in the same imitation

modes.reason: Imitation practice across a range of different pattern models builds the repertoire students need to eventually invent their own patterns. Each model expands what they know is possible.

nodes.label: Inventing sound patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can invent their own sound patterns — creating original alliterative phrases or rhyming pairs — and share them with others.
criteria: Student produces at least one original alliterative phrase with correctly repeated initial sounds
Student produces at least one original rhyming pair with matching end sounds

width.minimum: Invent at least one original alliterative phrase and one original rhyming pair.
width.typical: Invent original sound patterns — alliterative phrases, rhyming couplets, or combined patterns — and incorporate them into short chants, poems or songs shared with others.
wider: Create a short original poem or chant that deliberately uses both alliteration and rhyme for effect
Share invented sound patterns orally with expression, using volume and pace to enhance the sound effect

modes.reason: Inventing sound patterns requires students to draw on recognition, understanding of effect, and imitation practice — it is the integration task that brings the full capability together.

descriptors.title: Retell using plot and language
descriptors.description: orally retell or adapt a familiar story using plot and characters, language features including vocabulary, and structure of a familiar text, through role-play, writing, drawing or digital tools
descriptors.knowledge: Students can retell and adapt familiar literary texts through play, performance, images or writing at Foundation level (AC9EFLE05). They have not yet deliberately drawn on plot, character, vocabulary choices and text structure as resources for retelling — the Year 1 expectation makes these elements explicit as tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students orally retell or adapt a familiar story using plot and characters, appropriate vocabulary and text structure, through role-play, writing, drawing or digital tools.

nodes.label: Retelling the plot in order
nodes.checkpoint: Students can orally retell the main events of a familiar story in sequence, including the key characters, problem and resolution.
criteria: Student retells events in sequence without major omissions or reversals
Student includes the problem and its resolution in their retelling

width.minimum: Retell the main events of a familiar story in order, including who is involved and how the problem is resolved.
width.typical: Orally retell a familiar story using plot sequence (beginning, middle, end with problem and resolution), naming key characters and describing their roles.
wider: Retell stories from multiple texts, comparing how different plots are structured
Retell a story from a different character's perspective — how does the plot feel different?

nodes.label: Using language features in retelling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use language features from the original text — vocabulary, dialogue, descriptive phrases — in their retelling.
criteria: Student includes at least two specific vocabulary items or language features from the original in their retelling
Student uses at least some language that goes beyond their own everyday speech

width.minimum: Incorporate at least two vocabulary items or language features from the original text into an oral retelling.
width.typical: Use vocabulary, descriptive phrases and where appropriate, dialogue from the original text in retelling, showing awareness that language choices shape how the story is told.
wider: Compare a retelling that uses the original vocabulary with one that substitutes everyday language — discuss how word choices affect the story
Experiment with adding new vocabulary to enrich the retelling beyond the original

modes.reason: Drawing on text language as a resource requires students to build a repertoire of how story vocabulary, dialogue and description function. More retelling practice across more texts expands this repertoire.

nodes.label: Adapting the story
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adapt a familiar story — changing a character, setting or event — while maintaining the recognisable plot structure and using appropriate vocabulary.
criteria: Student's adaptation changes at least one element while maintaining the recognisable plot structure
Student uses vocabulary and language appropriate to the story type in their adaptation

width.minimum: Adapt at least one element of a familiar story (change a character, setting or event) and retell the adapted version orally or through drawing/role-play.
width.typical: Adapt familiar stories by changing characters, settings or events, maintaining the underlying plot structure and using vocabulary and language features appropriate to the story type, through oral retelling, role-play, drawing or digital tools.
wider: Adapt a story into a different medium — e.g. turn a written story into a role-play with dialogue
Adapt a story to a different cultural setting and discuss what changes in the language, characters and events

modes.reason: Adapting while preserving structure requires students to coordinate their understanding of plot, character vocabulary and text structure — it is the integration task that brings all three elements together in creative production.

descriptors.title: Features indicate text purpose
descriptors.description: discuss different texts and identify some features that indicate their purposes
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify some familiar texts such as stories and informative texts and their purposes (AC9EFLY01). They have not yet identified specific textual features — language, layout, structural elements — as indicators of purpose.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss different texts and identify features that indicate their purposes.

nodes.label: Texts have purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the purpose of familiar texts and explain how they know.
criteria: Student correctly names the purpose of two different texts
Student gives a feature-based reason for each identification

width.minimum: State the purpose of at least two different texts and give a reason (e.g. 'it's a story because it has characters and events').
width.typical: Name and explain the purposes of a range of familiar texts — to entertain, inform, instruct, persuade — with reasons grounded in text features.
wider: Discuss texts that serve more than one purpose simultaneously
Compare how the same information might be presented in texts with different purposes (e.g. a report vs an advertisement)

nodes.label: Features signal purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific features of texts — language, layout, structural elements — and explain how each signals the text's purpose.
criteria: Student identifies at least two features and links each to the text's purpose
Student uses feature-based language ('the headings tell me it's trying to inform')
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only recognise narrative features as purpose signals cannot classify informative, procedural or persuasive texts in subsequent work — the feature-to-purpose link must be established across multiple text types before any downstream text-type analysis is possible.

width.minimum: Identify at least two features in a given text and explain how each indicates what the text is trying to do.
width.typical: Identify and discuss features that indicate purpose across a range of text types — headings and diagrams (informative), character names and events (narrative), numbered steps (procedural), opinion language (persuasive).
wider: Compare two texts with different purposes side by side, identifying the distinct features that mark each
Examine digital texts and identify which features indicate purpose in online versus print contexts

modes.reason: Students need to see features functioning as purpose signals across varied text types to generalise the concept. Encountering only narrative features risks students equating all text features with storytelling.

descriptors.title: Turn-taking and active listening
descriptors.description: use interaction skills including turn-taking, speaking clearly, using active listening behaviours and responding to the contributions of others, and contributing ideas and questions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interact in informal and structured situations by listening while others speak and using some features of spoken language (AC9EFLY02). They have not yet applied the full set of interaction skills systematically — turn-taking, active listening, responding to others' contributions, and contributing ideas and questions as a coordinated set.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use interaction skills including turn-taking, active listening, responding to others' contributions, and contributing ideas and questions in discussions.

nodes.label: Turn-taking and clear speaking
nodes.checkpoint: Students can take turns to speak in structured discussions and speak clearly enough to be understood by the group.
criteria: Student waits for their turn before speaking in a discussion
Student's contribution is audible and clear to the group

width.minimum: Wait for their turn and contribute at least one idea, speaking at an audible volume and pace.
width.typical: Consistently take turns in group and class discussions, speak clearly with appropriate volume and pace, and wait without interrupting.
wider: Practise turn-taking in different group sizes — pairs, small groups, whole class — and discuss how expectations shift
Explore how turn-taking conventions differ across formal and informal discussion contexts

modes.reason: Turn-taking requires repeated practice in varied group configurations before it becomes habitual. Students need many opportunities to build the self-regulation needed for consistent, non-interruptive turn-taking.

nodes.label: Active listening behaviours
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate active listening — attending to the speaker, making eye contact, showing they are following the contribution.
criteria: Student demonstrates at least two observable active listening behaviours
Student can name the behaviours and explain why they matter

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two active listening behaviours (e.g. eye contact, nodding, facing the speaker) during a discussion.
width.typical: Demonstrate a consistent set of active listening behaviours — eye contact, body orientation, nodding or other acknowledgement — across structured discussion activities.
wider: Discuss what it looks like from a speaker's perspective when the audience is and isn't actively listening
Explore how active listening behaviours may differ across cultural contexts

nodes.label: Responding to and building on contributions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to what others have said — acknowledging, agreeing, questioning or extending a previous contribution.
criteria: Student explicitly acknowledges a prior contribution before making their own
Student's response connects to what was previously said rather than introducing an unrelated idea

width.minimum: Respond to at least one contribution from another student, acknowledging what was said before adding their own idea.
width.typical: Respond to others' contributions in discussion, using language that acknowledges what was said (e.g. 'I agree with...', 'I also think...', 'But what about...') and adds a new idea or question.
wider: Practise restating another person's idea before responding — discuss how this changes the quality of the discussion
Explore how asking a question in response to a contribution extends the discussion in a different way than agreeing does

modes.reason: Responding to a contribution requires students to listen, hold what was said, and then connect their own response — a sequenced reasoning move. A simple scaffold ('I heard [name] say... and I think...') supports this coordination.

descriptors.title: Compare text types
descriptors.description: describe some similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify some differences between imaginative and informative texts (AC9EFLY03). They have not yet described similarities and differences systematically across all three text type categories — imaginative, informative and persuasive.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts.

nodes.label: Three text type categories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name imaginative, informative and persuasive as three categories of text and give an example of each.
criteria: Student correctly names all three text type categories
Student gives a plausible example of each

width.minimum: Name the three text type categories and give one example of each.
width.typical: Name and describe the three text type categories, give multiple examples of each, and explain what each category is trying to do.
wider: Collect examples of each text type category from classroom and home environments
Discuss how digital texts fit into these categories — does a website belong to one or more categories?

nodes.label: Describing differences between text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts — in purpose, features, and language.
criteria: Student describes at least two differences between two text types with feature-based reasoning
Student correctly categorises a new example text when presented
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not have a working three-category schema — particularly if persuasive remains conflated with informative — cannot select appropriate text types for a given purpose in N3, which is the descriptor's application endpoint.

width.minimum: Describe at least two differences between two of the three text types.
width.typical: Describe differences in purpose, structural features and language between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts, using specific text examples as evidence.
wider: Compare texts that 'tell stories' with those that 'give opinions' — discuss what features distinguish them
Find examples where a text has features of more than one type and discuss which category fits best

modes.reason: Students often know that stories and information books are different but struggle to articulate persuasive as a distinct category. Encountering opinion texts — simple reviews, letters of request — as a third category alongside examples clarifies the distinction.

nodes.label: Selecting texts for a purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select a text type appropriate for a given purpose or task and explain their choice.
criteria: Student selects an appropriate text type for a given task
Student explains their choice by linking the text type to the task's purpose

width.minimum: Given a specific task (e.g. find out how something works; enjoy a story; decide which is better), identify which text type would be most useful and explain why.
width.typical: Select appropriate texts for a range of tasks — finding information, entertainment, forming an opinion — and justify the selection by linking text type to purpose.
wider: Explore how the same topic might be addressed by all three text types (e.g. an animal could be in a story, a report, or an advertisement) and discuss what each offers
Evaluate a text choice — did it serve the purpose well? What would a different text type offer?

modes.reason: Selecting a text for a purpose requires students to integrate understanding of all three text types — it is the practical application that makes the category distinctions useful and demonstrates genuine understanding.

descriptors.title: Read with phrasing and fluency
descriptors.description: read decodable and authentic texts using developing phonic knowledge, phrasing and fluency, and monitoring meaning using context and grammatical knowledge
descriptors.knowledge: Students can read decodable and authentic texts using developing phonic knowledge and monitor meaning at Foundation level (AC9EFLY04). They have not yet developed consistent phrasing and fluency, or systematically used context and grammatical knowledge as monitoring strategies alongside phonics.
descriptors.endpoint: Students read decodable and authentic texts with developing phrasing and fluency, monitoring meaning using context and grammatical knowledge.

nodes.label: Applying phonic knowledge in reading
nodes.checkpoint: Students can decode unfamiliar words using developing phonic knowledge as a primary word-identification strategy.
criteria: Student attempts to decode an unfamiliar word using phonics before guessing or skipping
Student correctly blends phonemes in single-syllable decodable words
nodes.hinge_reason: Without fluent phonic decoding, cognitive resources cannot be directed toward comprehension — students who remain word-by-word decoders cannot develop the phrasing and fluency that N2 requires.

width.minimum: Use phonic knowledge to attempt to decode an unfamiliar word in a reading context.
width.typical: Consistently apply developing phonic knowledge — blending, digraphs, common patterns — to decode unfamiliar words encountered in decodable and authentic texts.
wider: Apply phonic knowledge to multi-syllable words, breaking them into decodable parts
Discuss what strategies help when phonics alone doesn't fully solve a word

modes.reason: Phonic decoding must become fluent and automatic before reading resources can be directed to comprehension. Repeated reading of decodable texts builds the automaticity required.

nodes.label: Phrasing and fluency
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read in phrases rather than word-by-word, with developing fluency and expression.
criteria: Student reads in phrases rather than word-by-word for at least a sentence
Student's pace and expression reflect the meaning and punctuation of the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who read word-by-word cannot effectively monitor for meaning in N3 — phrased reading is the processing unit through which semantic and grammatical checking operates.

width.minimum: Read a familiar text in phrases (groups of words) rather than word-by-word, at a pace that supports meaning.
width.typical: Read decodable and authentic texts with developing phrasing — grouping words into meaningful units — and fluency, including appropriate pace, expression and attention to punctuation.
wider: Read the same passage at different speeds and discuss how pace affects comprehension and listener experience
Practise reading aloud for an audience, using phrasing and expression to convey meaning

modes.reason: Fluent phrased reading requires substantial rehearsal — it develops through repeated reading of varied texts rather than instruction alone. Consolidation through wide reading practice is the primary lever.

nodes.label: Monitoring meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise when meaning breaks down and use context and grammatical knowledge to self-correct.
criteria: Student pauses or re-reads when a word doesn't make sense
Student attempts self-correction using context or grammatical knowledge (not just phonics)

width.minimum: Notice when a word they have read doesn't make sense and attempt a self-correction using context or grammatical knowledge.
width.typical: Consistently monitor for meaning when reading, noticing breakdowns and self-correcting using context (does it make sense?), grammatical knowledge (does it sound right?), and phonics together.
wider: Discuss what strategies a reader can use when meaning breaks down — model the internal monitoring process
Compare self-correction strategies: re-reading from the start of the sentence, using picture cues, using context after the word

modes.reason: Monitoring for meaning requires a deliberate self-checking routine — 'does this make sense? does it sound right?' — that students must learn to apply systematically. Explicit scaffolding of the three-way check (meaning, structure, phonics) supports this.

descriptors.title: Build literal and inferred meaning
descriptors.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising and questioning when listening, viewing and reading to build literal and inferred meaning by drawing on vocabulary and growing knowledge of context and text structures
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting and summarising at Foundation level (AC9EFLY05). They have not yet explicitly applied inferencing, questioning as a deliberate strategy, or drawn on vocabulary and text structure knowledge to build beyond literal meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, questioning — to build literal and inferred meaning when listening, viewing and reading.

nodes.label: Literal meaning: what the text says
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and retell information stated explicitly in a text — what the text directly says.
criteria: Student accurately retells at least two pieces of information stated explicitly in a text
Student can locate a specific piece of information when asked

width.minimum: Identify and retell at least two pieces of information stated directly in a text.
width.typical: Consistently identify explicitly stated information across listening, viewing and reading contexts, building factual understanding of what the text says.
wider: Distinguish between information stated in words versus information shown only in images
Locate specific literal information in response to questions across a range of text types

nodes.label: Predicting and connecting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make predictions before and during reading and connect text content to their own knowledge or experiences.
criteria: Student makes a prediction using a text clue (cover, image, title) and states the evidence for it
Student confirms or adjusts the prediction after reading

width.minimum: Make at least one prediction before or during reading and confirm or adjust it after reading.
width.typical: Make and adjust predictions using cover, title, illustrations and text clues; make connections to prior knowledge and personal experience; explain how connections help build understanding.
wider: Compare predictions made from cover and title with what actually happened — discuss what cues were most reliable
Make text-to-text connections across two texts on the same topic and discuss what each adds

modes.reason: Predicting and connecting are strategies that improve through repeated application across varied text types and topics. The range of contexts in which students practise these strategies determines how transferable they become.

nodes.label: Inferring meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw inferences — identify meaning that is implied but not directly stated — using clues from the text.
criteria: Student identifies at least one piece of implied meaning
Student names the specific clue(s) from the text that support the inference
nodes.hinge_reason: Inferencing is prerequisite for N4's multi-strategy coordination — students who cannot draw beyond-literal meaning cannot meaningfully apply visualising, questioning and summarising to anything other than surface content.

width.minimum: Identify at least one piece of information in a text that is not directly stated and explain what clues led to the inference.
width.typical: Draw inferences from text clues — character feelings, motivations, causes of events — and explain the clues used, across listening, viewing and reading contexts.
wider: Compare an inference based on text clues with one based on personal experience — discuss which the text supports more strongly
Explore how illustrations provide inference clues that are not in the words

modes.reason: Inferencing is the most difficult comprehension strategy at Year 1. Students need many opportunities to encounter implied meaning — in different text types and modes — before the strategy becomes reliable. Image-based inferences, emotional inferences and causal inferences each require their own encounters.

nodes.label: Visualising, questioning and summarising
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use visualising, questioning and summarising strategies to build and consolidate meaning.
criteria: Student uses at least two different comprehension strategies and names each
Student explains how each strategy helped them build or check meaning

width.minimum: Use at least two different comprehension strategies (e.g. visualise + summarise, or question + connect) within a single reading experience.
width.typical: Apply visualising (forming mental images), questioning (asking what/why/how about the text) and summarising (capturing main ideas) as deliberate strategies across listening, viewing and reading.
wider: Discuss which strategy is most useful for which kind of text or difficulty
Apply multiple strategies to the same text and discuss how each adds something different to understanding

modes.reason: Using multiple comprehension strategies together — rather than in isolation — is the mature capability this descriptor targets. The integration node requires students to select and coordinate strategies for the specific comprehension challenge they face.

descriptors.title: Create and edit written texts
descriptors.description: create and re-read to edit short written and/or multimodal texts to report on a topic, express an opinion or recount a real or imagined event, using grammatically correct simple sentences, some topic-specific vocabulary, sentence boundary punctuation and correct spelling of some one- and two-syllable words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and participate in shared editing of short written texts to record and retell experiences (AC9EFLY06). They have not yet independently created texts across three purposes (report, opinion, recount), or applied grammatically correct simple sentences, topic vocabulary, sentence punctuation and spelling as a coordinated set of writing conventions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and edit short written and/or multimodal texts to report, express opinion or recount, using simple sentences, topic vocabulary, sentence punctuation and correct spelling of some one- and two-syllable words.

nodes.label: Writing for a purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a short text for a specific purpose — report, opinion or recount — and identify the purpose of their text.
criteria: Student's text has a clear purpose (report, opinion or recount)
Student can name the purpose of their text when asked

width.minimum: Write a short text with a clear purpose (report, opinion or recount) and name the purpose.
width.typical: Create short written and/or multimodal texts across all three purposes — reporting on a topic, expressing an opinion and recounting an event — with content appropriate to each purpose.
wider: Write on the same topic for two different purposes (e.g. a recount of an event AND an opinion about it) and discuss how the text changes
Create a multimodal text combining images and words for a chosen purpose

nodes.label: Grammatically correct simple sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write grammatically correct simple sentences — with a participant, process and optional circumstances.
criteria: Each sentence contains an identifiable participant and process
Student can identify and fix a sentence fragment in their own writing
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot produce grammatically complete sentences cannot develop the writing quality needed for the remaining nodes — fragments undermine both topic vocabulary expression (N3) and the re-reading-to-edit process (N4), which assume sentences are already structurally present.

width.minimum: Write at least two simple sentences that are grammatically complete (participant + process).
width.typical: Write grammatically correct simple sentences across their texts, with appropriate participants and processes, and some circumstances for detail.
wider: Edit a piece of writing specifically to improve grammatical completeness — adding missing participants or processes
Experiment with varying sentence structure by moving circumstances to different positions

modes.reason: Writing grammatically complete sentences requires sustained practice — students frequently produce fragments or run-ons at this level. Consolidation through frequent writing and re-reading builds the automatic production of complete sentences.

nodes.label: Topic vocabulary and punctuation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use some topic-specific vocabulary and sentence boundary punctuation in their writing.
criteria: Student includes at least one topic-specific word correctly used in their text
Student uses sentence boundary punctuation at the end of each sentence

width.minimum: Include at least one topic-specific word and correct end punctuation in a short written text.
width.typical: Use topic-specific vocabulary appropriate to the text's subject matter and apply sentence boundary punctuation (full stops, question marks, exclamation marks) consistently throughout.
wider: Use a word resource (word wall, dictionary) to find and check topic vocabulary
Review a peer's writing and identify topic vocabulary and punctuation use

nodes.label: Re-reading to edit
nodes.checkpoint: Students can re-read their own writing to identify and fix errors — adding words for meaning, correcting spelling, checking punctuation.
criteria: Student re-reads their text and makes at least one deliberate edit
Student can explain what they changed and why

width.minimum: Re-read a piece of their own writing and make at least one change that improves it.
width.typical: Re-read writing to edit for meaning (adding or deleting words), spelling (using resources to check words they are unsure of), and punctuation, making concrete improvements.
wider: Discuss what to look for when editing — develop a simple personal editing checklist
Compare a first draft with an edited version and describe the improvements made

modes.reason: Re-reading to edit requires a deliberate and sequenced checking routine — students need to learn to read their own writing as a reader, not just a writer. A simple scaffold (Does it make sense? Are words spelt right? Does each sentence end with a mark?) supports the habit.

descriptors.title: Deliver structured presentations
descriptors.description: create and deliver short oral and/or multimodal presentations on personal and learnt topics, which include an opening, middle and concluding statement; some topic-specific vocabulary and appropriate gesture, volume and pace
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and deliver short spoken texts to report ideas and events to peers (AC9EFLY07). They have not yet structured presentations with explicit opening, middle and concluding statements, or deliberately used topic-specific vocabulary and paralinguistic features (gesture, volume, pace) as presenting tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and deliver short oral and/or multimodal presentations with an opening, middle and concluding statement, topic vocabulary, and appropriate gesture, volume and pace.

nodes.label: Structuring a presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can organise a short presentation with an identifiable opening, middle and concluding statement.
criteria: Student's presentation has an identifiable opening that introduces the topic
Student's presentation has a concluding statement that closes or summarises
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a planned three-part structure, students cannot deploy topic vocabulary or paralinguistic features purposefully in N2 and N3 — unstructured delivery makes both vocabulary placement and gesture/pace meaningless.

width.minimum: Plan and deliver a short presentation that has a beginning, a middle with at least one key idea, and a conclusion.
width.typical: Create and deliver presentations with a clear opening (introducing the topic), a structured middle (key information or ideas) and a concluding statement (summarising or closing).
wider: Experiment with different types of opening — a question, a statement, a surprising fact — and discuss which works best for the topic
Compare presentations with and without a clear structure and discuss the difference for the audience

modes.reason: Planning a three-part structure requires students to make deliberate sequencing decisions — what goes first, what is the main content, how do I end? A simple planning scaffold (opening / key ideas / conclusion) supports this reasoning before the performance.

nodes.label: Topic vocabulary in presentations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use topic-specific vocabulary in their presentations to communicate precisely about the topic.
criteria: Student uses at least two topic-specific words correctly in their presentation
Student's vocabulary choice is appropriate to the topic

width.minimum: Use at least two topic-specific words correctly in an oral presentation.
width.typical: Incorporate topic-specific vocabulary appropriate to the subject matter across the presentation, using words that communicate precisely about the topic.
wider: Explain an unfamiliar topic-specific word to the audience as part of the presentation
Compare presentations with and without topic vocabulary — discuss how precision changes the listener's understanding

nodes.label: Gesture, volume and pace
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use appropriate gesture, volume and pace when delivering a presentation to support meaning and engage the audience.
criteria: Student speaks at an audible volume throughout the presentation
Student uses at least one deliberate gesture to support meaning

width.minimum: Deliver a presentation at an audible volume, at a pace that allows the audience to follow, and with at least one deliberate gesture.
width.typical: Use appropriate volume (loud enough for the audience), pace (neither too fast nor too slow for the purpose), and gesture (to emphasise or demonstrate) when delivering presentations, varying these for effect.
wider: Experiment with volume and pace for different purposes — retelling a scary moment versus explaining how to make something
Record a presentation and review the use of gesture, volume and pace — identify one area to improve

modes.reason: Managing gesture, volume and pace simultaneously with content delivery requires repeated practice. Students need multiple presentation opportunities before paralinguistic features are used consistently and deliberately.

descriptors.title: Write with unjoined letters
descriptors.description: write words using unjoined lower-case and upper-case letters
descriptors.knowledge: Students have been developing foundational pencil grip and letter formation at Foundation level. They have not yet consolidated consistent, legible unjoined letter formation across both lower-case and upper-case letters in writing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students write words using unjoined lower-case and upper-case letters.

nodes.label: Functional pencil grip
nodes.checkpoint: Students can hold a pencil with a functional grip that allows sustained writing without fatigue or loss of control.
criteria: Student holds the pencil with a functional grip (not fist grip) consistently
Student can write a sentence without loss of control
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a functional grip, students cannot produce the controlled letter formation required for N2 and N3 — formation exercises collapse without physical control of the tool.

width.minimum: Demonstrate a functional pencil grip that allows them to write at least a sentence.
width.typical: Hold a pencil with a consistent functional grip across writing tasks, sustaining control and comfort through short writing activities.
wider: Explore alternative writing tools (marker, chalk, stylus) and discuss how grip adjusts
Reflect on grip comfort during longer writing tasks and adjust when needed

modes.reason: Pencil grip is a physical habit that requires repeated practice to consolidate. Regular writing activities build the muscle memory and automaticity needed for a functional, sustained grip.

nodes.label: Consistent lower-case letter formation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write all lower-case letters with consistent, recognisable formation.
criteria: Student writes all lower-case letters legibly with correct formation direction
Student distinguishes commonly confused letter pairs (b/d, p/q) consistently
nodes.hinge_reason: Lower-case letter formation errors — particularly reversals — cascade directly into spelling and reading tasks; students who write b/d or p/q interchangeably cannot reliably encode or decode CVC words.

width.minimum: Write all lower-case letters legibly with correct formation direction.
width.typical: Write lower-case letters with consistent size, orientation and formation direction, producing legible writing across words and sentences.
wider: Compare letter formation across different scripts or fonts — discuss what makes a letter recognisable despite variation
Identify and practise letters that are commonly confused or reversed (b/d, p/q)

modes.reason: Lower-case letter formation requires sustained practice — particularly reversal-prone letters (b/d, p/q). Regular writing across varied tasks builds the automaticity needed for fluent handwriting.

nodes.label: Upper-case letter formation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write all upper-case letters correctly and use them appropriately (sentence starts, proper nouns).
criteria: Student writes upper-case letters legibly in sentence-start and proper noun positions
Student does not apply upper-case letters mid-sentence incorrectly

width.minimum: Write upper-case letters for sentence beginnings and at least one proper noun.
width.typical: Write all upper-case letters with correct formation and apply them in the appropriate contexts — sentence beginnings and proper nouns — in continuous writing.
wider: Explore contexts where all-caps are used (headings, labels) and discuss the convention
Write a short text and identify all correct upper-case letter uses

descriptors.title: Segment phonemes in words
descriptors.description: segment words into separate phonemes (sounds) including consonant blends or clusters at the beginnings and ends of words (phonological awareness)
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and generate rhyming words, identify syllables and segment single-syllable CVC words into onset and rime at Foundation level (AC9EFLY15). They have not yet segmented words fully into individual phonemes, particularly those containing consonant blends or clusters.
descriptors.endpoint: Students segment words into all separate phonemes including consonant blends and clusters at word beginnings and ends.

nodes.label: Phoneme segmentation in simple words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can segment single-syllable words into all individual phonemes in sequence.
criteria: Student segments a single-syllable word into correct individual phonemes in order
Student counts phonemes accurately (not letters) in a given word
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate single-word phoneme segmentation is definitionally prerequisite for N2 and N3 — students who cannot segment simple words cannot isolate individual consonants within blends.

width.minimum: Segment at least three single-syllable words (including CVC and CVCC patterns) into individual phonemes in order.
width.typical: Segment single-syllable words into all phonemes in sequence, including words with initial and final consonants, across varied vowel patterns.
wider: Segment words with four phonemes and confirm count
Compare segmentation of words with similar spelling but different phoneme counts

modes.reason: Accurate phoneme segmentation requires repeated practice — students often blend phonemes rather than cleanly separating each one. Segmentation is a foundational decoding skill that underpins spelling and must be automated.

nodes.label: Segmenting words with initial consonant blends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can segment words that begin with consonant blends or clusters (e.g. sp-, st-, bl-, cr-) into their individual phonemes.
criteria: Student correctly segments a word with an initial consonant blend, treating each consonant as a separate phoneme
Student says phonemes in correct order for a blend word
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot segment initial blends into separate phonemes will merge blend consonants in N3 final blend segmentation — the strategy of treating each consonant individually must be established before the harder final-position work.

width.minimum: Segment at least two words with initial consonant blends (e.g. 'spoon', 'fist') into all phonemes.
width.typical: Segment a range of words with initial consonant blends — including two- and three-consonant clusters — into individual phonemes, saying sounds in order.
wider: Sort words by their initial consonant blend and compare the phoneme count
Compare segmenting a word with an initial blend versus without — e.g. 'lip' vs 'slip'

modes.reason: Initial consonant blends are segmented differently depending on the cluster (sp- vs str- vs bl-). Students need exposure to a range of initial blend types to build a flexible segmentation strategy rather than a pattern-specific one.

nodes.label: Segmenting words with final consonant blends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can segment words with final consonant blends or clusters into their individual phonemes.
criteria: Student correctly segments a word with a final consonant blend
Student does not merge the final blend consonants into a single sound
nodes.hinge_reason: Complete phoneme segmentation — including final blends — is prerequisite for AC9E1LY10 phoneme manipulation; students cannot delete, substitute or add phonemes within blend positions they have not learned to isolate.

width.minimum: Segment at least two words with final consonant blends (e.g. 'fist', 'lamp') into all phonemes.
width.typical: Segment words with final consonant blends — including common patterns such as -st, -nd, -mp, -nk — into individual phonemes.
wider: Segment words with both initial and final consonant blends (e.g. 'stamp', 'blend')
Discuss how segmenting words with final blends helps with spelling

modes.reason: Final consonant blends are harder to segment than initial blends for most students — the end of the word receives less articulatory attention. Repeated practice with final blends before moving to both-ends blending is important.

descriptors.title: Manipulate phonemes in words
descriptors.description: orally manipulate phonemes in spoken words by addition, deletion and substitution of initial, medial and final phonemes to generate new words (phonological awareness)
descriptors.knowledge: Students can segment words into separate phonemes including consonant blends (AC9E1LY09). They have not yet manipulated individual phonemes by adding, deleting or substituting them to generate new words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students manipulate phonemes in spoken words by addition, deletion and substitution in initial, medial and final positions to generate new words.

nodes.label: Phoneme deletion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can delete a phoneme from a spoken word to produce a new word.
criteria: Student correctly produces the new word after deleting an initial phoneme
Student correctly produces the new word after deleting a final phoneme
nodes.hinge_reason: Phoneme deletion is the foundational manipulation — students who cannot reliably delete cannot perform substitution (N2), which requires deleting and replacing, or addition (N3), which requires inserting into a held phoneme sequence.

width.minimum: Delete the initial or final phoneme from at least two words and correctly state the new word formed.
width.typical: Delete initial, medial and final phonemes from spoken words to produce new words across a range of word patterns.
wider: Delete phonemes from words with consonant blends — e.g. delete the /s/ from 'slip' to get 'lip'
Chain deletions: delete a phoneme, then delete another from the result

modes.reason: Phoneme deletion requires secure phoneme segmentation — students who cannot reliably segment cannot reliably delete. Repeated practice, especially at the medial position, builds the precision needed.

nodes.label: Phoneme substitution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can substitute an initial, medial or final phoneme in a spoken word to generate a new word.
criteria: Student correctly substitutes an initial phoneme to make a new word
Student correctly substitutes a medial vowel to make a new word (e.g. pin → pen)
nodes.hinge_reason: Medial vowel substitution specifically — the hardest manipulation — underpins the short and long vowel reading and spelling work in AC9E1LY11; students who cannot substitute medial vowels will struggle to distinguish vowel patterns in words.

width.minimum: Substitute at least one phoneme in a spoken word (at any position) and correctly state the new word.
width.typical: Substitute initial, medial and final phonemes to generate new words, including substituting medial vowel sounds in CVC words (e.g. pin→pen→pan) and final consonants (e.g. pet→peg).
wider: Build a phoneme substitution chain: change one phoneme at a time across a series of words
Use phoneme substitution to generate rhyme families by substituting initial phonemes

modes.reason: Medial substitution (changing the vowel) is harder than initial or final substitution because vowel sounds are more abstract. Students need specific practice with medial vowel substitution as a distinct skill, not just more of initial substitution.

nodes.label: Phoneme addition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can add a phoneme to a spoken word in initial, medial or final position to generate a new word.
criteria: Student correctly adds a phoneme to make a new word
Student states the position (beginning/middle/end) where they added the phoneme

width.minimum: Add a phoneme to at least two spoken words (at any position) and correctly state the new word.
width.typical: Add phonemes to initial, medial and final positions in spoken words to generate new words, including adding phonemes to make consonant blends (e.g. add /s/ to 'lip' to get 'slip').
wider: Explore how adding a final phoneme changes a word family (e.g. 'an' → 'and' → 'hand')
Combine addition and substitution tasks in oral word-play chains

descriptors.title: Use vowels and blends to read and write
descriptors.description: use short vowels, common long vowels, consonant blends and digraphs to write words, and blend these to read one- and two-syllable words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can manipulate phonemes by addition, deletion and substitution (AC9E1LY10). They have been developing phoneme-grapheme knowledge at Foundation level. They have not yet applied knowledge of long vowels, consonant blends and digraphs systematically to read and write one- and two-syllable words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use short vowels, common long vowels, consonant blends and digraphs to write words, and blend these to read one- and two-syllable words.

nodes.label: Short vowels in words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use short vowel sounds to read and write words with short vowel patterns.
criteria: Student reads single-syllable words with short vowels correctly
Student writes words with short vowels using correct graphemes
nodes.hinge_reason: Short vowel accuracy is foundational for the entire phonics sequence — errors in short vowels produce systematic misreadings that cascade into long vowel work (N2), digraph work (N3) and two-syllable reading (N4).

width.minimum: Read and write at least five single-syllable words using short vowel patterns (a, e, i, o, u).
width.typical: Apply knowledge of all five short vowel sounds to read and write a range of single-syllable words, including CVC and CVCC patterns.
wider: Compare minimal pairs with different short vowels (e.g. 'man', 'men', 'min', 'mon') and discuss how the vowel changes meaning
Sort words by short vowel sound across five families

modes.reason: Short vowel accuracy is foundational — errors in short vowels cascade through spelling and decoding. Fluent recognition and production of all five short vowel patterns requires sustained practice.

nodes.label: Common long vowels
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use common long vowel sounds to read and write words, applying common spelling patterns.
criteria: Student reads words with a common long vowel pattern correctly
Student applies at least one long vowel spelling pattern in writing
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who apply short vowel rules to long vowel words produce systematic misreadings — this misconception, if uncorrected, causes persistent errors in reading unfamiliar words with silent-e and other long vowel patterns.

width.minimum: Read and write at least three words using a common long vowel pattern (e.g. silent-e: 'time', 'make').
width.typical: Apply common long vowel spelling patterns — silent-e, and other common patterns — to read and write words with long vowel sounds.
wider: Explore that long vowels can be represented by different spelling patterns (e.g. the long /a/ in 'make', 'rain', 'play') — introduce at exposure level
Sort long vowel words by spelling pattern

modes.reason: Students frequently apply short vowel rules to long vowel words. Encountering long vowels in multiple spelling patterns — even just recognising they exist — helps prevent over-application of the short vowel schema.

nodes.label: Consonant blends and digraphs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use consonant blends and digraphs to read and write words.
criteria: Student reads single-syllable words containing consonant blends correctly
Student writes single-syllable words with common digraphs (sh, ch, th) correctly

width.minimum: Read and write at least two words with consonant blends and two words with digraphs.
width.typical: Apply consonant blend knowledge (initial and final: bl-, st-, cr-, -st, -nd) and common digraphs (sh, ch, th, wh) to read and write single-syllable words.
wider: Compare reading words with blends versus without (e.g. 'rest' vs 'rest' without the -st) to see how blends change meaning
Collect and categorise words by blend or digraph type

nodes.label: Reading two-syllable words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can blend phoneme knowledge to read one- and two-syllable words.
criteria: Student reads a two-syllable word by attempting to break it into syllables
Student correctly reads at least three two-syllable words using phonic knowledge

width.minimum: Read at least three two-syllable words by breaking them into syllables and blending.
width.typical: Apply blending skills to read one- and two-syllable words containing short vowels, long vowels, blends and digraphs, using syllable boundary knowledge to manage two-syllable words.
wider: Read two-syllable compound words and discuss how each syllable carries meaning
Explore how syllable boundaries are determined in two-syllable words

modes.reason: Reading two-syllable words requires integrating all prior phonics knowledge — vowel patterns, blends, digraphs — across multiple syllables. It is the integration task that demonstrates applied phonic knowledge.

descriptors.title: Letters represent multiple sounds
descriptors.description: understand that a letter can represent more than one sound and that a syllable must contain a vowel sound
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use short and long vowels, blends and digraphs to read and write words (AC9E1LY11). They have not yet explicitly understood that the relationship between letters and sounds is not one-to-one — a letter can represent multiple sounds depending on context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that a letter can represent more than one sound, and that every syllable must contain a vowel sound.

nodes.label: One letter, multiple sounds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify letters that represent more than one sound and give examples from their reading.
criteria: Student gives two examples of the same letter making different sounds
Student explains that letters can make different sounds in different words
nodes.hinge_reason: Students operating on a one-letter-one-sound assumption will produce systematic decoding errors when encountering unfamiliar words — this misconception propagates indefinitely without explicit resolution and undermines the AC9E1LY13 spelling work that depends on context-sensitive grapheme choice.

width.minimum: Identify at least one letter that can represent more than one sound and give two examples showing both sounds.
width.typical: Identify and discuss letters that represent multiple sounds — e.g. 'u' in 'cut', 'put' and 'use'; 'a' in 'cat', 'father' and 'any'; 'c' in 'cat' and 'cent' — and explain that context determines which sound is used.
wider: Explore how context (surrounding letters, word position) determines which sound a letter makes
Find examples in shared reading texts where the same letter makes different sounds

modes.reason: Students operating on a one-letter-one-sound assumption will struggle with unfamiliar words. Encountering multiple examples of the same letter making different sounds — across different vowels and consonants — resolves this misconception systematically.

nodes.label: One sound, multiple letters
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sounds that can be produced by different letters or letter combinations.
criteria: Student gives two words where the same sound is made by different letters
Student explains why this means some spelling cannot be worked out from sound alone

width.minimum: Give at least two examples of the same sound being produced by different letters (e.g. 's' in 'sat' and 'cent').
width.typical: Identify common examples where the same sound is produced by different graphemes — e.g. the /s/ sound in 'sat' and 'cent'; the /k/ sound in 'cat' and 'kit' — and explain that spelling must be learned, not just decoded from sound.
wider: Collect a bank of words where the same sound has multiple spelling options — discuss why this makes spelling harder than reading
Explore how this principle links to the need to learn some words as whole units

nodes.label: Syllables must have a vowel sound
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify syllables in words and confirm that each syllable contains a vowel sound.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the syllable count in two-syllable words
Student identifies the vowel sound in each syllable of a two-syllable word

width.minimum: Break a two-syllable word into syllables and identify the vowel sound in each syllable.
width.typical: Identify syllables in one- and two-syllable words, confirm each syllable contains a vowel sound, and use this understanding to support reading and spelling of unfamiliar words.
wider: Explore three-syllable words and confirm each syllable has a vowel
Discuss how the syllable-vowel rule helps identify syllable boundaries in longer words

modes.reason: The syllable-vowel principle is a reasoning tool — students can use it to check their syllable division by asking 'does each part have a vowel sound?' A brief scaffold makes this check explicit and transferable.

descriptors.title: Spell with common letter patterns
descriptors.description: spell one- and two-syllable words with common letter patterns
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand that letters represent multiple sounds and that syllables contain vowel sounds (AC9E1LY12). They have not yet applied this knowledge to spell a range of one- and two-syllable words using common letter patterns systematically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students spell one- and two-syllable words with common letter patterns.

nodes.label: Spelling one-syllable words with known patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can spell one-syllable words using known letter patterns — including short vowels, consonant blends and digraphs.
criteria: Student correctly spells at least five one-syllable words with known patterns
Student can apply known patterns to spell a new, unfamiliar one-syllable word
