nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable one-syllable spelling is the foundation for the two-syllable strategy in N2 — students who cannot spell single syllables accurately cannot apply the 'spell each part' strategy to longer words.

width.minimum: Correctly spell at least five one-syllable words containing known letter patterns (e.g. short vowel, blend).
width.typical: Spell a range of one-syllable words using known letter patterns — CVC, CVCC, CCVC, digraphs — applying phoneme-grapheme knowledge to spell previously unwritten words.
wider: Generate and spell multiple words from the same pattern family (e.g. words ending in -st, -nd, -ng)
Apply spelling knowledge to write one-syllable topic vocabulary in content area writing

modes.reason: Spelling requires more precision than reading — students can recognise correctly spelled words they cannot yet produce. Consolidation through varied writing contexts builds reliable spelling production.

nodes.label: Spelling two-syllable words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can spell one- and two-syllable words by applying syllable knowledge and known letter patterns.
criteria: Student correctly spells at least three two-syllable words
Student can describe the strategy they use to approach spelling a two-syllable word

width.minimum: Correctly spell at least three two-syllable words containing known blends or patterns.
width.typical: Spell two-syllable words by attending to each syllable separately, applying known letter patterns to each part — including words with common blends in either syllable.
wider: Explore two-syllable compound words and discuss how spelling each part separately helps
Write sentences using two-syllable topic vocabulary correctly spelled

modes.reason: Spelling two-syllable words requires a deliberate strategy: break the word into syllables, spell each part, then reassemble. A simple scaffold ('say it in parts, spell each part') makes this strategy explicit.

descriptors.title: Read and write high-frequency words
descriptors.description: read and write an increasing number of high-frequency words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can spell one- and two-syllable words with common letter patterns (AC9E1LY13). They have also been building a high-frequency word bank at Foundation level. They have not yet expanded this bank to the growing range expected at Year 1, including irregular high-frequency words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students read and write an increasing number of high-frequency words, including irregular forms.

nodes.label: Reading high-frequency words automatically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read an increasing number of high-frequency words automatically, without sounding out.
criteria: Student reads target high-frequency words automatically (without phoneme-by-phoneme decoding)
Student recognises high-frequency words in continuous text as well as in isolation
nodes.hinge_reason: Automatic high-frequency word recognition is a direct prerequisite for reading fluency — students who must decode common words cannot achieve the phrasing and pace needed for comprehension; their decoding load remains cognitively full on low-information words.

width.minimum: Read at least 20 Year 1-level high-frequency words automatically (at a glance, without decoding).
width.typical: Read an increasing bank of high-frequency words automatically when encountered in continuous text, including words with irregular phoneme-grapheme relationships (e.g. 'one', 'have', 'pretty').
wider: Read high-frequency words in varied sentence contexts — confirming they are recognised regardless of surrounding text
Identify high-frequency words in shared reading texts and discuss which are decodable and which need to be memorised

modes.reason: High-frequency word recognition is built through repeated exposure — seeing and reading words frequently until they are stored as sight words. Consolidation through wide reading and word-level practice is the primary lever.

nodes.label: Writing high-frequency words correctly
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write high-frequency words correctly, including irregular forms, in their own writing.
criteria: Student correctly spells at least 15 target high-frequency words in writing
Student's high-frequency word spelling is correct in independent writing contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: Incorrect spelling of high-frequency words in independent writing signals that phonics-only strategies are being applied to irregular forms — this produces persistent misspellings that, once habituated, become difficult to correct.

width.minimum: Correctly spell at least 15 Year 1-level high-frequency words from memory in a writing context.
width.typical: Write an increasing bank of high-frequency words correctly in continuous writing, applying memory for irregular forms rather than phonetic attempts.
wider: Identify and self-correct misspelled high-frequency words in draft writing
Discuss why some high-frequency words cannot be spelled from phonics alone — building awareness of the need to memorise irregular forms

modes.reason: Writing high-frequency words correctly requires memory, not just recognition. Students who can read a word may not yet reproduce it correctly from memory — repeated writing practice builds accurate production.

descriptors.title: Grammatical morphemes and word families
descriptors.description: recognise and know how to use grammatical morphemes to create word families
descriptors.knowledge: Students can read and write an increasing number of high-frequency words (AC9E1LY14). At Foundation level students understand that words can be made of more than one meaningful part (AC9EFLY15). They have not yet systematically used grammatical morphemes — inflectional endings such as -s, -ed, -ing, -er — to generate and recognise word families.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and use grammatical morphemes to create and read word families.

nodes.label: Morphemes carry meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that words can be made of more than one part (base word + morpheme) and that each part contributes meaning.
criteria: Student identifies the base word in a morphologically complex word
Student names the morpheme added and explains what it changes

width.minimum: Identify the base word and added morpheme in at least two examples (e.g. 'walk-ed', 'play-ing') and explain what each part contributes.
width.typical: Identify base words and grammatical morphemes in familiar words, explain how the morpheme changes the meaning or grammatical role of the base, using examples like 'play', 'plays', 'playing', 'played'.
wider: Explore how the same base word changes function with different morphemes — noun to verb, verb to adjective
Discuss how recognising a base word inside a longer word helps with reading and meaning

modes.reason: Identifying base word and morpheme requires a segmenting reasoning move — 'what is the core word, what was added?' A simple scaffold ('find the word inside the word') supports students in making this move reliably.

nodes.label: Common grammatical morphemes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and use common grammatical morphemes — -s, -es, -ed, -ing, -er — to create word family members.
criteria: Student correctly builds at least three word family members from a base word using different morphemes
Student reads a morphologically complex word by identifying the base word first
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not have a working set of common grammatical morphemes cannot apply morpheme knowledge as a reading and spelling strategy in N3 — the N3 integration task requires knowing what the morphemes are before using them as decoding and encoding tools.

width.minimum: Use at least three different grammatical morphemes to build new word forms from a given base word.
width.typical: Recognise and use common grammatical morphemes to create word families — plural -s/-es, past tense -ed, present continuous -ing, comparative -er — from familiar base words.
wider: Build extended word families from common morphemes and discuss what each form is used for
Explore morphological families that include compound forms (e.g. 'playground', 'playtime' from 'play')

modes.reason: Students often recognise -ing and -ed but miss plural and comparative morphemes. Encountering all common grammatical morphemes as a coherent family — not individual spelling rules — builds the broader morphological awareness needed.

nodes.label: Using morphemes to read and spell
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use morpheme knowledge to read unfamiliar words by recognising base words, and to spell by applying morpheme addition.
criteria: Student reads a morphologically complex word by identifying the base word
Student correctly spells a word formed by adding a familiar morpheme to a known base

width.minimum: Read an unfamiliar word by identifying the base word inside it; spell at least two words formed by adding a morpheme to a known base.
width.typical: Apply morpheme knowledge to read unfamiliar words — recognising the base word and then the morpheme — and to spell words formed by adding known morphemes to known base words.
wider: Discuss what happens to some base words when morphemes are added — e.g. 'hop' → 'hopped' (doubling) — at awareness level only
Use morpheme knowledge to self-correct reading errors — identify whether the base word was read correctly

modes.reason: Using morphemes as a reading and spelling tool integrates knowledge of base words and morpheme function into an active decoding and encoding strategy — the endpoint of this strand's progression at Year 1.

descriptors.title: Language varies by context
descriptors.description: investigate how interpersonal language choices vary depending on the context, including the different roles taken on in interactions
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how language, facial expressions and gestures are used in different types of interaction (AC9E1LA01). They have not yet investigated how language choices vary systematically by context and by the roles participants take on.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can investigate how interpersonal language choices vary depending on context and the roles taken on in interactions, including culturally specific greetings and expressions of politeness.

nodes.label: Context shapes language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that the same idea can be expressed using different language depending on who is speaking and who is listening.
criteria: Student can name at least one way their language would differ between a formal and informal context.
Student can explain what feature of the context causes the language to change (e.g. who they are talking to, the setting, the purpose).

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples where language changes depending on the situation — e.g. greeting a friend vs greeting a teacher.
width.typical: Identify and discuss how language choices change across multiple everyday contexts — formal and informal, familiar and unfamiliar — and name what makes those contexts different.
wider: Compare greetings and expressions of politeness used in different cultural settings, including school, home and community contexts
Explore how digital communication contexts (e.g. text message vs formal letter) create different language expectations

modes.reason: Students often treat language as fixed — 'you just say what you mean'. Exposure to multiple contrasting contexts helps break the assumption that language is context-neutral. More examples across varied settings (not more explanation of one example) resolves this misconception.

nodes.label: Roles in interaction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how the role a person takes on in an interaction — speaker, listener, questioner, responder — influences their language choices.
criteria: Student can identify at least two different roles in a given interaction and describe how the language differs for each.
Student can explain why a person speaking in one role would not use the same language as someone in a different role.

width.minimum: Identify how a speaker's language changes when they take on different roles in the same interaction (e.g. asking a question vs giving an answer).
width.typical: Discuss how multiple roles in an interaction (leader, questioner, responder, instruction-giver) each carry different language expectations, and identify examples from classroom and familiar texts.
wider: Investigate roles in formal ceremony contexts such as First Nations Australian Welcome to Country, where the role of greeter, guest and witness carry distinct language protocols
Compare teacher–student and student–student interaction patterns, noting how the same student shifts language depending on their role

nodes.label: Familiarity and formality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how the degree of familiarity between participants affects language formality and vocabulary choices.
criteria: Student can give an example of a language choice they would make differently with a familiar vs unfamiliar person.
Student can explain what familiarity means in this context and how it influences language.

width.minimum: Compare language used with a familiar person (friend, family member) vs an unfamiliar person (new adult, community member) and name a difference.
width.typical: Explore how familiarity influences word choice, tone and degree of formality across multiple pairs of contrasting contexts, including culturally specific greetings and expressions of politeness.
wider: Identify First Nations Australian greeting words and protocols used with different groups — community members, visitors, Elders — and discuss how familiarity and respect shape these choices
Compare formal and informal email or spoken message openings to a known vs unknown audience, noting vocabulary and register differences

modes.reason: Students often conflate familiarity with friendship and assume formal language is 'cold'. Multiple cultural and social contexts help reveal that formality is a marker of respect, not distance — a misconception that widening directly addresses.

descriptors.title: Language to appreciate and prefer
descriptors.description: explore how language can be used for appreciating texts and providing reasons for preferences
descriptors.knowledge: Students explore language used to give reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences (AC9E1LA02). They have not yet used more precise vocabulary to appreciate specific textual features, or explored verbs that express degree of preference.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can explore how language is used to appreciate texts and give reasoned explanations for preferences using more precise vocabulary.

nodes.label: Moving beyond 'I liked it'
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that appreciation language names what specifically they are responding to, not just that they liked something.
criteria: Student produces an appreciation statement that names a specific textual feature, not just a general response.
Student can explain what makes their statement an appreciation rather than just a preference.

width.minimum: Distinguish between a vague preference statement ('I liked it') and a statement that names a specific textual feature ('I liked how the author described the setting').
width.typical: Identify and practise appreciation language that names specific textual features — setting, character, language choice, illustration — across several texts.
wider: Compare appreciation statements made by different students about the same text and identify which features each person noticed
Examine book reviews or blurbs as examples of appreciation language used for an audience

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate 'liking' with 'appreciating'. The misconception is that preference is just emotional — widening to name what specifically is being liked (setting, character, language) resolves this. More textual examples across different features, not more repetition of the same example, is the productive move.

nodes.label: Preference verbs and degree
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select verbs that express different degrees of preference — liked, preferred, enjoyed, loved — and explain the difference.
criteria: Student can use at least two different preference verbs and explain what difference in degree each conveys.
Student can select the most appropriate preference verb for a given strength of response.

width.minimum: Identify that 'liked', 'preferred' and 'enjoyed' express different degrees of preference and use at least two in a statement.
width.typical: Explore a range of preference verbs and their degrees, choose appropriate verbs for different responses, and discuss why degree matters when giving a reason.
wider: Compare how degree of preference changes the persuasiveness of a recommendation — stronger verbs create stronger recommendations
Identify preference verbs in texts by different authors and consider why they chose that degree

modes.reason: Distinguishing degrees of preference is a precise vocabulary task. Students need practice — trying verbs in context, comparing them, choosing between them — rather than broader contexts. Fluency in selecting the right degree verb is the target.

nodes.label: Specific vocabulary for place and setting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use specific vocabulary — including place names and descriptive nouns — to make appreciation of setting more precise.
criteria: Student uses a specific vocabulary term (not a vague placeholder) when appreciating the setting of a text.
Student can explain why the specific word makes their appreciation more precise.

width.minimum: Replace a vague setting description ('the place') with a more specific term ('the forest', 'the outback') when appreciating a text.
width.typical: Explore how specific vocabulary for setting, including First Nations Australian language words specific to Country/Place where relevant, makes appreciation of a text more precise and vivid.
wider: Identify First Nations Australian language words specific to Country/Place used in texts and explore how using those words makes appreciation of the setting more specific and respectful
Compare appreciation of setting using general vs specific vocabulary and discuss the effect on the reader

descriptors.title: Texts organised by purpose
descriptors.description: identify how texts across the curriculum are organised differently and use language features depending on purposes
descriptors.knowledge: Students explore how texts are organised differently according to their purpose (AC9E1LA03). They have not yet identified specific structural and language features associated with distinct text types across curriculum areas, or recognised that the same purpose can be expressed in different forms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify how texts across the curriculum are organised differently and use specific language features depending on their purposes.

nodes.label: Purpose drives organisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a text and connect that purpose to at least one organisational feature.
criteria: Student can name the purpose of a given text and identify at least one organisational feature that serves that purpose.
Student does not claim that all texts of the same type are organised identically — they can acknowledge variation.

width.minimum: Identify the purpose of a familiar text type (e.g. narrative, procedure) and name one organisational feature that serves that purpose.
width.typical: Identify and compare the purposes of several text types and connect each purpose to its typical organisational features across narrative, recount, information report and procedure.
wider: Compare two texts with the same purpose but different organisations (e.g. a procedure as a list vs as a video) and discuss how the form affects the audience
Explore informative texts from Science or HASS and identify how their purpose shapes their organisation

modes.reason: Students often think organisational features are arbitrary rules rather than purposeful choices. Seeing the same purpose realised in different text types, and different purposes in similar formats, resolves the misconception that structure is fixed. Multiple text type examples across curriculum areas are the productive move.

nodes.label: Language features signal text type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language features — such as time connectives in recounts, imperative verbs in procedures, technical vocabulary in reports — that signal a text's type and purpose.
criteria: Student can name a language feature in a text and explain how it supports the text's purpose.
Student can distinguish language features across at least two different text types.

width.minimum: Identify one language feature in a text that signals its purpose (e.g. imperative verbs in a procedure, past tense in a recount).
width.typical: Identify and name language features in narratives, recounts, information reports, simple procedures, opinions and responses to texts, and explain how each feature supports the text's purpose.
wider: Compare how the same topic is presented in a narrative and an information report, identifying the different language features each uses
Identify language features in poetry that differ from prose text types and discuss how they serve poetic purposes

nodes.label: Same purpose, different forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that a single purpose (e.g. expressing an opinion) can be expressed through different text forms — poster, email, brochure — and that the form shapes the language features used.
criteria: Student can identify that the same purpose can take different forms.
Student can name at least one way language features or organisation changes when the form changes, even if the purpose stays the same.

width.minimum: Identify two different forms that serve the same purpose and name one way the language or organisation differs between them.
width.typical: Discuss how opinion, information or recount purposes can each be realised across multiple forms, and identify how the chosen form shapes language features, layout and audience expectations.
wider: Create or compare two versions of the same message in different forms (e.g. a recount as a letter and as a multimodal presentation) and discuss how the form changes the language
Identify texts in digital formats (website, infographic, ebook) and compare their organisation to print equivalents

modes.reason: This node integrates the two prior understandings — purpose drives organisation AND language features signal text type — and adds the insight that form is a third variable. Coordinating all three is the learning challenge here.

descriptors.title: Cohesion through pronouns
descriptors.description: understand how texts are made cohesive by using personal and possessive pronouns and by omitting words that can be inferred
descriptors.knowledge: Students explore how repetition, rhyme and rhythm create cohesion in poems, chants and songs (AC9E1LA04). They have not yet examined how pronouns and ellipsis create cohesion in prose and other text types by tracking referents and omitting recoverable information.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can understand how texts are made cohesive through personal and possessive pronouns and through ellipsis (omitting words that can be inferred).

nodes.label: Tracking a referent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can track how a person or thing is referred to across a section of text — by name, then by pronoun — and identify which pronoun refers to which entity.
criteria: Student can identify the referent of a personal pronoun in a given sentence.
Student does not default to naming the most recently mentioned noun as the referent in cases where this would be incorrect.

width.minimum: In a short passage, identify the noun that a given pronoun refers back to (the referent).
width.typical: Map pronoun reference chains across a paragraph — tracking how 'Isy', 'she', 'I', 'sister' all refer to the same character — in both narrative and informative texts.
wider: Track reference chains across multiple characters in a narrative and identify where pronoun reference becomes ambiguous
Compare pronoun reference chains in first-person vs third-person narratives and discuss how each affects the reader's relationship to the story

modes.reason: Students commonly assume the most recently mentioned noun is always the referent — a positional heuristic that fails with complex reference chains. Multiple textual examples across different pronouns (she/he/they/it) and referent types resolve this. More texts, not more explanation of one example.

nodes.label: Personal and possessive pronouns in cohesion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that personal and possessive pronouns create cohesion by linking back to previously named entities and avoiding repetition.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the referent of both personal and possessive pronouns in a passage.
Student can substitute a repeated noun phrase with an appropriate pronoun without introducing ambiguity.
nodes.hinge_reason: Pronoun misuse — wrong case or ambiguous reference — produces incoherent text in all written production tasks downstream. Students whose pronoun use is unreliable carry that incoherence into extended writing regardless of other improvements made.

width.minimum: Replace repeated nouns in a short passage with appropriate personal or possessive pronouns and explain why the text flows better.
width.typical: Identify personal and possessive pronouns in a range of texts, explain their referents, and discuss how they prevent awkward repetition and create cohesive text flow.
wider: Compare a version of a text with pronouns to a version with all referents named repeatedly, and discuss the effect on the reader
Write a short passage about a topic that requires tracking multiple entities, using pronouns deliberately for cohesion

modes.reason: Using pronouns correctly — particularly possessive forms — requires precision and practice. Students who overuse or misapply pronouns (wrong case, ambiguous reference) produce incoherent text. Targeted practice in identifying and producing accurate pronoun use is more effective here than widening contexts.

nodes.label: Ellipsis — inferring omitted words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify words that have been omitted from a text and explain what can be inferred from the surrounding context.
criteria: Student can identify an instance of ellipsis and name what can be inferred.
Student understands that the omission is intentional and that context makes it recoverable.

width.minimum: Identify a sentence where a word or phrase has been omitted and state what the missing word is — e.g. 'Xanthe went to school. She had a lovely day [at school is inferred].'
width.typical: Identify multiple examples of ellipsis across different text types, explain what is inferred and why the omission is possible, and discuss how ellipsis contributes to text flow.
wider: Compare spoken and written texts to identify where ellipsis is more common and discuss why speakers omit more than writers
Identify ellipsis in dialogue in a narrative and discuss how it creates natural-sounding conversation

modes.reason: Students often perceive omitted words as errors or gaps rather than as deliberate cohesive choices. Examples across both spoken and written contexts, and across formal and informal registers, help students see that ellipsis is purposeful and reader-serving. Multiple context types resolve the 'it's missing' misconception.

descriptors.title: Navigate print and screen texts
descriptors.description: navigate print and screen texts using chapters, tables of contents, indexes, side-bar menus, drop-down menus or links
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how print and screen texts are organised using navigation and structural features such as page numbers, headings and links (AC9E1LA05). They have not yet actively navigated these features to locate specific information — their prior knowledge is understanding how features work, not using them purposefully.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can navigate print and screen texts using chapters, tables of contents, indexes, side-bar menus, drop-down menus and links to locate specific information.

nodes.label: How print navigation features work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how chapters, tables of contents and indexes are organised to support information access — numbering, alphabetical order, page reference — and use at least one to locate information.
criteria: Student can use a table of contents to locate a chapter and an index to locate a specific term.
Student can explain how the alphabetical order of an index speeds up information retrieval.

width.minimum: Use a table of contents to locate a specific chapter or section in a non-fiction book.
width.typical: Use tables of contents, chapters and indexes across several non-fiction books; explain how numbered chapters and alphabetical indexes are organised to support access; use an index to locate a specific term.
wider: Compare the organisation of indexes across two different non-fiction books and discuss why some terms are included and others are not
Create a simple table of contents for a class-made information text, making decisions about chapter sequence

nodes.label: How digital navigation features work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use website navigation tools — side-bar menus, drop-down menus and links — to locate information on a familiar website.
criteria: Student can use at least one digital navigation feature to locate specified information.
Student can name the navigation feature they used and explain what it does.

width.minimum: Use a side-bar menu or navigation link on a familiar website to locate a specific piece of information.
width.typical: Explore navigation tools on different websites — side-bar menus, drop-down menus, links, search bars — and explain how each tool helps users locate information.
wider: Compare the navigation structures of two different websites with similar purposes (e.g. two library or museum sites) and discuss which is easier to use and why
Identify how navigation menus on mobile and desktop versions of the same site differ

nodes.label: Choosing the right navigation tool
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select the appropriate navigation tool — print or digital — for a given information retrieval task and explain their choice.
criteria: Student can select an appropriate navigation tool for a given task and explain why they chose it.
Student can use both a print and a digital navigation feature to locate specific information.

width.minimum: Given a specific information-finding task, identify whether an index, table of contents or a website menu is the most efficient tool to use.
width.typical: Compare print and digital navigation tools and discuss when each is more efficient; navigate both types to locate information for a purpose and reflect on the experience.
wider: Compare information retrieval using a print index vs a website search bar for the same topic, and discuss the trade-offs
Explore how accessibility features (text-to-speech, screen-reader navigation) change how digital navigation works for different users

modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of print and digital navigation tools and applies them to a purposeful retrieval task. Coordinating knowledge of both tool types to make an informed choice is the new cognitive demand.

descriptors.title: Compound sentences
descriptors.description: understand that connections can be made between ideas by using a compound sentence with 2 or more independent clauses usually linked by a coordinating conjunction
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that a simple sentence is a single independent clause representing one event or idea (AC9E1LA06). They have not yet connected independent clauses into compound sentences or understood how coordinating conjunctions signal the relationship between clauses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can understand that compound sentences connect two or more independent clauses using coordinating conjunctions, and can identify the relationship between ideas that each conjunction signals.

nodes.label: Independent clauses can be joined
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that a compound sentence contains two or more complete ideas, each of which could stand alone, joined by a linking word.
criteria: Student can identify both independent clauses in a compound sentence.
Student can confirm that each clause makes sense without the other.

width.minimum: Identify the two independent clauses in a given compound sentence and confirm that each makes sense on its own.
width.typical: Identify and construct compound sentences from pairs of simple sentences across a range of topics; verify that each clause is independent.
wider: Sort a set of sentences into simple and compound, explaining the reasoning
Identify compound sentences in familiar picture books and shared reading texts

nodes.label: Conjunctions signal relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how 'and', 'but' and 'so' each signal a different relationship between ideas — addition, contrast and consequence — and choose the correct conjunction for a given pair of clauses.
criteria: Student selects the correct conjunction for a given relationship between two clauses.
Student can name the relationship ('and' = addition, 'but' = contrast, 'so' = consequence) for at least two conjunctions.

width.minimum: Identify whether 'and', 'but' or 'so' is appropriate to connect two given clauses and explain the relationship.
width.typical: Construct compound sentences using 'and', 'but' and 'so', explaining the relationship each conjunction signals; identify these conjunctions in a range of texts.
wider: Compare sentences where the conjunction is changed (e.g. 'and' to 'but') and discuss how meaning changes
Identify compound sentences in informative texts and discuss whether the conjunction was the best choice

modes.reason: Students often default to 'and' for any conjunction slot, treating compound sentences as mere addition. Exposure to multiple contexts where 'but' (contrast) or 'so' (consequence) is required — and where the wrong conjunction changes meaning — resolves the over-reliance on 'and'. More contrasting examples, not more practice with 'and', is the productive move.

nodes.label: Constructing compound sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct their own compound sentences, connecting independent clauses with appropriate coordinating conjunctions to express related ideas clearly.
criteria: Student produces a compound sentence where both clauses are independent and the conjunction is appropriate.
Student does not produce a run-on sentence or a sentence where one clause is dependent.
nodes.hinge_reason: Compound sentence errors — run-on sentences, dependent clause errors, wrong conjunction — propagate into all written text production. Students who cannot construct these reliably carry grammatical incoherence into every subsequent writing task.

width.minimum: Write at least two compound sentences using different conjunctions ('and', 'but', 'so') in a short piece of writing.
width.typical: Use compound sentences with varied conjunctions flexibly across simple and compound sentence writing, adjusting conjunction choice to signal intended relationships.
wider: Experiment with compound sentences of three clauses (e.g. 'The wolf huffed / and he puffed / and he blew the house down!') and discuss the rhythmic effect
Revise a piece of writing by converting some simple sentences to compound sentences where the relationship between ideas warrants it

modes.reason: Constructing compound sentences correctly — ensuring both clauses are independent, choosing the right conjunction — requires practice and checking. Errors at this node (run-on sentences, clause-merging errors, wrong conjunction) propagate into written text production. Precision-focused practice is the productive investment here.

descriptors.title: Noun groups and verb groups
descriptors.description: understand that in sentences nouns may be extended into noun groups using articles and adjectives, and verbs may be expressed as verb groups
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand the major word classes — nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs (AC9E1LA07). They have not yet examined how these elements combine into extended noun groups and verb groups that carry richer meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can understand how nouns are extended into noun groups through articles and adjectives, and how verbs are expressed as verb groups.

nodes.label: Extending a noun into a noun group
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that articles and adjectives extend a bare noun into a noun group that provides more specific information.
criteria: Student can identify the head noun and at least one extending element (article or adjective) in a noun group.
Student can build an extended noun group from a bare noun by adding at least an article and one adjective.

width.minimum: Identify the noun, article and at least one adjective in a given noun group (e.g. 'the longest side').
width.typical: Identify noun groups in sentences from a range of texts, naming the head noun and the articles and adjectives that extend it; build extended noun groups from bare nouns by asking 'how many?', 'what type?', 'what's it like?'
wider: Compare noun groups across different text types — sparse noun groups in procedures vs rich noun groups in narratives — and discuss why each text type uses them differently
Build noun groups from bare nouns in cross-curriculum texts (e.g. 'the ancient Egyptian artefact') and discuss how each element adds information

modes.reason: Students often treat adjectives as decoration rather than as group-builders. Seeing noun groups across different text types — where some texts deliberately minimise them and others maximise them — helps students understand that noun group length is a purposeful choice, not random. More text-type examples is the productive move.

nodes.label: Verb groups
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that verbs can be expressed as verb groups — combining an auxiliary or modal verb with a main verb — and explain what the group adds over a simple verb.
criteria: Student can identify the main verb and auxiliary in a verb group.
Student can explain one way the auxiliary changes the meaning of the verb (e.g. tense, passive voice).

width.minimum: Identify a verb group in a sentence (e.g. 'was touched', 'is running') and identify the main verb and its auxiliary.
width.typical: Identify and build verb groups using auxiliaries ('was', 'is', 'has been') and discuss how they change meaning — tense, aspect — compared to a simple verb.
wider: Compare active and passive verb groups ('touched' vs 'was touched') and discuss the effect on who or what is foregrounded
Identify verb groups in shared reading texts from different subject areas and discuss what the auxiliary adds

nodes.label: Noun groups and verb groups in text
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify both noun groups and verb groups in sentences, and explain how they work together to create more precise and expressive sentences.
criteria: Student correctly identifies both the noun group and verb group in a given sentence.
Student can expand a simple sentence by extending at least its noun group or its verb group.

width.minimum: In a given sentence, identify the noun group and the verb group and name their key elements.
width.typical: Analyse sentences across several texts for noun group and verb group complexity; revise simple sentences by expanding noun groups and extending verb groups.
wider: Compare two versions of a sentence — one with simple nouns and verbs, one with extended groups — and discuss how the expanded version changes the image or meaning
Write a short descriptive paragraph deliberately using extended noun groups and verb groups, then annotate what was added and why

modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate noun group and verb group knowledge simultaneously within sentences — the two concepts reinforce and interact. Coordinated identification and production is the learning demand.

descriptors.title: Images add and multiply meaning
descriptors.description: understand that images add to or multiply the meanings of a text
descriptors.knowledge: Students compare how images in different text types contribute to meaning (AC9E1LA08). They have not yet distinguished between images that add new information not in the written text versus images that multiply meaning by amplifying what the written text already expresses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can understand that images add new meaning to a text or multiply existing meaning by amplifying what the written text expresses.

nodes.label: Images add meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an image in a text that adds information not present in the written text and explain what new meaning the image provides.
criteria: Student can identify an image and state at least one piece of information it provides that is not in the written text.
Student can distinguish between what the image adds and what the written text says.

width.minimum: Identify one image in a text that provides information not stated in the written text and explain what new information the image adds.
width.typical: Identify and discuss multiple examples of images that add meaning in factual and narrative texts — maps, tables, illustrations showing setting — distinguishing what comes from the image alone vs the written text.
wider: Compare a factual text with its images removed and discuss what information is lost or becomes unclear
Identify images in digital texts (infographics, diagrams) that carry information the body text does not — and discuss why this division of information is used

nodes.label: Images multiply meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an image that amplifies or extends the meaning of accompanying words — showing emotion, atmosphere or subtext that the words alone do not fully convey.
criteria: Student can identify an image that amplifies or extends the words and explain what additional meaning the image creates.
Student does not describe the image as merely 'showing the same thing' when it does more than this.

width.minimum: Identify an illustration in a narrative that shows a character's emotion or reaction and explain how it extends what the words say.
width.typical: Identify and discuss multiple examples of images that multiply meaning in narratives — characters' actions, reactions, speech bubbles, thought processes — and explain what each adds beyond the written text.
wider: Compare how the same event is represented in the words and the illustration of a picture book and discuss where the image extends, contradicts or enriches the written meaning
Identify an image whose meaning changes depending on the surrounding words — and discuss how the combination creates meaning neither could alone

modes.reason: Students often see illustration as merely decoration or as 'showing what the words say'. The multiply-meaning concept — where the image goes further than the text — is counterintuitive. Multiple narrative examples with different kinds of amplification (emotion, irony, subtext) resolve this. More picture-book examples across different image-text relationships is the productive move.

nodes.label: Add and multiply across text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether images in a given text are adding new meaning or multiplying existing meaning, across both factual and narrative texts.
criteria: Student can identify at least one image that adds meaning and explain what new information it provides.
Student can identify at least one image that multiplies meaning and explain how it extends what the words say.

width.minimum: For a given text, classify at least one image as 'adding' and one as 'multiplying' and explain each.
width.typical: Analyse several texts across factual and narrative genres, identifying instances of images adding meaning and images multiplying meaning, and explain the role of each image in relation to the written text.
wider: Compare the roles of images across a picture book (narrative), an information report and a digital news article — discussing how each text type uses images differently
Create a two-image storyboard where one image adds meaning and one multiplies it, explaining the distinction

modes.reason: Applying both concepts — adding and multiplying — simultaneously to a range of texts requires coordinating the two distinctions. The integration demand is in holding both concepts active while reading.

descriptors.title: Vocabulary choices for topic
descriptors.description: experiment with and begin to make conscious choices of vocabulary to suit the topic
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise vocabulary associated with different learning area topics (AC9E1LA09). They have not yet experimented with making conscious vocabulary choices — replacing everyday language with topic-specific alternatives.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can experiment with vocabulary choices to suit a topic, making conscious decisions to select topic-specific language over everyday alternatives.

nodes.label: Everyday language vs topic-specific language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that topic-specific vocabulary is more precise than everyday language for communicating about a topic, and give at least one example.
criteria: Student can replace at least one everyday word with a topic-specific alternative and explain why the specific word is more precise.
Student can identify topic-specific vocabulary in a given text and name the topic it belongs to.

width.minimum: Replace an everyday word with a topic-specific alternative in a given sentence (e.g. replacing 'went' with 'migrated' in a science text).
width.typical: Identify topic-specific vocabulary in learning area texts, discuss why it is more precise than everyday alternatives, and practise selecting topic-specific vocabulary across Science, HASS and English contexts.
wider: Compare the same information written using everyday language vs topic-specific vocabulary and discuss the difference in precision and audience expectations

Identify First Nations Australians' language words relevant to a specific topic (e.g. Country-related vocabulary in an environmental topic) and discuss what they communicate that everyday language does not

modes.reason: Students often perceive everyday language as 'normal' and topic-specific language as 'hard words'. Multiple subject-area contexts — each with their own topic vocabulary — help students see that specificity is purposeful and reader-serving, not an arbitrary difficulty increase. Cross-curriculum examples are the productive move.

nodes.label: Vocabulary for character description
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select specific nouns and adjectives to describe characters in narratives, moving beyond generic terms to precise vocabulary.
criteria: Student can select a specific noun or adjective for a character and explain what impression it creates.
Student can distinguish between two near-synonyms (e.g. 'timid' vs 'frightened') and explain the different impression each creates.

width.minimum: Replace a generic character description word ('wizard') with a more specific alternative or compare two specific terms ('magician', 'sorcerer', 'wizard') and discuss the difference.
width.typical: Explore vocabulary for character description in narratives — distinguishing between synonymous nouns and adjectives and selecting the most precise for a given character and context.
wider: Compare how different authors describe similar character types (e.g. powerful figures, children in danger) and identify the vocabulary choices that create distinct impressions
Experiment with changing one or two vocabulary choices in a character description and discuss how the impression of the character shifts

nodes.label: Making conscious vocabulary choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make conscious vocabulary choices when writing — experimenting with alternatives and selecting the word that best suits the topic and purpose.
criteria: Student can identify and explain at least one deliberate vocabulary choice in their own writing.
Student replaces at least one everyday word with a topic-specific or more precise alternative during editing.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without an explicit reasoning process for vocabulary selection, students default to the first word available throughout all writing — the conscious choice-making habit established here is required for the editing phase in any subsequent writing task.

width.minimum: In a short piece of writing, identify one vocabulary choice they made deliberately and explain why they chose that word over an alternative.
width.typical: During editing, make at least two deliberate vocabulary replacements — replacing everyday language with topic-specific or more precise vocabulary — and explain each choice.
wider: Use a vocabulary journal or word wall from a current topic to draw on topic-specific vocabulary when writing, making choices from the range available
Compare a draft and a revised version of their own writing, annotating the vocabulary changes and explaining the improvement

modes.reason: Making a conscious vocabulary choice involves a reasoning chain — what is the topic, who is the audience, what does this word mean vs this one, which is more precise? Making that reasoning explicit (through think-aloud, annotation or discussion) helps students internalise the process rather than defaulting to the first word that comes to mind.

descriptors.title: Capitals in titles, commas in lists
descriptors.description: recognise that capital letters are used in titles and commas are used to separate items in lists
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand sentence boundary punctuation and capital letters for proper nouns and sentence beginnings (AC9E1LA10). They have not yet recognised capital letters as a title-marking convention or commas as list separators.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise that capital letters mark titles and that commas separate items in lists.

nodes.label: Capital letters in titles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify capital letters used in the titles of texts and explain that this is a convention for marking titles, distinct from sentence-start capitals.
criteria: Student can identify capitals in a title and explain this as a title convention.
Student does not confuse title capitalisation with sentence-start capitalisation.

width.minimum: Identify capital letters in the title of a text and explain that titles are capitalised by convention.
width.typical: Identify and compare capital letter usage in titles across different text types — books, news articles, posters, headings — and discuss what counts as a title.
wider: Compare different capitalisation conventions in titles (all words vs content words only vs first word only) across different text types and contexts
Identify titles in digital contexts (website headings, video titles, app names) and compare capitalisation conventions with print texts

modes.reason: Students need to build accurate recognition of title capitalisation as a distinct convention from sentence-start capitals. Precision in distinguishing these two uses requires targeted practice — more examples across text types, with attention to what is and isn't capitalised in titles.

nodes.label: Commas in lists
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify commas used to separate items in a list and explain their function as separators.
criteria: Student can identify commas separating items in a list.
Student can explain that commas separate list items and that 'and' typically precedes the final item.

width.minimum: Identify the commas in a sentence with a list of items and explain that they separate the items.
width.typical: Identify commas in lists across a variety of texts — shopping lists, class descriptions, informative texts — and discuss where commas appear vs where 'and' is used instead.
wider: Compare list punctuation with and without commas in different contexts and discuss how commas prevent ambiguity
Identify lists in multimodal texts (e.g. dot-point lists vs running-text lists) and compare how commas function in each

modes.reason: Accurate comma placement in lists is a precision skill. Students commonly omit the comma before 'and' or insert commas where they are not needed. Targeted practice — reading and producing lists — builds the fluency needed before this skill appears in writing.

descriptors.title: Characters and settings across contexts
descriptors.description: discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature created by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss how language and images create characters, settings and events in literature from First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors (AC9E1LE01). They have not yet examined how the connection between character and setting varies across different cultural and national literary traditions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature from First Nations Australian, wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators.

nodes.label: Character-setting connections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how a character belongs to or is shaped by the setting they inhabit in a literary text.
criteria: Student can identify a specific connection between a character and their setting in a given text.
Student can explain how the setting influences at least one aspect of the character's behaviour or experience.

width.minimum: Identify one way a character in a familiar text is connected to their setting — e.g. the character's actions, knowledge or challenges are shaped by where they are.
width.typical: Discuss character-setting connections across several texts — narrative, picture book, short story — identifying how setting shapes what characters do, what they know and what problems they face.
wider: Compare two texts with very different settings and discuss how each shapes the types of characters who inhabit them
Discuss how the Australian landscape shapes Australian characters differently from European fairy-tale settings

nodes.label: World literature traditions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how character-setting connections are used in literature from different world traditions and identify recurring patterns.
criteria: Student can identify a recurring character-setting pattern in at least one literary tradition.
Student can explain why certain characters and settings recur together in that tradition.

width.minimum: Identify a recurring character-setting pattern in a familiar world literary tradition — e.g. children in forests in European fairy tales, royalty in castles.
width.typical: Discuss recurring character-setting patterns across several world literary traditions, exploring why certain settings recur with certain types of characters and what cultural meanings they carry.
wider: Compare the settings used for similar character archetypes (e.g. powerful figures, lost children) across European, Asian and African literary traditions
Investigate how illustrators from different cultural backgrounds depict settings differently for similar story types

modes.reason: Understanding that character-setting conventions vary across world traditions requires students to accumulate examples from different literary traditions. Schema for 'what is typical for this tradition' only forms once enough varied examples have been experienced. Breadth of literary traditions is the productive investment.

nodes.label: First Nations Australian literature
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how First Nations Australian authors use character-setting connections that reflect relationships with Country and Place.
criteria: Student can identify a character-setting connection in a text by a First Nations Australian author.
Student can discuss at least one feature of how this connection differs from or enriches their understanding beyond other literary traditions.

width.minimum: Identify a character-setting connection in a text by a First Nations Australian author and discuss one way it differs from or is similar to connections in other texts they have read.
width.typical: Discuss how First Nations Australian authors depict characters whose identities and actions are connected to Country, Place and community; recognise recurring character types in texts by First Nations Australian authors.
wider: Compare how the same geographical setting (e.g. a specific country or region) is depicted by a First Nations Australian author vs a non-First Nations author, discussing differences in the relationship between character and place
Explore how illustrations in texts by First Nations Australian illustrators visually represent character-Country connections

descriptors.title: Features and personal preferences
descriptors.description: identify features of literary texts, such as characters and settings, and give reasons for personal preferences
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss literary texts and share responses connecting to their own experiences (AC9E1LE02). They have not yet identified specific literary features as the basis for preference — their responses remain experience-anchored rather than feature-anchored.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify features of literary texts such as characters and settings and give reasoned explanations for personal preferences.

nodes.label: Naming features as a basis for preference
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a specific literary feature — character, setting, plot event — as the basis for a preference, rather than giving an undifferentiated response.
criteria: Student names a specific literary feature as the basis for a preference.
Student's reason references what the feature does or is, not just how they felt.

width.minimum: Name one literary feature they responded to and explain why it created their preference.
width.typical: Identify multiple literary features across several texts and give reasons for preferences that reference specific features — character type, setting, narrative structure — rather than general feeling.
wider: Compare preferences for stories set in familiar vs unfamiliar worlds and discuss what makes each type appealing
Discuss preferences for characters whose lives are like or unlike their own, naming what draws them to each type

modes.reason: Students commonly give vague preference statements ('it was fun') or purely experiential ones ('it was like my life'). Moving to feature-anchored preference language ('I preferred the character because the setting made her actions surprising') requires exposure to multiple texts where different features create different preference responses. More texts, not more practice with one, is the productive move.

nodes.label: Responding to character behaviour
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss their feelings about characters' positive and negative behaviours and explain how these behaviours influence their preference for the text.
criteria: Student can identify a character behaviour and explain how it shaped their preference for the text.
Student can distinguish between liking a character and liking a text — explaining that a preference can be based on a character they found compelling rather than likeable.

width.minimum: Identify a character behaviour (positive or negative) and explain how it influenced their response to the text.
width.typical: Discuss responses to multiple character types — non-human characters including animals, characters with mixed behaviours — giving reasoned explanations for how behaviour shapes preference.
wider: Compare responses to the same character whose behaviour changes across a narrative — e.g. a villain who shows sympathy — and discuss how this complexity affects preference
Discuss non-human characters (animals, fantasy creatures) whose behaviour follows or subverts human expectations, and how this creates a preference response

descriptors.title: Language presents characters and settings
descriptors.description: discuss the characters and settings of a range of texts and identify how language is used to present these features in different ways
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss plot, character and setting as features of stories (AC9E1LE03). They have not yet examined how specific language choices present characters and settings differently across texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify how language is used to present characters and settings in different ways across a range of texts.

nodes.label: Language that describes character
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language — specific nouns and adjectives — used to describe a character's appearance and personality, and explain what impression that language creates.
criteria: Student can identify specific language used to describe a character and explain the impression it creates.
Student can name at least one noun and one adjective from the character description and explain how each contributes.

width.minimum: Identify two language features — at least one noun and one adjective — used to describe a character and explain the impression each creates.
width.typical: Identify and compare the language used to describe characters across multiple texts, noticing how different word choices create different impressions of similar character types.
wider: Compare how a hero and a villain in the same text are described using contrasting language choices, and discuss how the author uses language to position the reader
Examine how a character is described at the start vs the end of a narrative and identify how language reflects character change

nodes.label: Language that creates a sense of place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language used to create a sense of place in a text — specific nouns, adjectives and verbs — and explain how they establish the setting.
criteria: Student can identify specific language used to describe a setting and explain what it contributes to the sense of place.
Student can compare language features across at least two settings from different texts.

width.minimum: Identify two language features used to describe a setting and explain what they contribute to the sense of place.
width.typical: Identify and discuss setting language across multiple texts — urban, natural, fantastical, familiar — comparing how language features create different atmospheric effects.
wider: Compare how two authors describe the same type of setting (e.g. a forest, a beach) using different language choices, and discuss the different effects
Identify language that creates a sense of Australian place — including references to specific landscapes, flora and fauna — and compare with settings from world literature

nodes.label: Different presentations of the same feature
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that different authors use different language to present similar characters or settings, and discuss the different effects produced.
criteria: Student can name a language difference between two texts presenting similar features and explain the different effect each creates.
Student can discuss why different authors might choose different language to present similar characters or settings.

width.minimum: Compare two texts with a similar character type or setting and name one language difference that creates a different presentation.
width.typical: Discuss how a range of texts present similar features differently — through vocabulary, tone, description density — and explain how different language choices produce different effects on the reader.
wider: Compare presentations of a familiar character archetype (e.g. the wise elder, the brave child) across texts from different cultural contexts and discuss how cultural context shapes the language
Identify how the same setting is presented differently in a narrative vs an information text and discuss what this reveals about purpose and language

modes.reason: This node integrates character-language and setting-language knowledge across texts. Holding multiple texts in view simultaneously and comparing specific language choices is the coordination demand.

descriptors.title: Experiment with sound and word patterns
descriptors.description: identify, reproduce and experiment with rhythmic sound and word patterns in poems, chants, rhymes or songs
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss and imitate sound patterns including alliteration and rhyme in poems, chants and songs (AC9E1LE04). They have not yet reproduced patterns with accuracy or experimented with inventing new rhythmic sound and word patterns.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify, reproduce and experiment with rhythmic sound and word patterns in poems, chants, rhymes and songs.

nodes.label: Identifying rhythmic patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the rhythmic pattern in a poem, chant or rhyme — including where stresses fall and where lines repeat — and describe the pattern.
criteria: Student can describe the rhythmic pattern of a given poem or chant.
Student can identify where stresses fall or where repetition occurs in the pattern.

width.minimum: Identify the rhythmic pattern in a simple poem or chant by marking stressed syllables or describing the pattern of repetition.
width.typical: Identify and compare rhythmic patterns across multiple poems, chants and songs — noting patterns of stress, repetition and line length — and discuss the effects of different patterns.
wider: Compare the rhythmic patterns of chants from different cultural traditions and discuss how rhythm serves the purpose (ceremony, play, story)
Identify rhythmic patterns in poems with irregular rhythms and discuss the effect of variation

nodes.label: Reproducing sound patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reproduce a rhythmic sound or word pattern from a poem, chant, rhyme or song with accuracy.
criteria: Student can reproduce the key features of a rhythmic pattern — stress, repetition, rhyme — with reasonable accuracy.
Student maintains the pattern across the whole poem or chant, not just the first line.

width.minimum: Read or recite a poem or chant maintaining its rhythmic pattern with reasonable accuracy.
width.typical: Reproduce rhythmic patterns from multiple poems and chants across different forms — rhyming couplets, repetitive refrains, alliterative patterns — maintaining the pattern's key features.
wider: Perform a chant or poem with deliberate variation in volume, pace and emphasis to highlight the rhythmic pattern
Reproduce a rhythmic pattern in a different context — e.g. applying the pattern from one poem to new content

modes.reason: Reproducing rhythmic patterns accurately requires repeated practice — the motor and auditory memory involved in maintaining a pattern across performance needs consolidation. Practice across multiple performances is more productive than widening the types of patterns at this stage.

nodes.label: Experimenting with new patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with creating their own rhythmic sound and word patterns — inventing new words, changing syllables, substituting sounds — to produce a poem, chant or rhyming sequence.
criteria: Student produces an original rhythmic sequence with an identifiable pattern.
Student can explain what sound or word pattern they used and what effect they were aiming for.

width.minimum: Create a short original rhythmic sequence (at least two lines) that uses a deliberate sound or word pattern.
width.typical: Experiment with syllable manipulation, invented words and sound substitution to create original rhythmic sequences; explore how poets use word sounds to create effects for an audience.
wider: Create a new verse for an existing poem or chant that maintains the original rhythmic pattern
Invent nonsense words using known sound patterns and discuss how sound can create meaning even when words are invented

modes.reason: Experimenting with sound patterns benefits from an explicit creative reasoning scaffold — what pattern am I using, what sound effect am I going for, does my line fit the pattern? Making this process visible helps students move from accidental to deliberate sound play.

descriptors.title: Create texts using literary features
descriptors.description: create imaginative texts or adaptations of texts using key features of literary texts appropriate to Year 2
descriptors.knowledge: Students retell or adapt familiar stories using plot, characters, language features and structure (AC9E1LE05). They have not yet independently created imaginative texts or adaptations that deliberately apply key literary features as design choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can create imaginative texts or adaptations using key literary features including character, setting, and narrative structure appropriate to Year 2.

nodes.label: Identifying features to use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify key literary features in a model text and articulate how they will use those features in their own creation.
criteria: Student can name at least two literary features from a model text.
Student can articulate how they will use each feature in their own creation before drafting.
nodes.hinge_reason: Shallow feature identification at this node cascades directly into Nodes 2 and 3 — students who have not clearly identified which features they will use produce character and setting descriptions that lack deliberate design, and narratives with no coherent structural basis.

width.minimum: Identify at least two literary features in a model text and state which they will use in their own creation.
width.typical: Analyse a model text for literary features — character type, setting, structural pattern, language choices — and make deliberate decisions about which to use and how to adapt them for their own text.
wider: Compare features across two model texts with different tones or purposes and discuss which features would suit their intended creation
Use a planning frame to map their intended character, setting and narrative structure before drafting

modes.reason: In Mode B, the planning phase is a hinge — shallow analysis of the model text cascades into an underdeveloped creation. Making the feature-identification and feature-selection reasoning explicit before drafting begins prevents downstream phase collapse.

nodes.label: Creating character and setting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a character and setting for their imaginative text using deliberate language choices that establish each feature.
criteria: Student creates a character with at least one specific language choice that establishes personality or appearance.
Student creates a setting with at least one language choice that establishes a sense of place.
Student's character and setting are meaningfully connected — the setting is not arbitrary.

width.minimum: Write a character description and setting description using at least one specific language choice for each.
width.typical: Create characters with distinct personalities and settings with a clear sense of place, using specific vocabulary — nouns, adjectives — and establishing how character and setting connect.
wider: Create a character who is transformed by or in conflict with their setting, using language that makes the connection explicit
Adapt an existing character into a different setting and discuss how the change affects the character's behaviour and the language used to describe them

nodes.label: Structuring a narrative
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a short narrative or adaptation with a recognisable narrative structure — orientation, complication, resolution — and review it for coherence.
criteria: Student's narrative has an identifiable orientation, complication and resolution.
Student's character and setting are established using specific language features.
Student can review their text and identify at least one aspect they revised.

width.minimum: Write a short narrative with an identifiable orientation, complication and resolution.
width.typical: Create or adapt a complete narrative with a coherent structure, using language features studied — noun groups, character description, setting language — and review for structural completeness and vocabulary choices.
wider: Create an adaptation that changes a familiar story's setting or character and discuss how the change affects the plot and resolution
Write a narrative with a complication that requires the character to draw on the setting — using character-setting connection as a narrative device

modes.reason: Creating a complete narrative requires students to coordinate character creation, setting establishment, and narrative structure simultaneously — integrating all the literary features studied. Coordinated execution across all components is the learning demand of this phase.

descriptors.title: Similar topics in different texts
descriptors.description: identify how similar topics and information are presented in different types of texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss different texts and identify features that indicate their purposes (AC9E1LY01). They have not yet compared how the same topic is presented across different text types — their prior work focused on identifying features within single texts, not across texts on the same topic.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify how similar topics and information are presented in different types of texts.

nodes.label: Same topic, different text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that the same topic can be presented in different text types and name at least two text types that cover a given topic.
criteria: Student can name at least two text types that present the same topic.
Student can identify the purpose of each text type they name.

width.minimum: Identify two different text types that cover the same topic and name each type.
width.typical: Explore a topic across three or more text types — e.g. lifecycle in a poem, a narrative and an information report — and identify what each type is called and what its purpose is.
wider: Compare how a practical topic (e.g. recipes) is presented in print books, food packets, short video clips and digital apps — noting shared purpose and different forms
Identify a topic covered in a school subject and find multiple text types (textbook, website, picture book) that address it

nodes.label: What changes across text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least one way the presentation of information differs across text types covering the same topic — e.g. organisation, language, detail level.
criteria: Student can name one difference between how the same information is presented in two different text types.
Student can explain one reason why the text types present the information differently.

width.minimum: Identify one difference in how the same information is presented in two different text types.
width.typical: Compare how a topic is presented across two or more text types — discussing differences in organisation, vocabulary, level of detail, use of images — and explain why each text type presents the topic in its distinctive way.
wider: Discuss what is learned from each text type about the same topic that cannot be learned from the others alone
Compare how a poem and an information report about the same topic use language differently and discuss why

modes.reason: Students often assume that one text type gives them all the information they need. Comparing multiple text types on the same topic — and noticing what each adds or emphasises differently — resolves the single-text misconception. More topic-and-text-type pairings is the productive investment.

descriptors.title: Express and respond to opinions
descriptors.description: use interaction skills when engaging with topics, actively listening to others, receiving instructions and extending own ideas, speaking appropriately, expressing and responding to opinions, making statements, and giving instructions
descriptors.knowledge: Students use interaction skills including turn-taking, active listening and responding to others' contributions (AC9E1LY02). They have not yet expressed and responded to opinions using specific sentence frames, or given instructions to others.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can use interaction skills to actively listen, express and respond to opinions, extend their own ideas, and give instructions in discussions.

nodes.label: Active listening and responding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate active listening by paraphrasing or responding to a partner's contribution before extending the discussion.
criteria: Student demonstrates at least one active listening behaviour (paraphrasing, acknowledgement) before adding their own contribution.
Student's response is connected to what the previous speaker said.

width.minimum: Paraphrase or summarise a partner's contribution before adding their own idea in a think-pair-share activity.
width.typical: Demonstrate active listening behaviours — eye contact, paraphrasing, responding to what was said — across different discussion contexts including class discussion, partner talk and small group work.
wider: Use sentence starters that acknowledge the speaker before responding: 'I agree that ... and I'd add ...', 'I heard you say ... and I think ...'
Identify when a response in a discussion did not acknowledge the previous speaker and discuss the effect on the conversation

modes.reason: Active listening in practice — actually paraphrasing before responding, not just nodding — requires repeated rehearsal across many discussion contexts. The skill does not vary meaningfully across topics; what varies is whether students habitually deploy it. Practice, not more types of listening, is the productive investment.

nodes.label: Expressing and responding to opinions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express an opinion using appropriate language and respond to another's opinion — agreeing, disagreeing or offering an alternative — respectfully.
criteria: Student expresses an opinion using an appropriate sentence frame.
Student responds to another's opinion in a way that acknowledges it and either agrees, disagrees or offers an alternative.

width.minimum: Express an opinion on a topic using a sentence starter, and respond to a classmate's opinion with at least one appropriate response frame.
width.typical: Express opinions using varied sentence starters across multiple discussion contexts; respond to others using frames that agree, disagree or offer an alternative; understand how to disagree respectfully.
wider: Compare how the same opinion sounds with a confident vs tentative sentence starter and discuss when each is appropriate
Practise a discussion where the task requires each participant to disagree respectfully with the previous speaker

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of sentence starters and response frames — agreeing, disagreeing, offering alternatives, extending. No single frame covers all interaction contexts. Building a usable repertoire across multiple discussion tasks is the productive investment.

nodes.label: Giving and receiving instructions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can give clear instructions and receive instructions, asking clarifying questions where needed.
