criteria: Student gives instructions in an appropriate sequence that a listener could follow.
Student can receive instructions and ask a clarifying question if something is unclear.

width.minimum: Give a set of at least two instructions for a familiar task in an appropriate sequence.
width.typical: Give and receive instructions across different contexts — classroom tasks, game rules, procedures — using appropriate sequencing language and checking for understanding.
wider: Compare instructions given verbally vs in written procedure form and discuss what each mode does well
Give instructions to a partner who must follow them without additional help, then evaluate clarity and completeness together

descriptors.title: Purpose and audience of texts
descriptors.description: identify the purpose and audience of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students describe similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts (AC9E1LY03). They have not yet identified specific intended audiences and distinguished these from general purposes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify the purpose and audience of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts.

nodes.label: Identifying text purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a given text — to entertain, to inform, to persuade — and connect this to the type of text.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the purpose of an imaginative, an informative and a persuasive text.
Student can name at least one text feature that signals the purpose of each text.

width.minimum: Identify the purpose of one imaginative, one informative and one persuasive text.
width.typical: Identify and discuss the purposes of a range of texts across all three types, including texts by First Nations Australian authors, explaining what the purpose is and what text features signal it.
wider: Identify texts written by First Nations Australian authors and discuss their purposes — noting where purposes may include preserving cultural knowledge, sharing stories of Country, or engaging with specific communities
Identify advertisements and signs as persuasive texts and discuss what they are trying to persuade the audience to do or believe

nodes.label: Identifying intended audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the intended audience of a text and explain how they know — using features such as vocabulary, illustrations, form and content as evidence.
criteria: Student can identify the intended audience of a text.
Student can name at least one text feature that signals who the intended audience is.

width.minimum: Identify the intended audience of a given text and name one feature that indicates this.
width.typical: Identify intended audiences across several texts — different age groups, community members, consumers — and discuss how text features (vocabulary level, illustrations, context) signal who the audience is.
wider: Compare the audiences for two versions of similar information aimed at different groups (e.g. a children's and an adult's book on the same topic) and identify what features change
Identify the audience for an advertisement or sign and discuss what the creator assumed about that audience

modes.reason: Students often think 'audience' means 'people' in a general sense. The concept of a specific, designed-for audience — and the features that mark it — only becomes clear across multiple examples with different audiences. More varied audience examples, not more explanation of one, is the productive move.

descriptors.title: Read with fluency and self-correct
descriptors.description: read texts with phrasing and fluency, using phonic and word knowledge, and monitoring meaning by re-reading and self-correcting
descriptors.knowledge: Students read texts with developing phrasing and fluency, monitoring meaning using context and grammar (AC9E1LY04). They have not yet self-corrected systematically using phonic and word knowledge, or re-read specifically to restore lost meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can read texts with phrasing and fluency, using phonic and word knowledge, and monitor meaning by re-reading and self-correcting.

nodes.label: Using phonic and word knowledge to decode
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use phonic (sound-letter) and morphemic knowledge, and knowledge of high-frequency words, to decode unfamiliar words during reading.
criteria: Student applies a decoding strategy when encountering an unfamiliar word rather than stopping or guessing randomly.
Student correctly decodes a range of word types using appropriate strategies.
nodes.hinge_reason: Automatic decoding is a prerequisite for Nodes 2 and 3 — students who cannot decode without conscious effort cannot allocate attention to monitoring meaning or self-correcting. Decoding bottlenecks collapse the monitoring and self-correction work that follows.

width.minimum: Apply at least one decoding strategy — phonic, morphemic or sight word — when encountering an unfamiliar word in a text.
width.typical: Use phonic knowledge, morphemic knowledge and high-frequency word recognition in combination when decoding, selecting the most appropriate strategy for different word types.
wider: Identify which decoding strategy was most useful for a given unfamiliar word and explain why
Read texts with increasing complexity of word patterns — compound words, silent letters, vowel digraphs — applying appropriate decoding strategies

modes.reason: Reliable decoding requires fluency — automatic application of phonic and word knowledge without slowing comprehension. Practice across multiple reading contexts builds the automaticity this node requires. More reading practice is more productive than widening decoding strategy types at this stage.

nodes.label: Monitoring meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can monitor their own comprehension during reading and identify when meaning has broken down.
criteria: Student can identify a point in a text where meaning broke down and name a reason.
Student pauses voluntarily when meaning is lost rather than continuing without comprehension.
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying where meaning has broken down is a prerequisite for Node 3 self-correcting — students who cannot locate the comprehension failure point cannot apply a targeted correction strategy.

width.minimum: Identify a moment during reading when meaning is lost and describe what caused the breakdown.
width.typical: Monitor comprehension during reading across different text types, pausing when meaning breaks down and identifying whether the problem is a word, sentence or whole-text level issue.
wider: Practise metacognitive reading commentary — thinking aloud about comprehension monitoring — to make the monitoring process visible
Compare the experience of reading with and without monitoring comprehension and discuss what is missed when monitoring is not active

modes.reason: Monitoring comprehension requires an explicit internal reasoning process — 'Does this make sense? Where did I lose meaning? Is it a word or a sentence?' Making this process visible through think-aloud or commentary helps students develop self-monitoring as a deliberate habit rather than a passive one.

nodes.label: Re-reading and self-correcting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can re-read and self-correct when meaning breaks down, using available cues — phonic knowledge, syntax, context — to restore accurate reading.
criteria: Student self-corrects reading errors without prompting from the teacher.
Student can explain what cue they used to identify and correct the error.

width.minimum: Re-read a sentence where meaning was lost and produce a corrected reading, explaining what cue was used to self-correct.
width.typical: Self-correct spontaneously across a range of reading texts and text types, using phonic, syntactic and semantic cues; re-read sections when correction is needed rather than continuing past the error.
wider: Analyse a reading error — 'I said X, I should have said Y' — and identify which cue (sound, meaning, grammar) was used to detect and correct it
Compare the effect of self-correcting vs not self-correcting on overall comprehension of a passage

descriptors.title: Build and monitor meaning
descriptors.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning to build literal and inferred meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students use comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning, drawing on vocabulary and knowledge of text structures (AC9E1LY05). They have not yet added monitoring and summarising strategies, or made inferences by integrating print, image and prior knowledge simultaneously.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can use comprehension strategies including visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning to build literal and inferred meaning.

nodes.label: Predicting and connecting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use prior knowledge and text cues to predict content and vocabulary, and connect text to personal experience or prior knowledge.
criteria: Student makes a prediction supported by a text cue or prior knowledge before reading.
Student makes at least one connection between the text and prior knowledge or experience during or after reading.

width.minimum: Make one prediction before or during reading that is supported by at least one text cue or prior knowledge.
width.typical: Use predicting strategies — vocabulary prediction from topic and purpose, content prediction from images and headings — across a range of text types; connect texts to personal experience or prior knowledge and discuss the connections.
wider: Predict vocabulary likely to appear in texts from different subjects based on topic knowledge, then verify predictions during reading
Connect two texts on the same topic and discuss what each adds to or changes about prior knowledge

nodes.label: Making inferences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make a supportable inference by integrating information from print, images and prior knowledge.
criteria: Student makes an inference that integrates at least two sources of information.
Student can identify which sources of information support the inference (text, image, prior knowledge).

width.minimum: Make one inference and identify at least two sources of information used to support it (e.g. text + image, text + prior knowledge).
width.typical: Make inferences across a range of text types — narrative and informative — integrating print, image and prior knowledge; identify the main idea of a text as a form of inference.
wider: Use a graphic organiser to record text evidence, image evidence and prior knowledge used to support an inference, then discuss how confident the inference is
Compare inferences made by different readers about the same text and discuss why they might differ

modes.reason: Students often treat inference as guessing. The key misconception is that inferences are unsupported. Multiple text examples — where the inference is clearly grounded in combinations of evidence sources — resolve this. More text-type and evidence-source combinations is the productive investment.

nodes.label: Monitoring, summarising and questioning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can monitor their comprehension, identify key information for summarising, and generate questions during and after reading.
criteria: Student can identify the main idea of a text.
Student generates at least one question during or after reading that goes beyond what was explicitly stated.
Student identifies when their comprehension has broken down and takes a monitoring action.

width.minimum: Identify the main idea of a text and generate at least one question about something they want to know more about.
width.typical: Apply monitoring, summarising and questioning strategies across informative and persuasive texts — identifying main idea, tracking comprehension, generating questions before, during and after reading.
wider: Use a graphic organiser to represent connections between characters, order of events or sequence of information after reading
Compare summaries made by different students of the same text and discuss what was included or omitted and why

modes.reason: This node requires students to deploy multiple comprehension strategies simultaneously — monitoring while reading, identifying key ideas for summarising, generating questions throughout. Coordinating these as a set of active reading behaviours is the integration demand.

descriptors.title: Create texts for familiar audiences
descriptors.description: create and edit short imaginative, informative and persuasive written and/or multimodal texts for familiar audiences, using text structure appropriate to purpose, simple and compound sentences, noun groups and verb groups, topic-specific vocabulary, simple punctuation and common 2-syllable words
descriptors.knowledge: Students create and edit short written and multimodal texts using simple sentences, topic vocabulary and sentence boundary punctuation (AC9E1LY06). They have not yet created persuasive texts, used compound sentences, extended noun groups or verb groups, or edited for vocabulary precision.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can create and edit short imaginative, informative and persuasive written or multimodal texts for familiar audiences using appropriate structure, grammar, vocabulary and punctuation.

nodes.label: Selecting structure for purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select or plan a text structure appropriate to their purpose — imaginative, informative or persuasive — before writing.
criteria: Student can name the purpose of their text before drafting.
Student selects a text structure appropriate to that purpose.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a structural plan established here, Nodes 2 and 3 lack a framework — students produce sentences and vocabulary that are grammatically capable but structurally incoherent, rendering the editing node unable to recover the text.

width.minimum: Identify the purpose of their text and name a text structure appropriate to that purpose before drafting.
width.typical: Plan texts across all three purposes — identifying structural features appropriate to each — and use planning tools (graphic organisers, sequence frames) to organise ideas before drafting.
wider: Compare two possible structures for the same purpose and decide which suits the intended audience better
Plan a multimodal text considering how written and visual elements each contribute to the structure

modes.reason: In Mode B, planning is the phase that governs all downstream creation. A student who begins writing without a clear structural plan produces incoherent texts. Making the planning reasoning explicit — purpose, audience, structure — before drafting prevents phase collapse.

nodes.label: Constructing sentences with noun and verb groups
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use simple and compound sentences with extended noun groups and verb groups correctly and flexibly in their writing.
criteria: Student produces at least one compound sentence with two independent clauses correctly joined.
Student uses at least one extended noun group (noun + article + adjective) in their writing.
nodes.hinge_reason: Errors in compound sentence construction and noun group extension produced at this node carry into Node 3 — the editing node requires a draft with these features present to review; without them there is nothing to improve and the editing task collapses to surface punctuation only.

width.minimum: Write at least one sentence with an extended noun group and one compound sentence in a short piece of writing.
width.typical: Use simple and compound sentences flexibly across a short text, including extended noun groups and verb groups where appropriate to express ideas precisely.
wider: Review a draft by identifying places where noun groups could be extended to add precision or where compound sentences could be used to show relationships between ideas
Compare a draft with simple sentences only to a revised version with compound sentences and noun groups, discussing the improvement

modes.reason: Correct and flexible use of compound sentences and extended noun groups in produced text requires repeated practice with self-checking. Students who understand the concepts in isolation still produce errors in extended writing. Practice in writing and reviewing is the productive investment.

nodes.label: Editing for vocabulary and accuracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit their own writing by making deliberate vocabulary replacements and reviewing grammatical accuracy.
criteria: Student makes at least one vocabulary change during editing and can explain why the change improves the text.
Student reviews for at least one grammatical feature (pronoun use or sentence construction) during editing.

width.minimum: Identify and change at least one vocabulary item (replacing everyday language with topic-specific vocabulary) during editing.
width.typical: Edit writing for vocabulary precision — replacing everyday nouns with topic-specific alternatives — and grammatical accuracy — reviewing pronoun use and sentence construction — using digital tools where appropriate.
wider: Use a revision checklist to guide editing across vocabulary, grammar and punctuation simultaneously
Compare a first draft and an edited version, annotating what was changed and explaining why each change improves the text

modes.reason: Editing requires students to coordinate structural awareness, vocabulary knowledge and grammatical knowledge simultaneously. Holding all three dimensions active while reviewing a produced text is the integration demand of this phase.

descriptors.title: Deliver presentations with purpose
descriptors.description: create, rehearse and deliver short oral and/or multimodal presentations for familiar audiences and purposes, using text structure appropriate to purpose and topic-specific vocabulary, and varying tone, volume and pace
descriptors.knowledge: Students create and deliver short presentations with clear structure, topic vocabulary and appropriate gesture, volume and pace (AC9E1LY07). They have not yet deliberately rehearsed presentations or varied tone, volume and pace as purposeful delivery strategies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can create, rehearse and deliver short oral or multimodal presentations for familiar audiences and purposes, varying tone, volume and pace.

nodes.label: Planning structure and vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a short presentation with a structure appropriate to its purpose and identify topic-specific vocabulary they will use.
criteria: Student plans a presentation with an identifiable structure appropriate to its purpose.
Student identifies at least two topic-specific vocabulary items to use in the presentation.

width.minimum: Plan a presentation with an identifiable structure (e.g. introduction, key points, conclusion) and identify at least two topic-specific vocabulary items to use.
width.typical: Plan presentations across different purposes — informative, persuasive — using structures appropriate to each, identifying topic-specific vocabulary and sequencing ideas or events logically.
wider: Compare the planning structure for an informative vs a persuasive presentation and discuss what changes
Plan a multimodal presentation, deciding which ideas will be communicated through speech vs through visual elements

nodes.label: Rehearsing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can rehearse a presentation, practising appropriate tone, volume and pace.
criteria: Student rehearses the presentation and identifies at least one delivery element to improve.
Student implements at least one change in the final delivery based on rehearsal.

width.minimum: Rehearse a presentation at least once and identify one aspect of delivery (tone, volume or pace) to improve.
width.typical: Rehearse presentations using feedback — self, peer or teacher — to improve delivery elements including volume, pace and tone; practise adjusting volume and tone for more formal delivery contexts.
wider: Rehearse with a specific audience in mind and discuss how the delivery changes for different audiences
Record a rehearsal and use the recording to identify specific delivery improvements

modes.reason: Rehearsal requires repetition — practising the same presentation multiple times with deliberate attention to delivery elements. The productive investment is repeated practice with feedback, not widening delivery contexts before the basics are established.

nodes.label: Delivering with varied tone, volume and pace
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliver a presentation varying tone, volume and pace deliberately to serve the purpose and engage the audience.
criteria: Student delivers a presentation with at least one variation in tone, volume or pace.
Student uses topic-specific vocabulary in the delivered presentation.
Student maintains appropriate delivery for the context — volume audible, pace not rushed — throughout.

width.minimum: Deliver a presentation with at least one deliberate variation in tone, volume or pace.
width.typical: Deliver presentations with varied tone, volume and pace appropriate to purpose — adjusting for more formal situations — and use topic-specific vocabulary consistently.
wider: Evaluate their own or a peer's delivery using specific criteria for tone, volume and pace, and discuss what the variation achieved
Deliver the same content with two different delivery styles (e.g. formal vs informal) and discuss the effect on the audience

descriptors.title: Write legibly with growing fluency
descriptors.description: write words legibly and with growing fluency using unjoined upper-case and lower-case letters
descriptors.knowledge: Students write letters with developing formation using unjoined upper- and lower-case letters (Foundation). They have not yet written with growing fluency — consistent letter forms that do not slow down writing production.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can write words legibly with growing fluency using consistent unjoined upper-case and lower-case letters.

nodes.label: Consistent letter formation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can form upper-case and lower-case letters consistently and legibly across a short piece of writing.
criteria: Student's letters are recognisably correct and legible across a short piece of writing.
Student demonstrates a functional pencil grip/grasp.
nodes.hinge_reason: If letter formation is not automatic, cognitive load from handwriting displaces the composition capacity needed for all written production tasks — students who must consciously form letters cannot simultaneously plan, draft or edit what they are writing.

width.minimum: Write a short passage where all letters are correctly formed and legible.
width.typical: Sustain consistent and legible letter formation across varied writing tasks — short compositions, lists, labels — maintaining correct pencil grip/grasp.
wider: Limited width — consistent letter formation does not vary meaningfully across contexts. Extensions such as speed writing or letter size variation go further in one dimension rather than broadening the skill.

modes.reason: Letter formation is a fluency and automaticity task. Students need repeated practice to consolidate accurate, legible formation so that handwriting does not consume cognitive resources needed for composition. Practice and habit-forming is the productive investment — width is thin.

nodes.label: Growing writing fluency
nodes.checkpoint: Students write at a pace that does not impede composition — forming letters without significant pausing or re-forming.
criteria: Student completes writing tasks without pausing significantly to re-form individual letters.
Writing pace is sufficient that ideas are not lost while forming letters.
nodes.hinge_reason: Writing pace that cannot keep up with ideas causes composition to stall regardless of vocabulary or grammar knowledge — students lose their intended ideas before they can be recorded, undermining all subsequent written composition tasks.

width.minimum: Complete a short timed writing task (e.g. two or three sentences) without significant slowdown due to letter formation difficulty.
width.typical: Write across varied tasks with growing fluency — speed does not need to be fast, but letter formation should not be the bottleneck for ideas.
wider: Limited width — writing fluency is a developmental capacity built through practice volume, not breadth of contexts.

modes.reason: Fluency is built through volume of practice. This is a consolidation node — what students need is more writing time, not more types of writing contexts. Thin width acknowledged.

descriptors.title: Manipulate complex sounds
descriptors.description: manipulate more complex sounds in spoken words and use knowledge of blending, segmenting, phoneme deletion and phoneme substitution to read and write words
descriptors.knowledge: Students segment words into separate phonemes including consonant blends and clusters, and manipulate phonemes by addition, deletion and substitution to generate new words (AC9E1LY09/10). They have not yet applied these skills to more complex phoneme sequences including multi-phoneme blends and medial substitution.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can manipulate complex sounds in spoken words using blending, segmenting, deletion and substitution to read and write words.

nodes.label: Blending and segmenting complex patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can blend and segment spoken words with more complex phoneme patterns — multi-consonant blends, digraphs within clusters — to support reading and writing.
criteria: Student correctly segments a word with a multi-phoneme cluster into its component sounds.
Student correctly blends a sequence of phonemes including a digraph or complex cluster into a recognisable word.
nodes.hinge_reason: Fluent blending and segmenting of complex patterns is prerequisite for Node 2 deletion and substitution — students who cannot reliably segment complex words cannot accurately identify or manipulate the phoneme at a specified position.

width.minimum: Blend and segment a word with a consonant cluster or digraph (e.g. 'b-r-o-th-er', 'c-l-ou-d-y') correctly.
width.typical: Blend and segment a range of words with complex patterns — multi-consonant initial clusters, medial digraphs, final clusters — connecting spoken manipulation to written word recognition and production.
wider: Compare segmentation of words with similar-sounding clusters and discuss how spelling relates to the sounds (e.g. 'scratch' vs 'catch' — similar endings, different spellings)
Segment and blend words from different word families to identify common phoneme patterns

modes.reason: Blending and segmenting complex patterns requires accumulated practice — repeated application across many word examples builds the automatic phoneme-level processing needed for fluent reading and writing. Practice volume is more productive than widening pattern types before fluency is established.

nodes.label: Deletion and substitution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can delete or substitute phonemes in spoken words — at initial, medial and final positions — to form new words.
criteria: Student correctly deletes a phoneme at a specified position in a spoken word.
Student correctly substitutes a phoneme at a specified position to form a new word.

width.minimum: Delete or substitute a phoneme at a specified position in a spoken word to form a new word (e.g. delete 'scr' from 'scratch' to get 'atch'; substitute medial vowel in 'stack' to get 'stick').
width.typical: Apply deletion and substitution at initial, medial and final positions across a range of words, connecting spoken manipulation to reading and writing new words.
wider: Generate word families through systematic substitution at a single position and discuss what the pattern reveals about English sound-spelling relationships
Apply deletion and substitution to read new words encountered during reading rather than only in isolation

descriptors.title: Vowel digraphs and consonant clusters
descriptors.description: use phoneme–grapheme (sound–letter/s) matches, including vowel digraphs, less common long vowel patterns, consonant clusters and silent letters when reading and writing words of one or more syllables, including compound words
descriptors.knowledge: Students use short and long vowels, blends and digraphs to write words and read one- and two-syllable words (AC9E1LY11). They have not yet applied less common long vowel patterns, silent letters or multi-syllabic and compound word decoding.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can use vowel digraphs, less common long vowel patterns, consonant clusters and silent letters when reading and writing words of one or more syllables including compound words.

nodes.label: Vowel digraphs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and write words containing vowel digraphs — including common and less common patterns — applying correct sound-letter matches.
criteria: Student correctly reads words containing vowel digraphs without sounding out individual letters.
Student correctly writes words with common vowel digraphs.
nodes.hinge_reason: Vowel digraph automaticity is prerequisite for Node 3 multi-syllabic decoding — students who cannot reliably apply digraph patterns to individual syllables cannot decode multi-syllabic words where digraphs appear within a syllable.

width.minimum: Read and write words with common vowel digraphs ('ee', 'oo', 'ai', 'ay', 'ea') correctly.
width.typical: Apply vowel digraph knowledge across common and less common patterns in reading and writing, including words encountered in shared texts and learning area vocabulary.
wider: Compare vowel digraphs with the same sound but different spelling (e.g. 'ee' and 'ea' for the same vowel sound) and discuss how context helps choose the correct spelling
Identify vowel digraphs in content-area vocabulary (Science, HASS) and practise reading and writing them in context

modes.reason: Vowel digraph recognition and production requires repeated application across many words before it becomes automatic. Students who understand the concept still misread or misspell digraphs in new words. Practice volume builds automaticity more than breadth of pattern types at this stage.

nodes.label: Less common long vowel patterns and silent letters
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and write words with less common long vowel patterns (e.g. 'ight') and silent letters (e.g. 'knife', 'thumb').
criteria: Student correctly reads a word with a less common long vowel pattern or silent letter.
Student correctly writes a word with a silent letter without misspelling it phonetically.
nodes.hinge_reason: Less common long vowel patterns and silent letters appear within multi-syllabic words — students who cannot read these patterns reliably cannot decode Node 3 words where these patterns are embedded within a syllable.

width.minimum: Read a word with a less common long vowel pattern or silent letter correctly and use it in writing.
width.typical: Apply knowledge of less common long vowel patterns and silent letters across a range of words encountered in reading and writing contexts.
wider: Identify silent letters across a word family (e.g. 'knife', 'knot', 'know') and discuss the pattern
Compare less common long vowel patterns across word families (e.g. 'ight' words) and discuss how recognising the pattern speeds up reading

modes.reason: Silent letters and less common patterns are irregular in sound-spelling mapping and require memorisation plus pattern recognition. Precision and repeated exposure is more productive than widening to new pattern types before current ones are reliable.

nodes.label: Multi-syllabic and compound words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can decode and write words of two or more syllables, including compound words, applying phoneme-grapheme knowledge to each syllable.
criteria: Student can decode a two-syllable word by applying phoneme-grapheme knowledge to each syllable.
Student can identify the two constituent words in a compound word.

width.minimum: Decode a two-syllable word by applying phoneme-grapheme knowledge to each syllable separately.
width.typical: Read and write multi-syllabic and compound words — applying decoding strategies syllable-by-syllable and recognising constituent words in compound words — across reading and writing contexts.
wider: Identify compound words in learning area texts and decompose them into constituent words, discussing how the parts contribute to meaning
Compare two-syllable words with different stress patterns and discuss how stress affects pronunciation

modes.reason: Decoding multi-syllabic words requires students to coordinate vowel digraph knowledge, consonant cluster knowledge and silent letter knowledge simultaneously, applying each to different syllables within the same word. Coordinated application is the integration demand.

descriptors.title: Spelling patterns and morphemes
descriptors.description: use knowledge of spelling patterns and morphemes to read and write words whose spelling is not completely predictable from their sounds, including high-frequency words
descriptors.knowledge: Students spell one- and two-syllable words using common letter patterns, and read and write an increasing number of high-frequency words (AC9E1LY13/14). They have not yet applied morphemic knowledge to words with irregular or unpredictable sound-spelling relationships.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can use spelling patterns and morphemes to read and write words whose spelling is not completely predictable from their sounds, including high-frequency words.

nodes.label: Spelling patterns for irregular words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply known spelling patterns to read and write words with unpredictable sound-spelling relationships.
criteria: Student correctly spells a set of irregular high-frequency words in their writing.
Student can use context to select the correct pronunciation when a word is ambiguous.

width.minimum: Apply a known spelling pattern to write an irregular high-frequency word correctly (e.g. 'one', 'once').
width.typical: Apply spelling pattern knowledge to a range of irregular words and high-frequency words; use context to select the correct form when a word has more than one plausible pronunciation.
wider: Group irregular words by shared spelling pattern and discuss what the pattern reveals about English spelling history
Use context clues in a sentence to read a word with multiple plausible pronunciations (e.g. 'read' — present vs past tense)

modes.reason: Spelling irregular words correctly requires memorisation and pattern recognition built through repeated exposure and writing practice. Width is thin — the skill does not vary meaningfully across contexts. Repeated correct production in writing is the productive investment.

nodes.label: Using morphemes to spell unknown words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply morphemic knowledge — recognising base words, prefixes and suffixes — to spell unknown words by analogy with known words.
criteria: Student correctly spells an unknown word by applying morphemic knowledge from a known word.
Student can identify the morphemic relationship between a known and an unknown word.

width.minimum: Use a known word to spell a related unknown word through morphemic analogy (e.g. use 'one' to spell 'once', use 'cover' to spell 'uncover').
width.typical: Apply morphemic knowledge across a range of word families — using base words and affixes to generate correct spellings of unknown words — in both isolated practice and writing contexts.
wider: Build a word family from a known base word and discuss how morphemic knowledge generalises to new words
Identify morphemic relationships between words encountered in learning area texts and use them to unlock unknown words during reading

descriptors.title: Prefixes, suffixes and word families
descriptors.description: build morphemic word families using knowledge of prefixes and suffixes
descriptors.knowledge: Students use grammatical morphemes to create and recognise word families (AC9E1LY15). They have not yet systematically built word families using a range of named prefixes and suffixes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can build morphemic word families using knowledge of prefixes and suffixes.

nodes.label: What prefixes and suffixes do
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that prefixes and suffixes change the meaning or grammatical function of a base word and give at least one example of each.
criteria: Student can identify a prefix or suffix and name the base word.
Student can explain what the prefix or suffix adds to the base word's meaning or grammatical function.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that prefixes and suffixes are separable, meaningful elements is conceptually prerequisite for Node 2 — students who see affixes as arbitrary word-parts cannot systematically build word families by adding or removing them.

width.minimum: Identify a prefix or suffix on a given word and explain what it adds to the base word (e.g. 'un-' changes meaning; '-ing' changes tense).
width.typical: Identify prefixes and suffixes across a range of words, explain what each adds, and distinguish between meaning-changing prefixes (un-, re-) and grammatical suffixes (-ing, -ed, -er, -est).
wider: Compare words with the same prefix or suffix across multiple examples and discuss what pattern of meaning the prefix/suffix creates
Identify prefixes and suffixes encountered in learning area vocabulary and discuss how knowing the affix helps with word meaning

modes.reason: Students often think 'un-' or '-ing' are just part of the word, not added elements. Multiple examples across different base words — showing that the same prefix changes different base words in the same way — resolves the misconception that affixes are arbitrary. More base word examples, not more explanation of one, is productive.

nodes.label: Building word families
nodes.checkpoint: Students can build a word family from a base word by adding prefixes and suffixes, producing correctly spelled related words.
criteria: Student correctly builds at least three words in a family from a known base word.
Student correctly spells the words in the family, including words formed by combining the base with both a prefix and a suffix.

width.minimum: Build at least three words in a family from a known base word using prefixes or suffixes (e.g. 'friend' → 'friendly', 'friendship', 'unfriendly').
width.typical: Build word families from several base words, applying prefixes and suffixes correctly; use morphemic knowledge to write unknown words by analogy with known family members.
wider: Use a known word family to write unknown words encountered during reading or writing across subject areas
Compare word families with the same base word built using different affixes (e.g. 'cover', 'uncover', 'covering', 'recover', 'discovery') and map the family structure

modes.reason: Building word families requires accumulating examples — each new base word and its family members adds to the student's morphemic vocabulary. Schema for how prefixes and suffixes work only forms once a sufficient range of examples has been encountered. Breadth of base words is the productive investment.

descriptors.title: Social conventions and turn-taking
descriptors.description: understand that cooperation with others depends on shared understanding of social conventions, including turn-taking patterns, acknowledgement and body language
descriptors.knowledge: Students investigate how language choices vary according to context and roles in interaction (AC9E2LA01). They have not yet examined the specific conventions — turn-taking, acknowledgement, body language — that enable cooperation in group situations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that cooperation depends on shared social conventions including turn-taking patterns, acknowledgement and body language.

nodes.label: Turn-taking and collaborative language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify turn-taking conventions and collaborative language in group and pair work, and explain how they enable cooperation.
criteria: Student identifies at least two specific turn-taking or collaborative language conventions
Student explains how one convention helps people cooperate — not just that it's polite

width.minimum: Identify at least two collaborative language conventions (e.g. initiating, inviting, responding) and explain how they help a group work together.
width.typical: Recognise and use collaborative language for initiating, inviting, responding and extending in group and pair work; explain how turn-taking patterns and language choices support cooperative interaction.
wider: Compare how turn-taking conventions differ across formal group discussions versus casual conversations, and explain why different contexts have different rules
Examine specific First Nations Australian cultural protocols and speaking/listening conventions, and discuss how understanding different conventions helps people cooperate respectfully

modes.reason: Students often see turn-taking as a single set of rules rather than as context-dependent conventions. Comparing different group contexts — and especially different cultural protocols — reveals that cooperation requires understanding which conventions apply in which situation.

nodes.label: Acknowledgement and body language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify acknowledgement behaviours and body language that signal cooperation, and explain their role in shared understanding.
criteria: Student identifies an acknowledgement behaviour and a body language signal in an observed or enacted interaction
Student explains how these signals show that participants share understanding and are cooperating

width.minimum: Identify at least one acknowledgement behaviour and one body language signal in an interaction and explain how each supports the interaction.
width.typical: Recognise how acknowledgement (e.g. nodding, verbal feedback, building on others' ideas) and body language (eye contact, orientation, gesture) signal engagement and cooperation in a range of interaction contexts.
wider: Discuss how body language conventions vary across cultures — identifying examples where the same gesture or behaviour has different meanings for different groups
Reflect on an interaction where miscommunication occurred and identify which conventions were unclear or differently understood

descriptors.title: Language of evaluation and emotion
descriptors.description: understand how the language of evaluation and emotion, such as modal verbs, can be used to express and respond to opinions
descriptors.knowledge: Students explore how language is used to appreciate texts and give reasons for preferences (AC9E2LA02). They have not yet examined the specific language resources — modal verbs, evaluative adverbs/nouns/verbs, and emotional language — that enable expressing degrees of certainty and responding to opinions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how modal verbs, evaluative vocabulary and emotional language are used to express and respond to opinions.

nodes.label: Modal verbs and degrees of certainty
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify modal verbs and explain what degree of possibility, probability or necessity each expresses.
criteria: Student identifies a modal verb and names the degree of possibility/necessity it signals (high/medium/low)
Student explains how swapping one modal for another changes the strength of the statement

width.minimum: Identify at least two modal verbs (e.g. 'must', 'might', 'could') and explain the different degree of certainty or possibility each signals.
width.typical: Explore how modal verbs indicate degrees of possibility, probability and necessity — distinguishing high modality ('must', 'will') from medium ('should', 'would') and low ('might', 'could') — and explain how the choice changes the strength of an opinion or claim.
wider: Compare how the same sentence changes meaning when different modal verbs are substituted, and discuss what this reveals about how writers signal confidence in their claims
Find examples of modal verbs in persuasive texts (e.g. advertisements, arguments) and analyse how modality is used to make claims seem stronger or more flexible

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of modal verbs across the certainty scale before they can use or analyse them flexibly. Building familiarity with examples from high to low modality is the prerequisite for understanding degree.

nodes.label: Evaluative and emotional vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify evaluative and emotional vocabulary choices and explain how they express the speaker's or writer's feelings and opinions about characters, events or ideas.
criteria: Student identifies evaluative or emotional vocabulary and names the opinion or feeling it expresses
Student explains how the word choice shows the speaker's/writer's position — not just that it describes the character or event

width.minimum: Identify evaluative or emotional word choices in a text (adverbs, nouns or verbs) and explain what opinion or feeling each expresses.
width.typical: Recognise how adverb, noun and verb choices present different evaluations of characters and events; explore emotional language that demonstrates a range of emotions and positions; build vocabulary for expressing opinions and feelings.
wider: Compare how the same character is described with different evaluative vocabulary in two versions of the same story, and discuss what this reveals about point of view
Create a short text about the same event from two different emotional perspectives, choosing vocabulary deliberately to show the different positions

modes.reason: Students often see emotional vocabulary as simply positive or negative. Exploring different text types — narrative, persuasion, news — and different versions of the same story reveals that evaluative language constructs a specific perspective, not just a mood.

descriptors.title: Text language features by purpose
descriptors.description: describe how texts across the curriculum use different language features and structures to serve their purpose
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify how texts across the curriculum are organised differently depending on purpose (AC9E2LA03). They have not yet described the specific language features — as distinct from structures — that serve each text type's purpose.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe how texts across the curriculum use specific language features and structures to serve their purpose.

nodes.label: Structure and language features of factual texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the typical structure and language features of factual text types including recounts, autobiographies, procedures and reports.
criteria: Student names the structure of a factual text type (its stages/sections)
Student identifies at least two language features of that text type and connects each to the text's purpose

width.minimum: Describe the structure and at least two language features of one factual text type (e.g. recount, procedure, report) and explain how they serve the text's purpose.
width.typical: Describe the typical text structure and language features of factual recounts, autobiographies, procedures and reports — connecting each structural stage and language feature to the text's purpose.
wider: Compare language features across two factual text types with different purposes (e.g. procedure vs report) and explain why different features are needed
Identify a text that mixes features from more than one text type and discuss why the author might have made those choices

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate descriptions of multiple text types before they can generalise about how purpose drives structural and language choices. Building a repertoire across factual text types is the prerequisite for the comparative understanding the descriptor targets.

nodes.label: Structure of arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the stages of a basic argument structure (introduction, arguments, conclusion) and describe the language features that support each stage.
criteria: Student identifies at least two stages of a basic argument in a text
Student describes at least one language feature in a named stage and connects it to what that stage is trying to do

width.minimum: Identify the introduction, at least one argument and the conclusion in a simple persuasive text, and describe one language feature in any stage.
width.typical: Identify and describe the stages of a basic argument (introduction, argument 1, argument 2, conclusion) and the language features that signal and support each stage.
wider: Compare the argument structure in a children's persuasive text with a media advertisement, identifying what differs and discussing why
Write a simple argument using the identified structure and language features, then check whether each stage does its job

modes.reason: Argument structure is a reasoning scaffold as much as a text structure at Y3 — students need to understand what each stage does (state position, give evidence, restate) before the structure becomes usable for reading and writing.

descriptors.title: Paragraphs group information
descriptors.description: understand that paragraphs are a key organisational feature of the stages of written texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how cohesion devices including overviews and paragraph structure guide readers (AC9E2LA04 — implicitly). They have not yet examined how paragraphs function as the primary organisational unit that groups information into the stages of a text.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that paragraphs are a key organisational feature — grouping related information and marking the stages of written texts.

nodes.label: Paragraphs in informative texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that paragraphs in informative texts group related information together, often beginning with a topic sentence.
criteria: Student identifies what information a paragraph groups together
Student explains why those pieces of information belong in the same paragraph (what makes them related)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who haven't established the informative paragraph model at N1 have no baseline rule to contrast with at N2 — the narrative paragraphing lesson depends on students first understanding (and potentially over-applying) the topic-sentence convention.

width.minimum: Identify at least two paragraphs in an informative text and explain what related information each groups together.
width.typical: Recognise that informative texts are organised into paragraphs beginning with a topic sentence, grouping related ideas; examine models of well-constructed paragraphs and identify their features.
wider: Examine how the topic sentences of successive paragraphs map the overall structure of an informative text — reading just the first sentences to get the main ideas
Compare two versions of the same information — one organised into paragraphs, one without — and discuss the effect on the reader

modes.reason: Students often see paragraph breaks as arbitrary or stylistic. Examining models across different informative text types — reports, explanations, recounts — helps students see that paragraph breaks always signal a shift in focus, regardless of text type.

nodes.label: Paragraphs in narrative texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that paragraphs in narrative texts vary in length and serve different purposes — they do not always follow a predictable pattern formula.
criteria: Student identifies that narrative paragraphs vary in length
Student explains one example of why a paragraph starts or ends at a particular point in a narrative

width.minimum: Identify paragraphs in a narrative text and notice that they vary in length, explaining one example of why a short or long paragraph is used at a particular point.
width.typical: Recognise that narrative paragraphs vary in length and purpose — some build tension, some shift scene, some develop character — and do not always follow a topic-sentence pattern. Examine models of effective narrative paragraphing.
wider: Compare how a very short paragraph (even one sentence) is used for effect in a narrative versus a long descriptive paragraph — discuss what each achieves
Experiment with changing the paragraph breaks in a narrative extract and evaluate how it changes the reading experience

modes.reason: Students taught the topic-sentence rule may misapply it to narrative. Seeing that narrative paragraphing follows different logic — and that variation itself is a tool — prevents the misconception that all paragraphs work the same way.

descriptors.title: Layout and navigation features
descriptors.description: identify the purpose of layout features in print and digital texts and the words used for headings and hyperlinks
descriptors.knowledge: Students navigate print and screen texts using structural and navigation features (AC9E2LA05). They have not yet focused on identifying the purpose of specific layout features and the language choices made for headings and hyperlinks.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify the purpose of layout features in print and digital texts including headings, subheadings, chapter headings and hyperlinks.

nodes.label: Purpose of headings and subheadings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify headings and subheadings in print and digital texts and explain what purpose each serves for the reader.
criteria: Student names the type of layout feature (heading, subheading, chapter heading)
Student explains what the feature does for the reader — not just that it 'tells you what's there'

width.minimum: Identify at least two headings or subheadings in an informative text and explain what purpose each serves for the reader.
width.typical: Discuss the words used as headings and subheadings in digital and print information texts and chapter headings in narratives, explaining how each guides the reader.
wider: Compare the words chosen as headings across two information texts on the same topic and discuss how different heading choices change what the reader expects
Create alternative headings for sections of a text and evaluate which heading best serves the reader's needs

nodes.label: Hyperlinks in digital texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify hyperlinks in digital texts and explain the language choices made for hyperlink words and their purpose.
criteria: Student identifies a hyperlink and explains what the hyperlink word tells the reader
Student explains how the hyperlink serves a navigational purpose for the reader

width.minimum: Identify at least one hyperlink in a digital text and explain what the hyperlink word signals to the reader about where it will lead.
width.typical: Examine the words used as hyperlinks in digital texts and explain how the language choices signal what the reader will find if they follow the link.
wider: Compare how hyperlink words in a children's website versus a news website differ in their language choices, and discuss what this reveals about audience
Discuss how hyperlinks change the way a reader moves through a digital text compared with a print text — and what this means for navigation

descriptors.title: Clauses with subject-verb agreement
descriptors.description: understand that a clause is a unit of grammar usually containing a subject and a verb, and that subject-verb agreement is required
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how compound sentences connect ideas using coordinating conjunctions (AC9E2LA06). They have not yet examined the internal structure of a clause — specifically the subject-verb relationship — or the agreement rule.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that a clause contains a subject and a verb, and that subjects and verbs must agree in number.

nodes.label: Identifying clause elements
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the verb and subject in a clause.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the verb in a clause
Student correctly identifies the subject that goes with that verb
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably identify the subject and verb in a clause cannot apply subject-verb agreement rules at N2 — agreement requires knowing which subject the verb must match.

width.minimum: Identify the verb and subject in at least three clauses by locating the verb first, then finding what or who the verb is about.
width.typical: Identify clauses by locating verbs and the key words that link to the verbs; practise identifying subjects and verbs across different sentence types and text contexts.
wider: Find clauses in different text types (narrative, information, instruction) and compare how subjects vary — from simple nouns to noun groups
Explore what happens to a clause when the subject is removed — discussing why subjects are necessary for meaning

modes.reason: Clause identification is a precision skill — knowing the definition doesn't translate automatically into reliable identification. Students need repeated practice across varied examples before subject and verb identification becomes fluent.

nodes.label: Subject-verb agreement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify when a singular subject requires a singular verb form and a plural subject requires a plural verb form.
criteria: Student identifies whether a subject is singular or plural
Student selects or confirms the correct verb form to match the subject

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of subject-verb agreement (one singular, one plural) and explain why the verb form matches the subject.
width.typical: Understand and apply subject-verb agreement: singular subjects take singular verbs, plural subjects take plural verbs — recognise and correct agreement errors.
wider: Identify tricky agreement cases (e.g. collective nouns, compound subjects) and discuss why they are harder to get right
Find subject-verb agreement errors in student-level writing samples and explain the correction

modes.reason: Subject-verb agreement errors are common in student writing and persist without targeted practice. This is a precision skill that requires repeated application across varied sentence types, not just comprehension of the rule.

descriptors.title: Verb types and processes
descriptors.description: understand how verbs represent different processes for doing, feeling, thinking, saying and relating
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how nouns extend into noun groups and verbs into verb groups (AC9E2LA07). They have not yet examined the different types of verbs — doing, saying, sensing, relating — and how each represents a distinct kind of process.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how verbs represent different processes: doing, feeling, thinking, saying and relating.

nodes.label: Doing and saying verbs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify doing verbs (action) and saying verbs in narrative texts and explain what each type tells the reader.
criteria: Student identifies a doing verb and a saying verb, naming the type of each
Student explains what information each verb type provides — beyond just 'it's an action'

width.minimum: Identify at least two doing verbs and one saying verb in a narrative text and explain what each type of verb tells the reader.
width.typical: Explore doing and saying verbs in narrative texts, understanding how doing verbs show action and saying verbs indicate how characters speak — and how the choice of saying verb (e.g. 'whispered', 'shouted') adds information.
wider: Compare the doing verbs in an action sequence versus a description in the same narrative, discussing what the verb type choices reveal about the pacing
Explore how different saying verbs in dialogue change the reader's interpretation of the character's emotion or intention

nodes.label: Sensing and relating verbs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sensing verbs (feeling, thinking, perceiving) and relating verbs (defining, describing) and explain how they construct meaning differently from doing verbs.
criteria: Student identifies a sensing or relating verb and names its process type
Student explains how the sensing or relating verb contributes differently to meaning than a doing verb would

width.minimum: Identify at least one sensing verb and one relating verb in a text and explain what type of process each represents.
width.typical: Explore sensing verbs (feeling, thinking, perceiving) and relating verbs (constructing definitions and descriptions) — identifying different types and explaining how they control meaning in a clause differently from doing verbs.
wider: Find sensing verbs in a narrative text and discuss how they let readers understand what characters are thinking and feeling without being told directly
Compare a description written with relating verbs versus adjectives and discuss what each choice achieves

modes.reason: Sensing and relating verbs don't look like 'typical verbs' to students. Seeing them in multiple different text contexts — narrative, information, description — helps students recognise the full range of what verbs can do beyond physical action.

descriptors.title: Verbs anchored in tense
descriptors.description: understand that verbs are anchored in time through tense
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how compound sentences connect ideas using coordinating conjunctions (AC9E2LA06). They have encountered verbs but have not yet examined how tense anchors verbs to time — including the distinction between regular and irregular past tense forms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that verbs are anchored in time through tense, including regular and irregular past tense forms.

nodes.label: Tense anchors verbs in time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify present and past tense verbs and explain how tense anchors the action in time.
criteria: Student identifies the tense of a verb (present or past)
Student explains what time period the tense anchors the event in
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who haven't grasped that tense anchors verbs in time at N1 lack the conceptual framework for N2 — understanding why regular and irregular past forms exist requires knowing what past tense is doing.

width.minimum: Identify at least two verbs — one present tense, one past tense — and explain what time period each is anchored in.
width.typical: Learn how time is represented through verb tense — present tense anchors events now, past tense anchors them earlier — and identify tense in a range of texts including narratives and recounts.
wider: Examine why recounts use past tense while instructions typically use present tense, connecting tense choice to text purpose
Explore future tense forms and discuss how they anchor events differently from present and past

modes.reason: The concept of tense as time-anchoring is best grasped through examples across different text types — recounts use past, instructions use present, narratives mix both. Seeing tense as a systematic choice (not a verb ending rule) requires contrast across contexts.

nodes.label: Regular and irregular past tense
nodes.checkpoint: Students can form regular past tense by adding '-ed' and identify irregular past tense verbs that change form differently.
criteria: Student correctly forms regular past tense using '-ed'
Student correctly produces at least three irregular past tense forms

width.minimum: Form the past tense of at least two regular verbs correctly, and identify at least two irregular past tense verbs (e.g. 'ran', 'caught').
width.typical: Learn that regular past tense is formed by adding '-ed' (walked, jumped) and that irregular verbs change form differently (ran, caught, came); apply this knowledge in reading and writing.
wider: Collect a class list of common irregular past tense verbs, grouping them by their pattern of change
Find regular and irregular past tense verbs in a narrative text and discuss how they create the time frame of the story

modes.reason: Irregular past tense forms must be memorised — there are no rules to apply. Students need repeated exposure and practice rather than more contexts, which makes this a consolidation point rather than a hinge.

descriptors.title: Images extend meaning
descriptors.description: identify how images extend the meaning of a text
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that images add to or multiply meaning in texts (AC9E2LA08). They have not yet focused on how images extend meaning specifically — adding information or dimensions that the written text alone does not provide.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify how images extend the meaning of a text.

nodes.label: Images add information not in the words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify information that an image provides that is not stated in the accompanying written text.
criteria: Student identifies specific information in the image that is not stated in the written text
Student explains what meaning the image adds — not just that 'it shows what's happening'
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who still treat images as illustrations of what the words say (rather than as extending meaning) lack the analytical stance needed for N2 — gaze, angle and distance analysis requires students to already be reading images as meaning-makers.

width.minimum: Identify at least one piece of information an image adds that is not in the written text, and explain what the image tells the reader.
width.typical: Recognise how images extend meaning by adding information not in the words — including how the relationship between characters can be depicted through position, expression and gesture that the words don't explicitly describe.
wider: Compare what a text with its images says versus the same text without them — discussing what meaning is lost when the images are removed
Examine how the same event is shown in an image versus described in words, and discuss what each mode does better

modes.reason: Students often treat images as illustrations of what the words already say. Multiple examples where the image adds genuinely new information — not just pictures of what is written — helps students see extending as distinct from illustrating.

nodes.label: Images construct relationship with viewer
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how images construct a relationship between the depicted content and the viewer through gaze, angle and distance.
criteria: Student identifies a specific image feature (gaze, angle or distance)
Student explains what relationship or feeling that feature creates for the viewer

width.minimum: Identify one image feature (e.g. direct gaze, close distance, angle) and explain how it creates a particular relationship or feeling for the viewer.
width.typical: Recognise how images construct a relationship with the viewer through direct gaze into the camera, social distance and angle — explaining what each choice creates for the viewer.
wider: Compare two images of the same subject using different angles and distances, and discuss how the choices change the viewer's relationship with the subject
Find examples in picture books or media where image choices position the viewer to feel sympathy, distance, or power, and discuss how the technical choices create that effect

modes.reason: The connection between technical image choices (gaze, angle, distance) and their effect on the viewer requires explicit reasoning — students need the chain from 'the character is looking at me' to 'this creates a sense of connection/invitation'. The reasoning link doesn't come automatically.

descriptors.title: Topic and technical vocabulary
descriptors.description: extend topic-specific and technical vocabulary and know that words can have different meanings in different contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students experiment with and begin to make conscious vocabulary choices to suit a topic (AC9E2LA09). They have not yet examined how topic-specific and technical vocabulary works across disciplines, or how words shift meaning across contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students extend topic-specific and technical vocabulary and understand that words can have different meanings in different contexts.

nodes.label: Topic-specific and technical vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and use topic-specific and technical vocabulary for their learning area topics, including measurement terms and narrative terms.
criteria: Student uses at least two topic-specific or technical words accurately in context
Student can explain what each word means in that learning area context

width.minimum: Identify and use at least three technical or topic-specific words from a learning area topic and explain what each means in that context.
width.typical: Identify and use technical words for specific topics across the curriculum — e.g. metric length terms, narrative feature terms (character, setting, plot); extend vocabulary by adding prefixes and suffixes to known words.
wider: Compare technical vocabulary from two different subject areas (e.g. maths and science) and discuss how each subject builds its own specialised vocabulary
Investigate how adding a prefix or suffix to a word creates new vocabulary with related but different meaning

modes.reason: Vocabulary extension is inherently repertoire-based — students need to encounter and use topic-specific words repeatedly across different topics and subject areas to build a genuinely expanding vocabulary. Range across learning areas is the growth mechanism.

nodes.label: Words with different meanings in different contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify words that have different meanings in different contexts and explain how the context determines which meaning is active.
criteria: Student identifies a word with multiple meanings and names at least two contexts
Student explains what the word means in each context and how they know which applies

width.minimum: Identify one word that has different meanings in different contexts (e.g. 'warm' in everyday vs scientific contexts) and explain what it means in each context.
width.typical: Recognise and explore words that have different meanings in different contexts — everyday meanings versus technical meanings — and use context clues to determine which meaning is active.
wider: Find examples of the same word used in an everyday context and a subject-specific context in the same week of learning, and discuss how they know which meaning is intended
Explore how new words enter a topic vocabulary and what happens to the everyday word when a technical term takes over the same meaning

modes.reason: Students often assume a word has one meaning. Seeing the same word used differently across contexts — maths vs everyday, science vs everyday — reveals that meaning is context-dependent. Multiple contrast examples are necessary for this insight.

descriptors.title: Apostrophes for contraction and possession
descriptors.description: understand that apostrophes signal missing letters in contractions, and apostrophes show possession
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise how capital letters and commas are used in titles and lists (AC9E2LA10). They have not yet examined apostrophes — either for contraction or for possession.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that apostrophes signal missing letters in contractions and show possession (singular and plural).

nodes.label: Apostrophes in contractions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can form and interpret contractions using apostrophes to signal the missing letter(s).
criteria: Student correctly places the apostrophe in a contraction at the point of omission
Student can identify what letters have been removed to form the contraction

width.minimum: Form at least three contractions correctly using apostrophes (e.g. do not → don't, will not → won't) and explain what the apostrophe signals.
width.typical: Use apostrophes to create contractions from common word pairs; understand that the apostrophe marks where letters have been omitted; recognise contractions in reading.
wider: Investigate why 'won't' doesn't follow the expected pattern for 'will not', and explore other irregular contractions
Discuss when contractions are appropriate versus when full forms are preferred — comparing informal and formal text contexts

modes.reason: Apostrophe use in contractions is a precision convention — students understand the concept quickly but errors (especially 'wont', 'dont') persist in writing without targeted practice. Fluency requires repeated application.

nodes.label: Apostrophes for possession
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use apostrophes to show singular and plural possession.
criteria: Student correctly places the apostrophe for singular possession
Student correctly places the apostrophe for at least one regular plural possession

width.minimum: Correctly form singular possession (e.g. my friend's book) and at least one plural possession (e.g. the bees' hive) using an apostrophe.
width.typical: Use apostrophes to show singular possession (noun + 's) and plural possession (plural noun + ') in a range of contexts; recognise and correct possession apostrophe errors.
wider: Explore the irregular plural possessive (e.g. children's, men's) — where the apostrophe follows different rules — and discuss why
Compare possession expressed with an apostrophe versus a phrase (the book belonging to my friend) and discuss when each is preferred

modes.reason: Possessive apostrophe errors (especially plural possession and confusion with plural 's') are highly persistent in student writing. This is a mechanical precision skill where practice — not additional contexts — is the remedy.

The singular/plural possession distinction (friend's vs friends') is a genuine point where the rule changes. Seeing multiple examples of both types — and irregular cases — helps students develop reliable discrimination rather than guessing.

descriptors.title: Characters and events across contexts
descriptors.description: discuss characters, events and settings in different contexts in literature by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature from diverse contexts (AC9E2LE01). They have not yet compared how the same character type (e.g. the wolf) or story element is portrayed differently across texts from different cultural contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss characters, events and settings in different contexts in literature by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.

nodes.label: Same story, different tellings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how the same story or character type is told differently by different authors, identifying variations in characters, events and settings.
criteria: Student identifies at least two specific differences in character, event or setting across two versions of a story
Student discusses one reason why the versions might differ — not just listing differences

width.minimum: Compare two versions of the same story or story type and identify at least two differences in how characters, events or settings are presented.
width.typical: Explore how different wide-ranging authors tell the same story — identifying variations in character portrayal, setting and events; discuss how the same character type (e.g. the wolf) is portrayed differently in different versions.
wider: Compare a traditional story told by a First Nations Australian author with a mainstream version, discussing what is similar and what reflects different relationships with Country, family and community
Discuss why different authors might portray the same character type differently — connecting authorial choice to cultural perspective and purpose

modes.reason: Students easily accept a single version of a story as 'the real one'. Seeing multiple tellings — especially cross-cultural ones — reveals that character, setting and event are constructed choices, not fixed facts. This is a conceptual shift that multiple examples are needed to secure.

nodes.label: Australian settings in literature
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how Australian settings are portrayed in stories and identify distinctive features of how Australian places and environments are represented.
criteria: Student identifies a specific Australian setting in a text and names at least one feature of how it is described
Student discusses what the setting contributes to the story — not just where it is

width.minimum: Identify how one Australian setting is portrayed in a story and discuss at least one feature of how the setting is described.
width.typical: Explore how Australian settings are portrayed in stories — discussing distinctive landscape, environment and cultural features — and compare with how settings from other cultural contexts are presented.
wider: Compare how First Nations Australian authors portray Country/Place as a living, relational entity with how non-Indigenous Australian authors portray the same or similar landscapes
Discuss how the portrayal of Australian settings has changed across different time periods in children's literature

descriptors.title: Connect personal and character experiences
descriptors.description: discuss connections between personal experiences and character experiences in literary texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify features of literary texts and give reasons for personal preferences (AC9E2LE02). They have not yet focused specifically on drawing connections between their own experiences and those of characters — using prior knowledge and personal experience as a reading resource.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss connections between their own experiences and the experiences of characters in literary texts.

nodes.label: Drawing on prior knowledge to connect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw on relevant prior knowledge and personal experience to make meaningful connections to characters' situations in texts.
criteria: Student names a specific connection between their experience and a character's situation (not just 'I've been sad too')
Student explains how the connection helps them understand something about the character

width.minimum: Identify one connection between a character's experience in a text and a personal or known experience, and discuss what the connection helps them understand.
width.typical: Discuss relevant prior knowledge and past experiences to make meaningful connections to characters in texts — explaining how personal experience helps understand what a character might feel or do.
wider: Compare connections made by different students to the same character — discussing how different experiences lead to different connections and what this reveals about reading as a personal act
Explore a text where a character's experience is very different from one's own, and discuss how to make connections despite the unfamiliarity

modes.reason: Making a meaningful connection requires more than naming a similarity — students need the reasoning chain: this happened to the character → something similar happened to me → this helps me understand that the character felt/did X. The 'so what' of the connection needs explicit scaffolding.

nodes.label: Preferences grounded in experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and discuss favourite texts, explaining their preferences in ways that connect to personal experience and feelings.
criteria: Student states a preference for a text and gives a reason (not just 'I liked it')
