Student connects the preference to a personal experience or feeling the text evoked

width.minimum: Select a favourite text and explain at least one reason for the preference that connects to a personal experience or feeling.
width.typical: Select and discuss favourite texts, explaining reasons for assigning greater or lesser value — connecting preferences to what the text made them feel or reminded them of from their own experience.
wider: Compare preferences for the same text across a group and discuss why people connect differently — examining what different personal experiences lead to different preferences
Revisit a text that wasn't initially a favourite after a new personal experience, and discuss whether the connection changed

descriptors.title: Language, setting and mood
descriptors.description: discuss how an author uses language and illustrations to portray characters and settings and create mood
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss how language presents characters and settings differently across texts (AC9E2LE03). They have not yet examined how language and illustrations together create mood — the atmosphere or feeling a text establishes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss how authors use language and illustrations to portray characters and settings and create mood.

nodes.label: Language portrayals of character and setting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify descriptive language that creates character and setting, and discuss what the language choices reveal about traits, relationships and place.
criteria: Student identifies specific language choices (not just general description) that portray a character or setting
Student discusses what the language reveals — trait, relationship, place quality — not just what it describes
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify and interpret descriptive language choices at N1 lack the analytical vocabulary needed to discuss how language and illustration work together to create mood at N2.

width.minimum: Identify at least two descriptive language choices that portray a character or setting, and explain what each reveals.
width.typical: Identify and discuss how descriptive language creates setting, how it portrays character traits and actions, and how characters' speech and actions reveal personality — connecting language choices to their effect on the reader.
wider: Compare how the same character is described at different points in the story and discuss how the language changes as the character changes
Find language choices that portray setting in a First Nations Australian text and discuss how the relationship with Country/Place is constructed through language differently from other settings

modes.reason: Students need to encounter descriptive language choices across multiple text types — narrative, picture books, poetry — before the concept of language as a deliberate constructive choice becomes stable. A single exemplar risks anchoring the concept too narrowly.

nodes.label: Creating mood through language and illustration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify mood in a text and discuss how specific language choices and illustrations work together to create it.
criteria: Student names the mood created in a text (not just the character's emotion)
Student identifies at least one specific language or illustration choice that creates that mood and explains how

width.minimum: Identify the mood of a text or a section and explain at least one language or illustration choice that creates that mood.
width.typical: Discuss how descriptive language creates setting and influences mood; identify how illustrations portray mood alongside or beyond what the words say; discuss how language and illustration work together to create atmosphere.
wider: Compare the mood created at different points in the same story and discuss how the author shifts mood through language and illustration choices
Find a text where the illustration creates a different or ironic mood from the written language, and discuss the effect of that contrast

modes.reason: Students often identify mood as a feeling the character has, rather than an atmosphere the whole text creates for the reader. Multiple examples — across different genres, with and without illustrations — help students distinguish between character emotion and textual mood.

descriptors.title: Literary devices shape meaning
descriptors.description: discuss the effects of some literary devices used to enhance meaning and shape the reader's imagination and emotions
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify, reproduce and experiment with rhythmic sound and word patterns (AC9E2LE04). They have not yet discussed the effects of named literary devices — particularly imagery and sound devices like onomatopoeia — on meaning and the reader's experience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss the effects of literary devices including imagery, sound devices and figurative language that enhance meaning and shape imagination and emotions.

nodes.label: Imagery and its effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify imagery (visual, nature, sensory) in a text and discuss the effect it creates for the reader's imagination.
criteria: Student identifies imagery in a text (naming what is being described)
Student discusses the effect on the reader — what the imagery makes them imagine, see or feel

width.minimum: Identify one piece of imagery in a text and discuss what picture or sensation it creates for the reader.
width.typical: Discuss the effects of imagery in texts — including imagery related to nature, senses and familiar experiences — explaining what the imagery makes readers see, feel or imagine.
wider: Compare imagery used to describe the same natural phenomenon (e.g. a storm, a river) in two different texts and discuss how different choices create different effects
Explore how imagery in a First Nations Australian text conveys a relationship with Country/Place that goes beyond description

nodes.label: Sound devices and questions about effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sound devices such as onomatopoeia, alliteration and rhyme in texts and discuss why the poet or author chose them.
criteria: Student identifies a sound device and names its type (onomatopoeia, alliteration, rhyme)
Student discusses an effect the device creates — not just that it 'sounds good'

width.minimum: Identify at least one sound device in a text and discuss one effect it creates — answering the question of why the author might have used it.
width.typical: Generate questions to discuss the effects of literary devices; identify onomatopoeia, alliteration, rhyme and other sound devices and discuss how they enhance meaning, add rhythm or create sound effects that shape the reader's imagination.
wider: Experiment with replacing sound device words with neutral synonyms and compare the effect — discussing what is lost
Explore how onomatopoeia works across different languages and cultures — discussing whether sound imitation is universal or language-specific

modes.reason: Students can identify sound devices but struggle to discuss their effects beyond 'it sounds good'. Experiencing devices across poetry, narrative and non-fiction contexts — and generating questions about why authors chose them — builds analytical habit rather than just identification.

descriptors.title: Create using literary elements
descriptors.description: create and edit imaginative texts, using or adapting language features, characters, events and settings that reflect their own world
descriptors.knowledge: Students create and edit literary texts by adapting structures and language features of familiar texts (AC9E2LE05). They have not yet focused on using or adapting characters, events and settings that reflect their own world as a source for original imaginative text creation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and edit imaginative texts using or adapting language features, characters, events and settings that reflect their own world.

nodes.label: Drawing on literary texts for inspiration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw on literary texts they have read for inspiration and ideas, adapting settings or changing endings to create their own texts.
criteria: Student creates an imaginative text that draws identifiably on at least one element from a known literary text
Student can explain what was adapted and what reflects their own ideas or world

width.minimum: Create a short imaginative text that adapts at least one element (setting, character type, event or ending) from a read text, explaining what was borrowed and what was changed.
width.typical: Draw on literary texts for inspiration — adapting texts by changing setting or revising an ending; creating texts that reflect their own world through character, event or setting choices.
wider: Adapt a traditional story by shifting the setting to a familiar Australian or local context, and discuss how the story changes as a result
Create a text that uses a character type from a read text but places them in a situation from the student's own experience, discussing how the known character behaves in the new context

modes.reason: Creative text creation at Y3 is supported by having a repertoire of literary elements to draw from. Students who have encountered a range of character types, settings and event structures across their reading have more resources to adapt. This is a strand where reading breadth directly enables writing.

nodes.label: Using language features from literature in own writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use language features from literary texts they have studied (e.g. descriptive language, dialogue, imagery) in their own imaginative writing.
criteria: Student uses at least one identified language feature (naming it) in their own text
Student can explain why they chose that feature at that point in their writing

width.minimum: Use at least one language feature from a studied text (e.g. imagery, a specific type of descriptive language, dialogue) in an original imaginative text.
width.typical: Discuss characters encountered in literary texts and how those characters might behave in new situations; create imaginative texts using language features from studied texts including descriptive language, dialogue, imagery and characterisation techniques.
wider: Use literary devices discussed in LE04 (imagery, sound devices) deliberately in a creative text, and explain why each device was chosen
Compare a first draft with a revised version where a language feature has been deliberately improved — discussing what the revision achieves

modes.reason: Using literary language features in original writing requires students to integrate their knowledge of what devices do (from analysis) with creative composition decisions (when and where to use them). The bridge from reader to writer is the integration challenge at this node.

descriptors.title: Purpose and audience vary texts
descriptors.description: recognise how texts can be created for similar purposes but different audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify how similar topics and information are presented differently across text types (AC9E2LY01). They have not yet examined how the same purpose can produce different texts when the audience changes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise how texts created for similar purposes differ when aimed at different audiences.

nodes.label: Audience shapes text choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how texts with the same purpose are created differently for different audiences.
criteria: Student identifies at least two specific differences between two texts with the same purpose
Student connects each difference to the audience — explaining why the audience requires that particular choice

width.minimum: Compare two texts with the same purpose but different audiences (e.g. a safety campaign for adults vs children) and identify at least two ways the texts differ because of the audience.
width.typical: Identify how the same purpose (e.g. safety, instruction, persuasion) produces different texts for different audiences — examining vocabulary, images, examples and complexity as audience-driven choices.
wider: Compare instructions for assembling the same item written for different age groups, and discuss what specific changes are made to suit each audience
Find examples of similar-purpose texts aimed at children versus adults and evaluate whether the audience-related choices are effective

modes.reason: Students often see text differences as arbitrary or about topic rather than audience. Comparing texts with the same purpose but different audiences — across multiple examples — builds the insight that audience is a systematic determinant of textual choices.

descriptors.title: Share and extend ideas
descriptors.description: use interaction skills to contribute to conversations and discussions to share information and ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students use interaction skills to actively listen, extend ideas, express and respond to opinions and give instructions (AC9E2LY02). They have not yet focused on the specific skills of contributing as a group member across different roles — building on others, listening actively for specific information, and adjusting language to context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use interaction skills to contribute to conversations and discussions to share information and ideas.

nodes.label: Building on others' ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can build on and connect to ideas and opinions expressed by others in a discussion.
criteria: Student makes a contribution that acknowledges and builds on a previous speaker's point
Student demonstrates active listening by responding to specific content from earlier in the discussion

width.minimum: In a discussion, make at least one contribution that explicitly connects to or builds on a previous speaker's idea.
width.typical: Build on and connect ideas expressed by others; listen actively including for specific information; recognise the value of others' contributions; use language appropriately in different group contexts.
wider: Practice specific group roles (chairperson, recorder, reporter) and discuss how each role requires different interaction skills
Compare how the language used in a formal group discussion differs from casual conversation, and practise adjusting to each context

modes.reason: Building on others is a turn-taking skill that requires real-time listening under social pressure — it develops through repeated practice in genuine discussion contexts, not through more conceptual instruction.

nodes.label: Explaining to different audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adjust the language they use when explaining or presenting information depending on the context and audience.
criteria: Student demonstrates at least one adjustment to language or vocabulary for a different audience
Student can explain why the adjustment was made

width.minimum: Explain the same information to two different audiences (e.g. a peer and a teacher) using different language choices, and discuss what was changed and why.
width.typical: Use language appropriately in different situations — e.g. explaining a procedure, sharing information in different group contexts — adapting vocabulary, formality and examples to suit the audience.
wider: Explain a classroom learning activity to someone outside the class (e.g. through a recording or letter) and evaluate whether the explanation is clear to someone without shared context
Discuss how technical vocabulary from a learning area topic needs to be simplified or explained when talking to someone unfamiliar with it

descriptors.title: Identify audience and purpose
descriptors.description: identify the audience and purpose of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts, and discuss how language features are used to engage and influence the intended audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify the purpose and audience of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts (AC9E2LY03). They have not yet discussed how specific language features engage or influence the intended audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify the audience and purpose of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts and discuss how language features engage and influence the intended audience.

nodes.label: Identifying audience and purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the intended audience and purpose of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts.
criteria: Student identifies the intended audience and purpose of a text
Student provides at least one textual feature as evidence for their identification
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably identify the intended audience and purpose of a text cannot proceed to N2 — explaining how language features engage or influence requires knowing which audience and what purpose they are serving.

width.minimum: Identify the audience and purpose of at least two texts of different types (imaginative, informative or persuasive) and explain the evidence that shows each.
width.typical: Identify the audience and purpose of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts; identify words, phrases and images intended to persuade; identify the purpose of imaginative texts.
wider: Find a text where the intended audience is not explicit and discuss how you work out who it is from clues in the text
Compare two advertisements targeting different age groups and identify the specific features that signal each audience

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate examples across imaginative, informative and persuasive text types before the audience/purpose identification schema becomes reliable. A single text type is insufficient — the concept needs to crystallise across the full range before N2 analysis is workable.

nodes.label: Language features that engage and influence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how specific language features in texts engage the intended audience or work to persuade them.
criteria: Student identifies a language feature and names the intended audience
Student explains how the feature is designed to engage or persuade that specific audience

width.minimum: Identify at least one language feature in a persuasive or advertisement text and explain how it is designed to engage or persuade the target audience.
width.typical: Discuss how language features (including words, phrases and images) are used to engage and influence the intended audience across persuasive and imaginative texts — connecting feature choices to audience and purpose.
wider: Examine features of advertisements specifically targeting children and discuss how the language choices exploit what children find appealing or trustworthy
Compare how an imaginative text engages its audience differently from a persuasive text — identifying what different types of engagement look like

modes.reason: Connecting a language feature to its audience-influencing effect requires explicit reasoning — students need the chain: feature → how it works on this audience → the effect it creates. Without scaffolding, students say features are 'persuasive' without explaining why.

descriptors.title: Read accurately and fluently
descriptors.description: read a range of texts using phonic, semantic and grammatical knowledge to read accurately and fluently, and monitor and self-correct
descriptors.knowledge: Students read with phrasing and fluency, monitoring meaning by re-reading and self-correcting (AC9E2LY04). They have not yet applied all three knowledge types — phonic, semantic and grammatical — explicitly as coordinated reading tools across a wider range of texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students read a range of texts using phonic, semantic and grammatical knowledge to read accurately and fluently, monitoring and self-correcting.

nodes.label: Using multiple knowledge sources to decode
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use phonic, vocabulary and grammatical knowledge together to read unknown words accurately.
criteria: Student attempts to read unknown words using multiple sources (not just phonics alone or skipping)
Student self-corrects when an initial reading doesn't make sense
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not consolidated multi-source decoding cannot fluently monitor for meaning at N2 — monitoring requires decoding to be sufficiently automated that attention is freed for comprehension.

width.minimum: When encountering an unknown word, apply at least two knowledge sources (e.g. phonic knowledge + sentence grammar) and explain the decoding process.
width.typical: Use phonic knowledge, word knowledge, vocabulary and grammatical knowledge to read unknown words; read a wider range of texts from different learning areas including chapter books.
wider: Compare how you approach an unknown proper noun versus an unknown content word — discussing how different knowledge sources are more or less useful for each
Reflect on decoding strategies used across subject-area texts and identify which strategy is most useful for technical vocabulary

modes.reason: Fluent multi-source decoding develops through reading practice across a wide range of text types. Strategy knowledge is not the bottleneck — application under real reading conditions is.

nodes.label: Monitoring and self-correcting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can monitor their own reading for meaning and self-correct errors that disrupt comprehension.
criteria: Student notices when their reading doesn't make sense and stops to self-correct
Student applies at least one repair strategy (re-read, try alternative, use context) rather than continuing past the error

width.minimum: Demonstrate monitoring by identifying at least one point in a read text where meaning was disrupted, and explain what was done to repair it.
width.typical: Monitor meaning during reading and self-correct — re-reading, trying alternative decodings, using context — to maintain fluent and accurate reading across chapter books and curriculum texts.
wider: Discuss which self-correction strategies work best for different types of errors (unknown word vs wrong word that sounds similar)
Observe and compare the monitoring strategies of a proficient and a developing reader, discussing what makes the proficient reader effective

descriptors.title: Evaluate texts with comprehension strategies
descriptors.description: use comprehension strategies when listening and viewing to build literal and inferred meaning to evaluate information and ideas in texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students use comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning across texts (AC9E2LY05). They have not yet used comprehension strategies specifically to evaluate information and ideas — assessing relevance, importance and accuracy.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use comprehension strategies when listening and viewing to build literal and inferred meaning and evaluate information and ideas in texts.

nodes.label: Building literal and inferred meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use comprehension strategies including prediction, questioning and inference to build both literal and inferred meaning from texts.
criteria: Student applies at least two named comprehension strategies to a text
Student distinguishes between information stated directly (literal) and meaning they had to work out (inferred)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not built literal and inferred meaning using comprehension strategies cannot evaluate information and ideas at N2 — evaluation is downstream of comprehension, not parallel to it.

width.minimum: Apply at least two comprehension strategies (e.g. predicting, inferring, questioning) to build meaning from a text, explaining what each strategy helped them understand.
width.typical: Make predictions about a text; determine important ideas, events or details; draw inferences using text evidence and prior knowledge; learn new content and ask questions to expand understanding.
wider: Compare comprehension strategies used for narrative versus informative texts, discussing how purpose changes which strategies are most useful
Revisit predictions made before reading after completing a text and discuss whether and why they were confirmed or revised

modes.reason: Students at Y3 benefit from building a repertoire of named strategies that they can select and apply. Familiarity with multiple strategies — rather than defaulting to one — expands their comprehension toolkit across different text types.

nodes.label: Evaluating information and ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate information and ideas in texts — assessing relevance for a task, comparing how different texts present similar ideas, and determining importance.
criteria: Student makes an evaluative judgement about a text (relevant/important/trustworthy) and gives a reason
Student's reason is connected to a specific feature of the text — not just a general impression

width.minimum: Make at least one evaluative judgement about a text — e.g. whether it is relevant for a task, which information is most important, or whether two texts agree — and explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Compare and contrast how different texts present similar ideas or information; determine the relevance of a text for a particular task; evaluate information and ideas across texts when listening and viewing.
wider: Compare two texts that present conflicting information about the same topic and discuss how to decide which to trust
Evaluate which source (a book, a video, a website) is most useful for a specific research purpose and justify the choice

modes.reason: Evaluation requires criteria — students need reasoning scaffolds for what makes information important, relevant or trustworthy at Y3. Without criteria, evaluation defaults to preference. The reasoning structure (relevant/important/accurate because...) needs explicit modelling.

descriptors.title: Plan, create and publish texts
descriptors.description: plan, create, edit and publish imaginative, informative and persuasive written and multimodal texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students create and edit imaginative, informative and persuasive texts for familiar audiences using appropriate structure and language (AC9E2LY06). They have not yet focused on the full planning and editing cycle — including gathering ideas, selecting structure, using topic-specific vocabulary, and using digital tools and dictionaries.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, edit and publish imaginative, informative and persuasive written and multimodal texts.

nodes.label: Planning and structuring
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a text by gathering information and selecting an appropriate structure for their writing purpose.
criteria: Student produces a plan (notes, web, list or draft structure) that gathers ideas before writing
Student selects a text structure appropriate to the purpose and can explain why

width.minimum: Plan a text by gathering at least three ideas and selecting a text structure that suits the purpose, explaining why the structure was chosen.
width.typical: Gather information and ideas about a topic in preparation for writing; select appropriate text structure for the writing purpose and sequence content for clarity; use digital tools to plan, sequence and compose.
wider: Compare planning strategies for an imaginative text versus an informative text — discussing what is the same and what is different about each approach
Plan a multimodal text and discuss what additional decisions are needed compared with planning a written-only text

nodes.label: Creating with vocabulary and sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create texts using topic-specific vocabulary and appropriate simple and compound sentences to express and combine ideas.
criteria: Student uses at least one topic-specific vocabulary item in their text
Student uses both simple and compound sentences — not only one type
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not created a text with deliberate vocabulary and sentence choices have no substantive draft to bring to N3 editing — N3 requires a composed text as its input.

width.minimum: Create a text that includes at least two topic-specific vocabulary items and at least one compound sentence, explaining the purpose of each choice.
width.typical: Use appropriate simple and compound sentences to express and combine ideas; use vocabulary including topic-specific vocabulary relevant to the text type and purpose; select vocabulary deliberately to suit the topic.
wider: Compare vocabulary choices in a first draft with a revised draft and discuss how the vocabulary changes improved the text
Experiment with improving a generic sentence by replacing vague vocabulary with precise or topic-specific words, and evaluate the effect

modes.reason: Creating a text with deliberate vocabulary and sentence choices requires students to coordinate structural planning, grammatical knowledge (sentences, clauses) and vocabulary choice simultaneously. This is the composing integration that distinguishes planned, purposeful writing.

nodes.label: Editing and publishing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit a text for spelling, apostrophe use and content quality, and publish using digital tools.
criteria: Student makes at least one substantive edit (not just a surface fix) to a draft
Student correctly applies apostrophes for contractions and/or possession after editing

width.minimum: Edit a draft text by addressing at least one spelling or punctuation issue and one content improvement, explaining what was changed.
width.typical: Use print and online dictionaries and spellcheck to edit spelling, recognising that spellcheck doesn't catch all errors; check for correct apostrophe use for contractions and possession; use digital tools to publish texts.
wider: Compare a text before and after editing and evaluate whether the editing improved the text's clarity and accuracy
Develop personal editing strategies — a checklist approach — and apply it systematically to a draft

modes.reason: Editing is a skill that requires repeated practice — students improve through applying editing strategies across different texts and text types, not through additional conceptual instruction about what to check.

descriptors.title: Deliver elaborated presentations
descriptors.description: plan, create, rehearse and deliver short oral and/or multimodal presentations to inform and persuade
descriptors.knowledge: Students create, rehearse and deliver short presentations for familiar audiences, varying tone, volume and pace (AC9E2LY07). They have not yet planned and researched content for presentations, or used storyboards and sequencing as planning tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, rehearse and deliver short oral and/or multimodal presentations to inform and persuade.

nodes.label: Planning and researching a presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can research a topic and plan the sequence of ideas for a presentation using planning techniques such as storyboards.
criteria: Student produces a plan (storyboard, list or outline) that shows sequenced ideas before delivery
Student's plan includes enough content for a complete presentation — not just a title
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not planned and sequenced their presentation content cannot deliver at N2 — there is no content to pace or adjust tone for.

width.minimum: Research a topic for a presentation, gather at least three facts or ideas, and plan the sequence using a simple storyboard or list.
width.typical: Research a topic to prepare an oral or multimodal presentation; plan the sequence of ideas and information using techniques such as storyboards; explain ideas to a peer when planning.
wider: Compare how planning a multimodal presentation differs from planning an oral-only one — discussing what additional decisions are needed
Explain the planned presentation to a peer before delivery and use their feedback to make at least one improvement to the plan

modes.reason: Planning and sequencing a presentation is a procedural skill that develops through repeated practice across different topics and presentation types. Students need multiple opportunities to plan before the process becomes reliable enough to support deliberate delivery at N2.

nodes.label: Delivering with adjusted tone and pace
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliver a short oral or multimodal presentation that adjusts tone and pace to suit the purpose and audience.
criteria: Student delivers content clearly and at an appropriate pace for the audience
Student demonstrates at least one deliberate tonal or pacing choice that suits the purpose

width.minimum: Deliver a short presentation making at least one deliberate adjustment to tone or pace (e.g. slowing down for an important point, using an enthusiastic tone for persuasion).
width.typical: Adjust tone and pace to purpose and audience during delivery — informative presentations use clear, measured pace; persuasive presentations use engaging tone and appropriate emphasis.
wider: Record and review a presentation delivery, identifying one moment where tone or pace could be improved and why
Compare two deliveries of the same content with different tone choices and discuss which is more effective for the stated purpose

modes.reason: Deliberate voice control in delivery requires rehearsal — the skill develops through practice, not through more conceptual instruction about what tone and pace are. Students need multiple delivery opportunities across different presentation types.

descriptors.title: Joined letters consistent in size
descriptors.description: write words using joined letters that are clearly formed and consistent in size
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed letter formation in earlier years. They have not yet focused on joining letters consistently in handwriting.
descriptors.endpoint: Students write words using joined letters that are clearly formed and consistent in size.

nodes.label: Joined handwriting with consistent size
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write words using joined letters that are clearly formed and consistent in size.
criteria: Student's joined letters are clearly formed (distinguishable from each other)
Student maintains consistent letter size within a word and across a line

width.minimum: Write a set of words using joined letters, demonstrating clear letter formation and consistent size across a line of writing.
width.typical: Write words and sentences using joined letters that are clearly formed and consistent in size across extended writing tasks.
wider: Compare joined and unjoined writing of the same text and discuss how consistency of size and joining affects readability
Practise joins that students find most difficult and reflect on what makes those joins challenging

modes.reason: Handwriting is a motor skill — fluency and consistency develop through regular practice, not through conceptual extension. Repeated, distributed practice across varied writing tasks is the mechanism for improvement.

descriptors.title: Multisyllabic words and phonemes
descriptors.description: understand how to apply knowledge of phoneme-grapheme (sound-letter) relationships, syllables, and blending and segmenting to fluently read and write multisyllabic words with more complex letter patterns
descriptors.knowledge: Students manipulate complex sounds and use vowel digraphs, consonant clusters and silent letters to read and write multisyllabic words (AC9E2LY09-10). They have not yet applied this knowledge to more complex patterns including consonant digraphs representing different sounds.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply phoneme-grapheme knowledge and syllable patterns to fluently read and write multisyllabic words with more complex letter patterns.

nodes.label: Complex consonant patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and write words with consonant digraphs, consonant blends and digraphs that represent different sounds.
criteria: Student correctly reads multisyllabic words with complex consonant patterns
Student correctly segments a multisyllabic word into syllables when writing
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot flexibly apply phoneme-grapheme knowledge for complex consonant patterns will encounter systematic decoding errors when reading multisyllabic words — this blocks accurate reading across curriculum texts and underpins fluency in LY10 and LY11 morphological work.

width.minimum: Read and write at least four multisyllabic words with complex consonant patterns (digraphs, blends) and explain the sound each pattern represents.
width.typical: Read and write complex words with consonant digraphs and blends; apply knowledge to consonant digraphs that represent different sounds in different words (e.g. 'machine', 'chef' for 'ch'); use blending and segmenting across syllable boundaries.
wider: Collect examples of the same digraph representing different sounds (e.g. 'ch' in chair/chef/chorus) and sort them — discussing patterns in when each pronunciation applies
Explore how splitting words into syllables helps decode long unfamiliar words, practising across different syllable patterns

modes.reason: The key challenge is that digraphs like 'ch' don't always represent the same sound. Students need exposure to multiple examples across different words before they develop flexible pattern recognition rather than applying a single rule.

descriptors.title: Base words, prefixes and suffixes
descriptors.description: understand how to apply knowledge of common base words, prefixes, suffixes and generalisations for adding a suffix to a base word to read and comprehend new multimorphemic words
descriptors.knowledge: Students build morphemic word families using prefixes and suffixes (AC9E2LY12). They have not yet applied generalisations for adding suffixes to base words (e.g. doubling, dropping 'e').
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply knowledge of base words, prefixes and suffixes to read and comprehend new multimorphemic words.

nodes.label: Prefixes changing base word meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use knowledge of prefixes to change the meaning of a base word and read new multimorphemic words.
criteria: Student identifies the base word and prefix in a multimorphemic word
Student explains how the prefix changes the meaning of the base word

width.minimum: Identify the base word and prefix in at least three multimorphemic words, explain how the prefix changes the meaning, and read the words correctly.
width.typical: Use knowledge of prefixes to change the meaning of base words; read new multimorphemic words by recognising base + prefix structure.
wider: Collect words with the same prefix (e.g. 'un-') and generalise about what the prefix consistently does to meaning
Explore how knowing one prefix helps decode a whole family of unfamiliar words encountered in reading

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of common prefixes and their meanings to use morphological knowledge productively as a decoding strategy. Range of examples matters more than depth on a single prefix.

nodes.label: Suffix generalisations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply generalisations for adding a suffix to a base word (doubling, dropping 'e') to form plurals and past tense correctly.
criteria: Student correctly applies the doubling or 'drop e' rule when adding a suffix
Student can state the generalisation they applied

width.minimum: Apply at least two suffix generalisations correctly (e.g. double the final consonant before '-ing'/'-ed' for CVC words; drop the 'e' before a vowel suffix) and explain the rule applied.
width.typical: Use generalisations for adding a suffix to form plurals and past tense — including doubling the final consonant and dropping the 'e'; apply to form and read multimorphemic words.
wider: Find exceptions to the doubling rule and discuss why the exceptions exist — exploring what patterns predict when doubling applies
Compare suffix generalisations in English with known patterns in another language if applicable — discussing similarities and differences

modes.reason: Suffix generalisations are precision spelling rules that require repeated application in writing before they become automatic. Students know the rules but apply them inconsistently — practice across multiple words is the remedy.

descriptors.title: Less common letter patterns
descriptors.description: use phoneme-grapheme (sound-letter) relationships and less common letter patterns to spell words
descriptors.knowledge: Students use spelling patterns and morphemes to read and write words with unpredictable sound-spelling relationships (AC9E2LY11). They have not yet focused specifically on less common patterns after short vowels and 3-letter blends.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use phoneme-grapheme relationships and less common letter patterns to spell words.

nodes.label: Less common patterns after short vowels
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and spell words with less common letter patterns after short vowels (e.g. 'tch', 'dge').
criteria: Student correctly spells at least three words with a named less common pattern
Student can identify the pattern and explain why it appears at that position in the word

width.minimum: Correctly spell at least four words with less common patterns after short vowels (e.g. 'catch', 'bridge') and explain the pattern each uses.
width.typical: Use phonic knowledge to explore less common letter patterns after short vowels (e.g. 'tch', 'dge'); apply to spell words correctly in writing.
wider: Collect words with 'tch' and 'ch' after a short vowel and explore when each is used — developing a generalisation about the pattern
Find less common patterns in words from different curriculum areas and discuss how knowing the pattern helps spelling

modes.reason: Less common letter patterns are only identifiable through exposure to multiple examples. Students need to see enough instances of each pattern to recognise it reliably rather than treating each new word as unique.

nodes.label: 3-letter blends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and write words with 3-letter consonant blends.
criteria: Student correctly reads words with 3-letter blends without sounding out each letter separately
Student correctly spells words with 3-letter blends from memory or dictation

width.minimum: Read and write at least four words with 3-letter blends (e.g. 'str-', 'spr-', 'thr-') correctly.
width.typical: Use phonic knowledge and knowledge of letter patterns to spell words with 3-letter blends across reading and writing contexts.
wider: Collect a set of 3-letter blend words and sort by the blend at the start — discussing whether certain blends appear more in certain types of words
Apply 3-letter blend knowledge to read unfamiliar words encountered in subject-area texts

modes.reason: 3-letter blend reading and spelling develops through repeated practice with varied examples. Recognition becomes automatic through exposure rather than through more conceptual instruction.

descriptors.title: High-frequency words and homophones
descriptors.description: recognise and know how to write most high-frequency words including some homophones
descriptors.knowledge: Students use contextual and syntactic knowledge to spell some homophones (referenced in Y2). They have not yet focused on reliable recognition and writing of most high-frequency words as a distinct target, or on using context systematically to identify correct homophone spelling.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and write most high-frequency words including some homophones.

nodes.label: High-frequency word recognition and writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and write most high-frequency words automatically.
criteria: Student reads high-frequency words without decoding (automatic recognition)
Student writes high-frequency words correctly in the context of their own writing

width.minimum: Read and write at least 20 high-frequency words correctly and automatically (without sounding out).
width.typical: Recognise and write most high-frequency words automatically in both reading and writing contexts, including in extended writing tasks.
wider: Identify which high-frequency words are still causing errors in personal writing and develop a targeted strategy to learn those specific words
Examine how high-frequency words are often irregular and cannot be decoded phonically — discussing what strategies work for learning these words

modes.reason: High-frequency word recognition is built through repeated encounters — it is essentially a memorisation task. Practice and exposure are the mechanisms, not conceptual extension.

nodes.label: Homophones and context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use context and syntactic knowledge to identify and spell the correct form of common homophones.
criteria: Student selects the correct homophone form in a sentence context
Student can explain how the sentence context signals which form is correct

width.minimum: Correctly select and spell the right homophone (e.g. 'break' or 'brake', 'their' or 'there') in at least three sentence contexts and explain how the context was used to decide.
width.typical: Use context and syntactic knowledge to spell homophones correctly — identifying common homophone pairs and applying context clues to select the right form in reading and writing.
wider: Find homophone errors in a passage and explain how to use context clues to correct each one
Explore less common homophones encountered in reading and build a personal reference list with example sentences for each

modes.reason: Homophone selection errors persist because students learn word forms in isolation rather than in context. Multiple different sentence contexts for each homophone pair help students develop reliable context-based discrimination.

descriptors.title: Language in formal and informal contexts
descriptors.description: explore language used to develop relationships in formal and informal situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how cooperation depends on shared social conventions that vary with formality (AC9E3LA01). They have not yet explored how language relationships vary across formal/informal contexts and how cultural background influences interaction.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify how language choices — including register, vocabulary and inclusive phrasing — vary across formal and informal situations, and explain how factors such as age, expertise, familiarity and cultural background shape these choices.

nodes.label: Register and formality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that language changes depending on whether a situation is formal or informal, and give examples of the same idea expressed in each register.
criteria: Can identify a formal and an informal version of the same communicative act and name at least one language feature that marks the difference
Does not treat formal language as simply 'more correct' — can explain that both registers serve different purposes
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's analysis of how factors like age and expertise shape language choices requires students to understand register as contextually appropriate — without dispelling the formal=correct misconception, N2 analysis produces distorted conclusions about why language varies.

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of formal and informal language in a provided text or scenario and explain why the register differs.
width.typical: Compare formal and informal language across two or more familiar contexts (e.g. playground vs classroom report) and identify specific features — vocabulary choices, sentence structure, tone — that signal formality.
wider: Compare written formal and informal registers in the same genre across different purposes, such as a formal letter vs a text message covering the same request
Examine how digital communication contexts (email, chat, social media) sit on the formality spectrum and what signals register in each

modes.reason: Students often conflate formal language with 'correct' language and informal with 'wrong'. Encountering multiple contexts where informal register is appropriate — and where formal register would be odd — helps displace this misconception.

nodes.label: Factors shaping language choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how age, expertise and familiarity between speakers influence language choices in an interaction.
criteria: Can name at least two factors (age, expertise, familiarity) that influence language choices and link each to a concrete example
Can explain why the same person might use different language in two different relationships

width.minimum: Identify how one factor (e.g. talking to an expert vs a peer) changes the language used in a specific interaction.
width.typical: Analyse interactions across at least two relationship types (adult/child, expert/novice, friend/friend) and describe how each factor shapes vocabulary, tone and degree of formality.
wider: Compare how the same information is communicated differently depending on the audience's expertise — such as a scientist explaining an idea to colleagues versus to primary students
Examine how familiarity changes language over time in a relationship, using text-based examples such as letter exchanges or dialogue sequences

nodes.label: Inclusive language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify inclusive and non-inclusive language choices and explain why inclusive language matters in different contexts.
criteria: Can identify a non-inclusive phrasing and suggest an inclusive alternative with a reason
Understands that inclusive language is a relational choice, not just a rule

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of inclusive language and explain why it is used rather than an alternative phrasing.
width.typical: Recognise inclusive language principles in a range of texts and contexts, including gender-neutral terms, respectful naming and avoiding assumptions; explain the relational purpose of inclusive choices.
wider: Explore how language expectations around inclusion have changed over time by comparing older texts with contemporary equivalents
Research language used in formal contexts such as school communications or public signage, identifying where inclusive language is and is not used and suggesting revisions

nodes.label: Cultural conventions in interaction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how greeting conventions and respectful forms of address vary across cultures, including First Nations Australian practices.
criteria: Can describe at least one First Nations Australian convention for greeting or addressing Elders and explain its cultural significance
Does not treat one cultural convention as the default — can explain that conventions reflect cultural values

width.minimum: Describe at least one cultural convention that shapes how people greet or address each other formally.
width.typical: Compare greeting and address conventions across at least two cultural contexts, including First Nations Australian conventions for respecting Elders, and explain how these reflect cultural values about relationships.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian protocols for greeting, introducing and acknowledging Country and Elders, and compare these with conventions in other cultural groups represented in the class community
Investigate how formal greetings and terms of address differ across a range of cultures represented in Australian society and discuss what these differences reveal about values and relationships

modes.reason: Without encountering diverse examples, students default to a single cultural norm as the standard. Multiple cultural contexts help students understand conventions as culturally situated rather than universal.

descriptors.title: Subjective and objective language
descriptors.description: identify the subjective language of opinion and feeling, and the objective language of factual reporting
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how evaluative and emotive language including modal verbs can vary in forcefulness (AC9E3LA02). They have not yet distinguished subjective language of opinion/feeling from objective language of factual reporting as distinct registers with different purposes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify subjective language (opinion, feeling, thinking verbs) and objective language (factual reporting, summary verbs) in texts, explain the different purposes each serves, and recognise when each is appropriate.

nodes.label: Language of opinion and feeling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify thinking verbs and emotive vocabulary that signal a subjective point of view in a text.
criteria: Can identify at least two thinking verbs in a text and explain that they signal personal opinion
Can distinguish emotive vocabulary (e.g. 'wonderful', 'terrible') from neutral descriptors
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying objective language in N2 requires students to know what subjective features look like — the contrast between thinking verbs/emotive vocabulary (N1) and summary verbs/neutral vocabulary (N2) is how students distinguish the two registers.

width.minimum: Identify thinking verbs (e.g. 'I think', 'I believe', 'I feel') in a provided text and explain that these signal the writer's personal view.
width.typical: Identify a range of subjective language features across texts — thinking verbs, emotive adjectives, evaluative adverbs — and explain how these position the reader to share or consider the author's viewpoint.
wider: Compare the use of subjective language across different opinion text types — a review, a letter to the editor, a persuasive speech — and identify which features are consistent and which vary by genre
Explore how First Nations Australian authors use subjective voice to position readers in relation to cultural knowledge and experience

modes.reason: Subjective language features vary widely across opinion text types — students need multiple examples before the pattern is distinguishable from genre-specific features, and before the subjective/objective contrast is reliably seen.

nodes.label: Language of factual reporting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify summary verbs and neutral vocabulary that signal objective, factual reporting in a text.
criteria: Can identify at least one summary verb and explain that it reports a finding rather than expressing an opinion
Can distinguish 'The man has 6 cats' (objective) from 'The man has too many noisy cats' (subjective) and name the feature that marks each
nodes.hinge_reason: N3's explanation of why writers choose each register requires students to accurately characterise what each register consists of — the misconception about objective language from N2 produces inaccurate purpose analysis in N3.

width.minimum: Identify summary verbs (e.g. 'we concluded', 'the report found', 'results showed') in a provided text and explain that these signal reported facts rather than personal views.
width.typical: Identify objective language features across informational texts — summary verbs, precise nouns, impersonal constructions, present tense for facts — and explain how these create an effect of factual authority.
wider: Compare how objective language is used differently in scientific reports, news articles and encyclopaedia entries — same information, different degrees of formality
Examine how news reporting attempts objectivity and identify moments where subjective language creeps in

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate objective language with 'no adjectives' or 'short sentences'. Precision about what objective language features are — summary verbs, impersonal constructions — requires consolidation through multiple examples.

nodes.label: Purpose and context of each register
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why writers choose subjective or objective language depending on the purpose and context of their text.
criteria: Can explain why a specific text uses the register it does by naming its purpose
Does not assume that only reports are objective — can identify register choices in any text type

width.minimum: Explain why a particular text uses subjective or objective language by linking the language choice to the text's purpose.
width.typical: Compare two texts on similar topics — one subjective (review, opinion piece), one objective (report, news article) — and explain how the purpose of each text drives its language choices.
wider: Analyse a text that mixes subjective and objective language (e.g. a persuasive essay using reported evidence) and explain why the author moves between registers
Write a short objective and subjective version of the same information about a familiar topic, then discuss the effect of each on the reader

modes.reason: Students often assume all informational texts should be objective and all personal texts subjective. Mixed-register texts — persuasive essays, biographies — help students see that purpose, not text type alone, determines register.

descriptors.title: Text stages and language features
descriptors.description: identify how texts across the curriculum have different language features and are typically organised into characteristic stages depending on purposes
descriptors.knowledge: Students describe how language features and structures in curriculum texts vary according to purpose (AC9E3LA03). They have not yet identified the characteristic stages of specific text types and how stage organisation serves social purposes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify the characteristic stages and language features of a range of curriculum text types — including narratives, information reports, explanations and arguments — and explain how stage organisation and language features together serve each text's social purpose.

nodes.label: Stages and purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that texts are organised into stages and that stages serve the text's social purpose.
criteria: Can identify the stages of a given text type and name what each stage does
Does not confuse stage with paragraph — can explain that a stage may span multiple paragraphs
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying language features by text type in N2 requires students to understand what each stage is trying to do — students who conflate stages with paragraphs cannot explain why specific language features serve the stage's function.

width.minimum: Identify the stages of one familiar text type (e.g. narrative: orientation, complication, resolution) and explain what each stage does for the reader.
width.typical: Identify and label the stages of at least three text types from different curriculum areas — such as a narrative, an information report and an explanation — and explain the purpose each stage serves.
wider: Compare how the same social purpose (e.g. persuading) is achieved through different stage structures in different text types — argument vs advertisement vs speech
Examine how digital text forms (e.g. blog posts, infographics) adapt or modify traditional stage structures

modes.reason: Students often think 'stages' means paragraphs. Encountering multiple text types with labelled stages helps shift understanding from structural to functional — each stage exists because the text needs to do something at that point.

nodes.label: Language features by text type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific language features associated with particular text types and explain how these features serve the text's purpose.
criteria: Can name a language feature in a text and connect it to what the text is trying to do at that point
Can identify at least two different language features, not just one repeated example
nodes.hinge_reason: Distinguishing explanation from report structure in N3 requires students to recognise their different language features — without the feature repertoire from N2, students can only compare surface structure, not the linguistic choices that produce it.

width.minimum: Identify at least two language features in a provided text and explain why those features suit that text type (e.g. action verbs in a recount, timeless present tense in a report).
width.typical: Identify language features across a range of text types — including verb choices, tense, noun group structure, connectives — and explain how each feature contributes to the text's purpose and stage structure.
wider: Compare language features across texts on the same topic but in different text types (e.g. an explanation and a report about the water cycle)
Examine how multimodal texts combine language features with visual features to serve the text's purpose

modes.reason: Language features vary across text types — students need to accumulate examples across multiple types before the distinctions between them stabilise and become reliably distinguishable.

nodes.label: Explanations and reports — structural differences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish sequential and causal explanations from comparative and part-whole information reports by their stages and language features.
criteria: Can identify whether a text explains a process or reports information, and name a structural feature supporting that identification
Does not confuse sequential explanation (how something happens) with information report (what something is)

width.minimum: Identify whether a given text is an explanation or an information report and name one structural feature that supports the identification.
width.typical: Compare sequential/causal explanation structures with comparative/part-whole report structures across two or more texts, identifying the stages and language features that distinguish them.
wider: Locate examples of sequential, causal and comparative structures in texts from different curriculum areas (science, HASS, maths) and explain how the structure suits the subject content
Create a short explanation and a short report on the same topic and compare the structural choices made

modes.reason: Distinguishing explanation from report structure requires explicit attention to the logic of each — cause-effect chains vs classification-description hierarchies. A reasoning scaffold helps students see why the structures differ, not just that they do.

nodes.label: Form vs stage organisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between a text's form (poster, email, list) and its stage organisation, explaining that different forms can realise the same stages.
criteria: Can name a text's form and separately identify its stage structure
Understands that the same form (e.g. email) can realise different text types with different stage organisations

width.minimum: Explain the difference between a text's form and its stage organisation using one example (e.g. a poster that realises an argument has a form of 'poster' but stages of 'position, argument, conclusion').
width.typical: Identify the form and stage organisation of several texts, including cases where the same social purpose appears in different forms, and explain why form and stage organisation are separate considerations.
wider: Investigate how digital forms (social media posts, websites, infographics) organise stages differently from print equivalents while serving the same social purpose
Compare how First Nations Australian authors use different forms to structure storytelling, and consider how traditional narrative stages operate across oral and written forms

descriptors.title: Text connectives and cohesion
descriptors.description: identify how text connectives including temporal and conditional words, and topic word associations are used to sequence and connect ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how paragraphs group related information within stages of written texts (AC9E3LA04). They have not yet identified text connectives as the explicit devices that sequence and connect ideas across sentences and sections.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify temporal, conditional and additive text connectives, explain their role in sequencing and connecting ideas, and recognise how pronouns and determiners maintain cohesion across a text.

nodes.label: Pronouns and determiners as cohesive links
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how pronouns and determiners link back to previously mentioned information in a text.
criteria: Can identify a pronoun in a text and name the noun it refers back to
Can identify a demonstrative determiner (this/that/these/those) and explain what it is pointing to

width.minimum: Identify a pronoun or determiner (this, that, these, those) in a text and explain what it refers back to.
width.typical: Identify multiple cohesive devices — pronouns and demonstrative determiners — across a text and explain how they keep the reader connected to the subject without repetition.
wider: Examine how cohesion breaks down in texts where pronoun reference is unclear, and revise to restore it
Compare how pronouns and determiners create cohesion differently in narrative versus informational texts

modes.reason: Students often read past pronouns without tracking their referents. Identifying the reference chain requires sustained attention and practice — this is a fluency-building node, not a conceptual one.

nodes.label: Connectives between sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify text connectives that create logical links between sentences and explain the relationship each signals.
criteria: Can identify a connective and name the type of relationship it signals (contrast, cause, addition)
Does not treat all connectives as interchangeable — can explain why substituting 'however' for 'therefore' changes meaning

width.minimum: Identify a sentence-level connective (e.g. however, therefore, in addition) and explain the relationship it signals between the two sentences.
width.typical: Identify a range of connective types — adversative (however, nevertheless), causal (therefore, as a result), additive (in addition, furthermore) — across informational texts and explain what logical relationship each signals.
wider: Compare how connectives are used in argument texts versus explanation texts — which types predominate and why
Examine how removing or substituting connectives changes the logic of a paragraph, using a range of text types

modes.reason: Students often know 'however means contrast' but apply it mechanically without understanding the claim-counter relationship it creates. Multiple text contexts showing connectives doing real logical work helps build genuine functional understanding.

nodes.label: Temporal connectives and sequencing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify temporal connectives and explain how they sequence events or steps through time.
criteria: Can identify at least three temporal connectives in a sequence text and explain the order they create
Understands that temporal connectives signal time relationships, not just list items

width.minimum: Identify temporal connectives (firstly, then, next, finally) in a text and explain how they signal sequence.
width.typical: Identify temporal connectives across sequential texts — procedures, recounts, explanations — and explain how they create a clear time-ordered structure that guides the reader.
wider: Compare temporal sequencing in a recount (past sequence) versus a procedure (imperative sequence) and explain how the text type changes the connective choices
Examine how First Nations Australian oral narrative traditions use temporal sequencing in storytelling, and compare with written sequential texts

descriptors.title: Online text navigation features
descriptors.description: identify text navigation features of online texts that enhance readability including headlines, drop-down menus, links, graphics and layout
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify the purpose of layout and navigation features in print and digital texts (AC9E3LA05). They have not yet examined the specific navigation features of online texts — headlines, drop-down menus, links, graphics and layout — as readability-enhancing choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify and explain the purpose of online text navigation features including headlines, drop-down menus, hyperlinks, graphics and layout, and describe how these features help readers select and navigate content purposefully.

nodes.label: Print vs online navigation features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how print and online texts use different navigation features and explain what each type of feature does for the reader.
criteria: Can name at least two online-specific navigation features and explain their readability function
Can identify at least one way online navigation differs from print navigation

width.minimum: Name two navigation features specific to online texts (e.g. links, drop-down menus) and explain how each helps a reader.
width.typical: Compare navigation features in a print text (headings, subheadings, table of contents) with their online equivalents (home pages, subpages, hyperlinks, drop-down menus) and explain how online features extend or replace print conventions.
wider: Compare navigation features across two different websites on similar topics (e.g. two science information sites for students) and evaluate which is more readable and why
Design a navigation structure for a hypothetical webpage on a familiar topic and explain the purpose of each feature chosen

nodes.label: Headlines, graphics and layout
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how headlines, graphics and layout work together in online texts to guide reader selection and comprehension.
criteria: Can explain how a specific headline helps a reader decide whether to read further
Can explain how a graphic adds to rather than just repeats the text

width.minimum: Identify a headline, a graphic and a layout feature in an online text and explain what each contributes to readability.
width.typical: Analyse how headlines, graphics and layout in an online text work together to signal what is important, guide navigation and support comprehension — including how graphics and captions add meaning beyond the body text.
wider: Compare how headlines and layout differ across online news sites for different audiences (children vs adults) and explain the design choices
Examine how the same story is presented with different headlines and layouts across two sites and discuss how design affects meaning

descriptors.title: Complex sentences
descriptors.description: understand that complex sentences contain one independent clause and at least one dependent clause typically joined by a subordinating conjunction to create relationships, such as time and causality
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that clauses contain subjects and verbs that must agree (AC9E3LA06). They have not yet examined complex sentences with independent and dependent clauses joined by subordinating conjunctions to create time or causal relationships.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify independent and dependent clauses in complex sentences, name the subordinating conjunctions that join them, and explain what relationship — time, cause, condition, concession — the dependent clause adds to the main clause.

nodes.label: Independent and dependent clauses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the independent clause and at least one dependent clause in a complex sentence.
criteria: Can correctly identify the independent clause in a complex sentence (including when the dependent clause comes first)
Can identify the dependent clause and explain that it cannot stand alone as a sentence
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying subordinating conjunctions in N2 requires students to have reliably located the two clauses they join — without clause identification, conjunction identification has no structure to work from.

width.minimum: Identify the independent clause and the dependent clause in a provided complex sentence.
width.typical: Identify independent and dependent clauses across a range of complex sentences, including sentences where the dependent clause comes first, and explain what each clause contributes.
wider: Examine complex sentences in texts from different curriculum areas (science, HASS) and identify how dependent clauses carry different types of additional information
Transform simple sentences into complex sentences by adding dependent clauses and explain how meaning changes

modes.reason: Identifying dependent clauses — especially when fronted — requires reliable parsing skill. Students need practice across a range of sentence structures before this becomes automatic.

nodes.label: Subordinating conjunctions and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify subordinating conjunctions and explain the relationship each creates between clauses.
criteria: Can name the subordinating conjunction in a complex sentence and identify the relationship type it signals
Does not confuse coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or) with subordinating conjunctions
nodes.hinge_reason: Creating complex sentences for meaning in N3 requires students to select conjunctions that encode the intended relationship — without N2's conjunction-relationship repertoire, N3 choices are arbitrary.

width.minimum: Identify a subordinating conjunction in a complex sentence and name the relationship it creates (time, cause, condition, concession).
width.typical: Identify a range of subordinating conjunctions across texts — temporal (when, until, before, after), causal (because, since), conditional (if, unless), concessive (although, even though) — and explain what relationship each signals.
wider: Compare how temporal and causal subordinating conjunctions are used differently in narrative (to sequence events) versus explanation texts (to signal causation)
Examine how the position of the dependent clause (before or after the main clause) affects emphasis and meaning in a complex sentence

modes.reason: Students often learn 'because = reason' without understanding that multiple subordinating conjunctions signal cause, and that the specific choice creates different nuances. Multiple contexts help build a richer repertoire.

nodes.label: Using complex sentences for richer meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create complex sentences that use dependent clauses to add information about time, cause, manner or condition, making sentences more specific and detailed.
criteria: Can write a complex sentence with a dependent clause that adds time or cause information
Can explain how the dependent clause makes the sentence more specific than the simple sentence it expanded

width.minimum: Expand a simple sentence by adding a dependent clause to create a complex sentence that adds time or cause information.
width.typical: Create complex sentences across a range of relationship types — time, cause, condition, manner — and explain how each dependent clause makes the main clause more specific and the writing more precise.
wider: Revise a piece of writing to replace simple sentences with complex sentences and evaluate the effect on precision and readability
Compare complex sentence use across two texts at different complexity levels (e.g. a Year 2 reader vs a Year 4 informational text) and describe the difference in sentence structure

modes.reason: Creating complex sentences integrates knowledge of clauses, subordinating conjunctions and semantic relationships — the building blocks from nodes 1 and 2 coordinated in production.

descriptors.title: Direct and indirect speech
descriptors.description: investigate how quoted (direct) and reported (indirect) speech are used
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how different verb types represent doing, feeling, thinking, saying and relating (AC9E3LA07). They have not yet investigated how quoted (direct) and reported (indirect) speech work as distinct grammatical and textual choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify direct and indirect speech in texts, explain the grammatical and punctuation differences between them, and describe why a writer might choose one over the other in context.

nodes.label: Direct speech features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify direct speech in a text and describe its key features — quotation marks, saying verb, speaker identification.
criteria: Can identify direct speech in a text and name quotation marks and a saying verb as features
Understands that direct speech presents the speaker's exact words
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding indirect speech in N2 requires students to know direct speech as the contrast case — indirect features (no quotation marks, tense shift, pronoun change) are defined by how they differ from direct.

width.minimum: Identify direct speech in a text and name at least two features that mark it as direct speech.
width.typical: Identify direct speech across narrative and non-narrative texts, naming features including quotation marks, saying verbs, punctuation conventions and speaker identification, and explain what effect hearing the exact words creates.
wider: Compare how direct speech is used in narrative (to reveal character) versus news reporting (to attribute claims) and explain how purpose changes the role of direct speech
Investigate how dialogue in First Nations Australian literary texts uses direct speech to convey voice, community and cultural perspective

modes.reason: Direct speech appears across narrative and non-narrative texts with different purposes — students need multiple text contexts to understand it as a deliberate choice, not just 'what people say', before the contrast with indirect speech is meaningful.

nodes.label: Indirect speech features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify indirect speech in a text and describe its key grammatical features — no quotation marks, tense shift, pronoun change.
criteria: Can identify indirect speech and note that there are no quotation marks
Can explain that indirect speech reports what was said without using the exact words
nodes.hinge_reason: Explaining the effect of choosing direct versus indirect in N3 requires students to be able to transform between them — students who cannot produce indirect speech accurately cannot evaluate the choice meaningfully.

width.minimum: Identify indirect speech in a text and name at least one grammatical feature that distinguishes it from direct speech.
width.typical: Identify indirect speech across texts and describe its features — reporting verb, subordinate clause with 'that', tense shift, pronoun change — and explain why indirect speech is used to summarise or report rather than quote exactly.
wider: Compare how indirect speech is used differently across text types — reports, recounts, news — and explain why summarising is preferred over quoting in each
Examine how reported speech can change the meaning or emphasis of what was said, and discuss implications for fairness in reporting

modes.reason: The tense shift and pronoun change in indirect speech are mechanical features students commonly get wrong. Practice across multiple examples is needed before transformation between direct and indirect becomes reliable.

nodes.label: Choosing between direct and indirect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why a writer might choose direct speech over indirect speech (or vice versa) in a specific context.
criteria: Can explain why direct speech is used in a narrative (e.g. to show character, create immediacy) and why indirect speech is used in a report (e.g. to summarise efficiently)
Can transform a direct speech sentence into indirect speech correctly

width.minimum: Explain one reason why a writer uses direct speech in a narrative and one reason indirect speech is used in an informational text.
