width.typical: Analyse how direct and indirect speech are used purposefully across narrative and non-narrative texts, explaining the effect of each choice on authenticity, pace, summary and reader engagement.
wider: Rewrite a passage, converting direct to indirect speech and vice versa, and evaluate the effect on tone, pace and authenticity
Compare how direct and indirect speech are used across different media formats — written story, film script, news article — and explain how the medium influences speech choices

modes.reason: Students often see direct speech as simply 'what people say' without understanding it as a deliberate stylistic choice. Multiple genre contexts show how writers use speech differently depending on purpose.

descriptors.title: Adverb and prepositional phrases
descriptors.description: understand how adverb groups/phrases and prepositional phrases work in different ways to provide circumstantial details about an activity
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how different verb types and tense work in clauses (AC9E3LA07, AC9E3LA08). They have not yet examined how adverb groups/phrases and prepositional phrases provide circumstantial details of time, place, manner and cause around activities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify adverb groups/phrases and prepositional phrases in sentences, classify the type of circumstantial detail each provides (time, place, manner, cause), and explain how these phrases add precision to descriptions of activities.

nodes.label: Circumstantial details — what, when, where, how
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that sentences can include additional information about the circumstances surrounding an activity — when it happened, where, how and why.
criteria: Can identify at least three types of circumstantial detail in a sentence and name the question each answers (when? where? how?)
Can explain that circumstantial phrases add detail to the main activity without changing what the activity is
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying adverb and prepositional phrases in N2 and N3 requires students to know what type of circumstantial detail they are providing — without N1's time/place/manner/cause framework, classification in N2 and N3 is impossible.

width.minimum: Identify at least two different types of circumstantial detail in a provided sentence (e.g. time and place) and name what question each answers.
width.typical: Identify all four types of circumstantial detail — time, place, manner, cause — across a range of sentences and explain how each adds precision to the description of an activity.
wider: Compare how circumstantial detail is used differently in narrative (for atmosphere and pace) versus scientific description (for precision and replicability)
Examine how removing circumstantial phrases changes the meaning and specificity of a sentence across different text types

modes.reason: Circumstantial detail types appear across narrative and factual texts with different distributions — multiple contexts help students see how each type functions differently across purposes, before they encounter them as adverb and prepositional phrases.

nodes.label: Adverb groups and phrases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify adverb groups and adverb phrases in sentences and explain what circumstantial detail each provides.
criteria: Can identify an adverb phrase (not just a single adverb) in a sentence
Can name what type of circumstance the phrase provides

width.minimum: Identify an adverb group or phrase in a sentence and name the type of circumstantial information it provides.
width.typical: Identify adverb groups and phrases of time, place, manner and cause across texts, noting how they differ from single adverbs and explaining what each adds to the activity described.
wider: Collect adverb phrases from texts in different subject areas and analyse what types of circumstantial information are most common in each (e.g. manner in science descriptions, time in recounts)
Create sentences using adverb phrases in different positions (initial, medial, final) and evaluate how placement changes emphasis

modes.reason: Students readily identify single adverbs but often miss adverb phrases (e.g. 'with great care', 'in the early morning'). Recognition of phrases rather than single words requires repeated practice.

nodes.label: Prepositional phrases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify prepositional phrases and explain the circumstantial detail each provides about an activity.
criteria: Can identify a prepositional phrase and name the preposition that begins it
Can explain what circumstantial information the phrase provides

width.minimum: Identify a prepositional phrase in a sentence and explain what circumstantial detail it adds (e.g. place, time).
width.typical: Identify prepositional phrases providing different circumstantial details across texts — locative (from the chair, into the forest), temporal (at midnight, during the storm), manner (with a smile, in silence) — and explain what each adds to the activity.
wider: Compare prepositional phrase use in literary and factual texts — how do authors use prepositional phrases for atmosphere versus precision?
Examine how stacking multiple prepositional phrases in one sentence (as in the elaboration example) builds richly circumstantiated description

modes.reason: Prepositional phrase repertoire is built through encountering many examples across literary and factual texts — accumulation enables the stacked-phrase authorial control that the wider tier describes.

descriptors.title: Past, present and future tense
descriptors.description: understand past, present and future tenses and their impact on meaning in a sentence
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that verbs are anchored in time through tense (AC9E3LA08). They have not yet examined the three-tense system and the impact of tense choices on meaning across different text types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify past, present and future tense in sentences and texts, explain the impact of tense choice on meaning, and identify why particular text types are typically written in particular tenses.

nodes.label: The three tenses — identification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify past, present and future tense in sentences and name the verb forms that signal each.
criteria: Can correctly identify past, present and future tense in at least three different sentences
Can name the verb form change that signals tense (e.g. 'walked' for past, 'will walk' for future)
nodes.hinge_reason: Explaining why text types use particular tenses in N2 requires students to reliably identify the tense being used — tense misidentification in N1 produces incorrect pattern analysis in N2.

width.minimum: Identify the tense of at least three sentences and name the verb form used in each.
width.typical: Identify past, present and future tense across a range of sentences and texts, noting the different verb forms used to express each tense (simple, progressive, perfect forms where they appear).
wider: Examine how tense varies within a single text (e.g. a narrative that uses past tense for events but present tense for dialogue or reflection) and explain the shifts
Compare how different languages mark tense and explore whether tense is always marked by verb form

modes.reason: Reliable identification of tense — especially in complex verb groups — requires practice. Students commonly mis-identify tense when auxiliary verbs are involved.

nodes.label: Tense and text type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why particular text types are typically written in particular tenses and identify examples.
criteria: Can name the typical tense of two different text types and explain why
Does not assume all texts are written in past tense

width.minimum: Name one text type and the tense it is typically written in, and explain why that tense suits the text's purpose.
width.typical: Identify the typical tense of at least three text types — informative texts (present), recounts (past), procedures (imperative/present), narratives (past) — and explain how tense choice serves each text's purpose.
wider: Examine a text that mixes tenses (e.g. a biography moving between past narrative and present reflection) and explain why the tense shifts occur
Compare tense use in First Nations Australian storytelling texts, considering how tense relates to the living nature of story in oral traditions versus written texts

modes.reason: Students often learn tense rules for one text type and then over-apply them. Encountering multiple text types with explicit tense-purpose discussion builds flexible understanding rather than rigid rules.

descriptors.title: Image composition and framing
descriptors.description: explore the effect of choices when framing an image, placement of elements in the image and salience on composition of still and moving images in texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify how images extend the meaning of a text (AC9E3LA09). They have not yet examined how framing, element placement and salience are deliberate compositional choices that influence viewer response in still and moving images.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify framing, element placement and salience in still and moving images, explain how each compositional choice influences viewer response, and use metalanguage to describe visual techniques.

nodes.label: Framing choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how framing choices — close-up, mid-shot, wide shot — affect what the viewer sees and feels about an image.
criteria: Can identify the framing type of an image and link it to at least one effect on the viewer
Can explain that framing is a deliberate choice, not an accident

width.minimum: Identify the framing of an image (close-up, mid or wide shot) and explain one effect the framing has on the viewer.
width.typical: Compare framing choices across a range of still and moving images, explaining how close-up frames emphasise detail and emotion, mid shots show action and relationship, and wide shots establish setting and scale.
wider: Compare how the same subject photographed with different framings creates different emotional responses, using a sequence of images
Examine how framing choices in film or television advertising position the viewer in relation to the product or character

nodes.label: Element placement and salience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the placement of elements within an image and the use of salience direct the viewer's attention and create meaning.
criteria: Can identify the most salient element in an image and give at least one technical reason (size, colour, placement) for why it stands out
Can explain how placement (foreground vs background, centre vs margin) contributes to meaning

width.minimum: Identify the most salient element in an image and explain one reason why the image-maker has made it stand out.
width.typical: Analyse how element placement (foreground/background, centre/margin, left/right) and salience (size, colour, focus, contrast) work together to direct the viewer's attention and convey meaning across a range of images.
wider: Compare how image composition changes across different cultural contexts — for example, how First Nations Australian visual art uses composition and salience differently from Western photographic conventions
Analyse how moving images use camera movement and cut to create dynamic salience across time, compared with the fixed salience of a still image

modes.reason: Students often focus only on the most obvious salient element without understanding how placement creates a hierarchy of attention. Multiple varied images help build understanding of composition as a system of choices.

descriptors.title: Synonyms and antonyms
descriptors.description: expand vocabulary by exploring a range of synonyms and antonyms, and using words encountered in a range of sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students extend topic-specific vocabulary and understand that words can have different meanings in different contexts (AC9E3LA10). They have not yet explored synonyms and antonyms as vocabulary-expanding tools with shades of meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify synonyms and antonyms for words, explain how synonyms differ in shade of meaning, and apply new vocabulary from a range of sources — including First Nations Australian language words — in their own writing and discussion.

nodes.label: Synonyms and shades of meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify synonyms for a word and explain how synonyms differ in intensity, formality or connotation.
criteria: Can name two synonyms for a given word and explain one difference in their meaning or connotation
Does not treat all synonyms as interchangeable — understands that word choice carries shade of meaning

width.minimum: Identify two synonyms for a given word and explain one way they differ in meaning or use.
width.typical: Explore synonym clusters across a range of words (e.g. walk: stride, stroll, march, shuffle) and explain how the shades of meaning differ in intensity, formality and connotation, selecting the most precise synonym for specific contexts.
wider: Build synonym clusters for key vocabulary from a current cross-curriculum topic and compare shades of meaning to make precise choices in writing
Explore how synonyms can carry different cultural or emotional weights by examining words borrowed from First Nations Australian languages now used in Australian English

modes.reason: Synonym knowledge is accumulative — the richer the synonym repertoire, the more precise and varied a student's writing. This node rewards ongoing vocabulary collection across contexts.

nodes.label: Antonyms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify antonyms and explain how antonym pairs help clarify meaning through contrast.
criteria: Can identify the antonym of a given word
Can explain how using an antonym pair in a sentence creates a contrast that clarifies meaning

width.minimum: Identify the antonym of a given word and explain how the contrast helps clarify meaning.
width.typical: Identify antonym pairs across a range of vocabulary domains and explain how antonyms are used in texts to create contrast, emphasise differences and clarify meaning.
wider: Examine how antonyms are used in persuasive texts to set up contrast between positions (e.g. safe vs dangerous, fair vs unfair)
Explore how antonym pairs shift across contexts — words that are antonyms in one context may not be in another

nodes.label: Encountering and using new vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use words encountered in reading and research — including technical, learning-area and First Nations Australian vocabulary — in their own spoken and written language.
criteria: Can use a newly encountered word accurately in their own writing or speech
Can explain the meaning of the word and where they encountered it

width.minimum: Use at least two new vocabulary words encountered in a text or research task in their own writing or discussion, explaining the meaning of each.
width.typical: Deliberately collect and use new vocabulary from a range of sources — including subject-specific texts, research and texts by First Nations Australian authors — applying words in writing and discussion with attention to precision and appropriateness.
wider: Research words from First Nations Australian languages used in Australian English (e.g. place names, flora and fauna terms) and explore their origins and meanings
Create a personal vocabulary notebook organised by topic, collecting new words from cross-curriculum reading with definitions, synonyms and example sentences

modes.reason: Vocabulary expansion is fundamentally about accumulation. Students who encounter new words but do not use them do not retain them. Structured collection and active use across contexts builds lasting vocabulary range.

descriptors.title: Punctuation for dialogue
descriptors.description: understand that punctuation signals dialogue through quotation marks and that dialogue follows conventions for the use of capital letters, commas and boundary punctuation
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how apostrophes signal contractions and possession (AC9E3LA11). They have not yet examined how quotation marks and associated punctuation conventions signal and organise dialogue within texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify and apply dialogue punctuation conventions — quotation marks, capital letters, commas, boundary punctuation — and explain how each convention signals the structure of dialogue in a text.

nodes.label: Quotation marks signal dialogue
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify quotation marks in a text and explain that they enclose the exact words of a speaker.
criteria: Can identify quotation marks in a text and explain that they mark the spoken words
Knows that the punctuation before the closing quotation mark sits inside the marks
nodes.hinge_reason: Applying boundary punctuation conventions in N2 requires students to know where quoted speech begins and ends — without reliable quotation mark identification from N1, students cannot place commas and full stops correctly relative to them.

width.minimum: Identify quoted speech in a text, note the quotation marks and explain what they signal to the reader.
width.typical: Identify the role of quotation marks across a range of narrative and non-narrative texts, distinguishing dialogue quotation from other uses of quotation marks (e.g. titles, reported speech emphasis).
wider: Compare how different published authors punctuate dialogue — some use single quotation marks, some double — and discuss conventions across Australian published texts
Examine how dialogue is punctuated differently across cultures and publishing traditions

modes.reason: Recognising quotation marks as the frame for dialogue punctuation requires repeated encounter before the convention is reliably noticed and understood as a signal — not just known as a rule.

nodes.label: Capital letters, commas and boundary punctuation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply the conventions for capital letters, commas and boundary punctuation in dialogue correctly.
criteria: Can punctuate a basic dialogue sentence (said tag after speech) with all conventions correct
Knows that a comma, not a full stop, precedes a said tag when the dialogue continues the sentence

width.minimum: Punctuate a short piece of dialogue correctly using quotation marks, a capital letter to open quoted speech and appropriate boundary punctuation.
width.typical: Apply all dialogue punctuation conventions across a range of dialogue patterns — speech first with said tag, said tag first, speech interrupted by said tag — explaining the purpose of each convention.
wider: Edit a piece of dialogue with punctuation errors and explain each correction made
Analyse how published authors use dialogue punctuation for pace — short, rapid exchanges versus longer speeches — and identify punctuation choices that support each

modes.reason: Dialogue punctuation involves several co-occurring conventions (quotation marks, capital, comma/period placement, said tag positioning) that students commonly confuse. Sustained practice across varied dialogue patterns is the remedy.

descriptors.title: Storylines across contexts
descriptors.description: recognise similar storylines, ideas and relationships in different contexts in literary texts by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss characters, events and settings across different cultural and contextual contexts in literature (AC9E3LE01). They have not yet recognised similar storylines, ideas and relationships across First Nations Australian, Australian and world literary texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify common storylines, themes and relationship patterns across literary texts from different cultural contexts — including First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors — and explain how context shapes the way these universal patterns are expressed.

nodes.label: Identifying recurring storylines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a recurring storyline pattern (e.g. journey, transformation, conflict and resolution) across two or more texts from different contexts.
criteria: Can identify a shared storyline pattern across two texts from different cultural contexts
Can explain what makes the storylines similar despite being set in different contexts

width.minimum: Identify a similar storyline in two texts from different cultural contexts and explain what makes the storylines similar.
width.typical: Identify recurring storyline patterns — journey, transformation, rescue, coming-of-age, conflict — across at least three texts from different cultural contexts, including at least one First Nations Australian text, and explain what the patterns share.
wider: Investigate how the same universal storyline pattern (e.g. the hero's journey) appears in First Nations Australian, European and Asian literary traditions and discuss similarities and differences
Read texts by the same author and track how recurring storyline patterns or character relationships appear across their work

modes.reason: Recognising storyline patterns is a capability built through encountering many texts. The wider the textual repertoire, the stronger the pattern-recognition ability becomes.

nodes.label: Themes and connections to experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the theme of a literary text and connect it to their own experience, other texts and the wider world.
criteria: Can name the theme of a text and explain it in their own words
Can make at least one connection between the theme and their own experience or another text

width.minimum: Identify the theme of a literary text and make one connection to personal experience, another text or a real-world issue.
width.typical: Identify themes across a range of texts from different cultural contexts, making connections between texts and between texts and the world, and explaining how themes carry meaning beyond the specific story.
wider: Compare how a theme (e.g. belonging, courage, loss) is treated differently across texts from different cultural contexts and discuss what each treatment reveals about cultural values
Explore how themes in First Nations Australian literature connect to Country, community and cultural knowledge, and consider how these themes differ from Western literary treatments of similar ideas

nodes.label: Characters, settings and cultural context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how cultural context shapes the way characters, settings and relationships are portrayed in a text, even when the underlying storyline is familiar.
criteria: Can explain one way that cultural context shapes how a character or relationship is portrayed in a specific text
Does not treat cultural difference as superficial decoration — can explain how context shapes meaning

width.minimum: Explain one way that the cultural context of a text shapes how a familiar character type or relationship is portrayed.
width.typical: Compare how characters, settings and relationships in texts from different cultural backgrounds reflect the values and contexts of their origins, while sharing underlying patterns with texts from other cultures.
wider: Explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander characters and settings in First Nations Australian literature reflect cultural knowledge and relationships with Country that differ from Western literary portrayals
Research an author from a culture different from one's own and examine how their biography and cultural context appears in their literary work

modes.reason: Without encountering diverse cultural examples, students default to a Western literary norm and treat cultural difference as surface decoration. Multiple cultural contexts — especially First Nations Australian — help students understand how context shapes meaning, not just setting.

descriptors.title: Effects of text structure
descriptors.description: describe the effects of text structures and language features when responding to and sharing opinions about texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss how literary devices enhance meaning and shape reader response (AC9E3LE04). They have not yet described the effects of text structures and language features in formal responses to texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can describe how specific text structures and language features produce effects in a literary text, use metalanguage to support their responses, and share opinions about texts by connecting personal response to specific textual evidence.

nodes.label: Identifying structural and language choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific text structure choices and language features in a literary text and name them using metalanguage.
criteria: Can name a structural feature and a language feature in a text using metalanguage
Does not describe effects without naming the specific feature producing them
nodes.hinge_reason: Students must have metalanguage to name features before they can describe effects in N2 — without named features, the 'feature to effect' structure in N2 has nothing to anchor to.

width.minimum: Identify one structural feature and one language feature in a literary text and name each using appropriate metalanguage.
width.typical: Identify a range of structural choices (chapter structure, flashback, circular ending, section breaks) and language features (repetition, figurative language, dialogue, tense choices) across literary texts, naming each with metalanguage.
wider: Compare structural and language feature choices across two texts by different authors writing in the same genre, identifying what each author does differently
Examine how illustrators in picture books use visual structural choices (double-page spreads, white space, sequence) alongside author language choices to create effects

modes.reason: The metalanguage repertoire for describing structural and language features is built through repeated exposure across varied texts. Students need to encounter features named in context to build a usable vocabulary for literary response.

nodes.label: Describing effects on reader response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the effect that a specific structural or language choice has on a reader, linking the choice to the response it creates.
criteria: Can name a specific feature and describe the effect it has on the reader
Does not just describe personal feeling — connects feeling to a specific textual choice
nodes.hinge_reason: N3 requires students to support opinions with reference to specific features and their effects. Students who cannot complete the feature→effect link in N2 have nothing to cite in N3.

width.minimum: Describe the effect of one identified structural or language feature on the reader, using the structure 'The author uses [feature] to [effect]'.
width.typical: Describe the effects of a range of structural and language choices across a text, explaining how each choice shapes reader response — creating tension, building empathy, creating humour, establishing mood.
wider: Compare the effects of the same language feature (e.g. repetition) used in two different texts and explain why the effect differs depending on context
Write a short alternative version of a passage using different structural or language choices and describe how the effect changes

modes.reason: Connecting a specific textual feature to a specific reader effect requires a reasoning scaffold — students often describe their feelings without linking them to what in the text produced the feeling. The 'feature to effect' structure is the scaffold.

nodes.label: Sharing opinions using evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share an opinion about a text and support it with reference to specific text structures and language features.
criteria: Can state a clear opinion about a text and support it with at least one specific textual reference
Does not offer only plot summary — the response engages with how the text is constructed, not just what happens

width.minimum: State an opinion about a text and support it with at least one reference to a specific text structure or language feature.
width.typical: Share a reasoned opinion about a literary text in a discussion or written response, supporting the opinion with multiple references to specific structural and language features and explaining how these features support the view.
wider: Compare personal responses to a text with a peer's, identifying where opinions differ and examining whether different textual features are being prioritised
Respond to a First Nations Australian literary text using metalanguage to describe structural and language features, with attention to how cultural context shapes interpretive choices

modes.reason: Sharing a supported opinion integrates identification (node 1) and effect description (node 2) into a coherent reader-response — the full capability the descriptor demands.

descriptors.title: Character, setting and plot tension
descriptors.description: discuss how authors develop characters, setting and plot tension in literary texts, and the connection between setting and mood
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss how authors use language and illustrations to portray characters and how settings influence mood (AC9E3LE03). They have not yet examined how character, setting and plot tension work together as interconnected authorial choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can discuss how authors develop characters through action, dialogue and description; how setting choices create mood; and how plot tension is built through conflict, pacing and structure — explaining the connections between these elements.

nodes.label: Character development techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least three techniques authors use to develop characters and explain how each reveals character.
criteria: Can name at least three character development techniques and give an example of each from a text
Can explain what a specific technique reveals about a character that another technique would not

width.minimum: Identify two techniques an author uses to develop a character (e.g. what the character says and what they do) and explain what each reveals.
width.typical: Identify and discuss the full range of character development techniques — dialogue, action, direct description, narrator commentary, other characters' reactions — across at least two characters in a text, explaining how each technique reveals different dimensions of character.
wider: Compare how character is developed differently in a picture book (through illustration and sparse text) versus a chapter book (through extended description and dialogue)
Examine how First Nations Australian authors develop characters through relationship with Country and community, and how this differs from individualised Western character development

modes.reason: Character development awareness is built through encountering many examples across many texts. Students who have only seen one or two techniques for character development apply them too broadly in their own writing.

nodes.label: Setting and mood
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how an author's setting choices create mood, identifying specific language and visual features that produce the mood.
criteria: Can name the mood created by a setting and identify at least one specific language feature (e.g. a specific adjective or sensory detail) that creates it
Does not just name the setting — connects specific features to the mood produced

width.minimum: Identify the mood created by a setting in a literary text and name one specific language or visual feature that creates it.
width.typical: Analyse how setting choices — time of day, weather, landscape, sensory details, colour — create mood across a range of literary texts, explaining how the author's specific choices produce specific emotional atmospheres.
wider: Compare how two authors create contrasting moods through setting description in texts in the same genre (e.g. two adventure stories with different settings)
Examine how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors portray Country as an active participant in setting mood, and discuss how this differs from Western landscape description

nodes.label: Plot tension
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how an author builds plot tension through conflict, pacing and structural choices, and explain the connection between tension and reader engagement.
criteria: Can identify the main conflict in a text and name one technique the author uses to build tension
Does not describe tension as just 'exciting' — can explain what the author did to create the feeling

width.minimum: Identify the main conflict in a text and explain one way the author builds tension around it.
width.typical: Discuss how authors build plot tension across a text through conflict (character vs character, character vs self, character vs situation), pacing choices (short sentences, cliffhangers, delayed resolution) and structural choices (chapter endings, withholding information).
wider: Compare how tension is built differently in two texts in the same genre — what techniques are shared and what differs?
Map the tension curve of a text, identifying moments of rising tension, release and climax, and analyse the structural choices the author made to create this shape

modes.reason: Understanding tension as a constructed, technical product of specific authorial choices requires a reasoning scaffold. Students instinctively feel tension but need explicit analysis of what creates it.

descriptors.title: Literary devices and word play
descriptors.description: examine how literary devices including figurative language, deliberate word play and rhythm can be used for particular effects in poetry and literary texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss how literary devices including rhythm and onomatopoeia enhance meaning (AC9E3LE04). They have not yet examined how figurative language, deliberate word play and rhythm produce particular effects in poetry and literary texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify figurative language (simile, personification, alliteration), deliberate word play (puns, ambiguity) and rhythm in poetry and literary texts, and examine how each produces specific effects on meaning and reader response.

nodes.label: Figurative language — simile, personification, alliteration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify similes, personification and alliteration in texts and explain the specific effect each creates.
criteria: Can identify and name at least two different figurative devices in a text
Can explain the specific effect of at least one device, not just identify it

width.minimum: Identify one example each of simile, personification or alliteration and explain the effect it creates.
width.typical: Identify and discuss a range of figurative language devices across poetry and literary texts — simile, personification, alliteration — explaining how each device produces a specific effect: comparison, animation, sound pattern.
wider: Compare how the same figurative device (e.g. simile) is used for different effects in two different texts — one creating beauty, one creating horror
Examine figurative language in First Nations Australian poetry, including how imagery draws on Country, seasonal cycles and cultural knowledge for its effects

modes.reason: Recognition of figurative language and ability to explain its effect is built through encountering many examples across many texts. Students who have only seen one or two examples apply the device labels superficially.

nodes.label: Word play — puns, ambiguity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify deliberate word play including puns and ambiguity, and explain why the author made the choice.
criteria: Can identify a pun and explain both meanings it activates
Understands that word play is deliberate — the author chose to create the double meaning

width.minimum: Identify a pun or deliberately ambiguous word and explain the double meaning the author is using.
width.typical: Identify deliberate word play across a range of texts — puns, jokes, deliberate use of ambiguity — and explain both the double meaning and the effect it creates: humour, irony, mystery.
wider: Collect examples of word play from a range of sources (poetry, advertisements, jokes, books) and categorise by type and effect
Examine how word play in poetry creates multiple layers of meaning simultaneously and discuss why this is a valued poetic technique

nodes.label: Rhythm and sound effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify rhythm and sound patterns in poetry and literary texts and explain the effect each creates on meaning and reader experience.
criteria: Can identify a rhythm or sound pattern in a poem and explain one effect it has
Does not describe sound patterns as just 'nice sounding' — can connect the pattern to a specific effect

width.minimum: Identify a rhythmic or sound pattern in a poem (e.g. regular beat, alliteration pattern) and explain one effect it has on the reader.
width.typical: Identify and discuss how rhythm — regular beat, varied pace, line length — and sound devices — alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia — work together in poetry to create effects of pace, mood, emphasis and pleasure.
wider: Compare the rhythm of a traditional children's poem with a contemporary free-verse poem and explain how the different rhythmic choices produce different reading experiences
Explore how First Nations Australian song poetry uses rhythm and sound patterning for cultural, ceremonial and storytelling purposes

descriptors.title: Create and edit literary texts
descriptors.description: create and edit literary texts by developing storylines, characters and settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students create and edit imaginative texts using or adapting language features, characters, settings and plot structures (AC9E3LE05). They have not yet created and edited literary texts that deliberately develop storylines, characters and settings toward narrative effect.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can plan and create literary texts that develop a storyline, at least one character and a setting with intentional choices, and edit their texts by evaluating and improving those choices in collaboration with a peer.

nodes.label: Planning storyline, character and setting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a literary text by making deliberate choices about storyline shape, character and setting before writing.
criteria: Has made explicit choices about storyline shape, character and setting before writing begins
Can explain one reason for each planning choice
nodes.hinge_reason: Creating with deliberate craft in N2 requires students to have made explicit storyline, character and setting choices in planning — without a plan, N2's intentional craft choices cannot be made or evaluated.

width.minimum: Create a simple plan that identifies a storyline shape, one main character and a setting before beginning to write.
width.typical: Plan a literary text by making deliberate choices about storyline structure (orientation, complication, resolution), character development approach and setting with mood, explaining why each choice suits the text's intended effect.
wider: Experiment with alternative storyline structures (e.g. circular endings, flashbacks, multiple complications) and evaluate how each would change the text's effect
Study how a chosen author structures their planning — using author interviews, craft books or published drafts — and apply one technique to own planning

modes.reason: Making deliberate planning choices across storyline, character and setting requires explicit reasoning about why each choice suits the intended narrative effect — students without a scaffold default to writing whatever comes to mind rather than planning with purpose.

nodes.label: Creating with craft — sentences, dialogue and literary devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create literary texts using a range of sentence types, including dialogue and at least one literary device, to develop their storyline, character and setting.
criteria: Text includes correctly punctuated dialogue
Text includes at least one literary device used deliberately for effect
Storyline has an identifiable orientation, complication and resolution
nodes.hinge_reason: Peer editing in N3 requires a created literary text — N3 cannot proceed without the artefact N2 produces.

width.minimum: Create a literary text that includes at least one piece of punctuated dialogue and one literary device (e.g. simile, descriptive phrase, alliteration).
width.typical: Create a literary text that deliberately uses a range of sentence types for effect, dialogue that reveals character, and literary devices (figurative language, rhythm, word choice) to develop the storyline, character and setting toward an intended effect.
wider: Create literary texts in different forms — narrative, prose poem, short story — and compare how the same story content is shaped differently by each form
Create a literary text inspired by First Nations Australian storytelling structures or imagery, with attention to respectful and informed use of cultural elements

modes.reason: Creating a literary text with deliberate craft integrates knowledge from across the Language and Literature strands — sentence structure, dialogue punctuation, figurative language, structural choices — into a single coordinated performance.

nodes.label: Editing — peer feedback and revision
nodes.checkpoint: Students can give and receive specific feedback about choices in storyline, character and setting development, and revise their text in response to feedback.
criteria: Can give one specific piece of feedback about a storyline, character or setting choice in a peer's text
Has made at least one revision to own text in response to feedback received

width.minimum: Share a literary text with a peer, give one piece of specific feedback about a storyline, character or setting choice, and make at least one revision to their own text based on feedback received.
width.typical: Engage in structured peer editing focused on storyline, character and setting choices — identifying what is working, what could be developed, and giving specific, text-referenced feedback — and revise the text in response.
wider: Compare a draft and revised version of a text and explain what changed and why the revision improves the text
Use a published author's editing process (e.g. from interviews or manuscript facsimiles) as a model for own revision approach

modes.reason: Effective peer editing requires a structured framework — students without prompts default to 'it was good'. Explicit criteria for storyline, character and setting feedback provide the scaffold that makes editing generative.

descriptors.title: Texts across time and context
descriptors.description: compare texts from different times with similar purposes and audiences to identify similarities and differences in their depictions of events
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise how the same purpose can produce different texts when audiences differ (AC9E3LY01). They have not yet compared texts from different time periods to identify how historical context shapes depictions of events.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can compare texts from different historical periods with similar purposes and audiences, identifying similarities and differences in how events are depicted, and explain how the time period shapes the depiction.

nodes.label: Same purpose, different times
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify two texts from different time periods with the same purpose and explain what is similar and different about them.
criteria: Can identify two texts from different periods with the same purpose
Can describe at least one similarity and one difference in their depictions
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's analysis of how historical context shapes depiction requires students to have already identified two comparable texts from different periods — N1 provides the comparative base N2 builds from.

width.minimum: Identify two texts from different times with the same purpose and describe one similarity and one difference.
width.typical: Compare texts from different periods across at least two dimensions — language choices, visual conventions, what is included or excluded — and explain how each difference relates to the time period in which the text was made.
wider: Compare news coverage of the same type of event (e.g. a major sporting event) from different decades, examining how the depiction has changed
Compare family communication texts (letters, postcards, emails, texts) across different periods and explain how technology has changed the form while the purpose (staying in contact) remains similar

modes.reason: Students need to see multiple cross-period comparisons before the pattern of contextual shaping becomes visible — a single pair of texts is insufficient to reveal that depiction is always contextual rather than occasionally different.

nodes.label: How time period shapes depiction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the historical context of a text shapes how an event is depicted — what is emphasised, who is visible, what language is used.
criteria: Can explain one way that time period shapes how an event is depicted
Does not treat the more recent depiction as automatically more accurate — understands all depictions are contextual

width.minimum: Explain one way that the time period shapes how an event is depicted in a specific text.
width.typical: Analyse how historical context — available technology, social values, who has the power to tell stories — shapes what is included, emphasised and excluded in texts from different periods, drawing on at least two text comparisons.
wider: Examine how the same historical event is depicted in texts from different time periods, including how perspectives have changed as new voices have been included
Compare how First Nations Australian events or stories have been depicted in texts made at different times, discussing whose perspective is represented and how this has changed

modes.reason: Without multiple comparative examples, students tend to accept one period's depiction as neutral or accurate. Multiple cross-period comparisons help build critical awareness that all depictions are contextual.

descriptors.title: Acknowledge and extend in discussion
descriptors.description: listen for key points and information to carry out tasks and contribute to discussions, acknowledging another opinion, linking a response to the topic, and sharing and extending ideas and information
descriptors.knowledge: Students use interaction skills to contribute to conversations and discussions, sharing information and ideas (AC9E3LY02). They have not yet practised acknowledging another's opinion and linking responses to the topic while extending ideas.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can listen for key points in a discussion, acknowledge another's opinion, link their response to the topic, and share ideas that extend or build on what others have contributed.

nodes.label: Listening for key points
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify key points and information in what others say in a discussion and use these in their own contribution.
criteria: Can identify at least one key point from another person's contribution
Can reference that point in their own response
nodes.hinge_reason: Acknowledging another's opinion in N2 requires students to have identified key points from that contribution — N2 cannot be performed without N1's active listening.

width.minimum: After listening to a peer's contribution, identify one key point and reference it in a follow-up response.
width.typical: Listen actively across a discussion, taking notes or tracking key points, and reference what others have said in own contributions to demonstrate listening and build coherence in the discussion.
wider: Practise active listening in structured discussion formats (Socratic seminar, fishbowl) where referencing others' ideas is required
Reflect on one's own listening after a discussion, identifying what was easy and difficult to track and why

modes.reason: Active listening while tracking key points is a fluency habit requiring repeated practice across different discussion contexts before students can reliably identify what to reference.

nodes.label: Acknowledging and extending
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use language that acknowledges another's opinion and links their own response to the topic while extending or building on what was said.
criteria: Uses at least one acknowledgement phrase in a discussion contribution
Links own contribution to the topic rather than introducing an unrelated idea

width.minimum: Use at least one acknowledgement phrase ('I agree with... because...' or 'I see it differently because...') in a discussion contribution.
width.typical: Use a range of discussion language that acknowledges, extends, questions and links — including phrases that agree, partially agree, respectfully disagree and build on — across different types of classroom discussion.
wider: Compare formal discussion language conventions across different contexts (class meeting, debate, book club) and explain how the formality affects language choices
Examine how discussion skills differ across cultures and explore culturally appropriate ways to acknowledge and extend ideas

modes.reason: Extending another's idea rather than just starting a new thread is a discipline that requires sustained practice. Students need repeated structured opportunities across different discussion contexts.

descriptors.title: Characteristic features by purpose
descriptors.description: identify the characteristic features used in imaginative, informative and persuasive texts to meet the purpose of the text
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify audience and purpose of texts through language features and images (AC9E3LY03). They have not yet identified the characteristic features of imaginative, informative and persuasive text types as distinct categories.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify the characteristic language features, visual features and structural features of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts and explain how each feature serves the text's purpose.

nodes.label: Imaginative text features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify characteristic features of imaginative texts and explain how each feature helps create imaginary worlds and engage readers.
criteria: Can name two characteristic imaginative text features and link each to the text's purpose
Does not describe features as isolated techniques — connects each to the imaginary world or reader engagement

width.minimum: Identify two characteristic features of an imaginative text and explain how each contributes to its purpose.
width.typical: Identify and discuss a range of imaginative text features — descriptive language, figurative language, dialogue, narrative structure, character development — explaining how each feature creates the imaginary world and engages the reader.
wider: Compare imaginative text features across different forms — picture book, chapter book, graphic novel — and explain how the form affects which features predominate
Examine how First Nations Australian imaginative texts use features that reflect oral storytelling traditions and cultural knowledge

nodes.label: Informative text features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify characteristic features of informative texts and explain how each helps readers navigate, understand and use information.
criteria: Can name two characteristic informative text features and explain how each helps the reader
Can distinguish between a visual feature (image, diagram) and a language feature (heading, topic sentence)

width.minimum: Identify two characteristic features of an informative text and explain how each helps the reader access information.
width.typical: Identify and discuss a range of informative text features — headings, subheadings, captions, diagrams, bold text, topic sentences — explaining how each supports the reader's navigation and comprehension of information.
wider: Compare informative text features across digital and print formats — what features are shared and what differs, and why
Examine how informative texts use visual features (diagrams, charts, images) to complement or add to verbal information in a topic currently being studied

nodes.label: Persuasive text features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify characteristic features of persuasive texts and explain how each works to change the reader's views or actions.
criteria: Can name two persuasive features and explain how each attempts to influence the reader
Does not describe persuasive features as just 'convincing' — can explain the mechanism (e.g. emotive language makes readers feel something)

width.minimum: Identify two characteristic features of a persuasive text and explain how each attempts to influence the reader.
width.typical: Identify and discuss a range of persuasive text features — emotive language, rhetorical questions, evidence and statistics, repetition, call to action, inclusive pronouns — explaining how each is designed to position the reader to agree with the argument.
wider: Compare persuasive features across different persuasive text types — argument essay, advertisement, speech, opinion piece — and identify which features are shared and which are genre-specific
Examine how persuasive texts about topics related to Country, environment or community may use different persuasive strategies depending on the audience

modes.reason: Students often identify one or two persuasive features without understanding how they work together as a system. Multiple text types showing different combinations of features build a more complete understanding of persuasion.

descriptors.title: Integrate reading knowledge
descriptors.description: read different types of texts, integrating phonic, semantic and grammatical knowledge to read accurately and fluently, re-reading and self-correcting when needed
descriptors.knowledge: Students read a range of texts accurately and fluently using phonic, semantic and grammatical knowledge (AC9E3LY04). They have not yet practised integrating all three knowledge sources across different text types with self-correction strategies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can read different text types accurately and fluently by integrating phonic, semantic and grammatical knowledge simultaneously, and apply self-correction strategies — re-reading, pausing, cross-checking — when meaning breaks down.

nodes.label: Three knowledge sources working together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how phonic, semantic and grammatical knowledge each contribute to fluent reading and how they use all three simultaneously.
criteria: Can name and briefly describe all three knowledge sources
Can explain that fluent reading uses all three simultaneously, not one at a time
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's self-correction strategies require students to know which knowledge source has failed — without the three-source framework, students cannot diagnose breakdowns and apply targeted correction.

width.minimum: Explain what each of the three knowledge sources does for a reader: phonic (sounds/letters), semantic (meaning), grammatical (sentence structure).
width.typical: Demonstrate understanding that fluent reading requires simultaneous integration of all three sources, explaining how a reader uses all three when encountering an unknown word — checking sound, meaning and grammatical fit.
wider: Analyse what goes wrong when only one knowledge source is applied (e.g. a phonically correct but semantically wrong word choice) and explain how integration corrects this
Reflect on own reading using the three knowledge sources as a framework, identifying which source is strongest and which needs more attention

modes.reason: The concept of three integrated knowledge sources is abstract for Year 4 students who read fluently. Making the integration visible requires explicit reasoning about what each source does and how they cross-check.

nodes.label: Self-correction strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply self-correction strategies — re-reading, pausing, cross-checking — when reading breaks down.
criteria: Can name at least two self-correction strategies
Demonstrates re-reading or cross-checking when meaning breaks down in reading aloud

width.minimum: Identify one self-correction strategy and demonstrate its use when reading a challenging text aloud.
width.typical: Apply a range of self-correction strategies — re-reading from the start of the sentence, pausing to check meaning, cross-checking across all three knowledge sources — automatically when meaning breaks down in a range of text types.
wider: Reflect on which self-correction strategies are most useful for which types of breakdown (unfamiliar word, complex sentence, unfamiliar topic) and explain why
Apply self-correction strategies to increasingly complex texts, including subject-specific texts from other curriculum areas

modes.reason: Self-correction is a fluency habit built through practice. Students who understand the strategies intellectually still need repeated reading practice across texts to internalise them as automatic responses.

descriptors.title: Comprehension and evaluation strategies
descriptors.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning to build literal and inferred meaning, to expand topic knowledge and ideas, and evaluate texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students use comprehension strategies to build meaning and begin to evaluate texts using knowledge of context and structure (AC9E3LY05). They have not yet applied the full named repertoire — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning — to build literal and inferred meaning and evaluate texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can apply six named comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning, expand topic knowledge and evaluate texts, including texts by First Nations Australian authors, using evidence and reasoning to support their evaluations.

nodes.label: Literal meaning — main idea and supporting detail
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the main idea and supporting details in a text and explain the difference between literal and inferred meaning.
criteria: Can identify the main idea of a text in their own words
Can identify at least two supporting details and explain how they relate to the main idea
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's inference strategies require students to distinguish what is directly stated from what must be inferred — N1's literal/inferred distinction is the prerequisite for identifying when inference is needed.

width.minimum: Identify the main idea and at least two supporting details in an informational text.
width.typical: Identify main ideas and supporting details across a range of text types, explaining how topic-specific vocabulary builds understanding and how the author organises information to support the main idea.
wider: Compare how main ideas are signalled differently across text types — explicit topic sentences in reports versus embedded themes in narrative
Practise identifying main ideas in subject-specific texts from science, HASS and maths, noting how discipline language shapes meaning

modes.reason: Reliable identification of main idea and supporting details — and the literal/inferred distinction — requires practice across text types before students can dependably know what the text says versus what they are reading into it.

nodes.label: Inferred meaning — connecting, predicting, questioning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use connecting, predicting and questioning strategies to build inferred meaning from texts.
criteria: Can name an inference strategy and demonstrate its use with a specific textual example
Can distinguish an inference (meaning not directly stated) from a literal statement (meaning directly stated)

width.minimum: Use one inference strategy (connecting, predicting or questioning) to explain a meaning that is not directly stated in a text.
width.typical: Apply connecting (text-to-self, text-to-text, text-to-world), predicting (during reading, checking against text) and questioning (before, during, after) strategies to build inferred meaning across a range of texts.
wider: Make inferences from multimodal texts by connecting visual and verbal information, including texts that use images and layout to convey meaning not stated in words
Apply inference strategies to texts by First Nations Australian authors, considering how connecting to cultural context supports inference

modes.reason: Students often conflate inference with 'what I think' without connecting to textual evidence. Multiple text contexts — narrative, informational, multimodal — help students learn that inference is a text-grounded process across all text types.

nodes.label: Summarising and monitoring
nodes.checkpoint: Students can summarise the key ideas of a text in their own words and monitor their comprehension, identifying when meaning has broken down.
criteria: Can write a summary of a text that is significantly shorter than the original and in own words
Can identify a point in reading where meaning broke down and describe what strategy was used
nodes.hinge_reason: Text evaluation in N4 requires students to have accurately comprehended the text's claims and structure — students who cannot summarise key ideas will evaluate a misread text, producing unreliable evaluations.

width.minimum: Write a brief summary of a text in own words and identify one point during reading where meaning was unclear.
width.typical: Summarise key ideas from a range of texts in own words, applying monitoring strategies (re-reading, questioning unclear sections) to maintain comprehension throughout.
wider: Practise summarising across different text types — narrative summary (plot) versus informational summary (main points) — and compare the different challenges each presents
Apply monitoring and summarising to complex multimodal texts, tracking meaning across verbal and visual modes

modes.reason: Summarising in own words — as distinct from lifting sentences — requires practice across multiple texts. Many students at this level still paraphrase rather than genuinely restructure.

nodes.label: Evaluating texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a text by assessing the quality of its evidence, reasoning and argument, using textual evidence to support their evaluation.
criteria: Can state an evaluative judgement about a text with at least one text-referenced reason
Does not offer only unsupported opinion — evaluation is connected to specific textual evidence

width.minimum: Evaluate one aspect of a text (e.g. whether the evidence supports the argument) and give a reason supported by a specific reference to the text.
width.typical: Evaluate texts using multiple criteria — quality of evidence, strength of argument, author credibility, fairness of representation — giving text-referenced reasons for each evaluative judgement.
wider: Compare evaluations of the same text from two different readers and discuss how different values or prior knowledge lead to different evaluations
Evaluate how First Nations Australian perspectives are represented (or misrepresented) in texts, using criteria of fairness, accuracy and whose voice is heard

modes.reason: Evaluation requires explicit criteria and text-referenced reasoning — students default to vague value judgements without a structured reasoning scaffold. The criteria + evidence + reasoning structure is the scaffold.

descriptors.title: Plan, create and publish texts
descriptors.description: plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal imaginative, informative and persuasive texts, using visual features, relevant linked ideas, complex sentences, appropriate tense, synonyms and antonyms, correct spelling of multisyllabic words and simple punctuation
descriptors.knowledge: Students plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts using visual features, paragraphs and topic vocabulary (AC9E3LY06). They have not yet planned and created texts using complex sentences, linked ideas, synonyms/antonyms, multisyllabic word spelling and simple punctuation across all three text types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts across three text types — imaginative, informative and persuasive — using complex sentences, linked ideas, appropriate tense, precise vocabulary and correct spelling and punctuation.

nodes.label: Planning — structure and content
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a written or multimodal text by selecting appropriate structure, grouping ideas into logical sections and deciding on key vocabulary.
criteria: Plan includes identified text type structure with at least two sections
Plan includes key vocabulary noted before writing begins
nodes.hinge_reason: Creating with complex sentences and linked ideas in N2 requires a planned text structure — without a plan, students cannot make or evaluate deliberate organisational choices when drafting.

width.minimum: Create a plan for a text that identifies the text type structure, groups ideas into at least two sections and notes key vocabulary.
width.typical: Plan texts across all three text types — imaginative, informative and persuasive — selecting appropriate structure for each, organising ideas into logical paragraph groups and planning vocabulary including synonyms and precise terms.
wider: Use digital planning tools (mind-mapping, outline software) to organise and restructure ideas before writing, comparing the outcome with a handwritten plan
Plan a multimodal text, considering how visual and verbal elements will work together at each stage of the text

modes.reason: Planning across three text types requires explicit reasoning about how structure serves purpose — selecting between narrative, report and argument structures is not intuitive at Year 4 without a scaffolded decision process.

nodes.label: Creating — complex sentences and linked ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create texts using complex sentences and text connectives to link ideas coherently within and across paragraphs.
criteria: Text includes at least one complex sentence with a named subordinating conjunction
Text includes at least one text connective linking ideas between sentences
Tense is appropriate and consistent for the text type
nodes.hinge_reason: Editing in N3 requires a created text with vocabulary, spelling and punctuation choices to review — N3 cannot proceed without the artefact N2 produces.

width.minimum: Create a text that includes at least two complex sentences and one text connective linking ideas between sentences.
width.typical: Create texts using a range of complex sentences (with temporal, causal and conditional subordination) and text connectives to link ideas coherently within and across paragraphs, with appropriate tense for text type.
wider: Create texts in two different text types on the same topic and compare how sentence structure and connective choices change to suit each purpose
Create a multimodal informative text that integrates verbal and visual elements to communicate linked ideas

modes.reason: Creating a cohesive text integrates knowledge from across Language — complex sentences, text connectives, tense, vocabulary — into a coordinated writing performance. This is the integration node for the whole writing system.

nodes.label: Editing — vocabulary, spelling and punctuation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit their texts to improve vocabulary choices (synonyms, precise terms), correct multisyllabic spelling and ensure consistent punctuation.
criteria: Has changed at least one word to a more precise or varied synonym
Has corrected at least one multisyllabic word spelling
Punctuation is consistent throughout the text

width.minimum: Edit a piece of writing by changing at least one word to a more precise synonym and checking the spelling of at least two multisyllabic words.
width.typical: Edit texts systematically for vocabulary precision (selecting synonyms, replacing vague words), correct spelling of multisyllabic words and consistent simple punctuation — reviewing each dimension as a separate editing pass.
wider: Develop a personal editing checklist based on recurring errors and apply it to successive drafts across different text types
Compare first draft and edited version, annotating specific changes and explaining the reason for each improvement

modes.reason: Editing for vocabulary, spelling and punctuation requires habitual checking — students who understand what to look for still need practice making systematic review automatic rather than selective.

descriptors.title: Structured oral and multimodal presentations
descriptors.description: plan, create, rehearse and deliver structured oral and/or multimodal presentations to report on a topic, tell a story, recount events or present an argument using subjective and objective language, complex sentences, visual features, tone, pace, pitch and volume
descriptors.knowledge: Students plan, create and deliver presentations using clear structure, elaborated details and precise vocabulary (AC9E3LY07). They have not yet planned, rehearsed and delivered structured presentations using subjective/objective language, complex sentences and deliberate voice features.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can plan, create, rehearse and deliver structured oral and/or multimodal presentations for a range of purposes — report, story, recount, argument — using appropriate language register, complex sentences, visual features and deliberate voice control.

nodes.label: Planning the presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a structured presentation by selecting appropriate structure, language register (subjective or objective) and key visual features for the purpose.
criteria: Plan identifies the presentation's structure and purpose
Plan notes whether subjective or objective language is appropriate and gives a reason
nodes.hinge_reason: Rehearsing in N2 requires a structured presentation to practise — voice feedback cannot be applied to language and structural choices that haven't yet been made.

width.minimum: Plan a presentation that identifies structure, notes whether subjective or objective language is appropriate and lists at least one visual feature to include.
width.typical: Plan presentations across a range of purposes — report (objective), argument (subjective), recount (narrative past) — selecting appropriate structure, language register and visual features for each, with notes for key points rather than a script.
wider: Plan a multimodal presentation that combines spoken language with slides, images or props, and explain how visual and verbal elements complement each other
Plan a presentation for a specific audience (e.g. school assembly, parent information night) and explain how audience shapes planning choices

modes.reason: Planning across presentation purposes requires explicit reasoning about register, structure and visual feature choices — the decision between objective/subjective language and appropriate structure is not intuitive without a scaffold.

nodes.label: Rehearsing — voice features and feedback
nodes.checkpoint: Students can rehearse a presentation with a peer, receiving and applying feedback about tone, pace, pitch and volume.
criteria: Has rehearsed with a peer and can name one piece of specific voice feedback received
Has made at least one change to delivery based on feedback
nodes.hinge_reason: Delivery in N3 requires the voice features — tone, pace, pitch, volume — to have been practised and adjusted in N2 — unrehearsed delivery cannot demonstrate deliberate voice control.

width.minimum: Rehearse a presentation with a peer and make at least one change to tone, pace, pitch or volume based on feedback.
width.typical: Rehearse presentations with explicit attention to all four voice features — tone, pace, pitch, volume — receiving peer feedback using specific criteria and making adjustments to voice and language choices before delivery.
wider: Rehearse a presentation multiple times, tracking changes made after each rehearsal and evaluating which changes had the most impact on the presentation's effectiveness
Compare rehearsal feedback from a peer with self-evaluation using a recording and discuss where perceptions differ

modes.reason: Voice feature control — using pace, pitch, volume and tone deliberately — is a performance skill that requires repeated rehearsal across multiple contexts to become reliably available.

nodes.label: Delivering the presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliver a structured presentation using appropriate language, complex sentences, visual features and deliberate voice control for the purpose and audience.
criteria: Presentation has a clear structure with introduction and conclusion
At least one complex sentence is used in delivery
At least one deliberate voice feature is evident — pace, volume, pitch or tone varied for effect

width.minimum: Deliver a structured presentation on a topic using at least one complex sentence and at least one deliberate voice feature (e.g. slowing pace for emphasis).
width.typical: Deliver presentations across a range of purposes — report, argument, recount — with appropriate language register, complex sentences, integrated visual features and deliberate voice control (tone, pace, pitch, volume) suited to purpose and audience.
wider: Deliver the same content in two different presentation contexts (e.g. formal classroom vs informal small group) and reflect on how delivery changes across contexts
Deliver a presentation incorporating First Nations Australian content with attention to respectful language choices and appropriate acknowledgement conventions

modes.reason: Delivering a presentation integrates planning, language knowledge and rehearsed voice control into a single live performance — the full capability of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Joined handwriting fluency
descriptors.description: write words using clearly formed joined letters, with developing fluency and automaticity
descriptors.knowledge: Students form letters with developing consistency (prior year handwriting). They have not yet developed fluency and automaticity with clearly formed joined letters.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can write words using clearly formed joined letters with developing fluency and automaticity, so that handwriting does not impede composition.

nodes.label: Clearly formed joined letters
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write words using correctly formed joined letters that are legible to a reader.
criteria: Joined letters are legible — a reader can identify all letters without assistance
Letter formation is consistent across a piece of writing
nodes.hinge_reason: Developing fluency and automaticity in N2 requires correctly formed letters — practising at speed with incorrect formation reinforces the wrong habits and is harder to remediate later.

width.minimum: Write a short piece of text using joined letters that are legible and consistently formed.
width.typical: Write extended pieces using joined letters across a range of tasks, maintaining legibility and consistent letter formation throughout.
wider: Limited width — joined handwriting fluency is a motor skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. Extension involves writing at greater length and speed while maintaining legibility, not broadening application across contexts.

modes.reason: Handwriting automaticity is built through practice volume. Fluency and automaticity with joined letters require sustained practice — there is no conceptual breadth to exploit, only time on task.

nodes.label: Developing fluency and automaticity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write with developing speed and fluency so that handwriting does not slow down or interrupt the composition process.
criteria: Can complete a sustained writing task without stopping to think about letter formation
Writing pace is sufficient for the task demand

width.minimum: Write a short piece at a pace that does not significantly interrupt the flow of ideas — composition is not held up by letter formation.
width.typical: Write extended texts with developing automaticity — letter formation is sufficiently fluent that students can focus cognitive attention on composing rather than forming letters.
wider: Limited width — handwriting automaticity is a motor fluency target, not a conceptual one. The enrichment direction is sustained practice with increasing text length.

modes.reason: Automaticity is achieved through practice volume, not conceptual breadth. Students need extended writing practice to develop the fluency this descriptor targets.

descriptors.title: Complex letter combinations
descriptors.description: understand how to use and apply phonological and morphological knowledge to read and write multisyllabic words with more complex letter combinations, including a variety of vowel sounds and known prefixes and suffixes
descriptors.knowledge: Students apply phoneme-grapheme knowledge and syllable patterns to fluently read and write multisyllabic words (AC9E3LY09). They have not yet applied this knowledge to more complex letter combinations including a variety of vowel sounds and known prefixes and suffixes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can read and write multisyllabic words with more complex letter combinations — including a variety of vowel sounds and known prefixes and suffixes — by applying phonological and morphological knowledge.

nodes.label: Complex vowel sounds in multisyllabic words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply complex vowel patterns in multisyllabic words, including unstressed vowels.
criteria: Can correctly read at least five multisyllabic words with complex vowel combinations
Can correctly write at least five multisyllabic words with complex vowel combinations
nodes.hinge_reason: Adding prefixes and suffixes in N2 requires accurate reading and writing of the base word — vowel errors in the stem produce compounded errors when morphemes are attached.

width.minimum: Identify the vowel pattern in at least two multisyllabic words with complex letter combinations and read/write them correctly.
width.typical: Apply knowledge of a range of complex vowel patterns — unstressed vowels, vowel digraphs in multisyllabic words — to read and write words accurately, including words such as 'builder', 'animal', 'straightaway', 'thoughtful'.
wider: Sort multisyllabic words by vowel pattern and identify rules or generalisations that help predict spelling
Use morphological analysis to identify how vowel sounds shift across word families (e.g. explain vs explanation)

modes.reason: Unstressed vowels in multisyllabic words are a common source of spelling errors at Year 4. Reliable reading and writing of these patterns requires practice across many exemplars before automaticity is achieved.

nodes.label: Prefixes and suffixes in multisyllabic words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify known prefixes and suffixes in multisyllabic words and use this knowledge to decode and spell them.
criteria: Can identify a prefix or suffix in a multisyllabic word and name its meaning
