Can use prefix/suffix knowledge to decode or spell an unfamiliar word

width.minimum: Identify a prefix or suffix in a multisyllabic word and use this morphological knowledge to read or spell the word correctly.
width.typical: Apply knowledge of known prefixes (un-, re-, pre-, dis-) and suffixes (-ful, -less, -ness, -tion, -ing, -ed) to decode and spell a range of multisyllabic words, explaining how the morpheme changes or adds meaning.
wider: Explore how the same prefix or suffix appears across multiple words from different word families and generalise about its meaning contribution
Use morphological decomposition as a decoding strategy for unfamiliar long words in subject texts

modes.reason: Morphological awareness grows through accumulating prefix and suffix families across contexts — each new morpheme learned expands the decoding and spelling range transferably across vocabulary domains.

descriptors.title: Spelling generalisations and origins
descriptors.description: understand how to use knowledge of letter patterns, including double letters, spelling generalisations, morphological word families, common prefixes and suffixes, and word origins, to spell more complex words
descriptors.knowledge: Students apply knowledge of base words, prefixes and suffixes to read and comprehend multimorphemic words (AC9E3LY10). They have not yet used spelling generalisations, morphological word families and word origins as systematic strategies for spelling more complex words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can apply spelling generalisations, morphological word family knowledge, prefix and suffix rules and word origin knowledge to spell more complex words accurately.

nodes.label: Spelling generalisations — double letters and affixes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply spelling generalisations including rules for doubling letters when adding suffixes.
criteria: Can correctly apply a doubling rule (e.g. begin → beginning) and name the rule
Can apply a drop-e rule (e.g. hope → hoping) and name the rule
nodes.hinge_reason: Building word families in N2 requires correct application of suffixing rules (doubling, drop-e) — without N1's generalisations, students produce spelling errors when inflecting or deriving words within families.

width.minimum: Apply one spelling generalisation (e.g. doubling the final consonant before -ing: begin → beginning) to at least three words correctly.
width.typical: Apply a range of spelling generalisations — doubling rules, drop-e rules, change-y-to-i rules — across a range of words when adding common affixes, explaining the rule in each case.
wider: Investigate which spelling generalisations have exceptions and explore why (e.g. words of Latin origin may follow different doubling patterns)
Apply spelling generalisations systematically when editing own writing, developing a check habit

modes.reason: Spelling generalisations are procedural rules that require practice across many word examples before they become reliable. Understanding a rule does not guarantee consistent application without sustained practice.

nodes.label: Morphological word families
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify word families built from the same base and use family relationships to spell unknown related words.
criteria: Can name at least three words in a word family and explain what they share
Can use word family knowledge to spell a related word they have not seen before

width.minimum: Build a word family from a base word (at least 3 members) and use the family to spell a word they might not know independently.
width.typical: Build and explore morphological word families across a range of base words and morphemes, explaining how meaning and spelling are preserved across the family and using family relationships as a spelling strategy.
wider: Explore word families from Latin and Greek roots (e.g. tri-: tricycle, tripod, triangle) and identify how knowing the root helps spell and define multiple words
Research the word families of key vocabulary from a current cross-curriculum unit and use family knowledge to spell related forms

modes.reason: Morphological family knowledge is accumulative — each new family learned expands the range of words a student can spell and define. Students benefit from ongoing collection across curriculum contexts.

descriptors.title: Homophones and context spelling
descriptors.description: read and write high-frequency words including homophones and know how to use context to identify correct spelling
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise and write most high-frequency words including some homophones (AC9E3LY12). They have not yet applied contextual and syntactical clues systematically to determine correct homophone spelling.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can read and write high-frequency words including homophones, applying contextual and syntactical clues to select the correct spelling in context.

nodes.label: Identifying homophone pairs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify homophone pairs and distinguish the meaning of each word in the pair.
criteria: Can name at least three homophone pairs
Can explain the different meaning of each word in at least two pairs
nodes.hinge_reason: Using context to select the correct homophone in N2 requires students to know both words in the pair — without knowing the alternatives, students cannot apply the meaning-check that N2 requires.

width.minimum: Identify at least three homophone pairs and give the meaning of each word.
width.typical: Identify a range of common homophone pairs (our/hour, their/there/they're, to/too/two, hear/here, wear/ware/where) and explain the distinct meaning of each, noting part of speech where relevant.
wider: Collect homophones encountered in reading across a week and build a personal homophone reference list with meanings and example sentences
Investigate near-homophones and confusables (e.g. affect/effect, then/than) and develop memory strategies for distinguishing them

modes.reason: Knowing homophone pairs is a memory task that requires repeated encounter to become reliable — students need to recognise both words in a pair before context checking is possible.

nodes.label: Using context to select correct spelling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use contextual and syntactical clues to identify and write the correct homophone in a sentence.
criteria: Can select the correct homophone in a sentence and name the context clue that determines the choice
Does not rely on sound alone — uses meaning or part of speech to determine the correct form

width.minimum: Select the correct homophone in at least three sentences using context clues and explain the clue used.
width.typical: Apply contextual and syntactical clues systematically to select the correct homophone across a range of sentences and texts, explaining why the context determines the spelling choice.
wider: Edit a piece of writing specifically for homophone errors, explaining the reasoning for each correction
Examine how homophone errors in published or digital texts change meaning and discuss the importance of proofreading

modes.reason: Correct homophone selection in context requires automatic triggering of the meaning-check habit. Students who know the pairs still make errors in fluent writing without consistent practice building the checking habit.

descriptors.title: Language signals social roles
descriptors.description: Understand that language is selected for social contexts and that it helps to signal social roles and relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore language used to develop relationships in formal and informal situations (AC9E4LA01). They have not yet examined how language choices actively signal social roles and relationships, or considered cultural protocols and how silence/formality norms vary across communities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how specific language choices signal social roles and relationships in context, identify how formality registers shift across situations, and describe how communication norms and protocols differ across cultural contexts including those of First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Register and social context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that language varies in formality according to the social context, and name examples of formal and informal language in familiar situations.
criteria: Identifies at least two ways language choices (vocabulary, sentence structure, tone) differ between formal and informal contexts.
Explains why a specific language choice is appropriate or inappropriate for a given social situation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Register as a context-sensitive continuum is foundational to Node 2's analysis of role-signalling and Node 4's multi-criteria language selection framework. Students who treat formality as binary (on/off) rather than as a contextually calibrated spectrum will be unable to reason about how fine-grained language choices signal specific roles and relationships in Node 2.

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of language choices that shift between a formal and informal version of the same communication (e.g. 'Could you please pass the report?' vs 'Can you grab that?').
width.typical: Identify and explain how language formality signals context across a range of situations: classroom, playground, formal presentation, adult conversation. Match language choices to context purpose and relationships involved.
wider: Explore how digital communication contexts (texting, email, social media) generate their own register norms, and how these sit on a formal–informal continuum
Examine transcripts or scripts from different social situations and sort language choices onto a formality spectrum, justifying placements

modes.reason: Students often treat formality as binary (formal/informal) rather than as a spectrum that shifts continuously with context. Encountering diverse situations — school, sport, family, online — helps students see that register is contextually calibrated, not switched on or off.

nodes.label: Language signals roles and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how particular language choices signal roles (e.g. chairperson, speaker, expert) and the relationships between participants in an interaction.
criteria: Identifies a specific language choice and explains which role it signals and for whom.
Explains how the relationship between participants shapes the language choice made (not just identifies the relationship).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 4's integration task requires students to apply criteria for language selection that explicitly include roles and relationships. Students who cannot explain how language choices signal roles — not just identify that formality shifts — will be unable to account for the roles-and-relationships criterion in Node 4's multi-criteria analysis.

width.minimum: Identify how language choices in a structured context (e.g. a classroom debate or formal discussion) signal who holds which role, and explain what those choices communicate about the relationship between participants.
width.typical: Analyse examples from debate, formal discussion, and workplace contexts to explain how language signals authority, deference, peer equality, or expertise. Explain the consequences of role-mismatched language choices.
wider: Compare how language signals roles in formal Australian institutional contexts (parliament, courtroom, formal ceremony) versus informal peer contexts, discussing what makes the role-signalling legible

Examine how roles and relationships are signalled in texts written by First Nations Australian authors, identifying language choices that reflect cultural protocols around seniority, kinship or ceremony

modes.reason: The connection between a specific language choice and the role it signals is not always transparent to students. A reasoning scaffold — 'what role does this language position the speaker in, and how does the listener know?' — helps students develop the analytical move needed to explain rather than just identify.

nodes.label: Cultural variation in communication norms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how communication norms — including degrees of formality, periods of silence, and cultural protocols — differ across cultures, including First Nations Australian practices.
criteria: Describes at least one communication norm from a cultural context different from their own and explains what social meaning it carries.
Avoids framing cultural communication differences as incorrect or inferior — explains differences as purposeful within their context.

width.minimum: Identify at least one way that communication norms differ between cultural contexts, and explain what those differences signal about social relationships or values in that context.
width.typical: Describe how communication norms vary across cultural contexts examined in class, including aspects such as silence, turn-taking, degrees of formality, and directness. Explain that these differences reflect different cultural understandings of respectful interaction, not deficits.
wider: Research and describe specific communication protocols of a First Nations Australian community, explaining the social or relational meaning those protocols carry
Compare responses to common requests across cultural contexts studied, identifying how the same communicative intent is expressed differently and what values underpin those differences

modes.reason: Students commonly interpret unfamiliar communication norms through a deficit lens ('why don't they just say it directly?'). Encountering multiple cultural communication contexts — including silence as meaningful, indirect as respectful, formal as relational — helps students understand variation as culturally purposeful rather than as error.

nodes.label: Selecting language for context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain and apply criteria for selecting language appropriate to a social context, accounting for purpose, roles, relationships and cultural norms.
criteria: Identifies at least three contextual factors that inform language selection and applies them to explain a specific language choice.
Evaluates a language choice in a sample text or interaction as appropriate or inappropriate to context, with reference to purpose, roles, and relationships.

width.minimum: For a given social situation, identify the key contextual factors (purpose, roles, relationships, cultural norms) and explain how those factors would inform specific language choices.
width.typical: Analyse and explain language choices across several contrasting social contexts, accounting for purpose, roles, relationships and cultural context. Apply these criteria to evaluate the appropriateness of language choices in sample texts or interactions.
wider: Examine how mismatches between language choice and social context create meaning effects (e.g. humour, irony, social friction, power assertion), and explain what those effects reveal about the social norms in play
Investigate how language in formal roles changes across time periods (e.g. parliamentary language, legal language) and discuss what those changes indicate about shifting social relationships

modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate register knowledge (node 1), role-signalling (node 2), and cultural variation (node 3) into a unified analytical framework for language selection. The integration — applying multiple criteria simultaneously to evaluate a language choice — is the learning at this node.

descriptors.title: Beyond assertions to evidence
descriptors.description: Understand how to move beyond making bare assertions by taking account of differing ideas or opinions and authoritative sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify subjective language of opinion and feeling, and objective language of factual reporting (AC9E4LA02). They have not yet examined the rhetorical mechanisms for tempering assertions — distancing language, sourcing, generalising support — or how these choices affect a claim's persuasive weight.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how bare assertions can be strengthened by using distancing language, recruiting support, or citing authoritative sources, and identify how these moves shift the persuasive weight and reliability of a claim.

nodes.label: What makes a bare assertion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a bare assertion and explain why it is insufficient as persuasive or informative language in contexts that require evidence or qualification.
criteria: Identifies a bare assertion in a sample text and explains what is missing (evidence, sourcing, qualification).
Distinguishes between a bare assertion and a qualified or evidenced claim in at least two examples.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to identify and explain tempering moves specifically as responses to what bare assertions lack — distancing compensates for unsubstantiated confidence, sourcing compensates for anonymity. Students who cannot identify what makes an assertion bare cannot analyse why or how specific tempering moves address those gaps.

width.minimum: Identify examples of bare assertions in texts and explain what is absent — evidence, qualification, or sourcing — that would make them more persuasive or reliable.
width.typical: Distinguish bare assertions from qualified or evidenced claims across a range of texts. Explain why bare assertions may not convince a reader and what a reader might need before accepting the claim.
wider: Examine advertising or social media posts where bare assertions function as persuasive technique, discussing why audiences accept or reject them

Limited width — this node is a conceptual foundation (what a bare assertion is) that does not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. Extensions connect to how bare assertions function rhetorically, explored in later nodes.

modes.reason: Students often confuse opinion-statements with bare assertions, and may not recognise that a claim can be factual but still function as a bare assertion if unsupported. Consolidation through multiple examples helps students develop reliable identification before moving to the tempering moves.

nodes.label: Tempering moves: distancing and recruiting support
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain how distancing language (impersonal it, modal verbs) and recruited support (anonymous or general sourcing) change the persuasive character of an assertion.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct tempering moves in a text and names what type of move each represents.
Explains how at least one tempering move changes the relationship between the writer, the claim, and the reader.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to compare the persuasive weight of anonymous versus specific sourcing — a comparison that only makes sense against a shared understanding of why sourcing matters at all. Students who have not grasped that distancing and recruited support are rhetorical moves with distinct effects cannot reason about the elevated credibility that named authoritative sourcing adds.

width.minimum: Identify at least two tempering moves (e.g. 'It could be said...' or 'Most people agree...') in a sample text and explain how each changes the claim's relationship to the reader.
width.typical: Identify and explain the full range of distancing and recruiting-support moves from the elaboration examples. Analyse how each move positions the writer in relation to the claim and the reader, and discuss when each move is more or less appropriate.
wider: Compare how academic writing, journalism, and everyday persuasive writing use these tempering moves differently, and explain what those differences signal about each genre's conventions
Examine political speeches or editorials and identify where and why writers choose to distance themselves from or recruit support for claims, discussing the rhetorical effect

modes.reason: Students commonly treat all tempering moves as equivalent ('they all just say you're not sure'). Encountering the moves across different genres and contexts helps students see that each move signals a distinct relationship between writer, claim, and evidence — distancing vs. sourcing serve different rhetorical purposes.

nodes.label: Citing authoritative sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how specifying an authoritative source strengthens a claim, and identify the difference in persuasive weight between general and specific sourcing.
criteria: Explains why specifying a named authoritative source makes a claim more persuasive than anonymous or general sourcing.
Identifies whether a cited source is authoritative in context and justifies that judgement.

width.minimum: Identify examples of specific source citation in a text and explain how naming the source changes the claim's credibility compared to anonymous or general sourcing.
width.typical: Compare examples ranging from anonymous support through general sourcing to specific authority citation, and explain how each level of specificity changes the claim's credibility and the reader's relationship to it. Discuss what makes a source 'authoritative' in context.
wider: Examine how citation conventions differ across genres (news report vs. academic text vs. student essay) and discuss what those conventions signal about each genre's standards of evidence
Investigate what makes a source authoritative in different contexts — who is considered an authority in science vs. community knowledge vs. sports — and discuss how this affects language choices

modes.reason: The reasoning chain — 'this source is authoritative because... and therefore citing it does this to the claim' — is not automatic for Year 5 students. A structured reasoning scaffold helps students move beyond 'it has a source' to understanding how source specificity and authority interact to shape a claim's persuasive weight.

descriptors.title: Text stages and phases
descriptors.description: Describe how spoken, written and multimodal texts use language features and are typically organised into characteristic stages and phases, depending on purposes in texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how texts across the curriculum have different language features and are organised for different purposes, and identify some characteristic stages (AC9E4LA03). They have not yet described the internal phase structure within stages, or compared how the same genre adapts across spoken, written and multimodal modes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the characteristic stages and phases of a range of text types — including narrative, procedure, argument, explanation, discussion and information report — explaining how language features within each stage serve the text's purpose, and how these structures adapt across spoken, written and multimodal modes.

nodes.label: Stages serve purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the characteristic stages of familiar text types and explain how each stage contributes to the text's overall purpose.
criteria: Labels the stages of a given text type correctly and explains the communicative function of each stage.
Explains why removing or reordering a stage would disrupt the text's purpose.
nodes.hinge_reason: Stage identification and purpose-function explanation is prerequisite for Node 2's phase analysis and Node 3's language-feature mapping. Students who cannot identify and explain stages cannot locate phases within them, and cannot reason about why particular language features cluster in particular structural positions.

width.minimum: Identify and label the stages of at least two text types (e.g. narrative, information report) and explain what communicative work each stage does.
width.typical: Map stages across a range of text types including narrative, procedure, argument, explanation, and information report. For each, explain how the sequence of stages builds toward the text's purpose, and why stages are ordered as they are.
wider: Compare how the same text type (e.g. argument) is staged differently across spoken, written and multimodal forms, and explain what the structural differences reveal about audience and context
Examine texts where conventional stage ordering is disrupted (e.g. in medias res narrative, or delayed thesis argument) and discuss the effect of that disruption

modes.reason: Stage identification across multiple text types requires practice to become reliable. Students who have mapped only narrative stages will apply narrative assumptions to argument or explanation text structures. Consolidation through deliberate practice across text types builds the cross-genre stage recognition that Node 2 and Node 3 depend on.

nodes.label: Phases within stages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify phases within stages and explain how phases build the communicative work of the stage they belong to.
criteria: Identifies at least one stage and describes two or more phases within it, explaining what communicative work each phase does.
Identifies a language feature (sentence opener, connective, paragraph structure) that signals a phase transition.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to explain language features characteristic of specific stages and phases. Students who cannot distinguish a phase from a paragraph or a stage cannot locate language features within their structural position, and therefore cannot explain why those features appear where they do.

width.minimum: In a text with identifiable stages, identify at least one stage and describe its internal phases — how the stage unfolds through a sequence of smaller moves.
width.typical: Describe the phase structure of multiple stages across at least two text types, explaining how phases sequence within stages and what language features signal phase transitions (e.g. paragraph openers, sentence starters, cohesive devices).
wider: Compare how paragraphs function as phase units differently in narrative, argument, and procedural recount texts — examining how topic sentence position and function shifts across text types
Examine how phases are signalled visually in multimodal texts (layout, headings, images) versus through language in written texts

modes.reason: The distinction between a stage and a phase — and what makes something a phase rather than just a sentence — requires explicit scaffolding. Students need a reasoning framework: 'What job is this paragraph doing? Is that job the whole stage's job, or part of it?' without this, students conflate paragraph with phase.

nodes.label: Language features signal structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific language features used in different stages and phases, and explain how those features serve the communicative purpose of that structural position.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific language features (e.g. relational verbs in information reports, action verbs in procedures) and explains why they appear in that stage.
Explains the relationship between a language feature and the stage it appears in — not just names the feature.

width.minimum: Identify at least two language features characteristic of a specific stage or phase in a text type, and explain why those features are suited to the stage's purpose.
width.typical: Describe the characteristic language features of stages across narrative, argument, explanation, discussion and information report texts. Explain how language choices are constrained by stage function — why certain verb tenses, clause types, or vocabulary fields cluster in particular stages.
wider: Compare how language features in equivalent stages differ across spoken, written and multimodal realisations of the same text type
Examine how writers deliberately violate expected language features for effect (e.g. using present tense in historical recount) and explain what effect the violation creates

modes.reason: The range of text types and the language feature patterns associated with their stages is a knowledge base students need to accumulate. Students who have only analysed narrative stages will struggle when encountering explanation or discussion text structures. Breadth across text types is the target at this node.

nodes.label: Describing texts across modes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how the same genre structures adapt across spoken, written and multimodal modes, identifying what changes and what remains consistent.
criteria: Describes at least two differences in structure or language features when comparing the same text type across two modes.
Explains why at least one of those differences is a consequence of the mode (not just describes that it exists).

width.minimum: Compare one text type realised in at least two modes (e.g. written argument and spoken argument) and describe at least two structural or language feature differences, explaining why the mode affects those features.
width.typical: Describe how genre structures and language features adapt across spoken, written, digital and multimodal forms for at least two text types. Explain what the constraints of each mode do to stage structure, phase organisation, and language feature choices.
wider: Analyse a digital or multimedia text that blends multiple genres (e.g. a documentary that combines information report and recount) and describe how stage structures from different genres are interwoven

Compare how narrative, argument and explanation texts are structured differently when composed in digital mind map, linear written, or spoken presentation form — discussing what the compositional medium makes possible or constrains

modes.reason: This node requires students to apply stage/phase knowledge (nodes 1–2) and language feature knowledge (node 3) simultaneously to texts across modes. The integration — tracking both structural and language feature shifts across modes — is the full demand of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Starting point and prominence
descriptors.description: Understand how texts can be made cohesive by using the starting point of a sentence or paragraph to give prominence to the message and to guide the reader through the text
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how text connectives including temporal and conditional words, and topic sentences, add cohesion to texts (AC9E4LA04). They have not yet examined how the starting position of a sentence signals what the sentence is about, or how writers manipulate theme position to guide readers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how sentence and paragraph starting points signal to readers what the text is about and how it is developing, identifying how writers use theme position to create cohesion and give prominence to the message.

nodes.label: Sentence openers signal topic
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the sentence opener as signalling what the sentence is about, and explain that the rest of the sentence typically provides new information about that starting point.
criteria: Identifies the sentence opener in at least three consecutive sentences and explains what topic or frame each one sets up.
Explains the relationship between the sentence opener and the new information that follows it.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2's cohesion analysis and Node 3's prominence explanation both depend on students recognising the sentence opener as a deliberate positional choice with a signalling function. Students who do not see the opener as a topic-signal cannot trace how opener sequences create cohesion or reason about why a writer has positioned a specific element first.

width.minimum: In a sample text, identify the starting element of several sentences and explain what topic or frame each one signals to the reader.
width.typical: Analyse a text to map how sentence openers establish what each sentence is about, and explain how the sequence of openers tracks the development of the text's topic for the reader.
wider: Compare how sentence opener choices differ between narrative, information report and argument texts — explaining why different genres favour different types of starting elements
Experiment with rewriting sentence openers in a sample text and discuss how those changes shift the reader's path through the text

modes.reason: Students often focus on the content of sentences rather than their structural organisation. Encountering sentence openers across different genres — narrative (time or character), report (topic noun), argument (stance or connector) — helps students see that the opener is a deliberate positional choice, not just where a sentence happens to start.

nodes.label: Theme position creates cohesion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how consistent or shifting sentence opener choices create cohesion and guide the reader through the development of a text.
criteria: Traces the sentence opener choices through a passage and explains how they contribute to cohesion.
Identifies at least one place where an opener choice creates a shift or break in topic continuity and explains the effect.

width.minimum: Identify in a sample text how the sequence of sentence openers creates a consistent thread or marks a shift in the text's focus, and explain the cohesive effect.
width.typical: Analyse how a writer uses sentence opener choices across a paragraph or passage to build cohesion — tracking how the starting points connect sentences into a coherent flow. Identify where opener choices create or break cohesion and explain the effect.
wider: Analyse how paragraphs use their opening sentence to signal to the reader what the paragraph is about, and how this creates cohesion at the paragraph level as well as the sentence level
Compare a cohesive text with a rewritten version where sentence openers have been randomised — discussing what is lost and why opener sequencing matters

nodes.label: Giving prominence through starting position
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how placing particular information at the start of a sentence or paragraph gives that information prominence, and identify why a writer has made that choice.
criteria: Identifies an element in starting position in a text and explains what prominence it receives as a result.
Explains why the writer chose to position that element first, connecting the choice to the text's purpose or the reader's expected path through the text.

width.minimum: Identify in at least two examples how moving an element to the starting position of a sentence changes what receives emphasis, and explain what the writer achieves by that positioning.
width.typical: Analyse and explain how writers use starting position to give prominence to time, concession, reason, contrast or topic across a range of text types. Apply this understanding to explain specific writer choices in a text, connecting the positioning decision to the text's communicative purpose.
wider: Experiment with repositioning elements in sentences from a given text and discuss how each repositioning changes the emphasis and the reader's experience of the text

Examine how different text types use different types of elements in the prominent starting position (e.g. time in recount, concession in argument, topic in report) and explain what this reflects about each text type's purpose

modes.reason: Students often understand that the start of a sentence is 'what it's about' but do not see prominence as an active writer choice. Encountering multiple examples where writers have moved different elements — concession, reason, time, contrast — to starting position helps students recognise prominence as deliberate and purposeful, not accidental.

Explaining why a writer chose to give prominence to a particular element requires reasoning from writer intent through structural choice to reader effect. This chain — 'the writer moved X to the front because... and the reader experiences...' — needs to be made explicit.

descriptors.title: Complex sentences for effect
descriptors.description: Understand that the structure of a complex sentence includes a main clause and at least one dependent clause, and understand how writers can use this structure for effect
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand that complex sentences contain one independent clause and at least one dependent clause, joined by a subordinating conjunction (AC9E4LA06). They have not yet examined how the specific type of dependent clause — reason, purpose, condition, concession, time — creates a particular logical relationship, or how the ordering of clauses affects emphasis and effect.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how complex sentence structure creates logical relationships between ideas — including reason, purpose, condition, concession and time — and identify how writers use clause ordering and subordinating conjunction choice to create particular effects on the reader.

nodes.label: Types of logical relationship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the type of logical relationship a dependent clause creates (reason, purpose, condition, concession, time) and match subordinating conjunctions to the relationships they signal.
criteria: Correctly identifies the relationship type (reason, purpose, condition, concession, or time) for at least four examples of complex sentences.
Names the subordinating conjunction and explains what logical work it performs in at least two examples.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2's clause-ordering analysis and Node 3's effect explanation both require students to know which type of logical relationship they are working with. Students who conflate condition and concession, or purpose and reason, will make errors in Node 2 when comparing clause orderings and will be unable to explain the specific effect a complex sentence creates in Node 3.

width.minimum: Given examples of complex sentences, identify the type of logical relationship the dependent clause establishes and name the subordinating conjunction that creates it.
width.typical: Identify and explain the five types of logical relationship (reason, purpose, condition, concession, time) across a range of complex sentence examples. Match subordinating conjunctions to relationship types and explain what logical work each conjunction performs.
wider: Collect examples of each relationship type from texts across different genres — narrative, argument, explanation — and discuss how the distribution of relationship types reflects the text's purpose
Examine how multiple complex sentence types appear in a single paragraph and discuss how the pattern of logical relationships builds the paragraph's argument or narrative

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse the five relationship types, particularly condition vs. concession and purpose vs. reason. Consolidation through varied examples — focusing on what question the dependent clause answers — builds the reliable identification needed before examining clause ordering and effect.

nodes.label: Clause ordering and prominence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the ordering of main and dependent clauses — which comes first — affects what is emphasised and how the reader processes the sentence.
criteria: Compares two clause orderings of the same sentence and explains which element receives prominence in each version.
Explains why a writer might prefer one ordering over the other in a specific context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to explain how writers use complex sentence structure — including relationship type and clause ordering — for specific effects. Students who cannot explain how clause ordering shifts emphasis cannot account for why a particular ordering serves a particular purpose, which is precisely what Node 3's effect explanation demands.

width.minimum: Compare two versions of the same complex sentence (main clause first vs. dependent clause first) and explain how the ordering affects emphasis and the reader's experience.
width.typical: Analyse how writers choose clause ordering for effect across a range of sentence types. Explain how placing the dependent clause first creates a different reading experience from placing it after the main clause, and identify contexts where each ordering is more effective.
wider: Examine how clause ordering interacts with theme position (from AC9E5LA04) — when a writer fronts a dependent clause, that clause becomes the theme, discussing what communicative choices are involved
Compare clause ordering patterns in formal and informal writing contexts, discussing how the same logical relationship can be packaged differently for different audiences

modes.reason: The effect of clause ordering — why fronting a concession clause before a main clause feels different to placing it after — requires reasoning about reader expectation and emphasis. Students need a scaffold for explaining effect, not just identifying that the order differs.

nodes.label: Using complex sentences for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how writers use complex sentence structure — including relationship type and clause ordering — to create specific effects such as building tension, constructing argument, explaining causation, or expressing qualification.
criteria: Identifies a complex sentence and explains the specific effect it creates, connecting the structural choice (relationship type and/or ordering) to the effect.
Explains how the writer's choice of complex sentence structure serves the text's overall purpose in at least two examples.

width.minimum: In a text or passage, identify how at least two complex sentences have been used for deliberate effect, and explain what the writer achieves through the structure choice.
width.typical: Analyse how complex sentence choices across a text contribute to its overall effect — how reason clauses build explanation, how concession clauses signal nuanced argument, how time clauses create narrative rhythm. Explain how complex sentence choices connect to the text's purpose.
wider: Compare how complex sentence structures are used differently in narrative (for tension, time manipulation), argument (for concession and condition), and explanation (for cause and effect) — building a picture of how genre shapes sentence choice
Examine a literary text by a First Nations Australian author and discuss how complex sentence structures contribute to voice and effect

modes.reason: This node requires students to bring together relationship type (node 1) and clause ordering (node 2) knowledge and apply it to explaining writer effect — the integrative demand of the descriptor's 'use this structure for effect' clause.

descriptors.title: Expanded noun groups
descriptors.description: Understand how noun groups can be expanded in a variety of ways to provide a fuller description of a person, place, thing or idea
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand how adverb groups/phrases and prepositional phrases work in different ways to provide circumstantial detail (AC9E4LA08). They have not yet examined how multiple modifiers are combined within a noun group to build a precise, layered description.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how noun groups are expanded by combining determiners, adjectives, classifiers and other modifiers, and identify how noun group expansion creates precision and richness of description across different text types.

nodes.label: Components of a noun group
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the head noun and the elements that modify it within a noun group, including determiners, adjectives and classifiers.
criteria: Identifies the head noun and at least two modifier types in a given noun group.
Does not confuse adjective with classifier — can explain the difference (adjective expresses quality; classifier indicates type or sub-category).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to combine multiple modifier types in a specific order, and Node 3 requires them to explain how those combinations create effect. Students who confuse adjectives and classifiers, or cannot distinguish modifier types, will make systematic errors when combining modifiers and will be unable to explain which component is creating which effect.

width.minimum: Identify the head noun and at least two types of modifying elements in several noun groups from sample texts.
width.typical: Map the components of noun groups from texts across different genres, identifying determiner, adjective, and classifier elements and explaining what descriptive work each component does.
wider: Compare noun group complexity across different text types — narrative, information report, argument — and discuss how text type shapes the typical complexity of noun groups

Limited width — the internal structure of noun groups is a grammatical system that does not vary meaningfully across contexts; extension involves analysing longer or more complex noun groups rather than encountering genuinely different contexts.

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate adjectives and classifiers, or miss that a preceding noun can function as a classifier (e.g. 'cattle dogs'). Consolidation through varied examples builds reliable identification of noun group components before expansion is examined.

nodes.label: Combining modifiers for precision
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how multiple modifiers are combined in a specific order within a noun group to provide a fuller, more precise description.
criteria: Constructs or identifies a noun group with at least three modifying elements and explains the descriptive work of each.
Explains why the modifiers are ordered as they are (e.g. opinion before size before colour before classifier).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to explain how noun group expansion choices create specific effects — precision, vividness, technical authority. Students who have not yet grasped how modifier combination produces layered precision cannot analyse what specific expansion choices achieve or connect grammatical decisions to communicative purpose.

width.minimum: Construct or identify noun groups that combine at least three modifier types and explain how the combination provides more precise description than any single modifier would.
width.typical: Analyse and construct expanded noun groups from model texts and guided composition, explaining how the layering of modifiers — determiners, number, adjectives (opinion, size, age, colour), classifiers, head noun — adds successive layers of precision. Discuss the conventional order of adjective types.
wider: Examine how noun group expansion is used to create vivid description in narrative compared to precise technical description in information texts — discussing how the same grammatical tool serves different purposes
Collect noun groups from texts by First Nations Australian authors and discuss how the modifiers chosen reflect the author's perspective and the world being described

modes.reason: Students often pile up adjectives without understanding the conventional ordering constraints or the distinction between precision and cumulative weight. Encountering expanded noun groups across narrative and informational contexts helps students see that expansion serves different precision goals in different genres — vividness vs. technical classification.

nodes.label: Noun group expansion for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how noun group expansion choices in a text create specific effects — precision, vividness, technical authority — and how these choices serve the text's purpose.
criteria: Explains how a specific noun group expansion creates a particular effect (precision, vividness, authority) with reference to the modifier choices made.
Connects the noun group choice to the text's purpose or genre conventions.

width.minimum: Identify a noun group in a text, explain the expansion choices the writer has made, and connect those choices to the effect they create for the reader.
width.typical: Analyse noun group choices across a text, explaining how expanded noun groups create the text's descriptive style and serve its purpose. Compare a passage with minimal noun groups to one with rich expansion, discussing what is gained and lost.
wider: Analyse how poets and literary authors use noun group expansion to create imagery and mood, comparing to how scientific or technical writers use expansion to create precision — examining what noun group choices reveal about each genre's values
Experiment with varying the level of noun group expansion in a piece of writing and reflect on how those choices affect reader experience

modes.reason: This node requires students to apply component knowledge (node 1) and combination knowledge (node 2) to explaining writer effect — connecting grammatical choice to communicative purpose across text types.

descriptors.title: Image sequence and meaning
descriptors.description: Explain how the sequence of images in print, digital and film texts has an effect on meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore the effect of choices when framing an image, placement of elements in the image, and colour (AC9E4LA10). They have not yet examined how the ordering and sequencing of images across a text — rather than single-image composition — creates meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how image sequences in print, digital and film texts create meaning through ordering, juxtaposition, and the relationship between images, identifying how sequencing choices affect the reader's or viewer's interpretation.

nodes.label: Images sequence to tell or guide
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that images in texts appear in a deliberate sequence, and explain how the ordering of images guides the reader's or viewer's path through the text.
criteria: Identifies the sequence of images in a text and explains how the ordering creates a reading or viewing path.
Explains what would change in meaning if the sequence were altered.

width.minimum: In a picture book or image sequence, identify how the order of images creates a narrative or reading path, and explain how changing the order would change the meaning.
width.typical: Analyse image sequences in wordless picture books, digital texts with hyperlink choices, and/or short films to explain how ordering guides interpretation. Identify moments where the sequence creates surprise, builds expectation, or controls information reveal.
wider: Compare how image sequences function differently in print (fixed order), digital (multiple possible paths via hyperlinks), and film (time-based) — explaining what each medium's constraints do to meaning-making
Analyse how the sequence of images in texts by First Nations Australian authors create meaning, discussing how image ordering reflects cultural storytelling practices

nodes.label: Juxtaposition and relationship between images
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how placing images adjacent to each other — juxtaposition — creates meaning through contrast, comparison or connection.
criteria: Identifies two adjacent images and explains the meaning created by their juxtaposition that neither image creates alone.
Names the type of relationship the juxtaposition creates (contrast, connection, comparison, irony, etc.).

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of juxtaposition in an image sequence and explain what meaning the pairing creates that the individual images do not.
width.typical: Analyse how juxtaposition is used across several image sequences to create contrast, irony, emotional connection, or narrative development. Explain how the relationship between consecutive images generates meaning beyond what each image contains individually.
wider: Examine how film editing techniques such as cut, dissolve, or match cut create meaning through the juxtaposition of consecutive shots — comparing this to how picture books use page turns to create similar effects
Analyse how image juxtaposition is used in advertising or persuasive texts to create implicit arguments, and discuss the ethical dimensions of that technique

modes.reason: Students focus on what individual images contain rather than on the relationship between consecutive images. Encountering juxtaposition across picture book, digital, and film contexts helps students see that meaning emerges from adjacency, not just content — a key conceptual shift.

nodes.label: Sound and sequence in film
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how removing or adding sound changes how an image sequence is interpreted, and describe how sound and image sequence work together in film to create meaning.
criteria: Explains at least two specific ways sound changes the interpretation of an image sequence.
Identifies a sound choice (music, dialogue, sound effect) and explains what it contributes to meaning in conjunction with the images.

width.minimum: Compare an image sequence or film clip viewed with and without sound, and explain at least two ways that sound changes the interpretation of the images.
width.typical: Analyse how sound (dialogue, music, sound effects) interacts with image sequence in a short film or clip to create meaning, explaining how each element contributes and what is lost when sound is removed. Discuss how interpretation changed between silent and sound viewings.
wider: Examine how music choice in film shapes the emotional meaning of an image sequence, and discuss how the same sequence can be reinterpreted with a different musical score
Analyse a scene where sound and image are deliberately mismatched for effect, discussing what meaning is created by the disconnect

modes.reason: Students often say 'the music makes it scary' without explaining the mechanism. A structured reasoning scaffold — 'the sound creates X because it does Y to how we interpret the image' — develops the analytical move from naming to explaining.

descriptors.title: Specialist vocabulary and word history
descriptors.description: Understand how vocabulary is used to express greater precision of meaning, including through the use of specialist and technical terms, and explore the history of words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can expand vocabulary by exploring synonyms and antonyms, and using words in context (AC9E4LA11). They have not yet examined how specialist and technical vocabulary achieves precision beyond synonymy, or how word origins (Greek, Latin roots) explain and extend vocabulary.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how specialist and technical vocabulary expresses greater precision than general vocabulary, and use knowledge of word origins including Greek and Latin roots to interpret and extend vocabulary.

nodes.label: Precision through specialist vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why specialist or technical vocabulary expresses more precise meaning than general vocabulary, using examples from at least one learning area.
criteria: Explains what a specialist term communicates that a general term does not, using a specific example.
Identifies at least two specialist terms in a learning area text and explains the precision each provides.

width.minimum: Compare a specialist term (e.g. 'humpback whale') with a general term (e.g. 'mammal') in context, and explain what precision is gained by using the specialist term.
width.typical: Analyse examples of specialist and general vocabulary across at least two learning areas, explaining in each case what the specialist term communicates that the general term does not. Discuss why precision matters in technical or informational contexts.
wider: Examine how the same concept is named differently in everyday vs. specialist discourse (e.g. 'heart attack' vs. 'myocardial infarction') and discuss why specialists choose their vocabulary and what that signals about audience
Collect specialist vocabulary from a learning area text being studied and map the precision it provides — explaining how the specialist lexis builds the field's way of knowing

nodes.label: Word origins: Greek and Latin roots
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify Greek and Latin roots in common words and use root meaning to interpret unfamiliar vocabulary.
criteria: Identifies the root meaning in at least two unfamiliar words and uses it to explain the word's meaning.
Demonstrates root knowledge transfer — can interpret a word containing a known root encountered in a new context.

width.minimum: Identify the meaning of at least two Greek or Latin roots and use that knowledge to explain the meaning of words containing those roots.
width.typical: Identify and explain the meaning of a range of Greek and Latin roots encountered in curriculum vocabulary, and use root knowledge to interpret unfamiliar words in context. Apply this to words across multiple learning areas.
wider: Explore how Greek and Latin roots cluster in specific learning area vocabulary (e.g. Greek roots in science and mathematics, Latin roots in law and formal writing) and discuss what this historical pattern reveals
Investigate how compound words built from roots create precise technical meaning (e.g. 'telescope', 'biology') and explore extending this pattern to create new coinages for invented concepts

modes.reason: Root knowledge is a vocabulary tool that grows in value as students accumulate more roots. No single root is a hinge; the goal is building a working repertoire of roots encountered across learning areas. Regular encounter and application — rather than deep analysis of a few roots — is the investment signal here.

nodes.label: Word history shapes meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a word's history — its origins and etymology — illuminates its current meaning or usage, and connect word history to vocabulary precision.
criteria: Explains how a word's history illuminates its current meaning with a specific example.
Connects etymology to precision — explains why a word from a particular origin expresses meaning in the way it does.

width.minimum: Explore the history of at least two words and explain how their origins contribute to understanding their current meaning.
width.typical: Explore the history of words from different origins — including Greek, Latin, and other language sources — and explain how etymology illuminates precision and meaning. Connect word history to why words are used as they are in specialist contexts.
wider: Research words that have entered English from Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages (e.g. boomerang, kangaroo, billabong) and discuss what their presence in English reveals about cultural contact and knowledge transfer

Explore how the same concept is named through different etymological pathways in different specialist fields (e.g. same structure named from Greek in medicine vs. Latin in botany) and discuss what this reveals about the history of each discipline

modes.reason: Word history often feels disconnected from current meaning to students. Encountering etymology across multiple word types — including words from First Nations Australian languages and other non-European sources — helps students see word history as living and purposeful rather than as trivia about the past.

descriptors.title: Commas and apostrophes
descriptors.description: Use commas to indicate prepositional phrases, and apostrophes where there is multiple possession
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand that punctuation signals dialogue through quotation marks and that different types of punctuation including commas signal meaning to a reader (AC9E4LA12). They have not yet applied commas to prepositional phrases or apostrophes in multiple-possession contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use commas to signal prepositional phrases at the beginning of sentences, and use apostrophes correctly for plural possession including regular plural nouns, irregular plural nouns, and proper nouns.

nodes.label: Commas with fronted prepositional phrases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a prepositional phrase at the start of a sentence and use a comma to signal its boundary from the main clause.
criteria: Correctly places a comma after a fronted prepositional phrase in at least three examples.
Identifies sentences where a comma is missing after a fronted prepositional phrase and explains where it should go.

width.minimum: Identify prepositional phrases fronted in sentences and add or verify commas to signal the boundary between the phrase and main clause.
width.typical: Apply comma use to fronted prepositional phrases across a range of sentence types and writing contexts. Identify sentences where the comma prevents ambiguity or signals the reader's parsing path, and explain why the comma is placed where it is.
wider: Examine how other sentence-opening elements — time clauses, adverbial clauses — also take a following comma, connecting the rule to the broader principle that sentence openers are separated from the main clause

Limited width — comma use with fronted prepositional phrases is a mechanical rule that does not vary meaningfully across contexts. Extension involves the general rule for sentence openers, not broader application of the same rule.

modes.reason: This is a mechanical punctuation rule with high error frequency in student writing. Consolidation through practice — identifying, applying, and checking — is the investment signal. Width is thin; practice and precision matter.

nodes.label: Apostrophes for plural possession
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply apostrophes correctly for plural possession, including regular plural nouns ending in -s, and explain the difference between singular and plural possession apostrophe placement.
criteria: Correctly applies the apostrophe for plural possession in at least three examples with regular plural nouns.
Distinguishes apostrophe placement for singular vs. plural possession (e.g. 'student's' vs. 'students'') and explains the rule.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3's multiple-ownership rule is an extension of the plural possession rule — students must have secure singular vs. plural apostrophe placement before they can reason about joint versus separate ownership, which requires holding both rules simultaneously. Students with unreliable plural possession will apply the wrong base rule in Node 3.

width.minimum: Apply the apostrophe rule for regular plural possessives (e.g. 'the students' classroom') and distinguish the placement from singular possessives (e.g. 'the student's classroom').
width.typical: Apply apostrophe rules for plural possession across a range of cases: regular plurals ending in -s, multiple owners with apostrophe on the last owner, and proper nouns. Explain the rule applied in each case.
wider: Investigate irregular plural possessives (e.g. 'the children's books', 'the women's team') where the apostrophe-s is added because the plural does not end in -s — connecting this to the underlying rule
Examine variant forms for proper nouns ending in -s (e.g. 'James's' or 'James'') and discuss why both are accepted in Standard Australian English

modes.reason: Apostrophe placement for possession — especially distinguishing singular from plural possessives — is a high-frequency error site. The rule is mechanical and consistent but students conflate the singular and plural cases. Consolidation through deliberate practice across case types is more useful than width.

nodes.label: Multiple possession and joint ownership
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply the apostrophe rule for multiple ownership (apostrophe on the last owner) and explain why the rule is placed as it is.
criteria: Correctly applies the apostrophe in a multiple-ownership sentence and explains why it is placed on the last owner.
Distinguishes between joint and separate ownership apostrophe placement with at least one example of each.

width.minimum: Apply the apostrophe correctly in at least two examples of multiple ownership (e.g. 'the cat and kitten's bowls') and explain why the apostrophe appears on the last owner.
width.typical: Apply the multiple-ownership rule across a range of examples, and distinguish between joint ownership (one apostrophe on last owner) and separate ownership (apostrophe on each). Explain the difference in meaning between 'James and Sarah's house' and 'James's and Sarah's houses'.
wider: Collect examples from authentic texts of possession apostrophe use — including errors — and create an annotated analysis distinguishing correct from incorrect usage and explaining each case
Examine how apostrophe use has changed over time in English (e.g. the 'greengrocers apostrophe') and discuss what those changes reveal about conventions in language

modes.reason: The multiple-ownership rule requires students to reason about what the apostrophe signals — 'who owns this?' — rather than applying a surface pattern. The joint vs. separate ownership distinction requires explicit reasoning about meaning, not just pattern matching.

descriptors.title: Historical and cultural contexts
descriptors.description: Identify aspects of literary texts that represent details or information about historical, social and cultural contexts in literature by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise similar storylines, ideas and relationships in different contexts in literary texts (AC9E4LE01). They have not yet examined how specific literary details — images, symbols, dialogue, character descriptions — represent historical, social and cultural contexts, or explored texts by First Nations Australian authors in relation to the events that shaped their lives.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and explain how specific literary details — including images, symbols, dialogue and character descriptions — represent historical, social and cultural contexts in texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.

nodes.label: Literary details carry context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific literary details — images, symbols, dialogue, character descriptions — and explain what historical, social or cultural information those details convey.
criteria: Identifies a specific literary detail and explains what historical, social or cultural context it represents — not just names the detail.
Explains how the detail reveals something about the world of the text beyond what is explicitly stated.
nodes.hinge_reason: The reasoning move from detail to contextual inference must be established here — Node 2 and Node 3 both require students to apply this same move to increasingly specific contexts (First Nations Australian literature, Australian ballads). Students who cannot explain what a detail reveals will not be able to engage analytically with culturally specific or historically situated texts in subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: In a literary text, identify at least two specific details (images, symbols, dialogue or character descriptions) and explain what each reveals about the context in which the text was created or is set.
width.typical: Analyse how a range of literary detail types across a text convey contextual information — building a picture of the historical, social or cultural world the text inhabits. Explain how specific detail choices by the author reflect their context.
wider: Compare how authors from different historical periods use different types of literary details to convey context — examining what each author chooses to make visible and what they leave implicit
Examine texts from wide-ranging world authors and identify literary details that are culturally specific, discussing what knowledge is needed to interpret those details

modes.reason: Students identify details but often do not connect them to context — 'this character is described as wearing traditional clothing' without explaining what that reveals about when or where the story is set or what it signals about the character's relationship to their culture. The reasoning move from detail to contextual inference needs to be made explicit.

nodes.label: First Nations Australian literary contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify aspects of First Nations Australian literary texts that convey information about historical context, cultural practice, or the impact of events on community life.
criteria: Identifies at least two aspects of a First Nations Australian literary text and explains what historical or cultural context they convey.
Explains how the author's perspective or cultural position shapes the representation of context in the text.

width.minimum: In a text by a First Nations Australian author, identify at least two aspects — images, language, dialogue, character description — that convey information about historical or cultural context, and explain what those aspects reveal.
width.typical: Explore and discuss texts by First Nations Australian authors about events that shaped or had an impact on their lives, identifying how literary choices represent historical context. Explain how First Nations Australian authors position readers in relation to those contexts.
wider: Explore historical context in texts by First Nations Australian authors about specific events (e.g. the Stolen Generations, land rights, community history) and discuss how literary choices make those events present for readers
Compare how the same historical events are represented in texts by First Nations Australian authors and by other Australian authors, examining what is foregrounded, backgrounded, or absent in each

modes.reason: Students may not have background knowledge about the historical and cultural contexts in First Nations Australian literature, making the literary details opaque. Engaging with a range of texts — and with contextual information about events they represent — helps students develop the interpretive knowledge needed to read these texts with understanding rather than surface recognition.

nodes.label: Ballads and historical context across Australian literature
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify aspects of Australian literary texts — including ballads from different times — that convey historical and social context, and discuss how those contexts are represented through literary choices.
criteria: Identifies aspects of an Australian literary text that convey its historical period and explains what those aspects reveal about the social world of the text.
Makes a connection between a specific literary choice (language, image, character detail) and the historical or social context it represents.

width.minimum: In an Australian literary text (including a ballad), identify at least two aspects that convey historical or social context and explain what those aspects reveal about the time or community represented.
width.typical: Explore a range of Australian literary texts including ballads from different time periods, identifying how literary choices — character, setting, language, imagery — represent the historical and social contexts of their time. Compare how different periods' concerns and values are made visible through literary choices.
wider: Compare how two Australian ballads from different historical periods represent the values, concerns and social conditions of their respective times — examining what has changed and what has stayed constant in Australian social life
Examine how contemporary Australian authors represent historical events from earlier periods, discussing how temporal distance affects literary representation

modes.reason: Building familiarity with texts from different periods and cultural contexts — First Nations Australian, colonial, contemporary Australian, and world literature — is the long-term goal. Each text adds to the repertoire of contextual knowledge students bring to reading. Breadth of text encounter is the investment signal here.

descriptors.title: Present opinion with literary terms
descriptors.description: Present an opinion on a literary text using specific terms about literary devices, text structures and language features, and reflect on the viewpoints of others
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the effects of text structures and language features in literary texts (AC9E4LE02). They have not yet used specific literary terminology to support and present an opinion, or reflected on how others' viewpoints differ from their own.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present an opinion on a literary text supported by specific references to literary devices, text structures and language features using relevant terminology, and reflect on how the viewpoints of others complement, challenge, or extend their own interpretation.

nodes.label: Opinion supported by textual evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state an opinion about a literary text and support it with specific references to the text, identifying the textual evidence for their view.
criteria: States an opinion and provides at least two specific textual references that support it.
Explains the connection between each reference and the opinion — does not just quote and leave the connection implicit.

width.minimum: State an opinion about a literary text and support it with at least two specific references to the text, explaining the connection between each reference and the opinion.
width.typical: Present an opinion on a literary text supported by several specific textual references, explaining how each reference supports the opinion. Select references that represent different types of evidence — plot, character, language — rather than the same type repeatedly.
wider: Examine how textual evidence can support multiple different opinions about the same text, discussing what this reveals about interpretation
Compare how different readers select different evidence for the same opinion and discuss why evidence selection varies

nodes.label: Using specific literary terms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use specific terms about literary devices, text structures and language features accurately when discussing a literary text and explaining their opinion.
criteria: Uses at least two specific literary terms correctly and with explanation — not just appended as labels.
The term is used accurately — the feature it names is present in the text at the place cited.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to integrate textual evidence, terminology, and reflection on others' viewpoints into a single discussion move. Students who cannot deploy literary terms accurately will be unable to participate meaningfully in the reflective discussion that Node 3 demands — the shared language of literary terms is the medium through which viewpoints are compared and extended.

width.minimum: Use at least two specific literary terms correctly in presenting an opinion about a literary text, explaining how the feature named by each term contributes to the effect being discussed.
width.typical: Use a range of specific literary terms — including terms for literary devices, text structural features, and language features — accurately in presenting a literary opinion. Apply terms from the Y5 literature curriculum including those from AC9E5LE03 (point of view), AC9E5LE04 (imagery, simile, metaphor, personification, sound devices) where appropriate.
wider: Compare how using specific vs. vague language when presenting a literary opinion changes the precision and persuasiveness of the opinion — examining what is gained by using exact terminology
Research and apply one literary term not yet studied, using it correctly in presenting an opinion and explaining what it adds to the discussion

modes.reason: Literary terminology is a vocabulary repertoire that grows across the year and across the curriculum. Students need encounter with terms across multiple texts and discussion contexts to develop reliable accurate use. No single term is a hinge; the goal is expanding the working repertoire of correctly used terms.

nodes.label: Engaging with the viewpoints of others
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on viewpoints expressed by others about a literary text, explaining how those viewpoints are the same as, different from, or extend their own interpretation.
criteria: Identifies a viewpoint from discussion that differs from their own and explains the difference — not just notes that it is different.
Reflects on how another viewpoint has affected their own interpretation, even if their opinion has not changed.

width.minimum: After a discussion of a literary text, identify at least one viewpoint expressed by another reader that differs from or extends their own, and explain how that viewpoint relates to their original opinion.
width.typical: Engage in discussion of a literary text by posing and responding to questions about character dilemmas and author choices. Reflect on how the discussion has deepened, challenged or confirmed their own interpretation. Begin making judgements about the dilemmas characters face, supported by reasons.
wider: Examine how the same literary text generates different opinions depending on readers' backgrounds or prior experiences, discussing what this reveals about the relationship between reader and text
Compare critical responses to a text from different contexts or perspectives and discuss what each viewpoint illuminates or overlooks

modes.reason: This node requires students to integrate textual evidence (node 1), terminology (node 2), and awareness of multiple interpretations into a reflective discussion move — the full demand of the descriptor's 'reflect on the viewpoints of others' clause.

descriptors.title: Point of view shapes response
descriptors.description: Recognise that the point of view in a literary text influences how readers interpret and respond to events and characters
descriptors.knowledge: Students can discuss how authors and illustrators make stories engaging through character, setting and plot (AC9E4LE03). They have not yet examined how narrative point of view — who tells the story and what they can or cannot know — shapes what readers have access to and how their sympathies are positioned.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and explain how the point of view in a literary text — including first and third person narration — determines what information readers can access and how it influences readers' interpretation of events and characters.

nodes.label: What point of view is
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a text uses first or third person narration and explain what each choice means for who is telling the story.
criteria: Correctly identifies the point of view (first or third person) in a given literary text.
Explains who the narrator is and what their relationship to the events of the story is.
nodes.hinge_reason: Correct identification of narrative person is definitionally prerequisite for Node 2 (information access analysis) and Node 3 (sympathy and interpretation). Students who confuse first and third person narration, or who cannot identify who the narrator is, cannot analyse what that narrator knows or how they position the reader.

width.minimum: Identify the point of view in a literary text as first or third person and explain who the narrator is and what their relationship to the story is.
width.typical: Identify point of view across several texts, explaining the difference between a first-person narrator (character in the story, subjective, limited knowledge) and a third-person narrator (outside the story, potentially more access). Introduce the concept of narrative distance.
wider: Examine second-person narration in texts (e.g. some picture books, choose-your-own-adventure formats) and discuss what effect the direct address creates for the reader
