Limited width — identifying narrative person is a relatively narrow grammatical recognition task; the conceptual richness is in what each point of view does to reader access and sympathy, explored in later nodes.

modes.reason: Point of view identification is a foundational recognition task that students need to perform reliably before analysis can proceed. Students who read first-person narration as objective or who conflate narrator with author need practice with varied examples across multiple text types until the distinction is secure.

nodes.label: Point of view controls information access
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the choice of point of view determines what information the audience can access — what they know, when they know it, and what remains hidden.
criteria: Explains at least two types of information that are available or unavailable to readers because of the text's point of view choice.
Explains why the author might have chosen to give readers the particular information access their point of view provides.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding information access is directly prerequisite for Node 3's analysis of how point of view shapes sympathy and interpretation. Students who cannot explain what readers can and cannot know from a given point of view will be unable to reason about how that restricted or expanded access positions readers emotionally and interpretively.

width.minimum: Compare what a reader would know if a text's point of view were changed (e.g. from first to third), and explain at least two types of information that would become available or unavailable as a result.
width.typical: Analyse how first-person narration limits reader knowledge to what the narrator observes, thinks, and feels, while third-person narration can offer broader access. Discuss why an author might choose to restrict or expand reader access to information — what narrative purposes does each choice serve?
wider: Examine unreliable first-person narrators in texts and discuss what clues allow readers to understand more than the narrator tells them
Compare the information access available to readers in two versions or adaptations of the same story told from different points of view

modes.reason: Students commonly think that first person is 'more honest' and third person is 'more distant' without understanding that point of view shapes information access as a deliberate craft choice. Encountering the same events from multiple points of view helps students see information access as variable and purposeful.

nodes.label: Point of view shapes sympathy and interpretation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how point of view influences readers' sympathies with characters and their interpretation of events — what point of view makes readers feel and believe.
criteria: Explains how the point of view positions readers to sympathise with or interpret a specific character in a particular way.
Identifies how a different point of view would change the reader's response to the same events or characters.

width.minimum: Identify how the point of view in a text positions readers to sympathise with or understand a particular character, and explain how a different point of view would change the reader's relationship to that character.
width.typical: Discuss why an author chose a particular point of view, explaining how that choice shapes reader sympathy, moral positioning, and interpretation of events. Examine how readers can access more than the narrator tells them by reading against or beyond the narrator's perspective.
wider: Compare texts narrated from a first person and third person point of view about similar events, discussing what information the audience can access and how this influences the audience's sympathies — drawing on the elaboration examples
Examine a text by a First Nations Australian author and discuss how point of view shapes the reader's access to and understanding of cultural context

modes.reason: This node requires students to integrate point of view identification (node 1) and information access understanding (node 2) into an account of how readers are positioned emotionally and interpretively — the full demand of the descriptor's 'influences how readers interpret and respond' clause.

descriptors.title: Imagery and sound devices
descriptors.description: Examine the effects of imagery, including simile, metaphor and personification, and sound devices in narratives, poetry and songs
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine the use of literary devices and deliberate word play including imagery and rhythm in literary texts (AC9E4LE04). They have not yet examined how specific imagery types — simile, metaphor, personification — create meaning through comparison, or how sound devices create effects in poetry and song.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine and explain the effects of simile, metaphor and personification, and sound devices in narratives, poetry and songs — explaining how each device creates meaning and what effect it has on the reader or listener.

nodes.label: Imagery: comparison and new ways of seeing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify simile, metaphor and personification in texts and explain how each works through comparison to create a new way of seeing something.
criteria: Identifies an example of simile, metaphor and personification and explains the comparison each makes.
Explains what new understanding or experience the comparison creates for the reader — not just names the device.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how each imagery type works through comparison is prerequisite for Node 2's analysis of effect. Students who cannot explain the comparison mechanism — what is being compared to what, and why — cannot reason about the specific emotional, sensory, or conceptual effect the comparison creates for the reader.

width.minimum: Identify examples of simile, metaphor and personification in a text and explain how each creates a comparison and what that comparison helps the reader understand or experience.
width.typical: Identify and explain the working mechanism of simile (explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as'), metaphor (implicit comparison asserting identity), and personification (attributing human qualities to non-human things) across narrative, poetry and song examples. Explain how each device creates a new way of looking at the world.
wider: Examine how simile and metaphor can be used to explore the same concept in different ways — comparing examples and discussing what each comparison makes visible that others do not
Investigate extended metaphors in texts and discuss how sustaining a comparison across a passage or poem creates particular effects

modes.reason: Students often identify imagery types as labels without understanding the comparison mechanism — 'that's a simile' without explaining what is being compared to what and what insight the comparison creates. Encountering diverse examples across narrative, poetry and song helps students develop the analytical move from identification to explanation of effect.

nodes.label: Imagery creates effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the specific effect that a piece of imagery creates for the reader — emotional, sensory, conceptual — connecting the comparison to the author's purpose.
criteria: Explains the effect of at least two pieces of imagery, connecting the comparison to a specific reader experience (emotional, sensory, or conceptual).
Connects the imagery choice to the author's purpose at that point in the text.

width.minimum: For at least two examples of imagery, explain the specific effect each creates for the reader and connect that effect to the author's purpose at that point in the text.
width.typical: Examine imagery across narratives, poems and songs, explaining in each case the specific effect created (emotional response, sensory experience, new conceptual understanding) and why the author chose that comparison at that point. Discuss how by appealing to imagination, figurative language provides new ways of looking at the world.
wider: Discuss how different readers might respond differently to the same imagery based on their prior experiences, examining what this reveals about the relationship between reader background and literary response
Compare how imagery functions differently in narrative prose versus poetry — examining how genre shapes how imagery works and what it can do

modes.reason: Explaining the effect of imagery — not just identifying it — requires a reasoning chain: 'This image compares X to Y. This makes the reader feel/see/understand Z because...'. This chain does not come automatically and benefits from explicit scaffolding.

nodes.label: Sound devices and their effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sound devices in poetry and songs and explain the effects they create for the reader or listener.
criteria: Identifies at least two sound devices by name and explains the specific effect each creates.
Connects at least one sound device to the poem or song's overall effect or purpose.

width.minimum: Identify at least two sound devices (e.g. alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, rhyme) in a poem or song and explain the specific effect each creates.
width.typical: Examine how sound devices — including alliteration, assonance, consonance, onomatopoeia, rhyme, and rhythm — are used in narratives, poetry and songs to create particular effects: musicality, mood, emphasis, sensory experience. Explain how sound devices work alongside imagery to create the text's full effect.
wider: Compare how sound devices function in a poem meant to be read silently versus one written to be performed or sung, discussing what the performance dimension adds

Examine how First Nations Australian songlines and oral poetry traditions use sound and repetition to create meaning and carry knowledge — discussing what these practices reveal about the relationship between sound, rhythm, and meaning-making

modes.reason: Sound device recognition is a terminology repertoire that students build through encounter across multiple poems and songs. No single device is a hinge; the goal is developing a working repertoire of identified and named devices students can apply analytically. Breadth of encounter across text types is the investment signal.

descriptors.title: Experiment with figurative language
descriptors.description: Create and edit literary texts, experimenting with figurative language, storylines, characters and settings from texts students have experienced
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and edit literary texts by developing storylines, characters and settings (AC9E4LE05). They have not yet experimented with figurative language — simile, metaphor, personification — as a deliberate craft tool, or used model texts as a source for experimental creative choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and edit literary texts that deliberately experiment with figurative language, storylines, characters and settings drawn from or inspired by texts they have experienced, demonstrating intentional craft choices in their writing.

nodes.label: Reading as a writer: noticing craft choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific craft choices in model texts — figurative language, character techniques, setting construction — and explain how those choices create effects they can learn from.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific craft choices in a model text and explains the effect each creates.
Connects the craft choice to something that can be applied in their own writing — not just appreciates it.

width.minimum: In a model literary text, identify at least two craft choices the author has made (figurative language, character detail, setting description) and explain what effect each creates and what can be learned from it.
width.typical: Analyse a range of model texts for craft choices, building a repertoire of specific techniques — types of figurative language used, how characters are introduced and developed, how settings are constructed — that can be drawn on in their own writing. Create a visual or written map of craft choices from texts experienced.
wider: Analyse how First Nations Australian authors and illustrators make craft choices — examining how figurative language, character description and setting construction reflect cultural ways of knowing and representing the world
Compare craft choices across literary texts in different forms (picture book, poem, short story) and discuss how the form shapes which craft choices are available

nodes.label: Experimenting with figurative language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliberately experiment with figurative language — simile, metaphor, personification — in their literary writing, making choices about which type of imagery to use and where to use it.
criteria: Includes at least two examples of figurative language (using different types) in their literary text.
Can explain the intended effect of each figurative language choice — the choice is deliberate, not accidental.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to draw on figurative language experimentation as source material for extended narrative creation, and Node 4 requires them to edit figurative language for effect. Students who have not yet made deliberate figurative language choices cannot meaningfully attempt either — their drafts will lack the intentional imagery that editing and narrative integration depends on.

width.minimum: In a draft literary text, include at least two examples of deliberately chosen figurative language (at least two different types) and explain the effect intended with each choice.
width.typical: Draft a literary text that demonstrates deliberate use of figurative language — simile, metaphor and/or personification — at key points. Explain the craft choices made: why this image here, what comparison is intended, what effect is sought. Draw on imagery from model texts as inspiration or starting points.
wider: Experiment with the same scene or description using different types of figurative language and compare the effects — developing a feel for when simile vs. metaphor vs. personification serves the moment better
Experiment with extended metaphor across a short piece, developing a central comparison and sustaining it throughout

modes.reason: Students often produce figurative language that is generic ('the sun was like a ball') rather than purposeful. Encountering a range of model images — including unexpected comparisons, culturally specific imagery, and imagery from texts that have been studied — helps students develop a broader sense of what is possible and what makes an image work.

nodes.label: Experimenting with storylines, characters and settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw on storylines, characters and settings from texts they have experienced as source material for their own literary writing, making deliberate choices about what to adapt, extend, or transform.
criteria: Creates a literary text that incorporates at least one element drawn from a model text and demonstrates how it has been transformed.
Can explain the creative choices made — what was borrowed, what was changed, and why.

width.minimum: Create a literary text that draws on at least one element — storyline, character, or setting — from a text they have experienced, explaining what they borrowed and how they transformed or extended it.
width.typical: Create a literary text that uses model texts as creative source material — adapting storylines, borrowing character types, transforming settings — and explain the creative choices made. Demonstrate awareness of what was taken from models and how it has been made their own.
wider: Experiment with retelling a story from a different point of view or in a different setting, discussing how the change transforms the narrative and what the experiment reveals about the original
Create a literary text inspired by texts from culturally different contexts — adapting story structures, characters or settings from those texts and reflecting on what the adaptation requires

modes.reason: This node requires students to bring together craft reading (node 1), figurative language experimentation (node 2), and narrative construction into a literary text that demonstrates authorial intentionality — the full demand of the descriptor's 'experimenting with figurative language, storylines, characters and settings' clause.

nodes.label: Editing for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can review and edit their literary writing to improve figurative language, narrative development, and characterisation, making changes with reference to intended effect.
criteria: Makes at least two deliberate editing changes to figurative language or narrative elements and explains the effect intended by each change.
Can identify the difference between surface-level editing (spelling, grammar) and craft-level editing (figurative language, characterisation) and demonstrates both.

width.minimum: Review a draft and identify at least two specific changes that would improve the text's use of figurative language or narrative elements, and make those changes with an explanation of the intended improvement.
width.typical: Edit a literary text using negotiated criteria, focusing on precision of figurative language choices, character development, and setting construction. Reflect on how the editing process has changed the text and what the changes have achieved.
wider: Exchange drafts with a peer and provide specific feedback on figurative language and narrative choices — practising the language of craft critique as well as authorship
Compare an early draft with a final version and trace how the editing choices have improved specific effects — developing metacognitive awareness of the revision process

modes.reason: Editing for effect requires students to reason from intended effect backwards to the text — 'I want the reader to feel X here, so I need to change Y in my figurative language'. This purposeful editing orientation needs to be made explicit; students without the scaffold tend to fix surface errors rather than craft choices.

descriptors.title: Texts reflect time and place
descriptors.description: Describe the ways in which a text reflects the time and place in which it was created
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare texts from different times with similar purposes and audiences to identify similarities and differences (AC9E4LY01). They have not yet examined how vocabulary, idiomatic expressions, and social expectations within texts reveal the time and place of their creation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe how vocabulary choices, idiomatic expressions, social expectations, and cultural values in a text reflect the time and place of its creation.

nodes.label: Vocabulary marks time and place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify vocabulary in a text that signals when and where it was created, and explain how vocabulary choices reflect the language use of a particular time and place.
criteria: Identifies at least two vocabulary choices or expressions in a text and explains what each signals about time and/or place.
Explains why a specific word choice reflects the language use of a particular period or location.

width.minimum: In a text, identify at least two vocabulary choices — including idiomatic expressions if present — that signal the time or place of the text's creation and explain what each reveals.
width.typical: Analyse vocabulary choices across texts from different time periods and places, identifying how idiomatic expressions, word choices, and naming conventions signal time and place. Explain why the same concept might be described differently across texts from different times.
wider: Examine how Australian English vocabulary has been influenced by time and place — including words from First Nations Australian languages and from waves of migration — and discuss what the vocabulary of texts reveals about their cultural context
Compare texts from the same time period but different places and discuss how vocabulary choices reflect regional and cultural variation

nodes.label: Social expectations in texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how the social expectations of the time and place of a text's creation are reflected in its content, characters, or events.
criteria: Identifies a social expectation in a text and explains how it is reflected in specific textual details.
Explains how that social expectation reflects the time and place of the text's creation rather than universal values.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to synthesise vocabulary evidence and social expectation evidence into a coherent description of how a text reflects its context. Students who have not yet established the social expectations analysis strand will produce Node 3 descriptions that are one-dimensional — relying only on vocabulary and missing the social values dimension that the descriptor explicitly requires.

width.minimum: Identify at least one social expectation embedded in a text and explain how it is reflected — through character behaviour, dialogue, plot events, or narrator attitude.
width.typical: Describe how texts from different times and places reflect the social expectations of their context, examining how values, norms, and social roles are represented. Explain how those expectations differ from contemporary social expectations and what those differences reveal about social change.
wider: Examine how texts from different historical periods reflect changing social expectations about gender, class, or community, and discuss what reading those texts from a contemporary perspective reveals
Compare how texts by First Nations Australian authors reflect the social expectations and values of their communities and the historical contexts that shaped them

modes.reason: Students often read social expectations in historical texts as simply 'wrong' without understanding that those texts were written within a different social context. Encountering a range of texts from different times and places — including First Nations Australian texts — helps students understand social expectations as context-specific rather than universal.

nodes.label: Describing how texts reflect their context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can bring together vocabulary and social expectation observations to provide a coherent description of how a text reflects the time and place of its creation.
criteria: Provides a description of how a text reflects its time and place using at least two types of evidence (vocabulary and social expectations).
The description explains how the evidence reflects context — not just notes that differences exist.

width.minimum: Write or present a brief description of how a text reflects its time and place, drawing on both vocabulary evidence and social expectation evidence.
width.typical: Describe comprehensively how a text reflects its time and place, synthesising evidence from vocabulary choices, idiomatic expressions, social expectations, and cultural values. Explain the relationship between the text's features and its context of creation.
wider: Compare two texts from different times and places and describe how each reflects its context, discussing what the comparison reveals about how time and place shape texts
Examine a contemporary text and describe what future readers might learn about our time and place from its vocabulary and social expectations

modes.reason: This node requires students to integrate vocabulary analysis (node 1) and social expectations analysis (node 2) into a coherent description — the full demand of the descriptor's 'describe the ways' clause.

descriptors.title: Paraphrase and justify opinions
descriptors.description: Use appropriate interaction skills including paraphrasing and questioning to clarify meaning, make connections to own experience, and present and justify an opinion or idea
descriptors.knowledge: Students can listen for key points and information and contribute to discussions by expressing opinions and making judgements (AC9E4LY02). They have not yet applied paraphrasing as a clarification strategy, or developed systematic approaches to questioning for meaning-making in discussion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use paraphrasing and purposeful questioning to clarify meaning in discussions, make connections between what they hear and their own experience, and present and justify opinions with supporting reasons.

nodes.label: Paraphrasing to clarify
nodes.checkpoint: Students can paraphrase what a speaker has said to check understanding and signal attention, and use this as a clarification strategy in discussion.
criteria: Paraphrases a speaker's contribution accurately — captures the meaning in own words without significantly distorting it.
Uses paraphrasing as a clarification strategy — checks understanding rather than just replaying what was said.

width.minimum: In a discussion context, paraphrase at least one contribution from another speaker to check understanding, and explain what paraphrasing does for the conversation.
width.typical: Use paraphrasing to check understanding and signal engagement across discussion contexts. Explain the difference between paraphrasing (capturing meaning in own words) and summarising (condensing) and echo (repeating). Apply paraphrasing as a strategy to keep conversations moving and build shared understanding.
wider: Practise paraphrasing in paired and group contexts with explicit feedback on accuracy — developing awareness of what is captured and what is lost in a paraphrase
Compare how paraphrasing functions differently in formal discussion versus informal conversation contexts — discussing when the strategy is most useful

modes.reason: Paraphrasing is a skill that requires practice to become automatic. Students often confuse paraphrasing with repeating or summarising. Consolidation through deliberate practice in structured discussion contexts builds reliable deployment before paraphrasing is integrated with questioning and justification.

nodes.label: Purposeful questioning for meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can ask specific questions to clarify a speaker's meaning, and use questioning to move a discussion forward rather than just to gather information.
criteria: Asks a specific clarifying question that targets meaning — not a display question or a factual check.
The question is purposeful — it opens up discussion or clarifies understanding rather than closing conversation down.

width.minimum: In a discussion, ask at least one specific clarifying question that targets a gap in understanding or an unstated assumption in what a speaker has said.
width.typical: Ask specific questions to clarify meaning, make constructive comments that keep conversation moving, and use questions to invite elaboration or probe assumptions. Apply a range of question types: clarifying, extending, probing, inviting connection.
wider: Explore how different question types serve different discussion purposes — comparing how clarifying questions, open questions, and devil's advocate questions function in building shared understanding
Examine question types across formal and informal discussion contexts and discuss how formality shapes which question types are appropriate

nodes.label: Present and justify opinions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present an opinion clearly and support it with reasons, making connections to their own experience where relevant and choosing vocabulary suited to the context.
criteria: Presents an opinion with at least two supporting reasons in a discussion context.
Responds to at least one other speaker — through paraphrasing, questioning, or building on their point — demonstrating interaction rather than turn-taking.

width.minimum: Present an opinion in a discussion context with at least two reasons supporting it, and respond to at least one contribution from another speaker in the discussion.
width.typical: Present and justify opinions across formal and informal discussion contexts, choosing vocabulary and sentence structures appropriate to purpose and formality. Make connections between their own contributions and those of others. Respond constructively to challenge or different perspectives.
wider: Participate in a structured debate or formal discussion, applying all interaction skills (paraphrasing, questioning, justifying) in an integrated performance and reflecting on what worked and what could be improved
Apply different registers — formal and informal — to presenting the same opinion in different contexts, and discuss how register choice affects persuasiveness and appropriateness

modes.reason: This node requires students to integrate paraphrasing (node 1), purposeful questioning (node 2), and opinion presentation into a coherent interactive performance — the full capability demand of the descriptor. Phase collapse here means students default to opinion-delivery without the interactive skills that make discussion productive.

descriptors.title: Explain characteristic features
descriptors.description: Explain characteristic features used in imaginative, informative and persuasive texts to meet the purpose of the text
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify the characteristic features used in imaginative, informative and persuasive texts (AC9E4LY03). They have not yet explained how those features meet the purpose of the text — moving from identification to purposive explanation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how characteristic features — structural, linguistic, and visual — used in imaginative, informative and persuasive texts are purposively chosen to meet the text's communicative goal.

nodes.label: Features serve purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a characteristic feature of a text type and explain how it serves the text's purpose — not just that it is present.
criteria: Identifies a characteristic feature and explains how it serves the text's purpose — explains the relationship, not just names the feature.
Applies the explanation to at least two different text types or two different features within a text type.
nodes.hinge_reason: The feature-serves-purpose reasoning move is the foundation on which Node 2's character analysis and Node 3's multi-feature integration both depend. Students who can only identify features without explaining their function cannot engage with the purposive reasoning that Node 2 and Node 3 require.

width.minimum: Identify at least two characteristic features of a text type and explain, for each, how it helps the text achieve its purpose.
width.typical: Explain how characteristic features across imaginative, informative and persuasive texts work to meet their respective purposes — examining how features such as character, dialogue, topic sentence, thesis statement, emotive language, and modal verbs are purposively chosen.
wider: Examine how the same feature (e.g. an emotive vocabulary choice) can serve different purposes in different text types — discussing how purpose shapes the use of the feature, not just the feature itself
Analyse a persuasive text about a local community issue and explain how its features work to achieve action — connecting the elaboration example to the broader principle

modes.reason: Students who have only explained features in narrative texts may apply narrative reasoning to persuasive or informative texts inappropriately. Encountering feature explanation across all three text-type categories builds the understanding that purpose determines feature function, not text type name alone.

nodes.label: Characters in persuasive texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how characters are used in persuasive texts to deliver a message, and analyse why real people might be replaced by constructed characters.
criteria: Explains why characters are used in a persuasive text and connects that choice to the persuasive purpose.
Analyses what the character choice communicates to the audience beyond the explicit message.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to explain how multiple characteristic features of a text type work together. Students who have not yet understood why particular choices are made — not just that characters appear in persuasive texts, but why this is more effective than other options — cannot produce the analytical accounts of feature function that Node 3 demands.

width.minimum: Identify a text where characters are used to deliver a persuasive message and explain how the character choice serves the persuasive purpose.
width.typical: Explain how characters function as persuasive vehicles in texts such as advertising or advocacy, discussing why characters (rather than factual claims) are used and what the character choice communicates to the audience. Apply this to at least one health or community advocacy example.
wider: Compare persuasive texts that use real people versus constructed characters to make the same argument — discussing what each choice does for the persuasive strategy and audience response
Examine how First Nations Australian community advocacy texts use character and voice, and discuss how the choice of spokesperson reflects community values and communication conventions

modes.reason: The reasoning chain — 'characters are used instead of real people because... and this achieves... for the audience' — requires explicit scaffolding. Students often accept that characters are used without reasoning about why that choice is more persuasively effective than other options.

nodes.label: Explaining features across text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce a coherent explanation of how the characteristic features of a text type work together to meet its purpose, accounting for multiple features across structural, linguistic, and visual dimensions.
criteria: Explains at least three characteristic features of a text type and how they work together to serve the text's purpose.
The explanation addresses how features function — not just lists them or describes their presence.

width.minimum: Provide an explanation of how at least three characteristic features of a given text type work together to meet its purpose.
width.typical: Explain characteristic features across all three text type categories (imaginative, informative, persuasive), demonstrating understanding of how different feature sets serve different purposes. Produce explanations that go beyond description to analysis of function.
wider: Examine a text that blends purposes (e.g. an informative text that also persuades, or a narrative that advocates) and explain how features from different text types are combined and why
Compare how the same purpose can be served by different feature configurations — discussing what this reveals about the relationship between feature and purpose

modes.reason: This node requires students to integrate feature identification, purpose explanation, and character analysis into coherent explanatory accounts across all three text type categories — the full demand of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Navigate texts for purpose
descriptors.description: Navigate and read texts for specific purposes, monitoring meaning using strategies such as skimming, scanning and confirming
descriptors.knowledge: Students can read different types of texts integrating phonic, semantic and grammatical knowledge using strategies including monitoring, predicting, confirming and rereading (AC9E4LY04). They have not yet applied skimming and scanning as distinct, purposeful navigation strategies, or used signposting features systematically to locate specific information.
descriptors.endpoint: Students navigate texts for specific purposes by applying skimming, scanning and confirming strategies, and by using signposting features such as headings, subheadings and homepage navigation to locate, evaluate and confirm relevant information.

nodes.label: Skimming and scanning as distinct strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish skimming (reading for gist) from scanning (searching for specific information) and apply each to an appropriate task.
criteria: Correctly applies skimming to determine relevance and scanning to locate specific information in separate task demonstrations.
Explains the difference between the two strategies and when each is used.
nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable distinction between skimming and scanning is prerequisite for Node 3's meaning-monitoring work, which requires students to select appropriate strategies purposefully during research reading. Students who conflate the two strategies or apply them randomly cannot monitor whether they are using the right strategy at the right moment.

width.minimum: Apply skimming to determine whether a text is broadly relevant to a purpose, and scanning to locate a specific piece of information in a text, and explain how the two strategies differ.
width.typical: Apply and explain skimming and scanning as distinct strategies across a range of text types and navigation tasks. Discuss when each strategy is appropriate and what each does for the reader — skimming checks pertinence, scanning locates specifics.
wider: Compare how skimming and scanning work differently in print texts versus digital texts with hyperlinks and navigation features — discussing how the strategies adapt to different reading environments
Apply skimming and scanning in a genuine research task, reflecting on which strategy was used when and why

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate skimming with slow reading or treat scanning as random. Applying both strategies to diverse text types and reading purposes helps students develop reliable, strategic deployment rather than guessing or applying the wrong strategy to a task.

nodes.label: Using signposting features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use headings, subheadings, homepages, and subpages to navigate texts and locate specific information efficiently.
criteria: Locates specific information in a text using at least two signposting features and explains how each feature supported the navigation.
Demonstrates efficient navigation — does not read from start to finish when signposting features enable targeted access.

width.minimum: Use at least two signposting features (headings, subheadings, navigation buttons, homepage structure) to locate specific information in a text, and explain how each feature guided the navigation.
width.typical: Navigate texts using signposting features including headings and subheadings, homepages and subpages, to read texts efficiently. Explain how signposting features function as navigation tools and how they help readers locate relevant information without reading the full text.
wider: Compare signposting conventions across different types of texts — informational websites, reference books, digital databases — and discuss how navigation feature design reflects audience expectations
Apply subject and technical vocabulary knowledge to use signposting features more effectively, connecting prior subject knowledge to navigation efficiency

nodes.label: Monitoring meaning and confirming
nodes.checkpoint: Students can monitor their understanding while reading for a purpose, recognise when meaning breaks down, and use confirming strategies to resolve confusion.
criteria: Identifies a moment of meaning confusion and describes the confirming strategy applied.
Explains how the strategy resolved the confusion — demonstrates monitoring and repair, not just continued reading.

width.minimum: During a purposeful reading task, identify at least one point where meaning was unclear, describe the strategy used to confirm or restore meaning, and explain how the confusion was resolved.
width.typical: Apply a range of meaning-monitoring strategies during purposeful reading: rereading, using context to infer, checking signposting features, and confirming against prior knowledge. Explain the strategy used in specific instances and why it helped.
wider: Develop a metacognitive reading log during a research task — tracking where skimming, scanning, confirming, and other strategies were applied — and reflect on reading strategy choices
Compare how monitoring and confirming strategies work differently in narrative texts versus informational texts, discussing what good comprehension monitoring looks like in each text type

modes.reason: Metacognitive reading — noticing when meaning has broken down and selecting a repair strategy — requires explicit attention. Students often read through confusion without monitoring or applying confirming strategies. A structured reasoning approach helps students develop the monitor-and-repair habit.

descriptors.title: Evaluate information and ideas
descriptors.description: Use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning to build literal and inferred meaning to evaluate information and ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning and to evaluate ideas and information (AC9E4LY05). They have not yet applied research skills systematically — identifying purpose, locating texts, evaluating source quality, and summarising across multiple sources.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply comprehension strategies including visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning to build literal and inferred meaning, evaluate information and ideas across sources, and conduct purposeful research including assessing source accuracy and currency.

nodes.label: Building literal and inferred meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply comprehension strategies — particularly connecting and questioning — to build meaning beyond the literal content of a text, making inferences supported by textual evidence.
criteria: Makes an inference about a text's meaning that goes beyond literal content and supports it with specific textual evidence.
Identifies which comprehension strategy was used to construct the inference.

width.minimum: Use at least two comprehension strategies to make and support an inference about a text's meaning that goes beyond what is explicitly stated.
width.typical: Apply a range of comprehension strategies (visualising, predicting, connecting, monitoring, questioning) to build understanding across a text. Distinguish between literal meaning (what the text says) and inferred meaning (what can be concluded from what the text says).
wider: Apply comprehension strategies to complex or challenging texts — including texts with technical vocabulary or unfamiliar cultural contexts — and discuss how strategy use changes when the text is less familiar
Compare how different comprehension strategies are more or less useful for different types of texts — building metacognitive awareness of which strategies to deploy when

nodes.label: Summarising and main idea
nodes.checkpoint: Students can summarise a text or passage to determine its main idea, distinguishing main ideas from supporting detail.
criteria: Produces a summary that captures the main idea rather than listing supporting details.
Can explain why their summary is a main-idea summary rather than a detail list.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3's research task requires students to summarise across multiple sources to distil and evaluate information. Students who cannot reliably identify main ideas — producing detail-lists rather than central-claim summaries — will be unable to synthesise across sources or evaluate whether a source's claims are accurate or relevant.

width.minimum: Summarise a text to identify its main idea, demonstrating that the summary captures the central point rather than listing details.
width.typical: Summarise ideas and information across texts to determine main ideas, identify supporting evidence, and distinguish central claims from supporting examples. Apply summarising in research contexts to distil information from multiple sources.
wider: Compare summaries of the same text produced by different readers, discussing what choices are made about what counts as 'main' versus 'supporting' and why those choices might differ
Apply summarising skills across texts on the same topic from different sources, synthesising the main ideas into a coherent overview

modes.reason: Summarising accurately — capturing the main idea without drifting into list-of-details — is a skill that requires practice. Students commonly produce summaries that are too detailed or that miss the central claim. Consolidation through varied texts and explicit feedback builds the reliable summarising that underpins research skills.

nodes.label: Evaluating sources and information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the accuracy and currency of information from print and digital sources, and identify the research purpose before selecting and organising information.
criteria: Identifies a research purpose and explains how it guides source selection.
Evaluates at least two sources using specific criteria (accuracy, currency, relevance) and explains the evaluation — does not simply accept or reject sources without reasoning.

width.minimum: Identify the research purpose for a task and evaluate at least two sources for their relevance and accuracy, explaining the basis for the evaluation.
width.typical: Apply research skills including identifying research purpose, locating texts, gathering and organising information, evaluating the accuracy and currency of print and digital sources, and summarising information from several sources. Explain the criteria used to evaluate source quality.
wider: Examine how the same topic is covered differently across sources of different types (encyclopedia, news article, personal blog, academic reference) and discuss what each source's characteristics suggest about its reliability and purpose
Apply information evaluation skills to a contested topic — where sources offer different claims — and discuss how to navigate conflicting information

modes.reason: Evaluating source accuracy and currency requires students to apply criteria rather than accept information at face value. The reasoning chain — 'this source is/isn't reliable because... based on criteria...' — needs to be made explicit; students without this scaffold tend to trust all sources equally or distrust all unfamiliar sources.

descriptors.title: Develop ideas with connectives
descriptors.description: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts whose purposes may be imaginative, informative and persuasive, developing ideas using visual features, text structure appropriate to the topic and purpose, text connectives, expanded noun groups, specialist and technical vocabulary, and punctuation including dialogue punctuation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts with complex sentences, expanded noun groups, specialist vocabulary, and dialogue punctuation (AC9E4LY06). They have not yet deliberately developed ideas using text connectives and visual features in combination, or applied these tools across all three text type purposes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts across imaginative, informative and persuasive purposes, deliberately developing ideas using text connectives, expanded noun groups, specialist vocabulary, appropriate text structure, and accurate punctuation including dialogue.

nodes.label: Planning for purpose and structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate text structure for their writing purpose and plan how content will be sequenced and grouped within that structure.
criteria: Produces a plan that reflects the correct text structure for the purpose and sequences content logically within it.
The plan distinguishes between introduction, body structure, and conclusion — not just a list of points.

width.minimum: For a writing task, identify the text type and its structure, and plan how their content will be organised — including how the topic will be introduced, how information will be grouped, and how the text will conclude.
width.typical: Select appropriate text structure for purpose and audience, and plan content sequencing including: introduction of topic, grouping of related information in well-sequenced paragraphs, and a concluding statement. Use planning to organise information gathered from research or experience before drafting.
wider: Compare planning approaches across different text type purposes (imaginative, informative, persuasive) — examining how the planning tools (narrative map, argument plan, information organiser) differ and why
Plan a multimodal text and decide how visual and written elements will be distributed across the text structure, explaining the distribution rationale

nodes.label: Developing ideas through language choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop ideas in their writing using text connectives, expanded noun groups, and specialist vocabulary, making deliberate choices about how these tools contribute to the text's development.
criteria: Uses text connectives to signal the logical relationship between ideas — not just as sentence openers.
Uses at least one expanded noun group and one specialist vocabulary choice and can explain the function of each in context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 4 requires students to edit for meaning, structure, and accuracy — including reviewing their connective choices, noun groups, and vocabulary for precision. Students who have not yet made deliberate language choices in drafting have nothing substantive to edit at the craft level; their editing will default to surface-level fixes rather than the meaning-development work Node 4 demands.

width.minimum: In a draft text, identify and explain at least two deliberate language choices — text connectives, expanded noun groups, or specialist vocabulary — and explain how each develops an idea or serves the text's purpose.
width.typical: Draft a text that demonstrates deliberate use of text connectives (to signal relationship and sequence), expanded noun groups (for precision and description), and specialist vocabulary (for technical accuracy and register). Explain the function of each type of language choice in developing the text's ideas.
wider: Examine how text connective choices differ across text type purposes — comparing how connectives in narrative (sequence, time), argument (concession, causation), and explanation (cause, condition) serve different ideational purposes
Apply specialist and technical vocabulary appropriate to a specific learning area in an informative text, and compare the precision achieved with and without specialist terms

modes.reason: Students often use text connectives as sentence-starters rather than as tools that signal the logical relationship between ideas. Encountering connective choices across argument, explanation, narrative, and informative writing contexts helps students see that connective selection is a meaning choice, not a formula.

nodes.label: Visual features in multimodal texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and create multimodal texts that use visual features deliberately to develop ideas alongside written language.
criteria: Includes visual features in a multimodal text and explains how they develop ideas or serve the text's purpose — not just decorates.
Demonstrates that visual feature placement or choice was deliberate, not incidental.

width.minimum: Create or annotate a multimodal text identifying at least two visual features and explaining how each contributes to the text's development of ideas or purpose.
width.typical: Plan and create a multimodal text in which visual features (images, layout, diagrams, typography) are selected and positioned deliberately to develop ideas alongside written language. Explain how the visual and written elements work together.
wider: Compare how visual features serve different purposes in imaginative versus informative multimodal texts — discussing how layout, image choice, and design conventions differ across text type purposes
Examine how digital composition tools affect visual feature choices and discuss how the medium shapes what is possible and expected

nodes.label: Editing for structure, meaning and accuracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit their own and others' texts for precision in text structure, meaning, grammar, spelling and punctuation including dialogue punctuation.
criteria: Makes at least three targeted editing changes addressing different editing dimensions (structure/meaning AND accuracy/punctuation).
Uses dialogue punctuation correctly in texts where dialogue appears.

width.minimum: Review a draft and make at least three targeted editing changes — at least one addressing text structure or meaning and at least one addressing grammatical accuracy or punctuation (including dialogue punctuation if present).
width.typical: Re-read and edit texts using negotiated criteria covering text structure and meaning accuracy, and grammar, spelling and punctuation including dialogue punctuation. Apply digital tools where appropriate for surface-level editing. Distinguish between editing for meaning/structure and editing for accuracy.
wider: Exchange texts with a peer and apply editing criteria collaboratively, discussing the feedback given and received and what criteria-based editing reveals about the text
Create a personal editing checklist based on recurring patterns in their own writing — developing metacognitive awareness of individual writing strengths and challenges

modes.reason: Editing requires students to apply planning knowledge (node 1), language choice knowledge (node 2), and visual feature knowledge (node 3) simultaneously to evaluate and improve a draft — the full Phase D demand of the capability cycle.

descriptors.title: Deliver elaborated spoken presentations
descriptors.description: Plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that include relevant, elaborated ideas, sequencing ideas and using complex sentences, specialist and technical vocabulary, pitch, tone, pace, volume, and visual and digital features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan, create, rehearse and deliver structured oral and/or multimodal presentations of arguments and recounts (AC9E4LY07). They have not yet applied a full range of vocal features — pitch, tone, pace, volume — as deliberate presentational tools, or integrated digital features into multimodal presentations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that elaborate ideas with relevant detail, sequence ideas logically using complex sentences and specialist vocabulary, and apply pitch, tone, pace and volume deliberately to support audience understanding and engagement.

nodes.label: Planning: sequencing and elaborating ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a spoken or multimodal presentation that sequences ideas logically and includes relevant, elaborated supporting detail for each main point.
criteria: Produces a plan that sequences main ideas logically and includes at least one elaborating detail per idea.
The plan distinguishes between main ideas and supporting elaborations.

width.minimum: Plan a presentation that sequences at least three main ideas logically and includes at least one piece of elaborating detail (supporting evidence, example, or explanation) for each idea.
width.typical: Plan a report or presentation on a topic with a logical idea sequence, supporting detail for each idea, and consideration of how graphics, sound or visuals can enhance audience understanding. Apply a planning strategy that distinguishes main ideas from supporting elaborations.
wider: Compare planning approaches for presentations with different purposes (report, argument, narrative) — examining how purpose shapes how ideas are sequenced and what counts as relevant elaboration
Plan a multimodal presentation that distributes ideas across spoken and visual channels — deciding which ideas are best presented through speech and which through visual support

nodes.label: Language choices for spoken presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use complex sentences and specialist vocabulary in a spoken presentation, making choices appropriate to the presentation's purpose and audience.
criteria: Uses at least two complex sentences in the presentation — the complexity is audible in delivery, not just in the written plan.
Applies specialist vocabulary accurately and in context — not just appended as labels.

width.minimum: In a rehearsed presentation, use at least two complex sentences and at least two specialist vocabulary items, and explain how each choice serves the presentation's purpose.
width.typical: Use complex sentence structures and specialist vocabulary appropriate to topic and audience in a spoken presentation. Apply new learning through vocabulary choices that reflect the presentation's subject knowledge. Choose vocabulary and sentence structures that are appropriate for formal presentation register.
wider: Compare a transcript of a spoken presentation with its written equivalent — examining how the same ideas are packaged differently in spoken and written language, and what complex sentences sound like versus how they read
Reflect on how new learning during research has been incorporated into vocabulary choices in the presentation — developing metacognitive awareness of how subject knowledge shapes language choices

nodes.label: Vocal features for engagement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply pitch, tone, pace and volume deliberately in a presentation to support audience understanding and engagement, and explain the effect of those choices.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two deliberate vocal feature variations in a presentation.
Can explain what each vocal choice was intended to achieve for the audience — the choice is deliberate, not accidental.

width.minimum: In a rehearsed presentation, demonstrate deliberate variation in at least two vocal features (pitch, tone, pace, or volume) and explain what each variation was intended to achieve.
width.typical: Experiment with vocal features — tone, volume, pitch and pace — in formal presentations, recognising the effects these have on audience understanding and engagement. Apply deliberate vocal variation at key points: slowing for emphasis, raising volume for impact, varying tone for distinction between ideas.
wider: Record and review a presentation, analysing how vocal feature choices actually landed versus the intended effect — using the recording as feedback data for refinement
Compare how vocal feature conventions differ across presentation contexts (classroom report, debate, storytelling, formal speech) and discuss how context shapes appropriate vocal choices

modes.reason: Students commonly treat vocal features as performance decoration rather than as communication tools. Experimenting with vocal variations across different presentation contexts — and seeing the audience effects — helps students understand that pitch, pace, tone and volume are meaning-making choices, not performance polish.

nodes.label: Integrating visual and digital features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and use visual and digital features in a multimodal presentation to support and extend the spoken content, explaining how each feature contributes to audience understanding.
criteria: Includes at least two visual or digital features and can explain how each contributes to audience understanding.
The visual/digital features support the spoken content — they are not just slides with repeated text.

width.minimum: Include at least two visual or digital features in a presentation and explain how each contributes to the audience's understanding of the ideas presented.
width.typical: Plan and deliver a multimodal presentation that integrates spoken content with visual and digital features — graphics, sound, visuals — selected to enhance audience engagement and understanding. Explain how the visual/digital and spoken channels work together, not independently.
wider: Compare how visual and digital features function differently in a live presentation versus a recorded or asynchronous presentation — discussing how audience and delivery context shape feature choices
Evaluate a peer's use of visual/digital features in a presentation and provide feedback on whether each feature enhanced or distracted from the spoken content

modes.reason: This node requires students to integrate planning (node 1), language choice (node 2), and vocal delivery (node 3) with visual/digital feature selection into a complete multimodal presentation — the full delivery demand of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Shared patterns, different sounds
descriptors.description: Use phonic, morphemic and vocabulary knowledge to read and spell words that share common letter patterns but have different pronunciations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use and apply phonological and morphological knowledge to read and spell complex letter combinations (AC9E4LY09). They have not yet focused on the specific challenge of words that share written patterns but diverge in pronunciation — cross-pattern reading requiring multiple knowledge sources.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use phonic, morphemic and vocabulary knowledge together to read and spell words that share common letter patterns with different pronunciations, recognising that spelling context and word meaning are resources for pronunciation.

nodes.label: Recognising pattern–pronunciation divergence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify words that share a common letter pattern but have different pronunciations, and explain that multiple pronunciation options are possible for the same pattern.
criteria: Identifies a letter pattern that can be pronounced in at least two ways and provides correct examples of each pronunciation.
Explains that phonic knowledge alone is not sufficient for these words — vocabulary or morphemic knowledge is also needed.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to apply phonic, morphemic and vocabulary knowledge together specifically because phonic knowledge alone is insufficient for pattern-divergent words. Students who have not grasped that the same pattern can map to multiple pronunciations will default to a single-source phonic strategy in Node 2 rather than engaging the multi-source reasoning the node demands.

width.minimum: Identify at least one letter pattern that can be pronounced in more than one way and provide word examples of each pronunciation.
width.typical: Identify and group words with common letter patterns that have different pronunciations (e.g. 'journey', 'your', 'tour', 'sour'). Explain that the same written pattern can map to different spoken sounds, and that phonic knowledge alone is insufficient for accurate reading of these words.
wider: Investigate other letter patterns with multiple pronunciations across English — examining how the range of pattern–sound mappings reflects the diverse origins of English vocabulary

Compare how pattern–pronunciation relationships differ between words derived from different language origins (e.g. French-derived vs Anglo-Saxon-derived words) and discuss what this reveals about English spelling history

modes.reason: Students may apply a single pronunciation rule to a pattern and not monitor when the result does not match a known word. Encountering diverse examples of pattern–pronunciation divergence helps students develop monitoring awareness and builds their lexical bank of known exceptions.

nodes.label: Using multiple knowledge sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw on phonic, morphemic and vocabulary knowledge together to determine the correct pronunciation or spelling of words with ambiguous letter patterns.
criteria: Can explain which knowledge source was decisive in determining the pronunciation or spelling of a specific word with an ambiguous pattern.
Demonstrates monitoring — recognises when a phonically-derived pronunciation does not match a known word and applies an alternative strategy.

width.minimum: For at least two examples of words with ambiguous letter patterns, explain which knowledge source (phonic, morphemic, vocabulary) provides the key information for determining correct pronunciation or spelling.
width.typical: Apply phonic, morphemic and vocabulary knowledge in combination when reading or spelling words with ambiguous patterns. Explain the decision-making process: what the phonic pattern suggests, what morphemic knowledge adds, and how vocabulary knowledge (knowing the word) confirms or overrides.
wider: Develop a personal 'tricky pattern' vocabulary — collecting words that required multiple knowledge sources and annotating what each knowledge source contributed to reading and spelling them accurately
Examine how encountering a new word with an ambiguous pattern in a reading context provides enough vocabulary knowledge to add the word to the known-word base

modes.reason: The three-knowledge-source reasoning process — phonic, morphemic, vocabulary — needs to be made explicit. Students who rely on one source in isolation will fail at pattern-divergent words. A structured reasoning scaffold ('what does the pattern suggest? what does the word part/meaning suggest? what does knowing this word suggest?') builds reliable multi-source decoding.

descriptors.title: Build words from known patterns
descriptors.description: Build and spell new words from knowledge of known words, base words, prefixes and suffixes, word origins, letter patterns and spelling generalisations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use knowledge of letter patterns, including double letters, spelling generalisations and word origins to spell unfamiliar words (AC9E4LY10). They have not yet applied this systematically to build new words from known base words, or applied spelling generalisations such as suffix-governed changes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use knowledge of known words, base words, prefixes, suffixes, word origins, letter patterns and spelling generalisations to build and spell new words accurately.

nodes.label: Known words and base words as building blocks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a known word or base word as a starting point for spelling related words, recognising meaning and spelling connections between base forms and derived forms.
criteria: Correctly builds at least two related words from a known base word and explains the spelling and meaning connection.
Uses base word knowledge to decode or spell an unfamiliar related form.

width.minimum: Starting from at least two known or base words, build a word family that demonstrates spelling and meaning connections (e.g. 'vision' → 'television', 'revision').
width.typical: Use known words and base words to build word families and spell derived forms, explaining the spelling and meaning connections. Identify base words in complex words and use them as a decoding and spelling resource.
wider: Investigate how the spelling of a base word may modify when a suffix is added — exploring the spelling changes required (doubling, dropping 'e', changing 'y' to 'i') and the generalisations that govern them
Examine word families across different learning areas and discuss how knowing the base word helps with both spelling and meaning in specialist vocabulary

nodes.label: Prefixes and suffixes: meaning and form
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how prefixes and suffixes modify the meaning or grammatical form of a word and use this knowledge to build and spell new words.
criteria: Correctly spells words with at least two different prefixes and two different suffixes.
Explains the meaning change each prefix or suffix makes to the base word.

width.minimum: For at least two prefix and two suffix examples, explain the meaning change each adds and spell at least two words correctly that use each affix.
width.typical: Build and spell new words using a range of prefixes and suffixes, explaining the meaning and grammatical changes each makes. Apply suffix knowledge including how suffixes such as '-tion' and '-ment' change verbs into nouns. Use this knowledge as a spelling strategy for unfamiliar words encountered in reading.
wider: Investigate how prefix and suffix knowledge transfers across learning area vocabulary — examining how scientific, mathematical and historical vocabulary uses Latin and Greek affixes systematically
Examine 'chameleon' prefixes (prefixes that change spelling before certain base word letters, e.g. 'in-/im-/ir-') and discuss why the spelling changes while the meaning stays the same

modes.reason: Prefix and suffix knowledge is a vocabulary and spelling tool that grows through accumulated encounter. No single affix is a hinge; the goal is a growing working repertoire that students can apply flexibly. Regular encounter and application across content areas is the investment signal.

nodes.label: Spelling generalisations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply spelling generalisations to spell unfamiliar words, including generalisations for suffix additions (e.g. 'suitable', 'likeable', 'collapsible').
criteria: Correctly applies at least two spelling generalisations to unfamiliar words and names the generalisation used.
Identifies whether a generalisation applies to a given word before attempting to spell it — demonstrates rule-checking, not guessing.

width.minimum: Apply at least two spelling generalisations to spell unfamiliar words correctly, and explain the rule applied in each case.
width.typical: Apply a range of spelling generalisations to spell unfamiliar words including those with suffix additions (-able/-ible choices, suffix-triggered base word changes). Explain the generalisation applied and identify exceptions that do not follow the rule.
wider: Investigate the historical origins of common spelling generalisations — understanding why rules developed and how they reflect patterns in English word origins
Create a personal spelling generalisation reference that categorises generalisations by type and includes examples and notable exceptions

modes.reason: Applying spelling generalisations reliably — particularly suffix-governed changes like -able/-ible — requires practice and consolidation. Students know the rule in the abstract but apply it inconsistently under composing conditions. Consolidation through varied examples and application in writing context builds reliable use.

descriptors.title: Plurals and suffix effects
descriptors.description: Explore less common plurals, and understand how a suffix changes the meaning or grammatical form of a word
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use and apply phonological and morphological knowledge to read and spell complex letter combinations (AC9E4LY09). They have not yet examined irregular plurals derived from word origins, or examined how suffixes systematically change the grammatical class of words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students read, spell and use less common plurals derived from word origins, and explain how specific suffixes change the grammatical form or meaning of words — including how '-tion' and '-ment' nominalise verbs.

nodes.label: Less common plurals and word origins
nodes.checkpoint: Students can spell and explain less common plurals whose forms are derived from their word origins (Greek, Latin, English), explaining why these plurals differ from the regular -s pattern.
criteria: Correctly spells at least three less common plurals from different origin patterns.
Explains why the less common plural form differs from the regular -s pattern — connects form to origin.

width.minimum: Identify and correctly spell at least three less common plural forms (e.g. 'cacti', 'lice', 'criteria') and explain that each follows the plural pattern of its language of origin.
width.typical: Explore less common plurals including Latin-origin plurals (-us/-i, -um/-a), Greek-origin plurals (-on/-a), and irregular English plurals (vowel changes such as 'louse/lice'). Explain how word origin determines the plural form and use this knowledge to interpret and spell unfamiliar plurals.
wider: Investigate how less common plural forms are used in specific learning area vocabulary — scientific (e.g. 'bacteria', 'stimuli'), mathematical (e.g. 'formulae', 'radii') — and discuss how knowing the origin helps with specialist reading
Examine how English speakers sometimes regularise less common plurals (e.g. 'forums' alongside 'fora') and discuss what this variation reveals about how language changes

modes.reason: Less common plural knowledge is a vocabulary repertoire that grows through encounter. No single plural form is a hinge; the goal is an accumulating working knowledge of plural patterns from different word origins that supports reading and spelling across learning areas.

nodes.label: Suffixes change grammatical form
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how specific suffixes change the grammatical form of a word and use this knowledge to build and recognise different word classes.
criteria: Identifies at least two suffixes that change grammatical form and gives correct examples of each.
Explains what grammatical change each suffix creates — not just names the suffix and a word.

width.minimum: Identify how at least two suffixes change the grammatical form of a word (e.g. '-tion' changing a verb to a noun) and provide two correct examples for each suffix.
width.typical: Explain how suffixes such as '-tion', '-ment', '-ness', '-er/-or', and '-ful/-less' change the grammatical class of words — converting verbs to nouns (nominalisation), adjectives to nouns, or words to other classes. Use this knowledge to recognise and build word forms in reading and writing contexts.
wider: Examine how nominalisation (verb-to-noun conversion via suffixes) is used in informational and academic texts to build compact, precise noun phrases — and discuss what nominalisations do to text register

Compare how the same base word generates different forms through different suffixes and explore what each form does grammatically (e.g. 'protect' → 'protection', 'protective', 'protectively', 'protector')

modes.reason: The connection between suffix and grammatical class change — and why that matters for reading and writing — requires explicit reasoning. Students who learn suffix patterns as lists without understanding the grammatical function miss the utility of the knowledge. A structured reasoning scaffold ('this suffix changes X class to Y class, which means in a sentence it can...') develops functional understanding.

descriptors.title: Language formality and social distance
descriptors.description: understand that language varies as levels of formality and social distance increase
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that language is selected for social contexts and that it helps to signal social roles and relationships (AC9E5LA01). They have not yet examined how formality and social distance interact as a continuum, or how formal address protocols function at institutional or ceremonial levels.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that language choices vary systematically with levels of formality and social distance, and can identify and apply appropriate language for a given context.

nodes.label: Formality as a continuum
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that language exists along a continuum from informal to formal and name the key registers (slang, colloquial, conversational, formal).
criteria: Names and correctly applies the four register labels (slang, colloquial, conversational, formal) to provided examples
Identifies at least one language feature (e.g. vocabulary choice, contraction use) that signals register
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate 'polite' with 'formal' or treat formality as binary cannot correctly reason about social distance in Node 2 — the two-variable model breaks down without a working continuum.

width.minimum: Identify at least three points on the formality continuum using provided examples; label each as slang, colloquial, conversational or formal.
width.typical: Discuss and sort a range of spoken and written examples across the full continuum; explain what features (vocabulary, sentence structure, tone) signal each register.
wider: Compare the same message expressed across all four registers (e.g. a request for help) and analyse how meaning and relationship signal shift
Examine how digital communication (texts, emails, social media posts) creates new registers that blend formal and informal features

modes.reason: Students often conflate 'polite' with 'formal' or assume formality is binary. Exposure to a range of register examples across spoken and written modes helps students build a more nuanced continuum model.

nodes.label: Social distance and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how social distance (familiarity, power relationship, audience) determines appropriate register choice.
criteria: Explains why a specific register is appropriate for a given social relationship using at least two contextual cues (familiarity, power, audience)
Identifies an example where register mismatch would be inappropriate and explains why
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot hold familiarity and power as two separate variables, their Node 3 register choices will rest on single-cue guessing — producing register mismatches in formal production tasks.

width.minimum: Explain the register appropriate for one contrasting pair of social relationships (e.g. talking to a friend vs. a principal) and justify why using at least one language feature.
width.typical: Analyse several social contexts (peer, teacher, community leader, ceremonial) and explain how both familiarity and relative power shape register expectations; identify how audience affects language selection.
wider: Investigate how social distance operates differently in cultures where respect is marked differently (e.g. formal pronoun systems in other languages compared with English address terms)
Compare formal address protocols across institutions (school, government, royalty) and identify what social values they encode

modes.reason: Students need to hold two variables simultaneously (familiarity AND power/status) to make register judgements. Making the reasoning chain explicit — 'I know this is formal because the relationship is distant AND the status differential is high' — prevents over-reliance on a single cue.

nodes.label: Applying register appropriately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use language appropriate to a given level of formality and social distance, and evaluate their choices.
criteria: Produces spoken or written language that consistently fits the specified register level
Explains at least one specific language choice (vocabulary, sentence structure, or tone) and how it signals the intended register

width.minimum: Present or write an idea at one specified register level appropriate to a given audience; identify one choice made and explain why it suits the context.
width.typical: Present ideas or opinions in at least two contrasting register contexts (e.g. peer discussion and a formal presentation); reflect on choices made and how they serve different audiences.
wider: Analyse a formal public speech or ceremonial address and identify specific language features that signal institutional formality
Draft the same argument for two different audiences (e.g. a class debate and a letter to a local council) and compare register choices
